exp.0:2:
It says that Job had enormous wealth. He owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen (each yoke is two oxen for plowing), five hundred female donkeys, and a great many servants, that is, household servants or workers. For this reason he was regarded as the greatest of all the people of the east, that is, of the peoples of the east.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not Job. He presents Job as an upright man who feared God, and shows that his wealth was great. The author sets the stage before the great test that is coming. The numbers suggest total abundance, though we do not know for certain whether they are exact or symbolic.

For today: possessions are not bad in themselves, but what was most valuable in Job was his character and his reverence for God. Use what you have with humility, and care first for your relationship with God and with your family.
exp.0:11:
God says to Satan that everything Job has is in his hand, that is, under Satan's power to test him. But God sets a limit: Satan may not touch Job himself. Afterward, Satan withdraws from the presence of the Lord.

The Lord speaks, responding to Satan's challenge in the heavenly court. Satan had said that Job served God only because God blessed him. God allows the test, but sets a boundary. The verses that follow show that Job's losses begin at once. The text does not explain every reason for the suffering; it only shows that God remains the one in charge.

When you go through pain, remember that no trial is outside God's control. He sets limits and does not abandon you. Trust Him even when you do not understand everything.
exp.0:13:
This verse tells us that a messenger came running to Job with news. He tells him that the oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing nearby. "Grazing" here means eating grass. The sentence is left incomplete, because the messenger keeps speaking in the next verse, where he describes the attack.

The messenger is a servant of Job who survived the attack of the Sabeans. This happens right after God allowed Satan to test Job, taking away his possessions but not touching his person. This begins a chain of misfortunes that arrive one after another. The account first describes a calm scene of ordinary work, so that the blow lands harder.

For today: tragedies often come in the middle of ordinary days and without warning. We cannot control that, but we can nurture our trust in God now, in everyday life. If we already have the habit of prayer and of reading his Word, we will have something to lean on when bad news arrives.
exp.0:16:
This verse tells of the third piece of bad news that Job receives. A servant arrives and says that the Chaldeans, divided into three groups, attacked Job's camels and carried them off. They also killed the young servants, that is, the younger attendants, with the sword. Only this servant escaped to bring the news.

The one speaking is a messenger. Job, a righteous man and very wealthy, is losing his possessions in a single day. The Chaldeans were a people who lived in that region, and here they act as raiders. The messages come one after another, leaving him no time to recover.

For today: sometimes blows come one on top of another, and we feel out of breath. This passage reminds us that we are not alone in our suffering. When everything falls apart, we can come to God honestly and ask him for strength, one day at a time.
exp.0:18:
This verse tells of the fourth and worst piece of news Job receives in a single day. A great wind came from the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead. Everyone died. The messenger was the only one who escaped to tell him.

A messenger speaks before Job, a rich and righteous man. Earlier, Job had already lost his animals and servants. Now he learns that his sons and daughters died in the house of their eldest brother. The book presents all of this as a trial that God allows, and Job does not understand why.

For today: when pain arrives all at once, you do not need immediate answers. You may weep, as Job did, and still return to God with honesty and trust.
exp.0:19:
Job gets up after hearing the worst news: all of his children have died. He tears his robe and shaves his head, which were ways of showing very deep grief in that time. He then falls to the ground, but not to give up. He does it to worship God.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Job had already lost his property and now loses his children, all in a single day. His reaction shows two things together: real pain and a faith that still stands. Job does not pretend the loss doesn't hurt, but he also does not turn away from God.

For today: you do not have to hide your pain to be faithful. You can grieve honestly and still draw near to God instead of pulling away from Him. Worship in the middle of suffering does not erase the sadness, but it places it in the right hands.
exp.0:20:
Job says that he came into the world with nothing and will leave it with nothing. He recognizes that everything he had was a gift from the Lord, and that the Lord also has the right to take it away. Even so, he blesses the name of God.

Job speaks as a man of integrity, upright and wealthy. In a single day he lost his possessions, his servants, and all his children. He has just heard the latest news: a great wind brought down the house where his children were. He tore his robe and shaved his head as a sign of mourning, and then he fell to the ground and worshiped. He does not know what has happened in heaven; he knows only his own grief.

We can grieve sincerely and, at the same time, worship. In loss, remembering that everything is a gift helps us give thanks for what we had and trust God, even when we do not understand.
exp.1:1:
In this verse, God asks Satan where he has come from. Satan answers that he has come from going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it, that is, from roaming it from one place to another.

This takes place at a gathering in heaven, where the sons of God (heavenly beings) present themselves before the Lord. God speaks first, and Satan answers. The question does not mean that God does not know anything; it opens the dialogue that leads to speaking about Job. Some scholars see in Satan's words a patrol of watchfulness, others an attitude of accuser.

For today: our adversary is active and always seeking, but he always answers before God and cannot act beyond his limits. We can rest in the knowledge that God remains in control.
exp.1:4:
Satan tells God to stretch out his hand and touch Job's body, his bones and his flesh. He is sure that then Job will curse God to his face. Here, "curse" means speaking badly of God or cursing him.

Satan, the accuser, is speaking in reply to God. Job had already lost his property and his children, but he remained faithful. Satan claims that Job serves God only as long as he has his health. The Bible does not say that God doubted Job; the account tests whether his faith is sincere.

For today: our faith should not depend only on everything going well for us. When pain or sickness comes, we can keep trusting God, even when we do not understand what is happening, and we can also be honest with him in prayer.
exp.1:7:
It says Job, his body covered with painful sores, used a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself and relieve the itching. He was sitting among ashes, which in that culture was a sign of mourning, grief and humiliation. The sores described a serious disease of the skin.

The narrator tells what happened after God allowed Satan to strike Job, but without taking his life. Job went from being a respected man to suffering alone and without comfort. This sets up the reaction of his wife and Job's firm reply, in which he still trusts in God.

When pain leaves you without strength, you do not have to pretend that you are well. Job sat in his suffering without ceasing to trust. You can bring your pain honestly to God, and look for someone to walk alongside you.
exp.1:9:
Job answers his wife firmly. He says she speaks like one of the foolish women. She is talking without thinking about God. Then he asks a question: if we accept the good things God gives us, shall we not also accept the evil ones? The text ends by saying that Job did not sin with his lips, that is, he did not speak against God.

Job is sitting among the ashes, sick, with his body covered in sores, after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His wife, in despair, suggests that he curse God and die. Job does not call her foolish as a person; he says she speaks as a foolish woman would. It is a firm correction, but without cursing. Then his three friends will arrive.

For today: when pain comes, we do not need to pretend that everything is fine, but we can take care with our words. Before we complain or give in to despair, let us remember that God is still worthy of trust, and let us bring him our complaint honestly.
exp.1:10:
Here it says that three friends of Job, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, heard about all the suffering that had come upon him. Each one set out from his own place, because they had made an appointment to go together. They wanted to mourn with him, that is, to share in his grief, and to comfort him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Job has just lost his possessions, his children, and his health, and even his wife advised him to give up. Yet he did not sin with his lips. The friends arrive afterward, and the text shows that at first their attitude is good: they weep and sit in silence for seven days. Later, their words will become a cause of argument and error.

For today: when someone suffers, the first thing is not speeches but being present. Call, visit, listen, and accompany them, even when you do not know what to say.
exp.1:12:
Their three friends sat down with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word, because they saw that his suffering was enormous.

The narrator of the book describes here the arrival of Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. They had heard about Job's tragedy: he lost his possessions, his children and his health. They came to comfort him. They wept, tore their robes and threw dust on their heads, signs of mourning in that culture. Later on, the friends will speak and get things wrong, but here the best thing they do is stay silent.

For today: when someone is suffering greatly, they do not always need explanations or quick advice. Sometimes the most loving thing is simply to be present, to listen and to stay with them patiently, without rushing to fix everything.
exp.2:3:
He says that Job wishes the day of his birth would turn dark, as if it were a sad day without any light. "Dark" here means gloomy and full of sorrow. The phrase about God not caring for it from above means that God would not take it into account or remember it. And that no brightness would shine on that day, that is, that it would disappear from history.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. He spent seven days in silence with his friends, and now he breaks that silence with a very deep pain. He does not curse God; he curses the day he was born. His lament is sincere and raw.

Today we can learn that there is no need to pretend strength before God. If you are suffering greatly, you can tell him honestly what you feel. He listens, and it is also wise to seek out someone you trust who can walk with you.
exp.2:6:
Job wishes that night, the night he was conceived or born, would be barren and empty, without joy. He wants no voice to be heard in it, no cry of celebration. The word "barren" can be understood as unproductive or without fruit.

It is Job speaking, a man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. After seven days of silence with his friends, he finally voices his pain. He does not curse God, but the day of his birth. It is poetic and anguished language, not a teaching to imitate.

For today: if you are in deep sorrow, you can be honest before God. The Bible does not hide these words, and that shows us that He can hear our lament without rejecting us. Speak with God, and also seek out someone you trust who can walk with you.
exp.2:8:
Job asks that the stars of the early dawn be dark, that the light wait for the morning and never come, and that he not see the eyelids of the morning, a poetic image for the first rays of the sun, as if they were eyes opening on waking. Dawn is the time when the day begins.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. He has sat in silence with his friends for seven days, and now he opens his mouth and curses the day he was born. He does not curse God, but expresses his pain in very strong and poetic language. He wishes that the night of his birth had never come to an end.

For today: when pain runs deep, you can tell God honestly what you feel, without disguising it. The Bible shows that God does not reject Job for his laments. Speak with God, and also seek out someone you trust who can walk with you.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that Job curses the night of his birth because it did not shut the doors of his mother's womb, that is, it did not prevent him from being born. It also did not hide from his eyes the sorrow that would come after.

Job speaks, a man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. After seven days of silence with his friends, he finally voices his anguish. He is not denying God; he is pouring out a pain so great that he wishes he had never been born. The Bible presents his complaint with honesty, without hiding it.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, even if the words are very harsh. Also seek someone you trust who will listen to you with patience, without rushing you or giving you easy explanations.
exp.2:12:
This verse says that, if Job had died at birth, he would now be at peace. Job compares death to a sleep in which, at last, there is no pain. It is not a plan but a cry of anguish.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends come and sit with him in silence. Then Job breaks the silence and curses the day of his birth. Here he expresses his deep weariness. The Bible does not hide his pain, and later God hears him and does not reject him.

Today we can be honest with God when we are exhausted. There is no need to pretend to be strong. If someone close to us suffers like this, let us accompany them with patience, without rushing to give speeches. And if there are thoughts of harming oneself, it is wise to speak soon with someone you trust or to seek professional help.
exp.2:13:
It says that if Job had died at birth, he would now be resting alongside the kings and counsellors of the earth. The phrase "which built desolate places for themselves" is difficult. Some believe it refers to ruins or ruined places that those great men rebuilt; others, to monuments or tombs they raised for themselves. The exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The one speaking is Job, after losing everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends have not yet answered him. He does not curse God, but he is in such pain that he wishes he had never been born. He pictures death as a place of rest, where even the powerful end up the same as everyone else.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you can be honest with God, as Job was. And remember that human power and human works do not last forever; only in God do we find true rest.
exp.2:15:
Job says it would have been better had he never been born. He asks why he was not hidden away, buried or gone, like a stillborn child, or like the babies who died before they ever saw the light of day. Here the idea is of a child born without life.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions and his health. He is in such deep pain that he wishes he had never existed. He pictures death as a place of rest, where suffering no longer reaches. It is a sincere cry of grief, not a lesson about how to view life. Later, God does not rebuke him for lamenting this way.

For today: if you are going through deep sorrow, you can be honest with God, even about your darkest thoughts. He listens without being frightened. And do not carry that anguish alone: seek out a brother or sister in faith, a pastor, or a trusted counselor who can walk with you.
exp.2:17:
There the prisoners rest together, and they no longer hear the voice of the oppressor, the one who drove them to work and demanded payment, and who treated slaves and prisoners harshly.

Job speaks, a man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is in such pain that he wishes he had never been born. He pictures death as an end to weariness and to oppression. This is the language of his suffering, not a complete teaching about what happens after death. The Bible presents it honestly, without hiding his anguish.

For today: if you are exhausted or under pressure, do not pretend you are fine. You can speak to God frankly, as Job did. And also seek practical help: a friend, a pastor, or a counselor who can walk with you and help you rest.
exp.2:18:
Job says that in death, which here is called "there," people are no longer divided by rank. The "small" is the one of little importance and the "great" is the one of great importance. Both rest in the same place. And the servant is free from his master, that is, the slave no longer has an owner giving him orders.

Job speaks, a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is full of pain and wishes he had never been born. He pictures death as a place of rest where struggles and abuses come to an end. This is his lament, not a complete teaching about what happens after death. The Bible says more on that subject in other passages.

When suffering overwhelms you, you can speak to God honestly, as Job did, without pretending. And remember that before God no one is worth more or less because of their position; treat everyone with dignity.
exp.2:20:
They say there are people who long for death and it does not come. They seek it more eagerly than someone searching for hidden treasure. "Long for" here means to desire strongly. It is not a calm sentence; it is the cry of someone who is suffering greatly.

Job is speaking after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His three friends sit with him in silence. Job curses the day of his birth and asks why life is given to those who live in bitterness. He does not say that God does not exist; he pours out his pain before Him, and the Bible records that complaint with honesty.

For today: if you are going through a very deep sadness, you can speak to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. And if you ever think about taking your own life, seek help now: talk with someone you trust, a pastor or a health professional.
exp.2:21:
They say there are people so worn down by suffering that they rejoice greatly, almost as at a celebration, when they find the grave. "Greatly" means very much, and "grave" is the place where a dead person is laid to rest. It is a powerful picture of the longing to rest from pain.

Job is speaking after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends sit beside him in silence. Job is not giving a lesson but pouring out his anguish. He wishes he had never been born and thinks death would bring relief. The Bible does not hide this complaint, and later God does not reject Job for voicing it.

For today: if you are exhausted by pain, you do not need to pretend to be strong. You can speak honestly with God, as Job did. And if you have thoughts of ending your life, tell someone you trust today or seek professional help.
exp.2:22:
This verse is part of a painful question: why is life given to a man who cannot see his way, who does not know where to go, and whom God has hemmed in on every side? The image is of being surrounded by walls, with no way out and no direction.

The one speaking is Job, after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends sit in silence beside him. Job does not curse God, but he does lament having been born. He feels confused and trapped. Some understand that Job acknowledges that God is in control, even though he does not understand what is happening; others see instead his honest outpouring.

For today: when you feel lost or without a way out, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did. And seek out trusted people who will stay with you while you wait for light.
exp.3:1:
Eliphaz wonders whether he should speak to Job at all, because he knows his words may hurt him. He admits that trying to say something might upset Job, but he also admits that he cannot stay silent: who can hold back from speaking?

Eliphaz is from Teman, one of Job's three friends. Job has just lamented his enormous suffering. Eliphaz begins politely, but it soon becomes clear that he wants to correct him, since he believes Job is suffering because of some sin. Later God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so their advice should be read with care.

For today: before advising someone who is suffering, listen first, and ask yourself whether you are truly helping them or just want to say what you think. Speak with humility, compassion and truth.
exp.3:2:
It says that Job had taught many people and that he strengthened the weak. The word "strengthened" in the verse above means giving strength or encouragement. Weak hands are tired hands with no strength left; they represent people who are discouraged and worn out.

Elifaz, Job's friend, speaks here, breaking the silence after Job's lament. He begins in a kind tone and acknowledges the good Job did for others. However, he will soon use this to tell Job that he is not now practicing what he taught. Elifaz interprets Job's suffering as if it were the result of some sin, and later God will say that his friends did not speak rightly about Him.

For today: when someone is suffering, it is not enough to repeat back to them what they themselves believed or said. Stay with them patiently, listen before explaining, and offer real encouragement without judging.
exp.3:3:
Job says he helped those who were about to fall.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. Job is suffering an enormous loss, and Eliphaz begins his first speech. He acknowledges the good Job did for others, but uses it to point out that he is now not applying that same encouragement to himself. Although it sounds kind, his tone is one of reproach, and the book itself shows that his advice was not correct.

Today, if you have been a support to others, it is also normal to need support when you suffer. Allow yourself to be accompanied, and when you comfort someone, do it with tenderness and without reproach.
exp.3:4:
Job, who used to help others through their troubles, now finds that suffering has come to him, and he feels its weight and is confused by it. The phrase about it being hard to bear means that it is difficult for him to endure. The idea of being troubled means that he is distressed and loses his composure.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He comes to comfort him, but his words sound like a rebuke, since he implies that Job is not living out what he taught. We should read this carefully: Eliphaz speaks with good intentions, but he is wrong to assume that Job's suffering is the result of his sin. At the end of the book, God corrects these friends.

For today: when someone is suffering, accompany them with tenderness and do not judge them. And if you are the one suffering, remember that being distressed does not make you any less faithful; you can bring your pain to God honestly.
exp.3:5:
What it says: Eliphaz asks Job whether his fear of God, his confidence, his hope, and the uprightness of his ways should not be his support now.

Context: Eliphaz is one of Job's three friends. Job has lost everything, and Eliphaz tries to comfort him, but with a tone of rebuke. He reminds Job that he used to encourage others, and now Job is shaken. Eliphaz implies that suffering comes from sin, an idea that God later corrects in the book (Job 42:7).

For today: When someone is suffering, let us avoid giving quick explanations or reproaches. It is better to stay with them with patience and kindness. And if we ourselves suffer, we can keep trusting God even without understanding the why.
exp.3:9:
It says that lions, which are strong and feared, can lose their power. Their roar goes silent and their teeth are broken. "Broken" here means shattered or destroyed. The lion in this verse is an image of powerful and violent people.

Elifaz, Job's friend, is the one speaking. He wants to explain Job's suffering by saying that wicked people fall under God's judgment. This is what he has observed in life. But the book later shows that Elifaz was wrong to apply this to Job, because Job was not suffering for being wicked.

For today: do not envy or fear the power of those who do harm, because it does not last forever. But do not use this truth to judge the pain of others, as Elifaz did. Instead, walk alongside the one who suffers with humility and compassion.
exp.3:10:
Here he says that even the lion, the strongest and most feared animal, can perish when it finds no prey to hunt. Then its cubs, who depended on it, are left scattered and without protection. "Perish" means to die, and "prey" is the animal the lion hunts to eat.

Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's friends, speaks here. He is trying to explain Job's suffering with an idea of his own: that the wicked are destroyed by God. He uses the image of lions to speak of powerful people who fall. But the book later shows that Eliphaz was wrong to apply this to Job, who was innocent.

Today it reminds us that no one is so strong as to have no need of God. It also invites us not to judge the pain of others lightly. When someone is suffering, it is better to accompany them with humility than to offer quick explanations.
exp.3:12:
Elifaz is said to have received a message in the middle of thoughts and visions of the night, just when people fall into a deep sleep. It is the beginning of the account of a night experience that left him deeply impressed.

The speaker is Elifaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to comfort and correct Job, and to give weight to his words he recounts this spiritual experience. The verses that follow describe a spirit and a message. The Bible does not fully clarify the origin of that voice, and later God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). For that reason it is wise to listen carefully.

For today: do not accept something as true just because it sounds very spiritual or was a striking experience. Compare everything with what God has already revealed in His Word, and speak with humility and compassion when you counsel someone who is suffering.
exp.3:15:
It stood still, but Eliphaz could not make out its form. The explanation says something appeared and stopped in front of Eliphaz's eyes, and that he could not recognize its shape. An image was before his eyes; it was a figure or an apparition. At first there was silence, and then he heard a voice speaking.

The one speaking is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's friends. He tries to comfort Job and to explain his suffering. He recounts a nighttime experience that frightened him and uses it as an authority. Note: later God says that Job's friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so not everything Eliphaz says is correct, even though the Bible records it.

For today: we should not base our faith on impressive experiences or visions, nor use them to judge others. Let us test everything by what God has revealed in His Word, and treat those who suffer with humility.
exp.3:18:
It says that if even the angels are not perfect before God, how much less are we human beings. Our body is compared to a house of clay, built upon the dust. The word "moth" refers to a small insect that destroys clothing; here it shows that we are fragile and easily broken. "Crushed" means destroyed or crushed to pieces.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He describes a night vision he had and uses it to tell Job that he must have sinned, since he is suffering. Be careful: at the end of the book, God himself says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about him, so his words contain some truth about human frailty, but he applies them wrongly to Job.

Today we can live with humility, remembering that we depend on God. But we must also take care not to judge those who suffer, as if their pain were always a punishment.
exp.3:19:
They are said to be like houses of clay, fragile, and able to be destroyed between morning and evening. They vanish forever, and no one stops to think about it; that is, they pass away without anyone caring or noticing.

Elifaz of Teman, one of Job's friends, speaks here. He recounts a night vision in which he is told that God is not unjust and that even the angels are not perfect before Him. His aim is to persuade Job that he suffers because of some sin. Note: later God says that Elifaz did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so his words are not a safe guide in every respect.

For today: life is brief and fragile, so it is wise to live it with humility and trust in God, without boasting about tomorrow. And when we see someone suffering, it is better to accompany them with compassion than to judge them.
exp.4:0:
He says Job may cry out for help, but no one will answer him. He also asks which of the "holy ones" Job will turn to. Here "holy ones" is usually understood to mean heavenly beings or angels, though some think it refers to godly people.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. Job is suffering greatly and has complained before God. Eliphaz answers him harshly, suggesting that his complaint is useless and that his suffering comes from some foolishness. Note: God himself, at the end of the book, says that the friends did not speak rightly about him.

For today: when someone is suffering, they do not need a speech that judges them, but companionship and compassion. And when you are the one suffering, remember that you can cry out directly to God, who does listen, even when others do not know what to say to you.
exp.4:2:
He says he saw a fool, that is, someone who lives without fearing God, who seemed to prosper and to take root like a firm tree. But suddenly he noticed that his house was heading toward ruin, and so he declared it cursed, that is, doomed to fail.

Eliphaz speaks, one of Job's friends. He believes suffering always comes as punishment for some sin, and he hints at this to explain Job's pain. The verses that follow describe the downfall of that fool's children and goods. Note: the book later shows that Eliphaz was wrong to apply this idea to Job (Job 42:7).

For today: do not judge other people's suffering as God's punishment. When someone suffers, accompany them with compassion and prayer, and trust that God sees what we cannot see.
exp.4:3:
It says that the children of the fool, that is, of the person who lives without wisdom, will be far from safety. Here "safety" means security and well-being. The gate was the place where the judges gathered and cases were settled; there the children will be crushed, that is, humbled and overcome, with no one to defend them.

Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. He tries to explain Job's suffering by saying that the fool comes to a bad end. But take note: Eliphaz generalizes, and at the end of this book God says that he did not speak rightly (Job 42:7). His words do not apply to every case, and certainly not to Job's.

Today we can learn not to explain other people's pain with easy answers. When someone is suffering, it is better to stand with them with compassion and to listen, rather than assume they are paying for something.
exp.4:6:
This verse compares human suffering to sparks that fly upward. Just as the sparks rising from a fire go up naturally, a person is born destined to pass through trouble, that is, through pain and hardship.

Elifaz, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. He is trying to explain to Job why he is suffering, and he says that troubles do not spring up from nothing. His underlying idea is that pain has a cause, and that Job should turn back to God. Note: later on, God says that Elifaz did not speak rightly about Him, so his words are not always correct.

For today: when difficulties come, do not be surprised or think that God has abandoned you. Seek God with confidence, and do not judge harshly those who are suffering.
exp.4:10:
This verse says that God lifts up the humble and sets them in a high place, that is, He gives them honor and safety. It also says that those who mourn, the ones who are in grief or deeply sad, are brought to safety. The word "safety" here means salvation, rescue, or well-being.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He is speaking about the power and goodness of God, who cares for creation with the rain and also cares for the weak. His general idea is true, but we must remember that Eliphaz later misapplies his ideas to Job, and God Himself corrects him at the end of the book.

When you are going through a moment of pain, or of being unimportant in the eyes of others, do not lose hope. Practice humility and bring your sorrow to God in prayer, trusting that He knows how to lift you up in His time.
exp.4:11:
The verse says that God frustrates the plans of the crafty, so that their hands cannot carry out what they devised. That is, those who are very skilled at deceiving or scheming evil. So their hands fail to accomplish anything they planned. The word "crafty" here does not refer to simple cleverness, but to a skill used with malice.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He is describing the power of God: he gives rain, lifts up the humble, and comforts those who mourn, but he also overturns the wicked. Note, however, that the book itself later shows Eliphaz applied these ideas wrongly to Job's situation, so his statement is true in general but does not explain Job's suffering.

For today: if you feel frustrated by injustice or by people who cheat, trust that God sees and has the final word. In the meantime, choose to act with honesty.
exp.4:14:
It says that God rescues the poor, the needy, from the sword, that is, from violence, and from the hurtful words of wicked people. He also delivers them from the violent hand, which speaks of the abuses of powerful people. The wicked are those who live without respect for God.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to comfort Job and explain that God corrects the proud and protects the weak. His words sound beautiful, but he assumes Job is suffering because of some sin, and at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. Even so, this truth about God's care for the poor also appears in other passages of the Bible.

Today, if you feel powerless before injustice, pray with confidence, for God sees the weak. And if you can, be a concrete help to someone in need.
exp.4:15:
It says that the poor person has hope, and that wickedness is silenced, left without any way to defend itself. The first word refers to someone in need who lacks the basics. The word for wickedness means injustice or evil, and here it is presented as if it were someone left without words.

The one speaking is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's friends. He teaches that God rescues the poor from the violent and the wicked. His words contain truths about God's care, but then he applies them wrongly to Job, as if his suffering were always the result of some sin of his own. The same book corrects that idea.

If today you feel small or in need, you can keep praying and waiting on God, for He cares about those who suffer. And if you have something to give, help someone in need this week with concrete actions.
exp.4:21:
The verse says that the person protected by God will be able to laugh, that is, to look on calmly and with confidence, both at ruin and at famine. Nor will they be afraid of wild animals. The word "destruction" speaks of ruin or devastation, and the "beasts of the earth" are the wild animals.

The one speaking is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's three friends. He tells Job that if he seeks God and accepts his correction, God will care for him in every calamity. Be careful: later God himself rebukes Eliphaz and his companions for not having spoken rightly about him (Job 42:7). Their words contain a general truth, but they apply it wrongly to Job's case.

Today we can trust that God cares for his own, without thinking that every suffering is a punishment. Faced with a crisis, let us ask for calm and confidence in him, and avoid judging others who suffer.
exp.4:22:
It says that the person who is right with God will live in harmony with creation. The phrase about being in league with the stones of the field means being in covenant or at peace with the stones of the field, that is, the stones will no longer be an obstacle to planting or to living there. And the wild animals will stop being a threat: they will be at peace with you.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, Job's friend. He believes that God protects those who accept correction and seek Him. That idea has some truth, but at the end of the book God Himself says that Eliphaz and his friends did not speak rightly about Him. Job's suffering was not punishment for sin, so these promises must not be used as a rule for judging anyone.

For today: trust that God cares for you, but do not use that trust to judge someone who is suffering. Walk alongside them with compassion, not with easy explanations.
exp.5:3:
He says that Job feels as if God had shot arrows into him, and that their poison reaches to the very depths of his soul. Furthermore, he feels that the terrors of God, that is, dreadful things coming from God, attack him like an army in battle.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friend Eliphaz has just told him that his suffering must have a cause. Job answers that his pain is as heavy as the sand of the sea, and that is why his words come out disordered. He understands his pain as something that comes from God, although the book shows that the story is more complex.

When someone is suffering, we do not need to correct their words right away. First we can listen with patience and compassion, and we can also bring our pain honestly to God, as Job did.
exp.5:5:
Job asks whether anything without taste or salt can be eaten, and whether the white of an egg has any flavor. The obvious answer is no. Some believe the Hebrew phrase refers to the white of an egg, and others to the juice of a slimy plant. Scholars are not sure.

Job speaks as one who is suffering enormously. He is responding to his friend Eliphaz, whose words seem to him bland and without comfort. Job compares Eliphaz's explanations to a tasteless meal that does not nourish someone who is wounded.

Today, when someone suffers, let us avoid stock phrases and cold advice. Better to listen, accompany, and speak with tenderness. And if you are the one suffering, you can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did.
exp.5:6:
Job says that he can no longer choose what he eats or what he endures. What his soul once refused, as if touching it made him sick, has now become his food because of his pain. Here "touch" means to come near or to taste, and "food" speaks of what he is forced to swallow. Some understand it to refer to his bitter words, others to his suffering itself.

Job speaks in reply to Eliphaz. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his friend tells him to calm down. Job answers that just as an animal does not complain when it has good pasture, he is not complaining without reason. His life has become tasteless and bitter.

For today: when you suffer, do not hide your pain. You can tell God honestly how bitter you feel. And if you walk alongside someone who is suffering, do not give quick answers; listen to them with patience and kindness.
exp.5:13:
It says that the one who suffers is owed comfort and support from his friend, even when he has lost his strength. Whoever does not give it sets aside the fear of God Almighty. The one who is afflicted is the person going through pain and distress; the friend is the close companion; and the Almighty is God, the All-Powerful. The second half of the verse is hard to translate, and scholars interpret it in different ways, but the general idea is that withholding compassion from the one who suffers is failing to show the reverence owed to God.

Job is speaking after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. Eliphaz has just addressed him with reproaches instead of tenderness. Job feels alone, and in the verses that follow he compares his friends to streams that dry up just when they are most needed.

When someone close to you is suffering, do not begin with explanations or judgments. Be present, listen, and accompany them. Often, your calm care is worth more than any advice.
exp.5:15:
This verse continues the comparison of the stream. It says the waters of the torrent are dark and dim because of the ice, and hidden under the snow. "Ice" is the frost or cold that covers the water. That is, in winter the stream looks full and strong, but that appearance depends on the cold.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. He is answering Eliphaz, one of his friends, who instead of comforting him judged him. Job says his friends are like desert streams: they seem to give hope, but when the heat comes, they dry up and disappear.

For today: it is not enough to look good when everything is going easily. We can ask ourselves whether we are steady when someone is suffering. Let us walk alongside others with patience, listen without accusing, and offer real support, especially when it is hard.
exp.5:19:
The explanation says the caravans came expecting to find the streams they hoped for, but they were left disappointed and embarrassed. The sense of the verse is that they were let down, and their hope was real, but the water was no longer there.

Job is speaking, and he is suffering greatly. He is answering his friend Eliphaz. In the verse before, he compares his friends to desert streams, which swell in winter but dry up in the heat. Teman and Sheba were regions from which caravans came. Job expected comfort from his friends, but he found accusations, and he felt let down.

For today: if someone has failed you when you needed them most, be honest with God about your pain, as Job was. And try to be a friend who does bring water: listen with patience, stay close, and do not judge without knowing the whole story.
exp.5:20:
Here Job tells his friends that they are like those desert streams that dry up.

Job speaks, a man who has lost everything and is sick and in pain. His friend Eliphaz has already spoken to him, and Job complains that he finds no compassion. Travelers from Tema and Sheba hoped for water in the streams, but when they arrived they were disappointed. Some think the friends were afraid that God would punish them too; the text does not fully explain this.

When someone is suffering, we do not need to have all the answers. Sometimes the best thing is to stay close, listen patiently, and offer a kind presence, without judging or running away out of fear or discomfort.
exp.5:23:
Job asks his friends to teach him and to make him understand where he has gone wrong. If they truly manage to do this, he will hold his tongue. He means that he will stop speaking and stop complaining.

Job is a man who suffers greatly, and he is answering Eliphaz. His friends accuse him of having sinned, but they do not point out any specific fault. Job did not ask them for money or a ransom, only an honest and clear correction. He is willing to listen if they show him the truth.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us not judge them without evidence. And if others correct us clearly and kindly, let us have the humility to listen. Correcting someone well requires knowing the facts, speaking with love, and staying with the person.
exp.5:26:
Job's friends have come to comfort him, but in this verse Job accuses them of treating him as though he were defenseless and could be taken advantage of, like an orphan with no one to protect him. He says they would even turn on a friend and trade him away for their own gain. It is a sharp accusation, and it shows how much Job felt betrayed by the people who should have stood by him.

Job speaks here in reply to Eliphaz. He is in terrible pain, and his friends answer with lectures instead of compassion. Job feels they are judging his cries of anguish as if they were empty arguments, when they are really the words of a desperate man. His rebuke is bitter, and it is meant to shake them out of their certainty.

For today: when someone is suffering, listen before you correct. They may not need your arguments as much as your company, your patience, and kind words that help them find the strength to stand up again.
exp.5:27:
Job asks his friends to look him straight in the face. "Look at me" means to pay close attention to him, to his face and to his condition. He tells them to judge for themselves whether he is lying. It is as if he were saying: "Look me in the eyes and decide whether I am sincere."

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends, such as Eliphaz, accuse him of having sinned in secret and rebuke him for his complaints. Job feels wounded and poorly understood. That is why he asks them to listen carefully, instead of criticizing his words of pain.

Before judging someone who is suffering, let us take the time to look at them and truly listen. Very often the person needs company and attentive ears, not hasty sermons. And if we are the ones who suffer, we can speak honestly before God and before trusted people.
exp.6:1:
Job compares his life to that of a tired servant who longs for the shade to rest, and to a day laborer who eagerly waits for the moment his workday ends and he receives his pay. "Longs for" means to desire something very strongly. A day laborer is someone who works for pay earned each day. The "shade" may be rest from the heat of the day, though some understand it as the evening shadow that signals the end of work.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and he answers his friend Eliphaz. He feels exhausted, without rest, and sees his days as a heavy labor that never ends. He says this honestly before God and before his friends.

For today: when you are weary or suffering, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God sincerely how you feel. The Bible shows that honest prayer, even with complaints, is welcome.
exp.6:4:
It says that Job's body is covered with worms and crusts of dry earth. His skin is split, with open wounds, and he looks disgusting.

Job speaks, a man who lost almost everything and now suffers a painful skin disease. He says this to God and also to his friends, in the middle of sleepless nights. He does not describe his suffering with decoration, but with complete honesty. The worms can be understood literally or as a way of painting his badly deteriorated condition.

For today: when you suffer, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how you feel, even with raw words. He listens, and you can also seek the support of people who walk with you without judging you.
exp.6:12:
Here Job says that when he lies down, he hopes his bed will bring him rest and calm his complaint. The phrase that would soften his complaints means that it would make them gentler, that it would ease his pain. Job seeks comfort in sleep, like any person who is tired and in pain.

Job speaks, a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is answering his friend Eliphaz and addresses God with complete sincerity. In the verses that follow, he says that not even sleep brings him peace, because he has nightmares. His pain is so great that he finds no relief anywhere.

For today: when the night brings you anguish and you cannot rest, do not pretend that everything is fine. Speak with God honestly, as Job did. He can hear your complaints without rejecting you, and praying sincerely is a good first step toward comfort.
exp.6:13:
Job tells God that when he tries to rest, God frightens him with dreams and terrifies him with visions. Here, to shake or startle hard means to scare someone badly, and to be stirred up means to be troubled or filled with terror. Job feels that even sleep brings him no relief.

Job speaks, a man who has lost everything and suffers pain in his body and in his soul. He hopes his bed will bring him comfort, but the nights are worse. He wonders whether he is some sea monster that needs to be watched. These are words of honest complaint; he attributes the dreams to God, although the book shows that his understanding of them was limited.

For today: when pain takes away your sleep, do not hide it. Tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did, and also seek the company of someone you trust who will pray with you.
exp.7:9:
This verse asks whether the older generations will not teach you and tell you. It says they will speak and bring words out of their heart, that is, they will share what they have truly lived and learned. Bringing words out of the heart means speaking with sincerity, from experience and not just from memory.

Bildad, one of Job's three friends, is the speaker. He is trying to explain to Job why he is suffering. He appeals to the wisdom of past generations, saying that our life is brief, like a shadow, and that we know little. His argument is that God punishes the wicked. Later, God Himself will say that Job's friends did not speak rightly about Him, so their counsel is not entirely correct.

For today: listen to people who are older and have experience in the faith, since they can offer you much wisdom. But always compare what you hear with the whole of the Bible, because even good advice can be applied wrongly.
exp.7:16:
It says this tree has its roots intertwined beside a spring of water, and that they grip firmly even among the stones. The phrase about the roots going on intertwining means that they keep winding around one another. It seems a strong, well-fed tree, with the look of security.

Bildad, Job's friend, is speaking, and he does so with a harsh idea: that whoever forgets God comes to a bad end. He describes a man who seems prosperous, but whose success does not last. The verses that follow show that such a tree can be uprooted and forgotten. Even so, the book of Job teaches that Bildad was wrong to apply this to Job.

For today: let us not measure anyone's life only by their prosperity or their suffering. Rather, let us seek to put down roots in God himself, who is the true spring, and treat with compassion those who suffer.
exp.7:18:
He says that the joy of the wicked is temporary. When they are pulled up from their place, the earth leaves no trace of them, and other plants spring up from that same ground. The verse's word "joy" is the thing being described here, and some readers take the phrase with bitter irony: that is all their joy amounts to.

Bildad, one of Job's friends, speaks. Using the image of a plant without firm roots, he insists that the wicked come to a bad end. He says this to convince Job that his suffering is punishment. But at the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: do not use a general truth to judge another person's pain. Walk alongside them with kindness. And seek to let your joy rest in God, not in things that pass away.
exp.7:20:
The explanation says that God can still fill a person's mouth with laughter and their lips with shouts of joy.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He believes God always rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked, so he tells Job that if he turns back to God sincerely, joy will return. However, at the end of the book God says that Job's friends did not speak rightly about Him. For that reason, this promise is beautiful, but it does not apply to every kind of suffering.

For today: when you go through pain, do not think that God is punishing you. Bring Him your heart with sincerity and wait on Him, trusting that He can restore your joy in His time.
exp.8:13:
Here Job wonders how he could answer God, if not even the powerful can stand against him. Job feels that, before the greatness of God, no clever speech would do much good.

The one speaking is Job, in the midst of great suffering. He answers his friend Bildad and acknowledges that God is wise and powerful. But Job feels helpless: he would like to defend his case, and he cannot see how to do it before a Judge so great. It is a sincere complaint, not a final teaching about God. Later the book will show a more complete picture.

For today: when you are confused or hurt, you do not need to speak to God with perfect phrases. You can pray with humility and honesty, and trust in his mercy more than in your arguments.
exp.8:18:
He says that, if it comes to strength or power, God is without doubt the stronger. And if it comes to judgment, no one can force God to appear before a court.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. He feels that God has struck him without cause and has filled his life with bitterness. In this verse he recognizes that he cannot win against God, either by strength or in a lawsuit. Note: Job expresses what he feels, and later God himself corrects some of his ideas.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, you can speak to God with complete honesty, even with your complaints. But trust that God is greater than your questions, and rest in his character, not only in your own explanations.
exp.8:21:
Job says there is one thing he can no longer keep quiet about: in the eyes of God, both the blameless person and the wicked person can end up in the same destruction. "Blameless" here means upright, with no visible fault. "Destroy" means to bring to an end, to ruin.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of his suffering. He is answering Bildad, who insists that God does not mistreat the righteous. Job, wounded, feels that his own experience does not fit that idea. Here he speaks out of his pain and confusion, not as a complete teaching about God. Later in the same book, it becomes clear that Job did not have the whole truth.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, you can tell God honestly how you feel. But do not conclude that God is unjust just because you cannot see his reasons. Keep seeking him with trust.
exp.8:33:
Job asks God to take away his rod, that is, the punishment or the rod of correction with which he feels God is striking him. He also asks that the terror of God, that is, the dread produced by God's greatness, not frighten him.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of his great suffering. He answers his friends and acknowledges that God is not a man as he is. For that reason he cannot argue with God as an equal. He longs for an arbiter who would lay a hand on both of them, but there is none. If God were to withdraw his awesome presence, Job could speak without fear.

When we suffer, we can be honest with God, even with our fear and confusion. Job sees the need for a mediator, and Christians see in Jesus the one who draws near to us and allows us to approach God with confidence (1 Timothy 2:5).
exp.9:9:
He says that God formed Job from the smallest and most fragile beginnings. Job uses the image of milk being poured out and cheese being set to describe how he was shaped in the womb. The first image is about being poured out like liquid, and the second about being firmly shaped, as milk becomes solid as it sets. It is a poetic comparison, not a scientific explanation.

Job is speaking in the middle of his great suffering. He feels confused and cries out to God with honest pain: if God made him with such care, why does He seem to be destroying him now? Job does not understand what is happening, and in this passage he speaks out of his anguish. The verses that follow remind us that God also gave him life and mercy.

For today: when you do not understand your pain, you can speak to God with complete honesty. Remember that He formed you with care and that your life matters to Him, even when you cannot see the reason for what you suffer.
exp.9:15:
Job's suffering is said to keep growing and growing. Job feels that God is hunting him like a fierce lion hunts its prey, and that God again shows his power against him through astonishing things, which for Job are painful.

Job speaks in the middle of his pain, after losing everything. He addresses God with honest, almost bold complaints. He believes God treats him as an enemy, though the book shows that this is not the case. His view is limited, and interpreters see this language as the outpouring of a wounded man, not as teaching about what God is like.

For today: when you suffer, you can speak to God with sincerity, without pretending. But remember that what you feel does not always describe what God is. Tell him your pain and keep trusting his character.
exp.9:18:
It says that Job wishes he had never existed, as though he had never lived, and that he would have been carried straight from his mother's womb to the grave.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering: he has lost his possessions, his children, and his health. He speaks to God with raw, painful honesty and holds nothing back. He feels that God is attacking him and does not understand why. This is a lament, not a lesson on how to view life. Scholars agree that Job is expressing his anguish, and the book shows that God hears that cry.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can speak to God with complete honesty, even with your darkest questions. He does not turn away from someone who weeps. And if someone beside you is suffering like this, stand with them patiently, without rushing them or offering easy answers.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that Job wants a little relief before he dies, before he goes to the place he will not return from. He speaks of death as "the land of darkness and the shadow of death," that is, a dark place without light.

Job speaks in the midst of enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and his friends judge him unjustly. Here he speaks to God with sincere pain and asks for a moment of respite. His view of death is bleak; the Bible shows his lament here, not a complete teaching about the life to come.

For today: when pain weighs on you, you can speak with God in complete honesty, without pretending to be strong. He listens to a sincere lament, and praying this way can be the first step toward receiving comfort.
exp.10:0:
This verse only introduces the one who is about to speak. Zophar the Naamathite (as the name is spelled today) takes up the word and answers Job.

Zophar is one of the three friends who came to comfort Job after his great suffering. Here he speaks for the first time, after Job's speeches. He is upset by everything Job has said and rebukes him harshly. About his origin, we only know that he is called the Naamathite; his exact location is uncertain. At the end of the book, God will show that the friends did not speak rightly about Him.

For today: before you answer someone who is suffering, listen with patience and humility. Holding a firm opinion is not the same as being right. Ask God for wisdom to comfort with compassion, not to judge in haste.
exp.10:1:
Here Zophar asks whether so many words should go unanswered, and whether a man who talks too much (the word means a chatterer, one who talks endlessly) will be declared righteous just for talking a lot. For him, talking a lot does not show that someone is right.

Zophar, Job's third friend, speaks up after Job has defended himself at length. He believes Job is suffering because of some sin and that his speeches are only excuses. Yet the book itself shows that Zophar is wrong to judge Job, although his point about the multitude of words contains some truth.

Today we can remember that being right does not depend on speaking louder or longer. Before we defend ourselves or correct others, it is wise to listen with humility, to speak with few words, and not to judge harshly those who are suffering.
exp.10:2:
Here Zophar asks whether Job's empty talk, his lies or hollow words, will silence everyone. He also asks whether Job will mock others without anyone rebuking him or making him ashamed.

Zophar speaks, one of Job's three friends. Job suffers greatly and insists he has done nothing that deserves such punishment. Zophar takes this as arrogance and believes Job talks too much. Note: the book itself shows at the end that the friends were not right in everything, so their words are not always good advice.

For today: before correcting someone who is suffering, listen with humility. We may have some truth and still wound others if we speak without compassion. Let us ask God for wisdom and tenderness.
exp.10:3:
Here, Job is accused of saying that his way of speaking and living is pure, and that he is clean before God.

Zophar, the third of Job's friends, speaks. He is annoyed by Job's many words and believes his suffering is punishment for some sin. Be careful: Zophar sums up what Job says in a somewhat exaggerated way. Job did defend his integrity, but he also acknowledged that no one is righteous before God (Job 9:2). Moreover, the book shows that Zophar is wrong to judge Job.

For today: before judging someone who is suffering, let us listen with humility and not accuse them without knowing the facts. And when it is our turn to suffer, let us speak with sincerity, while leaving God to be the final judge.
exp.10:7:
It says that God's greatness is higher than the heavens and deeper than the grave, and it describes the grave as the place of the dead, which is the Hebrew word Sheol. The questions ("What can you do?" and "What can you know?") mean that a human being cannot reach or measure God by his own effort.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He wants to correct Job and thinks Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. His point about God's greatness is true, but the conclusion he draws about Job is mistaken, as God himself shows at the end of the book.

For today: learn to trust God even when you do not understand what you are going through. Recognizing that God is greater than your explanations keeps you from judging others who suffer, and it invites you to rest in him.
exp.10:8:
He says God is so great that he cannot be measured. His "measure" is his extent or size, and it is longer than the earth and broader than the sea. It is a poetic way of saying that God does not fit within our measurements or our minds.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He tries to show that Job cannot understand God and, for that reason, should acknowledge his own limitation. It should be made clear that, at the end of the book, God says the friends did not speak rightly about him. So their words contain truths about the greatness of God, but they apply them badly to Job's suffering, by implying that he has some hidden sin.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, do not be anxious about having all the answers. Trust in a God who is greater than your questions, and rest in the knowledge that he knows you, even though you cannot grasp him.
exp.10:9:
It says that no one can stop God when he acts. Some understand that it speaks of God as a judge who arrests and calls people to trial; others understand it as his general power.

The one speaking is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He tries to show Job that God is so great that no one understands him or can question him. However, Zophar assumes that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about him. His view of God's power is true, but he applies it wrongly.

For today: trust that God is sovereign, even when you do not understand your situation. And be careful not to use that truth to judge someone who is suffering; stay with them with humility and compassion.
exp.10:11:
It says that a vain person, that is, empty and without judgment, would only become sensible if a colt of a wild donkey (a young wild ass, a symbol of stubbornness and untamability) were born already tamed. It is a way of saying that this is almost impossible.

Zophar, one of Job's three friends, speaks here. He accuses Job of speaking without knowledge and insists that God sees all iniquity. His idea is that Job must be in sin, although the book shows that Zophar is wrong in his diagnosis. This sentence sounds harsh and even cruel, because it indirectly calls Job a fool. Some understand it as a general proverb about foolishness.

For today: before judging someone's pain, let us listen with humility. And if we are the ones who suffer, let us ask God for wisdom instead of becoming defensive.
exp.10:12:
It says that if the person prepares their heart, that is, readies it and disposes it well, and reaches out their hands toward God, which is a picture of prayer and sincere seeking, something good will come. The sentence is left open, but the verses that follow show the answer.

It is Zophar speaking, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he calls him to repent. It is worth remembering that the book itself shows Zophar was wrong about Job; his words sound religious, but they do not describe Job's situation well. Even so, the invitation to prepare the heart and pray is a good biblical principle.

For today: before you pray, stop for a moment. Set aside the rush, be honest with God, and open your heart to him, without assuming that all suffering comes from a sin of your own.
exp.10:15:
The verse says that Job would leave his pain behind. If he remembered it, it would be like remembering the water of a river that has already passed: something that cannot be held onto and will not stop again.

Zophar, one of Job's three friends, speaks here. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and so he invites him to repent in order to regain peace. His promise of relief is beautiful, but his assumption is mistaken. At the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: God does heal and comfort, but not all suffering is punishment. Trust that your pain will not last forever, and when someone is suffering, walk alongside them with tenderness instead of judging them.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that the life of the person who returns to God will be clearer than the midday. Even darkness will become like a morning that is beginning, full of light and new opportunities.

The one speaking is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he promises that if Job repents, God will restore him. Be aware: the book shows that Zophar was wrong in his diagnosis, since Job was not suffering for that reason. Even so, his words describe beautifully what God can do.

For today: do not measure every suffering as a punishment, but do draw near to God sincerely in your dark times. He can bring light and rest, even though it may not always be the way we expect.
exp.11:2:
Here Job tells his friends that he too has understanding. He affirms that he is not inferior to them, and adds that anyone could say what they are saying, because it is nothing out of the ordinary.

Job speaks with irony to his friends, who accuse him of suffering because of some hidden sin. They talk as though they alone were wise, and Job feels hurt and mocked. He reminds them that he also knows what they keep repeating, and that their words do not explain his pain.

When someone is suffering, they do not need speeches that make them feel smaller. They need companionship, respect, and attentive listening. Before offering advice or explaining another person's pain, we can listen with humility, remembering that no one knows everything.
exp.11:5:
It says that robbers and those who defy God do well: their homes are peaceful and they feel secure. The word "tents" refers to their dwellings. The word "provoke" means to offend or defy; the old spelling of the word "to" is also used here. The last phrase can be understood in two ways: that God has placed in their hand what they have, or that they believe they hold everything in their own hand, as if it were their god. Scholars interpret it in both ways.

Job speaks, answering his friends, who claimed that God always punishes the wicked and blesses the good. Job, righteous and suffering, shows them that real life does not always work that way, and that they do not have all the wisdom they presume to have.

Today: if you see that unjust people do well, do not conclude that God does not see or that obeying him is not worth it. Nor should you judge someone who suffers as if they were guilty. Trust in God and treat with compassion those who are going through pain.
exp.11:12:
This verse says that true wisdom, power, good counsel, and understanding belong to God. "Strength" means power or force. "Counsel" is the ability to guide and to decide well. "Understanding" here means insight or discernment.

Job is speaking, answering his friend Zophar. His friends were claiming wisdom for themselves, saying that the elders know more. Job replies that he too understands, and that human wisdom is limited. Then he shows God acting with power: He tears down, shuts up, and holds back the waters. Commentators debate how much of this is irony aimed at his friends, but the central point is clear: God rules over all.

For today: before making an important decision, ask God for direction with humility. Listen to wise counsel, but remember that the final word and the best guidance come from Him.
exp.11:13:
He tears down, and what he tears down cannot be rebuilt. He shuts a person in, and there is no way out. The idea is that God's power has no rival.

Job is speaking, answering his friend Zophar. His friends believed they knew how God works, but Job tells them that he too knows God's greatness. In this passage he describes God's power over nations, waters, and people. Some read it as a bitter complaint, others as a sincere confession of faith in the middle of pain.

For today: when a situation seems closed or lost, remember that God governs even what you do not understand. Bring him your confusion with humility, and trust that he knows when to open and when to shut at exactly the right moment.
exp.11:14:
It says that God controls the waters. If He holds them back, everything dries up; if He lets them loose, they flood and sweep across the land. The image shows that not even nature moves outside His command. The reference to holding back means that He restrains or keeps them in check.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering, answering his friends, who were giving him advice as if they knew everything. Job tells them that he too recognizes the power of God. But his point is that God does things that humans cannot explain or predict, such as tearing down, shutting in, drying up, or flooding. Some think Job speaks with a certain bitterness; others think he simply exalts the sovereignty of God.

Today we can remember that we do not control everything or understand everything that happens. Instead of offering easy explanations for another person's pain, we can walk alongside them with humility and trust in God, even when we do not understand.
exp.11:16:
He leads counselors away stripped of their wisdom, and makes the judges look like fools. The explanation of this phrase says that God can leave counselors without counsel, meaning without wisdom or good ideas, and that he makes the judges foolish, that is, he takes away their good judgment and confuses them. Being left stripped is an image of being plundered, with nothing left to cover them.

The speaker is Job, answering his friends, who offer explanations about God and his suffering. Job tells them that he too knows God is sovereign. In these verses he describes how God acts over nature and over rulers: he brings down wise people and powerful people alike. Some readers see sadness or irony in Job's words here; the exact tone is understood in different ways.

For today: human wisdom and authority are limited. If you hold a position or give advice, do it with humility, and ask God for his guidance, without trusting only in your own judgment.
exp.11:17:
God takes away the power of those who rule harshly. The word "bond" can refer to the authority or the yoke with which they govern. Then he binds them with a belt, as one would a servant or a captive. Some understand that God frees kings from their chains and then puts them to his service. Others see that he strips them of their power. Both readings are possible in the original text.

Job speaks, answering his friends, who were saying that God only punishes the wicked. Job replies that God is sovereign and acts over kings, judges, and princes, and that his work cannot always be explained by simple formulas.

Today: do not place your final trust in any leader, system, or human power. Pray for those who govern, and remember that they too answer to God. That gives you calm when the world seems unjust.
exp.11:21:
He brings deep things out of the darkness and reveals the shadow of death to the light. Nothing is so hidden that God cannot make it known.

Job speaks here in reply to his friends, who insisted they knew why he was suffering. Job answers that he too knows the power and wisdom of God. In the verses nearby he describes God as one who acts in surprising ways with kings, judges, and nations. Some read these words as praise, others as a note of complaint, since Job does not understand what God is doing.

For today: if there is something dark in your life, such as a doubt, a pain, or a mistake, do not hide from God. Bring it to him with confidence; he sees what is deep and knows how to bring it into the light with care.
exp.11:22:
This verse says that God makes the nations grow, and he can also destroy them. He scatters them across the earth and then gathers them together again.

Here Job is speaking, answering his friend Zophar and the others. Job acknowledges that God has wisdom and power over kings, judges, and whole peoples. But he says it with a certain irony: he too knows these things, and yet he suffers without understanding why. Interpreters disagree about how much of this is complaint and how much is worship.

For today: when the world seems confusing, remember that no government or power lasts forever without God. Trust in him, pray for your country, and do not place your final hope in human leaders.
exp.11:24:
They grope in the dark, as people who walk in complete darkness and see nothing. Groping means moving forward by touch, not knowing where they are going. The word "stagger" here means to stumble and lose their way, like a drunken man who cannot walk straight.

Job is speaking, answering his friends, who were saying that God only punishes the wicked. Job replies that God has power over nations and their rulers: he raises them up, brings them down, and takes away their understanding. Many readers see that Job is exalting God's sovereignty, though there is also a tone of complaint about how hard it is to understand his ways.

For today: do not rely only on your own intelligence or on human leaders. Ask God for light and direction each day, and walk in humility, knowing that without his guidance anyone can lose the way.
exp.12:0:
Job says that everything his friends have been talking about, he has already seen with his own eyes, and he has heard and understood it with his own ears.

Job is a man who suffers greatly and has lost everything. His friends Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar have given him long speeches saying that his pain comes from some hidden sin. Job answers them that he is not ignorant of what they say about God. That is why, in the verses that follow, he prefers to speak directly with God.

For today: when someone suffers, listening is worth more than giving quick explanations. And when we suffer, we can bring our questions and our pain directly to God with sincerity.
exp.12:8:
Job asks his friends whether it would go well for them if God examined them thoroughly. To search someone out means to investigate carefully, to look even into what is hidden in the heart. He also asks whether they would dare to mock God the way one person deceives another, that is, to treat him lightly.

Job speaks while he is suffering greatly. His friends insist that his pain is punishment for some sin, and they claim to be defending God, but they do so with false and one-sided arguments. Job warns them that God cannot be fooled by fine-sounding words, and that they themselves would be judged.

For today: before explaining someone's suffering or speaking for God, let us examine our own hearts. It is better to accompany others with humility and truth than to give easy answers that God may never have given.
exp.12:9:
He says God will surely rebuke you if, even in secret, you show favoritism toward someone for the sake of advantage. Hiding it, or doing it without being seen, makes no difference to him. To show favoritism is to lean toward someone because of who they are rather than what is right.

Job is speaking, and he is suffering greatly. His friends tell him that his pain is a punishment for some sin, and they defend God with arguments that Job considers false. Job warns them that by speaking this way to please God, they are actually being unjust, and God himself will judge them.

For today: God desires truth and justice, not words that only sound pious. Before giving an opinion about another person's suffering, it is wise to listen with humility, without judging or defending God with easy answers. He sees the intentions of the heart.
exp.12:12:
Job asks his friends to be quiet and let him speak. He says that he will speak, and then let whatever must happen come to him.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly and has lost everything. His friends insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin, and they even defend this as if they were defending God. Job warns them that God is not pleased by false arguments. He decides to speak honestly, even though that puts him at risk, and to trust in God.

For today: when you are in pain, you can speak to God honestly, without pretending or repeating pretty phrases. Tell Him sincerely what you feel and wait on Him, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.12:13:
Job asks: "Why should I bite my flesh with my own teeth and carry my life in the palm of my hand?" These are two old expressions. They are understood as a way of saying that he is willing to risk everything, even his life, in order to speak frankly before God. Scholars explain them in somewhat different ways, but the general idea is that one.
