The speaker is Job, who is suffering greatly. His friends tell him that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job does not agree. He asks them to listen to him, and he would rather present his case before God, even though it will cost him dearly. His courage comes from a trust that has not yet died out.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not pretend or keep silent. Speak to God with sincerity, even with your doubts and pains, trusting that he hears you and is just.
exp.12:15:
He also says that God himself will be Job's salvation, meaning his deliverance. The word "salvation" here means rescue, not merely good physical health. The second part gives the reason: a hypocrite, that is, someone who pretends to be devout but has a false heart, would not dare to come before God.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job disagrees and decides to bring his case directly before God. His confidence does not come from thinking himself perfect, but from knowing that his faith is sincere and that he has nothing to pretend before God.

For today: when you are going through a trial, you can come to God with complete honesty, with your questions and your pain, without masks. He prefers an honest heart to a religiosity that is only for show.
exp.12:19:
It says that Job asks God for only two things: that God not do them. If God takes them away, Job promises not to hide from His presence. The two requests appear in the following verse: that God take away His heavy hand and that He not terrify him with His dread.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends tell him that he suffers because of some hidden sin, but he feels innocent and wants to defend his cause directly before God, as in a trial. He demands nothing with pride; he seeks fair treatment so that he can speak with freedom. Some understand his tone as courage, others as presumption, and the book itself later shows that Job did not understand everything.

For today: you can be honest with God about your pain and your questions. He is not offended by an honest prayer, although you may have to grow in trust and humility.
exp.12:21:
Job says to God: "Call me, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you answer me." It is like asking God to choose how they will talk: that God asks and Job answers, or that Job asks and God responds. The word "or" in this line is written differently in the original, and that is the same sense of choice expressed here.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends tell him he suffers because of some sin, but he does not feel guilty. So he asks God to lift his heavy hand and his terror, so that he can present his case without fear. Then he asks what his wrongs are. Some understand this as sincere courage; others see it as a complaint that God later corrects.

We can speak with God honestly, even with questions and pain. Prayer is not pretending to be calm, but coming near with trust, also willing to listen to his answer.
exp.12:23:
Job asks God directly: "Why do you turn away from me and treat me as if I were your enemy?" Hiding the face means withdrawing one's closeness and favor. Job feels that God has become distant and hostile.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends insist that he is suffering for some hidden sin, but he cannot find anything he has done to deserve it. So he asks God to show him his fault, if there is one. It is the sincere cry of someone who feels God's silence. Later on, God does not rebuke him for speaking with such honesty.

When you feel that God is far away, you do not have to pretend or stay silent. You can bring your hardest questions to him with sincerity and respect, trusting that he listens even when he does not answer right away.
exp.12:25:
Here Job says to God: "Why do you write bitter things against me?" It is as if God were keeping a record with harsh judgments against him. Job feels that God is charging him even for the sins of his youth.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends say he suffers because of some hidden sin. Job does not understand his pain and feels treated as an enemy. He sees himself as weak, like a dry leaf. Note: this is Job's feeling, not necessarily the truth about God. At the end of the book, God himself corrects that view.

When you suffer, you can speak to God with complete honesty, even with painful questions. But do not conclude that God is punishing you for your past. In Christ there is true forgiveness (Colossians 2:14).
exp.12:26:
It says God puts his feet in the stocks, that is, a wooden device used to secure prisoners. It also watches all his steps and leaves a mark on the soles of his feet, as if he wanted to follow his trail.

Job speaks, a man who suffers greatly and feels that God treats him as an enemy. His friends tell him he suffers for some hidden sin. Job, in his pain, complains before God and sees himself as a weak leaf pursued without reason. This is his sincere complaint; it does not mean that God truly acts this way, and the book itself later shows that the situation was different.

Today, when suffering makes us feel trapped or abandoned, we can speak to God with frankness, as Job did, instead of staying silent or pretending. Honest prayer is also faith.
exp.12:27:
He says Job feels his body wearing away little by little. He compares it to wood eaten away by woodworm, an insect that wears it down from inside, and to a piece of clothing that the moth is destroying.

Job speaks in the middle of his great suffering. He addresses God and feels that God treats him like a man on trial: He watches him, puts his feet in the stocks (a wooden device that held the prisoner) and even holds against him the sins of his youth. Job does not understand why he suffers, and here he appears weak and fragile. Scholars understand in different ways whether this verse continues his complaint or begins a general reflection on human frailty.

For today: when you feel tired or without strength, you can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did. He hears you and does not turn away from you.
exp.13:3:
Verse 4 asks a question and answers it right away: who can bring something clean out of what is unclean? No one. The word "unclean" here means dirty, impure. Job is speaking about the human condition: we cannot produce purity from ourselves.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering, addressing God. He has just described the human being as a flower that is cut down and a shadow that passes away. He wonders why God fixes his gaze on someone so fragile and brings him to judgment. Some understand that Job points to an inherited human weakness, while others take him to be simply acknowledging our frailty and limitation.

Today we can humbly recognize that we are not able to make ourselves righteous by our own effort. Instead of pretending to strength, we can come to God with sincerity, asking for forgiveness and help, trusting in his mercy.
exp.13:6:
It says that a cut-down tree still has hope. Even if it is chopped down, it can sprout again, and its new shoots (the young new branches) do not come to an end. The word "will sprout again" means that it will put out new growth once more. Job uses the picture of a tree that seems dead but comes back to life when it feels water.

Job is speaking in the middle of enormous pain. He has just said that human life is short and that God has set its limits. He compares the tree with a human being: the tree grows back, but he cannot see how a person could do the same. It is a sincere complaint, and at the same time a longing for hope. Later Job wonders whether a man will live again.

For today: if you feel cut down by a loss or a failure, do not keep silent before God. Bring him your pain honestly, and seek the living water of his Word and of your community. God knows how to give new beginnings.
exp.13:10:
This verse uses an image from nature: the water of the sea goes away, and a river runs dry until it is empty. The comparison points ahead to the next verse: just as the water disappears, a human being also comes to an end.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly and speaks to God with honesty. Earlier he said that a cut tree may sprout again with water, but that a man dies and is no longer seen. Here Job expresses his pain and his little hope for that moment. Some understand the "sea" as a lake or a large body of water, not necessarily the ocean.

For today: if you are going through a season of pain or weariness, you can speak to God honestly, as Job did, without pretending to be strong. Tell Him what you feel; He listens.
exp.13:14:
He says that God will call Job, and Job will answer him. The word "desire" here means that God would have affection and longing for the work of his hands, that is, for the human being he created. Job imagines a day when God seeks him out with tenderness, and he responds.

Job speaks while suffering greatly and feeling that God has treated him harshly. In the verses before, he wishes to hide in the grave until God's anger passes, and he wonders whether a person who dies lives again. Here he expresses a hope: that God will not forget him forever. Then he complains again. Scholars debate how much certainty of resurrection is present here; it is more a longing than a confident belief.

For today: even when you feel that God is far away, you can remember that he made you and values you. Speak to him honestly, even with your doubts, and wait for his answer with patience.
exp.13:19:
It says that God is always stronger than a human being, and that a person cannot resist him. Job describes how God overcomes him and changes his face (the expression is distorted, perhaps by death or by pain) and sends him away, that is, dismisses him from this life so that he does not return. The word "change" here means to alter or transform his appearance.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering, answering his friends. He reflects on how fragile and brief life is, comparing it to mountains that crumble and stones that water wears away. His tone is bitter and honest; he expresses what he feels, although not everything he says is the final word about God. Some readers see complaint here, others see an acknowledgment of divine power.

For today: when you feel small or without hope, you can speak to God honestly, as Job did. Recognizing that our life is fragile invites us to trust in the One who remains faithful, even when we do not understand what is happening.
exp.14:0:
This verse only introduces the one who is about to speak. Eliphaz, the man from Teman, takes up the word again to answer Job. "Temanite" means that he came from Teman, a place associated with the region of Edom. The spelling "Eliphaz" is the older form of the name.

Job is suffering greatly. His three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, came to comfort him, but they ended up arguing with him. Here the second round of speeches begins. Eliphaz thinks Job's suffering is due to some sin, and so he speaks to him harshly. At the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

Before speaking, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are truly listening. When someone is suffering, they do not always need explanations or quick corrections. They need companionship, patience and wise words, spoken with humility and compassion.
exp.14:1:
Eliphaz asks whether a wise man would speak with empty ideas, as if he filled his belly with the east wind. That wind was the wind from the east, hot and dry, which in Palestine scorched the plants and brought nothing good. A wise man of real substance does not speak with hollow and harmful words.

Eliphaz is one of Job's three friends. Here he begins his second speech. He is upset because Job has defended himself forcefully, and he accuses him of speaking without sense. Yet later God says that these friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so his criticism is not entirely fair.

For today: before we speak, especially when we are angry, it is good to think about whether our words help or merely make noise. And let us also take care not to judge harshly someone who is suffering.
exp.14:4:
It says that what Job speaks reveals what is in his heart. "Iniquity" here means guilt or wickedness. "The crafty" are people skilled at twisting words to justify themselves. Eliphaz maintains that Job chose this way of speaking, and that for this reason his own words accuse him.

The speaker is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's three friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for some hidden sin, so he interprets Job's complaints as arrogance. However, the book itself shows that Eliphaz is mistaken in this judgment: God will say later that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). For this reason this verse is a human accusation, not a verdict from God.

For today: before you speak, check whether your words seek the truth or only defend yourself. And when someone is suffering, listen to them with patience, without rushing to accuse them.
exp.14:5:
Job's own words, he says, are the evidence against him. Eliphaz claims there is no need for him to accuse Job, because what Job says with his mouth and lips already declares him guilty. "Condemn" here means to declare guilty.

The speaker is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job's suffering is punishment for some hidden sin. He is upset because Job defends his innocence and questions how God is treating him. For this reason he calls Job crafty and proud. However, at the end of the book God says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so his accusation is not a reliable guide.

For today: our words reveal what is in the heart, so it is wise to speak carefully, especially in pain. But let us also avoid judging harshly someone who is suffering, as Eliphaz did.
exp.14:6:
Elifaz asks Job, with irony, whether he was the first man ever born, or whether he existed before the hills. The question is not meant to be answered yes; it is meant to mock Job.

Elifaz is one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he is irritated that Job insists on his innocence. So he accuses Job of speaking as if he had a superior, ancient, and secret wisdom. Some think he means a wisdom that existed before all of humanity. The text does not fully explain this, but the sarcastic tone is clear.

For today: even when we are right about something, we should speak with humility and not use irony to hurt. And when someone is suffering, let us listen and walk alongside them before we judge. Only God knows everything.
exp.14:8:
Eliphaz asks Job what special knowledge he has that the others lack. It is a challenging question: "What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not also in us?" With it, he hints that Job thinks himself wiser than everyone.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. Job is suffering greatly, and Eliphaz accuses him of speaking with pride and of despising the wisdom of the elders. Note this: although Eliphaz says some things that are true, God later says that he and his friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). His harsh tone does not reflect the heart of God.

For today: let us learn to listen to others with humility, without thinking ourselves the owners of the truth. But let us also avoid using wisdom to judge someone who is suffering. In the face of another's pain, it is better to accompany with kindness than to correct with harshness.
exp.14:9:
It says that among Job's friends there are people with gray hair, elders, and even some who are older than Job's father. A man with white hair is one who is gray-headed, and someone who is very far along in years is one who is very aged.

It is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's three friends, who is speaking. He is upset because Job defends his innocence and does not accept his explanations. Eliphaz appeals to the experience of the older men to say that Job does not have a wisdom greater than theirs. Exactly whom he means by the elder is not made clear; some think he includes himself.

Today: age and experience have value, but they do not replace listening with humility. Eliphaz uses his authority to silence a man who is suffering. Before advising someone who is suffering, listen with kindness and do not rely only on your own experience.
exp.14:11:
What it says: Eliphaz asks Job why his heart carries him away, as if he were losing control, and why his eyes flash.

Context: The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, in his second speech. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin and that his complaints against God are pride. He relies on his age and on the wisdom of the elders. However, God will later say that Eliphaz did not speak correctly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: When someone is suffering, let us avoid judging their heart or their gestures. Before correcting, let us listen with patience and compassion. And when we are hurting, let us bring our emotions honestly to God.
exp.14:20:
He says the wicked person lives with constant fear. Even in the midst of calm, he hears noises that terrify him. The phrase about dreadful sounds refers to frightening sounds that bring terror. The word for ruin means to destroy or lay waste, so the destroyer who comes upon him is one who falls on him just when he felt secure.

The speaker is Eliphaz the Temanite, a friend of Job. He describes what, in his view, always happens to the wicked: they suffer inwardly and have no rest. But notice that Eliphaz implies Job suffers because he is wicked, and the book itself shows that this judgment was mistaken. God himself corrects Eliphaz at the end.

For today: true peace does not depend on everything going well or on trusting in our own strength. A clear conscience and trust in God bring calm. And let us be careful not to judge those who suffer, as if their pain were always punishment.
exp.14:21:
He does not believe that he will return out of darkness, and he is waited for by the sword.

Darkness refers to misfortune, distress, or ruin. The sword is a violent death. He lives with the constant fear that something like this will overtake him.

Elifaz, one of Job's friends, speaks in his second speech. He believes that suffering is always punishment for wickedness, and so he describes how the wicked person lives, to hint that Job is in that condition. His description has some truth to it, but the Bible later shows that it did not apply to Job (Job 42:7).

For today: a life without God can bring deep restlessness, but let us not judge someone who suffers as if they were guilty. Let us accompany them with humility and compassion, and turn to God with confidence when we feel fear.
exp.14:24:
He says this man stretched out his hand against God, that is, he openly challenged him. The phrase "strengtheneth himself against the Almighty" means he acted with stubbornness and pride, like someone who wants to fight against God. The word "for" explains the reason for what was said before: his distress comes from that rebellion.

Eliphaz, Job's friend, speaks in his second speech. He describes how he believes the wicked man ends: with fear and ruin. The problem is that Eliphaz takes for granted that Job suffers because he is rebellious, and the book shows that this conclusion was mistaken. His general description may be true, but applied to Job it is unjust.

For today: let us not challenge God with pride, but neither should we judge others by saying their pain is punishment. Better to draw near to God with humility and to accompany those who suffer with compassion.
exp.14:32:
He says the wicked person will lose his fruit before its time, like a vine that drops its grapes while still green, or an olive tree that lets its blossoms fall. The unripe grapes are the ones not yet ready, still green. In this way, that person will not live to see the fruit of his life; everything he hoped for will be left unfinished.

Eliphaz, Job's friend, is speaking in his second speech. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he describes the fate of the wicked, suggesting that Job is in that situation. But note this: at the end of the book, God says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). His description works as a general idea, but it is applied wrongly to Job.

For today: do not measure anyone's life, including your own, by their losses, as if every pain were punishment. Instead, take care of what you sow: honesty bears fruit that lasts, and deceit ends empty.
exp.15:0:
This verse is a simple introduction. It says that Job takes up the word and begins to speak. "Answered" does not mean that someone had asked him a new question, but that he replies to what his friend Eliphaz has just said in the previous chapter.

The one speaking is Job, a man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His three friends came to comfort him, but now they accuse him, suggesting that his suffering is punishment for some sin. Job responds with pain and frankness, and in the verses that follow he tells them that their comfort is troubling to him.

For today: before speaking with someone who is suffering, let us listen carefully. Sometimes the best help is not to give explanations but to accompany with humility, and we too can, like Job, express our pain honestly before God.
exp.15:9:
They opened their mouths wide against Job to speak to him with mockery and scorn. The phrase about being struck on the cheek with insult speaks of blows or slaps meant to humiliate him, though it can also be understood as insults that hurt just as much. Finally, the words about all of them joining together mean that many came together against him.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends, instead of comforting him, accuse him of having sinned. Job feels attacked by everyone and feels that even God seems to be against him. Scholars understand that he is describing his pain in a very intense way, as in a lament.

For today: when someone suffers, they need companionship and not judgment. If you are going through a moment like this, you can speak to God with sincerity, as Job did. And if you see someone who is hurting, treat them with tenderness and listen before you give your opinion.
exp.15:14:
Here Job says he sewed rough cloth, made of hair or sackcloth, directly onto his skin, and that he put dust on his head. The garment itself is the coarse cloth worn as a sign of mourning. Sewing it on means he did so firmly, as someone who has no intention of taking it off soon.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He feels that God attacks him like a warrior and, on top of that, his friends accuse him of having sinned. So he expresses his pain with signs of mourning typical of his time. He insists that his hands are free of wrongdoing and that his prayer was sincere.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, do not disguise it or pretend to be strong. You can bring your honest sadness before God, as Job did, and look for someone who will listen to you without judging you.
exp.15:15:
Here Job says that his face is red and swollen from so much weeping. His eyes are ringed with deep, dark shadows, the sign of sleepless nights and worn-out grief.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his property, and his health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. In this chapter he answers Eliphaz and feels that God himself is attacking him. Even so, in the next verse he insists that his hands are free of wickedness and that his prayer has been sincere.

For today: you do not have to hide your pain or pretend to be strong before God. You can weep honestly, as Job did, and keep praying even when you do not understand what is happening. God is not shocked by your tears.
exp.15:19:
Job's friends have turned into his critics. Instead of comforting him, they argue with him and treat his pain as if it were a failing. So Job lifts his eyes to God and pours out his tears before Him.

Job speaks out of a life that has lost nearly everything and an illness that wears him down. His friends are sure that his suffering is punishment for some hidden sin. Job insists that he is innocent. Feeling misunderstood, he calls on God as his witness in heaven, even though he cannot make sense of what God allows.

When the people close to us do not know how to comfort us, we can bring our tears to God honestly. And when we walk beside someone who is suffering, it is better to listen with tenderness than to argue or hunt for someone to blame.
exp.16:6:
Job says that his eyes have clouded over, so that he can hardly see, because of pain and bitterness. The word for his state of mind here refers to a very deep sorrow, a heaviness of the soul. In addition, all his thoughts have become like a shadow: thin, without strength, like something that is fading away.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He feels that God has made him an example of mockery before the people. Even so, in the verses that follow he acknowledges that the upright will be astonished, and that the righteous will keep to his way.

For today: when pain clouds your sight and your thoughts, do not pretend that you are fine. You can tell God honestly how you feel, as Job did, and keep taking one step at a time, trusting that He sustains you.
exp.16:7:
Upright people will be astonished at Job's suffering and at the injustice that surrounds him. The innocent will rise up, that is, become indignant and react, against the hypocrite, the one who appears devout but is not. Being astonished means being surprised or deeply struck.

Job speaks, aching and almost without strength. His friends tell him he suffers because of some hidden sin, and he feels mocked, treated as a byword for misfortune and as someone others make fun of. Interpreters understand this in different ways: some see a hope that the righteous will defend the truth; others see a lament over the lack of understanding.

Today, when we face the suffering of others, let us avoid judging in haste. Rather, let us listen, accompany, and defend what is right with humility, without pretending to a faith we do not live.
exp.16:12:
If Job still hopes for anything, the only thing he sees ahead is the grave. He speaks of the tomb as if it were his house, and of the darkness as the bed where he will lie down. The grave is the place of burial; "darkness" here refers to the dark of death.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends accuse him and make him feel more alone. At this point he is exhausted and feels that his days are running out. His words are an honest outpouring, not a doctrine to copy. The verses that follow show that he himself wonders where his hope has gone.

For today: when you feel weak and see no way out, you do not have to disguise your pain. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did. And look for someone you trust to walk with you, rather than facing the darkness alone.
exp.17:7:
He says that the wicked person will be caught in a net that they themselves step on without realizing it. The phrase about being caught by one's own feet means that the trap falls on the very steps they take, and the phrase about walking upon a snare means that moving forward across ground full of traps, where any step can entangle them.

Bildad, Job's friend, speaks here in his second speech. He holds that the wicked always fall because of their own bad choices, and he says this while hinting that Job suffers because of some sin. Later on, God shows that this conclusion was mistaken: Job was not suffering because he was wicked. So the principle has some truth in it, but Bildad applies it wrongly.

For today: when someone insists on deceit or injustice, sooner or later they become tangled in it. But let us be careful not to judge others by their pain, as Bildad did. It is better to accompany them with compassion and to examine our own path.
exp.17:11:
He says the wicked person will be left without strength, like someone who is hungry and weak. The idea is that disaster is already waiting at his side, ready to fall on him.

The one speaking is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. In this chapter he describes how the wicked person ends up, with traps and terrors on every side. But notice this: Bildad believes all suffering comes from wickedness, and so he suggests that Job is guilty. At the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: do not use these words to judge someone who is suffering. Pain is not always punishment. Instead, accompany with tenderness, listen, and pray, and examine your own heart with humility.
exp.17:13:
The explanation says that the wicked person's security will be taken away suddenly. "His tent" refers to his home, the place where he felt protected. The phrase about it being brought to the king of terrors is an image of death, seen as a monarch who causes terror.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He describes what, in his view, always happens to the wicked. His idea is that suffering comes only because of wickedness, and so he implies that Job is guilty. The book itself shows that this conclusion was mistaken.

For today: let us not place our trust in money, success, or health, because all of these can disappear. And let us be careful not to judge those who suffer, as Bildad did. Let us rest more firmly in God, who sustains the one who trusts in Him.
exp.17:14:
This verse says that the wicked person will live in his own home as a stranger, as if it no longer belongs to him. The "tent" is his dwelling, and "dwell" means that he will live there. The sulfur scattered over his home is an image of destruction and judgment, like a cursed and desolate place.

Here Bildad speaks, one of Job's three friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and he describes the fate of the wicked to suggest that Job deserves it. But at the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so their words should not be taken as a general rule.

For today: let us be careful not to judge another person's pain as God's punishment. Instead, let us walk alongside those who suffer with compassion, listening and prayer, without accusing them.
exp.17:15:
This verse uses the image of a tree. If the roots below dry up and the branches above are cut off, the tree is left without life and without a future. In this way the passage describes a person whose life comes to a complete end: they have no hidden support and no visible fruit.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's friends. In this speech he describes what, in his view, happens to the wicked. His words sound harsh because he wants to suggest that Job is suffering for some sin. But the book shows that Bildad is wrong to apply this idea to Job, since God himself recognizes him as a man of integrity.

For today: let us take care of our roots, that is, our life with God in what is hidden. And let us not judge others by their suffering, as Bildad did.
exp.18:7:
Job says that God has fenced in his way, like a wall or a hedge, so that he can no longer move forward. Furthermore, he feels that God has set darkness over his paths, the trails where he walks, so that he cannot see the direction he should take.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends tell him that he suffers because of some hidden sin, but he defends himself. Here he describes what he feels, not necessarily the whole truth about God. At the end of the book, God himself corrects the way both Job and his friends spoke.

For today: when you feel there is no way out and no light, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did, and seek out someone you trust to accompany you while you wait.
exp.18:9:
He has torn me down on every side, until I am finished. He is describing a man who feels that God has broken him down on every side, the way a house is pulled apart until only ruins are left. He says he is being used up, that he is coming to an end. He also compares his hope to a tree pulled up by the roots: it no longer has anything to hold it or any way to grow again.

Job speaks here, a man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends tell him he is suffering because of some sin, but he defends himself and feels that God is his adversary. In the middle of his anguish he describes his pain with strong images. This is how things look to him in the midst of distress, and the book shows that his view was not complete.

When you feel that your hope has been uprooted, you can be honest with God, as Job was. You do not have to pretend to be strong. Tell Him how you feel, and seek the support of people who will stand with you without judging you.
exp.18:15:
The passage says that Job called his servant, that is, a worker in his household, and the servant did not answer him. Job even pleaded with his own voice, speaking to him humbly.

Job is a man who lost everything: his possessions, his children, and his health. In this chapter he complains that relatives, friends, and even the people in his own household reject him. He used to be a respected man with authority over his servants; now he must beg them, and even then they do not attend to him. It is part of his pain from feeling lonely and humiliated.

For today: if someone is suffering, let us not leave them alone. A visit, a phone call, or a kind word can bring relief. And if you feel ignored, remember that you can speak to God with sincerity, as Job did.
exp.18:17:
Job says that even the little children, who normally show respect to their elders, mocked him. Every time he stood up, they spoke against him.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends tell him he is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he complains that his family, his servants, and now even the young people reject him. Some understand the young people as children and others as youths without respect; in either case, the verse shows his humiliation.

For today: if someone goes through a trial and people look down on him, we should not join in the mockery. We can approach him with respect, listen, and offer companionship. And if you are the one who is suffering, you can tell God your pain with sincerity, as Job did.
exp.18:19:
Job says that his bone clings to his skin and to his flesh, meaning that he is thin, worn down by suffering. "Skin" here refers to the outer covering of the body. Then he says he has escaped with only the skin of his teeth, a very unusual expression. It is understood to mean that he barely has any life left, almost nothing, as if only his gums remained. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: health, children, and possessions. He is sick, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. In this passage he describes his pain and his loneliness, since even the children and his close companions reject him. He asks for compassion.

For today: when someone suffers, there is no need to explain to them why. Simply accompany them with patience and tenderness. And if you are suffering, you can be honest with God about your pain, as Job was.
exp.18:23:
Job wants his words to be engraved forever. He asks that they be carved into stone with an iron pen, and that lead be used to fill the letters so they stand out more clearly. In other words, he wants his testimony to be kept from being erased or forgotten as time passes.

Job speaks as one who suffers greatly and feels attacked by his friends, who accuse him of having sinned. He insists he is innocent and feels that no one believes him. For that reason he wants to leave a lasting record of what he says. Right after this, he declares his confidence that his Redeemer lives. Some understand this as a hope that God will vindicate him; others see a hope of resurrection.

For today: when you feel misunderstood, do not keep your pain to yourself alone. Speak with God honestly, and lean on the hope that he lives and knows you.
exp.18:28:
Job warns his friends to be afraid of the sword, that is, of God's punishment. He says the sword reaches those who do evil, so that they will know God does judge.

Job speaks as a man who suffers greatly and is wounded by the accusations of his friends. They treat his pain as if it were punishment for some hidden sin. Job has just declared his confidence that he will see God, and now he warns them that they themselves should take care, because they are judging him unjustly. Some understand this as a serious warning; the text does not give more detail.

For today: before explaining someone's suffering, or criticizing it, approach them with humility and compassion. God is the judge, and we do not see the whole heart of another person.
exp.19:0:
This verse only introduces the one who is about to speak. Zophar the Naamathite takes up the word to answer Job. "Naamathite" probably indicates that he came from a place called Naamah, though it is not known for certain where that was.

Zophar is one of the three friends who came to comfort Job after his great suffering. Here his second speech begins. In the verses that follow it is clear that he is upset, because he feels that Job has corrected or offended him with his words. He speaks hastily and with great confidence, although the book later shows that his conclusions were not correct.

For today: before answering someone who is suffering, it is wise to listen calmly and not rush ahead out of pride or anger. A word spoken in haste can wound, while patience and compassion can truly help.
exp.19:2:
Sophar says he heard a rebuke that felt like an insult to him, a reproach that puts him to shame. So his spirit, that is, his understanding and his inner feelings, pushes him to answer. In other words: "I heard a correction that wounded me, and my mind will not let me stay silent."

Zophar is one of Job's three friends. Job had just defended himself and questioned their accusations. Zophar feels insulted and answers quickly and angrily. He then claims that the wicked always end badly, implying that Job suffers because of his sins. The Bible later shows that Zophar was wrong about Job (Job 42:7).

For today: when something bothers us or wounds our pride, it is wise to wait before answering. Praying and listening with humility keeps us from speaking harshly or judging without knowing the whole story.
exp.19:6:
This verse says that the wicked person, though he may look great, will vanish completely. "Dung" is a strong way of speaking of something despised, and "perish" means that he will come to an end. Those who knew him will ask in amazement, "Where is he?" His life, which seemed so firm, leaves nothing lasting behind.

It is Zophar speaking, one of Job's three friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he hints that Job is a hypocrite. But the book shows that Zophar is wrong to apply this idea to Job, although some of his words about the fall of pride sound true in other places in the Bible.

For today: do not trust in success, power, or fame, because all of that passes away. Seek instead an honest life before God. And avoid judging the one who suffers, for we do not always know his reasons.
exp.19:8:
He says the wicked person will vanish so completely that those who knew him will never see him again. Nor will his place, his house, or his position remember him or miss him.

Zophar, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. He believes that the wicked always fall quickly and that their prosperity does not last long. With this he hints that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. However, the book shows that Zophar is wrong to apply this to Job, since God himself says that his friends did not speak rightly about him.

Today we can remember that power and riches pass away, and that it is not wise to measure a person, or their suffering, only by what we see. Let us seek a life that has worth before God, and avoid judging others in haste.
exp.19:10:
It says that the bones of the wicked, which should have the strength of his youth, are full of the sins of his youth, that is, the wrongs and passions of his younger years. Those same sins will go with him to the grave, for he will be buried together with them in the dust.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, speaks in his second speech. He believes that the wicked always fall soon and that Job suffers because of some hidden sin. He describes the downfall of the wicked in detail. But the book shows that Zophar is wrong to apply this to Job, since God himself says that Job was blameless.

For today: the habits we feed from a young age put down deep roots. Today you can hand over to God a harmful habit and ask him for help to leave it, instead of letting it stay with you your whole life.
exp.19:22:
He says that just as the wicked man is about to be satisfied, God sends the heat of his anger upon him. That wrath rains down on him even while he is eating.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He holds that the wicked always come to a bad end, and he suggests that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. That idea was not right in Job's case, and in the end God rebukes the friends for not speaking rightly about Him. Even so, Zophar states something true: injustice and greed do not go unanswered.

For today: do not use this text to judge someone who is suffering, as Zophar did. Use it to examine your own heart. Ask yourself whether ambition is pushing you to always want more, and ask God to teach you to live with gratitude and justice.
exp.19:24:
It says that God's judgment is like a warrior who draws an arrow from his quiver (the case where arrows are kept). The bright arrow pierces the wicked man through to his inner parts, the bitter fluid of the body, an organ that symbolizes what is most inward in a person. In the end, terror falls upon him, a dread that overwhelms him.

Zophar speaks, one of Job's three friends. He insists that every wicked person comes to a bad end and that his prosperity does not last long. With this he implies that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. At the end, God will say that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: do not use the suffering of others to accuse anyone. God is just, but we do not always know why someone suffers. Accompany others with compassion, and examine your own heart with humility.
exp.20:11:
It says that the children of the wicked amuse themselves with music: they dance and rejoice to the sound of the tambourine (a small hand drum), the lyre (a stringed instrument something like a harp), and the pipe (here not a church organ, but a wind instrument such as a flute). It is a picture of festivity and a life without worries.

Job is speaking, answering his friends. They claimed that the wicked always suffer soon. Job answers with what he sees: some who ignore God prosper, have happy families, and live at ease. He does not say this is right, but that life is more complicated than his friends claim. Later on, Job also reminds us that their end will come.

For today: do not judge people, or yourself, only by prosperity or suffering. When you see others doing well without God, do not grow bitter or envy them. Trust that God sees everything and that He has the final word.
exp.20:15:
It says that the prosperity of the wicked is not in their own hands, meaning they do not control it or produce it themselves. Job also distances himself from their way of thinking: "the counsel of the wicked is far from me." The "wicked" are those who live without respect for God.

Job speaks here, answering his friends. They claimed that wicked people always end up suffering. Job observes that many wicked people prosper, even though they reject God. Some interpreters read this verse as Job's criticism of that prosperity. Others see it as a clarification: even though they prosper, he does not share their way of thinking.

For today: do not measure the right path by visible success. Even when someone seems to triumph without God, seek his wisdom and do not follow their advice. Everything good comes from God.
exp.20:24:
It says there is another person who dies with a soul full of bitterness, never having enjoyed food or life. This is the contrast with the man before, who died prosperous and at peace.

Job speaks here, answering his friends, who insist that God always punishes the wicked and rewards the good. Job answers them with reality: some die in abundance and others in suffering, and this does not always follow from their conduct. In the end, he says, both finish the same way in the dust.

For today: do not judge anyone's life by their comfort or their pain. If you are suffering, do not assume that God has rejected you. And if you see others suffering, come alongside them with compassion instead of offering easy explanations.
exp.20:25:
It says that, no matter how each person lived, rich or poor, content or bitter, everyone ends the same way: stretched out in the earth and covered with worms. The first sentence about lying down is simply saying they will be lying down. The word "dust" speaks of the grave.

Job is speaking in reply to his friends, who insisted that God always punishes the wicked with visible misfortune. Job shows them that real life does not always work that way: some wicked people prosper, others suffer, and death comes to all. For that reason he rejects their simple explanations about his pain.

For today: do not judge anyone by what you see, because neither their success nor their suffering proves what is in their heart. Remember that life is brief, and live with humility, trusting in God, who sees everything with justice.
exp.20:26:
Job tells his friends that he knows what they are thinking about him. "I know your thoughts" means that he can see their intentions. The schemes they are cooking up are the ideas and accusations they invent in their minds to attack him.

Job is speaking in reply to Zophar and his other friends. They insist that suffering is always punishment for sin. Job has said that sometimes the wicked prosper and that the good and the bad die alike. Here he warns that he understands the hidden argument: they consider him guilty and want to prove it. The verses that follow confirm this.

Today this invites us not to judge those who suffer or to assume that their pain is punishment. Before offering easy explanations, we can listen, accompany, and comfort. God looks at the heart, and we do not see the whole story.
exp.20:31:
He says that the wicked person, after living without anyone confronting him, will be carried to the grave with honor. The word "tomb" in the verse may refer to a raised mound or elevated sepulchre. Some translators understand that someone keeps watch over his tomb, but the exact meaning of the original is not entirely certain.

Job is speaking, answering his friends. They claimed that the wicked always suffer in this life, and that for this reason Job was suffering because of his sin. Job answers them with what he sees: sometimes the wicked prosper, die in peace, and are honored. For this reason their comforts seem empty to him.

For today: do not measure people, or yourself, only by visible success or suffering. Final justice belongs to God, and it is not always seen here. And when you comfort someone who is suffering, listen with humility instead of giving them easy explanations.
exp.21:6:
This verse says that Job did not give water to the exhausted person and refused bread to the one who was hungry. The phrase about withholding bread means that Job kept back what he had, that he did not want to share it, even though he had it.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for some sin, so he accuses Job of serious wrongs, such as oppressing the poor, the widows, and the orphans. The book itself presents Job as an upright man, so these accusations seem unjust and unsupported by evidence.

For today: do not refuse simple help to someone who needs it, such as food, water, or companionship. And also, before judging someone who is suffering, it is better to listen to them with humility, as Job's friends did not.
exp.21:12:
It says that someone thinks or claims: "What does God know? How can he judge if there is darkness?" It is a question full of doubt, as if God were so far away or so much in the dark that he could not see what we do. Here "judge" means making fair decisions about people's actions.

Elifaz, one of Job's friends, is the speaker. He is accusing Job of thinking this way and of living wrongly, although the book shows that the accusation was not fair. Elifaz uses the greatness of the heavens and the stars to say that God is very high. But he reaches a wrong conclusion, since he assumes that because God is high, he cannot see.

For today: when you feel that God does not see your pain or your decisions, remember that his greatness does not put him far from you. Pray with sincerity, and be careful about accusing others without knowing their hearts.
exp.21:13:
He says the clouds are like a hiding place or shelter for God: by this reasoning, they block his view, and so he does not see what happens on earth. Meanwhile, he only walks through the circuit of heaven, far away from us.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He is accusing Job of thinking this way, even though Job never said it. Eliphaz attributes ideas to Job in order to argue that Job is a hidden sinner. That is why God later says that these friends did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7).

For today: let us not think that God is distant or blind to what we go through. Nor should we use harsh words to judge the pain of others. Let us approach those who suffer with humility, listening more and accusing less.
exp.21:15:
They were taken away before their time, and the ground they stood on was swept away by a flood. He says those wicked men died suddenly, before their time. Their foundation, that is, what held up their lives and their plans, collapsed as if a river had overflowed and carried everything away.

Elihu is not in this passage; it is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, who speaks. He believes Job suffers because of his wickedness, and he warns him not to follow the path of the wicked of the past. According to Eliphaz, they thought God did not see them and told Him to leave them alone, even though He had filled their houses with good things. Note that the book shows Eliphaz is wrong to judge Job.

For today: do not build your life only on success or on the things you own, because these can fall quickly. Thank God for what He gives you and lean on Him. And do not judge the suffering of others as if it were always punishment.
exp.21:17:
He says that God had filled the houses of those wicked men with good things. The word "filled" means filled completely. Even so, the speaker sets himself apart from their way of thinking: "the counsel of the wicked is far from me," that is, he does not want to follow their ideas or their way of life.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He is accusing Job of being like the wicked people of the past, who told God to leave them alone even though He had blessed them. Note that Eliphaz is wrong to judge Job, and at the end of the book God corrects him. Even so, this verse shows a truth: blessings should not draw us away from God.

Today, when we have abundance, let us remember that it comes from God. Let us give thanks instead of becoming self-sufficient, and let us flee from counsel that urges us to live without Him.
exp.22:1:
Job says that today too his complaint is bitter. His pain is stronger than his groaning: however much he moans, he cannot express all that he suffers.

Job speaks, a man who has lost everything and suffers greatly. He is answering his friends, and in this case Eliphaz, who accused him of having sinned. Job feels misunderstood and wishes to present himself before God to lay out his case.

For today: when your pain is greater than your words, do not hide it. You can speak with God honestly, even with sadness or complaint. The Bible shows that God does not reject the one who suffers and speaks to him with an open heart.
exp.22:2:
Job says he wishes he knew where to find God. "Find" means to locate, and "seat" is his throne, the place from which God rules and judges. Job is willing to go all the way there to stand before Him.

Job speaks as a man who suffers terribly, and whose friends insist that his pain is punishment for some sin. He feels wounded and weary, and so he speaks with bitterness. He feels that God is far away and wants to lay out his case before Him, as in a trial, and hear His answer. Some readers see here a complaint; others, a faith that keeps searching for God in the middle of pain.

When suffering makes you feel that God is far away, you do not have to pretend strength. You can bring Him your questions and your pain with honesty, trusting that He listens.
exp.22:7:
Job says he searches for God in every direction and cannot find him. He goes toward the east, where the sun rises, and does not find him; he goes toward the west, where the sun sets, and does not notice him, that is, he cannot make him out or tell that he is there.

Job speaks as a man who suffers greatly without understanding why. His friends tell him he suffers because of his sin, but he wants to bring his case before God and be heard with justice. He feels that God is absent and silent. Yet in verse 10 he says that God knows his way and that he will come out like gold that has been tested.

For today: when you feel that God is far away and you receive no answers, do not be afraid or believe that he has abandoned you. Be honest with him in prayer, as Job was, and hold on to the truth that he sees your path even when you cannot see him.
exp.22:15:
He says that God has left Job's heart without strength and without courage, and that the Almighty has filled him with dread.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and his friends tell him he suffers because of his sin. Job knows he is innocent, but he does not understand God. He wants to make his case before Him, and yet he feels fear of His power. This is an honest outpouring, not a teaching about what God is like. Later on, God Himself hears him and answers him.

When pain leaves you weak and confused, do not pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, even without understanding everything, and keep seeking Him.
exp.23:0:
God, the Almighty, knows all times, that is, he knows when each thing happens. Then Job asks: if God knows everything, why do those who know him and trust in him not see "his days"? These "days" are understood as the day when God steps in and brings about justice. Some translators understand it this way; the Hebrew allows for nuances.

Job speaks in the middle of his debate with his friends. They say that the wicked always end up in trouble. Job responds with an honest complaint: he sees that the abuses continue, as the following verses show, where orphans and widows are robbed, and God seems slow to act.

For today: if you see injustice and feel that God is taking his time, you can tell him so honestly, as Job did. While you wait, do not stay silent: help those who suffer, and trust that God does see and will bring about justice in his own time.
exp.23:2:
It says there are wicked people who take what little the weakest have. The donkey and the ox were the means of work and livelihood for orphans and widows, who had no one to defend them.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He asks why God allows the wicked to keep doing harm, and why those who trust in God do not soon see his justice. Job does not offer a solution yet; he voices his complaint honestly. Job's friends used to say that bad things happen to wicked people right away, but he observes that this is not always so.

For today: God looks out for the vulnerable, and we should too. We can help a widow, an orphan, or a lonely person with something concrete, such as work, shopping, or standing up for their rights, and avoid taking advantage of someone who cannot respond.
exp.23:3:
They push the needy off the road: the poor of the land hide themselves out of fear. The wicked, he says, shove aside those who have nothing, and the poor of the country hide away so they will not be mistreated.

It is Job speaking, in the middle of his debate with his friends. They say that bad people suffer and good people prosper. Job answers that this does not always look that way: many times the unjust take advantage of the weak, and it seems nothing happens to them. So Job calls God to account, although he does not have all the answers.

For today: open your eyes to those who live in fear or are ignored, such as immigrants, the elderly, and workers who are underpaid. You can stand up for someone, pay what is fair, or support a work that helps the vulnerable, trusting that God sees the injustice.
exp.23:5:
They go out into the field and reap what they did not sow, and they gather the grapes of a vineyard that is not theirs. Gathering the grapes is cutting the fruit from the vine. The phrase about reaping their neighbor's pasture is hard to render; it may mean they harvest forage or grain that belongs to someone else, and some understand that they force others to work for them.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends said that God punishes the wicked right away. Job answers with what he sees: there are unjust people who take advantage of the poor and seem to get away with it. In this way he voices his complaint and his longing for God to act.

Today, this verse invites us not to profit from the work of others: to pay what is fair, to keep what we have promised, and to defend those who have no voice. And if we see injustice, we can trust that God sees it, even when he seems slow to act.
exp.23:8:
They pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor. The explanation says that there are unjust people who snatch the fatherless child from the breast. That is, they take an orphan baby away from the mother who nurses it, or they take the child as a slave or as security for a debt. Moreover, from the poor they take the pledge, which was an object, often clothing or a cloak, that someone left as security for a loan. In this way they take advantage of the weakest.

Job speaks in the middle of his dialogue with his friends. He complains that God seems not to punish the wicked quickly, while the poor suffer. Some understand that Job describes the injustice of the world; others, that he complains to God about his silence. The text does not resolve this here.

For today: open your eyes to the vulnerable. You can support a needy family, pay a fair wage, or refrain from abusing those who depend on you.
exp.23:9:
It says that the poor are left to walk about naked, without clothing, and that the hungry, who carry the sheaves of grain, are robbed of what they harvest. In other words, they work in someone else's field, but they are not allowed to eat any of what they gather.

Job speaks here, answering his friends, who said that wicked people always come to a bad end. Job points out that in real life many people abuse the weak, and it seems that nothing happens to them. Here he describes the injustice bluntly and asks why God does not step in (v. 12). Interpreters read this passage as a sincere complaint, not as a final explanation.

For today: do not stay silent in the face of injustice. Pay a fair wage, share your food or clothing, and support those who stand up for poor workers.
exp.23:13:
This verse describes a murderer who rises early, at first light, to kill the poor and the needy. When night comes, he acts like a thief.

Job speaks here in the middle of his debate with his friends. They maintained that God quickly punishes the wicked, but Job replies that often the unjust seem to go free while the weak suffer. His complaint is honest: God does not seem to intervene. Some scholars read the passage as a lament and others as a description of human wickedness; in either case, Job asks why God delays in acting.

For today: do not close your eyes to injustice against the poor. Pray with sincerity, even with questions, and do something concrete: support someone who is suffering, help a person in need, or defend the one who has no voice.
exp.23:16:
It says that for wrongdoers, the morning brings fear and not joy. For them the light of day is like the shadow of death, a dreadful darkness. If someone recognizes them, they are seized with deep terrors, because they fear being discovered.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. He is describing how the unjust, like the adulterer and the thief, take advantage of the night to sin and flee from the light. Job complains that God seems to allow them to act, although some understand that he is also describing their final downfall. Interpreters debate the exact tone of this section of the book.

For today: if there is something you could only do in secret, that is a sign you should stop. Live in such a way that you do not fear the light. If you have already failed, come to God with sincerity; in Christ there is forgiveness and peace.
exp.23:17:
They are light and unstable on the surface of the water, like something that moves and has no firm footing. Their share of the land is under a curse, and they will not walk the path of the vineyards; that is, they will not enjoy good labor and the fruit of life.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. He is describing those who do evil in the dark, like thieves, and he reflects on how their lives end. Some scholars think Job is here acknowledging the final punishment of the wicked, and others that he is repeating what his friends say. The Hebrew text is difficult and is translated in several ways.

For today: a life without integrity has no firm foundation. Seek to do what is right even when no one sees you, and trust that God is just, even when his justice sometimes takes a long time.
exp.23:18:
Dry heat and drought carry away the waters that come from melted snow, and in the same way the grave takes the sinners. The verse compares two things. Just as heat and drought quickly sweep away the water from melted snow, so the grave sweeps away sinners. The idea is that death overtakes them as surely as the sun dries up the waters.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his long debate with his friends. They held that bad people always soon meet trouble. Job points out that often the wicked seem to prosper and oppress the weak. Many understand that here he describes how everything ends in the end, though some scholars think Job is quoting or imitating his friends' argument. The passage is debated.

For today: do not become bitter over the apparent advantage of the unjust. Their time is short. Trust that God sees everything, and do good with patience.
exp.23:19:
The verse says that the wicked will be forgotten even by their own mother. The worms, which feed on the dead, will find them sweet, like a pleasant morsel. No one will remember them again, and their wickedness will be broken like a tree that splits apart.

Job is speaking, answering his friends. They maintained that things go badly for the wicked in this life, but Job had pointed out that many wicked people prosper. Here he describes the end that awaits them: death overtakes them and no one remembers them. Some scholars think Job speaks with irony or describes what his friends say; the passage is interpreted in several ways.

For today: do not envy someone who prospers by doing wrong. Their success is temporary. It is better to live with integrity, for that does leave a good and lasting memory.
exp.23:21:
It says that God, or according to some translations the wicked man, draws out or prolongs the mighty with his power. Although they rise up and seem firm, no one can be sure of his life.

Job speaks. In this chapter he complains that many oppressors seem to prosper, abuse the poor, the widow and the childless woman, and God does not stop them right away. Even so, Job recognizes that their success is fragile and will not last forever.

For today: do not lose heart or envy those who prosper by doing harm. Their power is uncertain. Rather, trust in God, practice justice and care for the weak, even when no one notices.
exp.23:23:
It says that the powerful wicked are lifted up for only a little while, but then they disappear. They are brought low like everyone else. The phrase about being shut up probably means that their life comes to an end, or that they are gathered in like grain. In the end they are cut down like the heads of grain, that is, the way ripe wheat is harvested. The words about being lifted up mean raised high or made great, and the words about being brought low mean struck down.

Job is speaking, answering his friends. He observes that many unjust people prosper and seem secure, even though God is watching them. Here he acknowledges that their success does not last forever. Some scholars see in this a hope for justice, and others see a complaint that it takes so long. Job ends by challenging anyone who would contradict him.

For today: do not lose heart or envy those who succeed through injustice. Their power is temporary. Keep doing what is right and trust that God sees everything and judges with justice.
exp.25:1:
Job speaks to his friend Bildad with irony. In essence, Job is saying that Bildad's speeches have given him no real support.

Job is suffering greatly. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends came to comfort him, but they ended up accusing him. Bildad has just spoken (chapter 25) and did not respond to Job's pain. That is why Job answers with harsh, sarcastic words, because he feels more wounded than helped.

For today: when someone is suffering, they do not need sermons or quick explanations. They need companionship, listening, and kind words. Before offering advice, ask yourself whether you are really upholding that person or are only talking.
exp.25:6:
He stretches out the north over empty space, and hangs the earth on nothing. It is a poetic image: the earth does not rest on visible pillars, but God holds it up by his power.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his suffering. He is answering his friends, who gave speeches about God without comforting him. Job shows that he too knows the greatness of God, which reaches to the world of the dead, the heavens, and the earth. Some think that "the north" refers to the northern sky; this is not entirely certain.

For today: if God holds up the whole earth with no visible support, he can sustain your life when you cannot see where help is coming from. Today, bring to him in prayer whatever worries you, and trust that he continues to hold you up.
exp.26:2:
Job says that as long as his life is in him and the breath of God is in his nostrils, that is, as long as he has life and is breathing, he will keep what follows in verse 4: he will not speak falsehood. Breath means the air we take in and let out, and nostrils refers to the nose. Job understands that his breathing is a gift from God.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends insist that he suffers for some hidden sin, but he maintains that he is innocent. Although he feels that God has treated him bitterly, he acknowledges him as the living God and does not give up his honesty. Some see here a solemn oath; others, simple firmness.

For today: every breath is a gift from God. Even when life hurts and others judge you wrongly, you can choose to remain sincere and not trade the truth for relief or approval.
exp.26:3:
Here Job says that he will never use his lips to speak evil things, nor his tongue to deceive. Job is not declaring a specific sin, but making a firm promise to speak with truth and integrity.

Job speaks in the midst of great suffering. His friends insist that he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job swears by God that, as long as he has life, he will not invent a guilt he does not have just to prove them right. He acknowledges that God has afflicted him, but maintains that he has not lived in wickedness. Interpreters debate whether his confidence in his own righteousness was entirely correct, since God later confronts him.

For today: when you are under pressure, do not lie or exaggerate to look good or to avoid conflict. Ask God for help to speak the truth, even when it is costly, and with humility.
exp.26:5:
Job says he holds fast to his righteousness and will not let it go. He will not give it up or surrender it. He states that his heart, that is, his conscience, will not accuse him as long as he lives.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends insist that he is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he refuses to agree with them or to lie about himself. He declares that he will keep his integrity until death. This does not mean that he thinks himself perfect, since in other passages he acknowledges his need of God. It is about his sincerity before Him.

For today: try to live in such a way that your conscience is clear before God. When you are wrongly accused or tempted to give in, stand firm in truth and honesty, and ask God to examine your heart.
exp.26:14:
The explanation says that the descendants of the wicked who survive the sword will die later and be buried because of death, meaning they will not escape that fate. And their widows will not weep for them. The phrase about those who survive of him is rendered in this reading as those who outlive his family. Some think there will be no mourning because the disaster is so sudden, or because death will come as judgment.

Job is speaking in reply to his friends. They taught that suffering always proves a hidden sin. Here Job describes what awaits the wicked according to God, although he insists that his own case is different and maintains his integrity.

For today: let us not put our trust in violence or injustice to secure our future. Let us seek to live with integrity and leave final justice in God's hands, without judging the pain of others lightly.
exp.26:19:
It says that terrors will overtake the wicked like a flood that seizes them, and that at night a whirlwind will carry them off suddenly. The image is of a swift fall, with no time to flee or to defend oneself.

The speaker is Job. His friends had been saying that he suffered because he was wicked. Here Job describes the fate of the wicked, using words similar to theirs. Some understand that Job reinforces that God does judge wickedness, though he insists that he himself is innocent. Others see a certain irony directed at his friends. Scholars interpret this in various ways.

For today: do not trust in riches or in a security that rises up without God, because they are as fragile as a hut. And be careful not to judge the suffering of others as punishment. Seek to live with humility and justice before God.
exp.26:22:
It says that people will clap their hands at the wicked when his end comes, and will hiss at him from wherever they stand. Clapping and hissing were old gestures of mockery and of relief at someone's downfall.

The one speaking is Job, answering his friends. Here he describes what, in his view, awaits the wicked: God's judgment and the rejection of everyone. Some scholars believe Job repeats the ideas of his friends; others think he is simply affirming that God does punish wickedness, even though he himself is innocent.

For today: there is no need to rejoice when someone falls. Instead, trust that God is just and leave in his hands what you cannot correct. Ask him to keep you from living in such a way that others have reason to mock you.
exp.27:1:
It says that iron is taken out of the earth, from the dust, and that the metal, that is, copper or bronze, is melted out of the stone. "Melted" means made liquid with fire so that it separates from the rock. It is part of a description of ancient mining.

Job speaks in the middle of his long debate with his friends. In this chapter he writes a poem about wisdom. He shows that human beings are very ingenious: they know how to find silver, gold, and iron hidden beneath the earth. But then he makes clear that true wisdom is not obtained in this way, and that only God knows where it is and gives it.

For today: value human talents and work, but do not confuse knowledge with wisdom. Ask God, with humility, for that wisdom which no skill of ours can dig out of the earth.
exp.27:4:
It says the earth produces bread on its surface, but beneath it the ground appears turned over, as if fire had overturned it. It is an image from mining: one digs deep and breaks the rock. Some think it refers to the use of fire to crack the stone, and others to the heat and the appearance of the deep parts of the earth.

This chapter is a poem attributed to Job. It describes what human beings accomplish through their ingenuity: they enter the darkness and bring out hidden treasures. It does this to contrast with wisdom, which is not found by digging. Only God knows where it is.

For today: value what you know how to do and what you have achieved, but do not confuse skill with wisdom. Before deciding something important, ask God for direction, because true wisdom begins with reverence for Him.
exp.27:5:
It says there are places in the earth, hidden beneath the ground, where the stones are sapphire and the dust holds gold. Here "sapphire" is a precious blue stone, and the dust of gold refers to particles or nuggets of gold mixed in with the earth. Some scholars think the sapphire of that time may have been what we today call lapis lazuli, but this is not certain.

Job is speaking in a poem about wisdom. He describes how people dig mines in deep and dangerous places that no bird or wild beast knows, in order to bring out treasures. Job wants to show that humans are able to find hidden riches, but true wisdom is not obtained that way. Later he says that the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

Today we can work very hard to earn money or achievements and neglect what is most valuable. This week, give the same effort to seeking God in prayer and in his Word, asking him for wisdom for your decisions.
exp.27:6:
It says there is a path, the one of the hidden mines beneath the earth, which no bird has known. Not even the vulture, famous for its sharp sight, has ever seen it.

Job speaks in a poem about wisdom. He describes how miners go down into dark and remote places to bring out sapphires, gold, and metals. His point is that human beings achieve remarkable things, but later he says that true wisdom cannot be found through that same skill. Only God knows where it is.

For today: we can admire what human intelligence accomplishes, but we should not trust it to understand the meaning of life. When something is beyond us, let us ask God for wisdom with humility, because He sees what no human eye can see.
exp.27:10:
It says that a person, searching for treasure in the mines, holds back the water that flows beneath the ground and brings to light what was hidden.

Job speaks in the middle of his long dialogue with his friends. In this poem he admires what people achieve when they dig into the earth, but he uses it as a contrast: the person finds silver and precious stones, and yet cannot find wisdom by his own means. Some understand that the passage refers to digging tunnels and controlling seepage of water.

Today we can be grateful for human intelligence and labor, but without trusting only in them. To live well we need wisdom, and this comes from God. Ask Him for it with humility every day.
exp.27:15:
This verse says that wisdom is worth more than the most expensive things in the world. The gold of Ophir was famous for its purity, and the onyx and the sapphire were gems that people valued highly. Even so, none of those riches is enough to pay for wisdom. The phrase "cannot be valued" means that its worth cannot be measured in those things.

Here Job is speaking, in the middle of his suffering and of his debates with his friends. In this poem he describes how people dig mines and find metals and gems, but cannot discover wisdom by their own effort. Later in the chapter it says that God knows it, and that to fear the Lord is wisdom (v. 28).

Today we can ask ourselves what we pursue more eagerly: money or wisdom. We can ask God for direction before we decide, and listen to his Word with humility.
exp.27:19:
Job asks where wisdom can be found and where true understanding lives. This question is repeated in this poem, as also in verse 12.

This chapter is a poem within the book of Job. It is usually understood as being spoken by Job after hearing his friends. Earlier he has described how people dig mines and find metals and jewels, but wisdom is not obtained that way. That is why the question does not seek a place on a map; rather, it shows that wisdom is beyond our reach. At the end of the chapter (v. 28), the answer is the fear of the Lord.

For today: do not seek wisdom only in your own effort, your studies, or your money. Ask God for it with humility, read it in his Word, and obey him in the small things of each day.
exp.27:21:
This verse says that wisdom is so hidden that not even destruction and death possess it; they have only heard of it, like a distant rumor. In Hebrew, the word for destruction is Abaddon, and the word for death is the grave. Here the verse is not speaking of a place of punishment, but of the realm of the dead.

Job is speaking in a poem about wisdom. Man knows how to bring silver and gold out of the earth, but he cannot find wisdom. Neither the living, nor the birds, nor the realm of the dead itself has it. Only God knows its way, as the verses that follow say.

For today: do not look for true wisdom only in your experience, your achievements, or your intelligence. Ask God for it, for He knows it and gives it to those who ask with humility.
exp.27:23:
He says that God looks to the farthest places on the earth and sees everything under the heavens. "The ends of the earth" means the most remote corners of the world. Nothing escapes his sight, neither what is hidden nor what is far away.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, in a poem about wisdom. He asks where true wisdom can be found. Neither death nor the treasures of the earth can give it; only God knows it. This verse explains why: God sees everything, and so he understands the origin and order of creation, as the following verses about the wind, the waters, and the rain show.

For today: when you feel that no one sees your situation or that you do not understand what is happening, remember that God sees the whole picture. You can ask him for wisdom with confidence, instead of relying only on your own understanding.
exp.28:4:
Job remembers a happy time when he felt that God, the "Almighty" (the All-Powerful), was close to him. He also remembers his children gathered around him, that is, a united family alive in his home.

The one speaking is Job, a man who has lost almost everything: his possessions, his health, and his children. In this chapter he looks back with longing and pain.
