He does not know why he suffers, and he misses the closeness with God that he once enjoyed. His words express sincere sadness, not a complaint against God that God would reject.

For today: when we go through hard times, we can remember with gratitude the good things God gave us, and honestly tell him what we feel. And in the meantime, let us value today the family and loved ones we have close by.
exp.28:5:
He says that in his best days, Job had such abundance that it seemed he washed his steps with butter (cream, or milk butter), and that even the rock poured out streams of olive oil for him. It is poetic language: his paths were so prosperous that he had more than enough of everything.

Job speaks here while already suffering greatly. He remembers with longing when God watched over him, his family was with him, and people showed him respect. Many understand the rock pouring out oil as a picture of unexpected blessings, although scholars do not fully agree on every detail of the image.

Today, we can thank God for the blessings we have, without taking them for granted. And if we are going through a hard time, remembering his past goodness can give us hope, even when we do not understand the present.
exp.28:7:
It says that when Job appeared in public, the young men would step aside or hide themselves out of respect, and the older men would rise to their feet to honor him. Standing up here means getting up as a sign of reverence. Some think the young men hid out of shyness before someone so respected; the text does not explain this further.

Job speaks while already suffering, remembering with longing his life before. He used to be a respected judge who sat at the city gate, the place where cases were settled. His reputation came not only from his wealth but from his justice and his help to those in need, as he describes in this same chapter.

For today: let us seek the respect that comes from living with integrity and serving others, not from position or money. And if we lose recognition, let us remember that our worth comes from God.
exp.28:9:
The explanation says that when Job arrived, the most important leaders would stop talking. The leaders are the chiefs or nobles of the city. The expression "their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth" means they fell completely silent out of respect.

The speaker is Job, who looks back with longing on his life before his suffering. In chapters 29 to 31 he describes how he was respected at the city gate, where decisions were made. That respect did not come only from his wealth, but from the fact that he defended the poor and the fatherless, as the following verses say.

For today: true respect is earned through a righteous life and service to those in need, not through power or image. Ask yourself whom you can help this week, without expecting applause.
exp.28:12:
It says that Job received the blessing, that is, the gratitude and kind words, from those who were about to be lost or die, such as the poor and the helpless. In addition, Job filled the widow's heart with joy, a widow who in that time was very vulnerable.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his suffering. He remembers with longing what his life was like before the disaster, when people respected him because he defended those in need. With this he also defends his integrity before his friends, who accused him of being a wicked man.

For today: look for someone who is going through a hard time, such as a widow, an orphan or a lonely person, and help them in a concrete way. A visit, a meal or a favor can give them back their hope.
exp.28:14:
It says that Job helped those who had a physical limitation. To be "eyes to the blind" means to guide and direct someone who cannot see the way. To be "feet to the lame" means to support and accompany someone who cannot walk on their own. It is not talking about miracles, but about constant and close help. The "lame" are those who have difficulty walking.

Job speaks, a man who lost everything and remembers his past life. In this chapter he defends his integrity before his friends, who kept insisting that his suffering was punishment for some sin. He mentions how he used his position to protect widows, orphans, and the needy, and how he lived with justice.

Today we can ask ourselves who near us is missing a guide or a support. Perhaps it is an elderly neighbor, a sick relative, or someone who feels lost. Accompanying them, taking them to an appointment, or patiently explaining something to them can be eyes and feet for that person.
exp.28:15:
This verse says that Job was like a father to those in need. The needy are people who are poor or who lack the basics of life. Job also says that when he did not understand a case, he searched it out carefully, so that he would not judge hastily.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He remembers with longing how he lived before losing everything. His friends accuse him of being wicked, and he answers by describing his righteous conduct: he helped the blind, the lame, and the poor, and he defended the oppressed against those who abused them.

For today: when someone goes through a need or a conflict, do not give your opinion quickly or keep your distance. Listen, ask questions, and get the facts right before you speak or judge. Then help in concrete ways, with your time, your voice, or your resources, as a good father cares for the one who needs him.
exp.28:16:
It says that Job broke the jaws of the wicked and made him release what he had caught in his teeth. It is an image of a fierce animal, like a lion, that seizes its prey. The wicked are those who act unjustly or do evil. The prey is the victim the wicked man had in his grip.

Job speaks here, remembering with nostalgia how his life was before his suffering. In chapter 29 he describes his good reputation: he helped the poor, the blind, and the fatherless. This phrase shows that he used his influence to defend the oppressed, stopping the abuse of the powerful. It is a poetic image, not a literal description of violence.

Today, God invites us to defend those who are mistreated, using our voice, time, or influence with justice and without violence. We can stand with someone who suffers abuse at work, at home, or financially, and help them seek protection and assistance.
exp.28:18:
He says that Job saw himself as a healthy tree. His root was spread out by the waters, that is, reaching toward the water and well nourished. And the dew lay all night upon my branch: the fresh moisture of the night rested on his branches the whole time. It is an image of strong, stable and blessed life.

Job speaks in chapter 29, remembering with longing his life before the suffering. He was sure he would die in peace, in his nest, after a long life. Then he had respect, God's protection and authority to help the weak. Now he suffers and feels abandoned, and that is why he remembers those days.

For today: a firm life needs roots near the source. Seek God steadily in prayer and in his Word, so that in good times you do not become complacent and in hard times you do not dry up.
exp.28:21:
After I spoke, they did not answer again, and my words fell gently on them.

Job is speaking, suffering greatly and remembering with longing his past days, when he was respected in his community. He describes how people listened to him closely and waited for his counsel. The verses that follow compare that waiting to the way the land waits for the rain it needs. Some believe Job is also defending his honor before his friends.

For today: let your words be like gentle rain, encouraging and guiding, not wounding. Speak with humility, listen first, and offer counsel that helps others grow.
exp.29:0:
He says that now men younger than he is mock him. They are the sons of people whom Job once looked down on so much that he would not have put them even with the dogs that guarded his flock. The phrase about being younger means men younger than he is, and the word for looked down on means he would have rejected them or held them in contempt.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of his suffering. He was once respected by everyone, but now he has lost almost everything, and even people of very low social standing humiliate him. Job is not boasting; he is lamenting the painful fall of his honor. His words reflect his pain, and are not necessarily a model to imitate.

For today: when someone suffers, let us not treat them with mockery or contempt. If we are the ones suffering, we can honestly tell God about our pain, as Job did, and treat every person with respect.
exp.29:8:
He says that Job has become an object of mockery. The word "song" refers to a mocking song, and the word "byword" is a popular saying used to ridicule someone. In other words, people now make fun of him and use him as an example of misfortune.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He used to be respected, but now even young people from marginalized families look down on him, and he describes them with harsh words (vv. 1-8). Job feels that public humiliation adds to his pain, and he thinks God himself has allowed this fall (v. 11). It is his sincere complaint, not a teaching about how to treat others.

For today: when someone suffers, let us avoid mocking or judging them. Let us approach them with respect and companionship. And if you are going through humiliation, you can express your pain to God with honesty, as Job did.
exp.29:9:
They detest me, Job says, and they keep their distance from me. They do not even hold back from spitting in my face. "Abhor" means that they loathe me or look at me with disgust. Spitting on someone was a very strong sign of contempt and humiliation.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. Once people respected him, but now he is insulted by younger men of low social standing, who even mock him in songs. Job feels that God has weakened him, and that gave them courage to attack him. This is his complaint, not an explanation from God of what is happening.

Today, if someone suffers rejection or ridicule, this text reminds us that God does not ask us to stay silent about our pain. We can bring it to him honestly. And when another person is going through a trial, instead of pulling away or judging them, we can draw near with respect, companionship, and kind words.
exp.29:13:
They came in on me like a wide breach in a wall, rushing in through the gap with nothing to stop them. The phrase about rolling over him in his ruin means they threw themselves upon him, pressing in on his disaster and using his downfall as an opportunity to strike him harder.

Job speaks here in his last great lament. He was once respected, but now young men without honor attack him and humiliate him. He feels defenseless, like a city whose wall has been torn down. The text does not explain further who these young men were, but Job's pain is clear: he is suffering, and on top of that he is despised.

For today: when someone is going through a weak moment, we should not take advantage or pile on more blows. We can be the ones who help repair the wall with a visit, a kind word, or practical help. And if you are the one suffering, you can speak to God honestly, as Job did.
exp.29:15:
He says he feels as if his soul is draining out of him, poured out like water emptying from inside. It is a way of saying he is worn out and without strength. The days of suffering have hold of him, gripping him tightly, and will not let him go.

Job speaks here, a man who has lost nearly everything: his possessions, his children, and his health. In this chapter he describes his physical pain and the mockery of others. He used to be respected, and now he feels that misfortunes break in on him as through an opening torn in a wall. He laments before God and before his friends.

For today: when pain leaves you feeling empty, there is no need to pretend to be strong. Job spoke with honesty, and the Bible does not silence him. You can tell God how you really feel, in simple words, and look for someone you trust to stay with you.
exp.29:16:
Job says that at night the pain pierces his bones, as if something were drilling into them from within. And his pulses, that is, his throbbing or aches, do not rest. Some translators understand this to refer to pains that gnaw at him without stopping. The Hebrew text is not entirely clear at this point.

Job speaks, a man who has lost almost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. In this chapter he contrasts his former honor with his present suffering. He complains before God with complete sincerity, and his nights are long and without relief.

For today: if pain, physical or of the soul, keeps you from sleep, do not hide it. Tell God honestly, as Job did, and also seek someone you trust or a doctor who can accompany you. Asking for help is not a lack of faith.
exp.29:17:
He says that, because of the great amount of matter (pus or discharge from his sores), his garment has changed its shape and no longer looks as it did before. Also, the robe tightens around his neck, as if it were choking him. Some scholars think the force of God distorts his garment; others think it is the disease that affects it. The Hebrew text is difficult and is translated in several ways.

Job speaks, a man who lost everything and suffers a painful illness. In this chapter he describes his physical pain and his humiliation, and he feels that God has left him without an answer. His friends have judged him, and he laments with sincerity.

Today, if you are suffering, you can speak to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. Job did not hide his pain, and the Bible records it. You can also look for someone who will walk with you with compassion, without judging you.
exp.29:23:
The verse says that God does not stretch out his hand against the grave. That is, he does not attack those who are already dead or strike the tombs. Then it asks whether those who are buried will call for help when he destroys them. This verse is difficult, and translators and commentators understand it in several ways.

Job speaks in the middle of his pain. He complains that God, whom he feels as an enemy, has lifted him up only to let him fall. He knows he is heading toward death, and he asks for relief in his distress, since his suffering makes no sense to him.

Today we can learn that it is right to bring our complaints and questions to God honestly, even when we do not understand what we are suffering. Job did not pretend to be fine, and God did not reject him.
exp.30:0:
Here Job says he made a serious commitment with his eyes, like a firm agreement: he would not let them look with desire at a young unmarried woman. A covenant is a solemn agreement. To think upon a maid means to fix the mind on her with desire, not merely to see her. And reward means payment or recompense.

Job speaks as a suffering man whose friends accuse him of having sinned in secret. In this chapter he defends himself and reviews his conduct, beginning with his inner purity. He knows that God sees everything, and that serious sin begins in the gaze and the thought. The verses that follow show that he recognizes God judges those who do wrong.

For today: decide in advance which things you will not let your eyes take in, whether in the street, on your phone, or on social media. A clear agreement with yourself and with God, made before temptation comes, helps you guard your heart and live with integrity.
exp.30:1:
Job asks what reward God would give from heaven to someone who lets his heart and his eyes wander. The question is rhetorical: if a person lives in impurity, he could not expect anything good from the Almighty.

Job speaks here as a man who is suffering greatly. In chapter 31 he defends himself against the accusations of his friends and reviews his conduct. He has just said that he made a covenant with his eyes so as not to look with desire at a woman. Then he remembers that God sees all his ways and that sin brings consequences.

Today we can remember that God also sees what is hidden. Before we look at, read, or think about something that tempts us, it is wise to ask ourselves: "Does this bring me closer to God or move me away from Him?" Setting clear limits, as Job did with his eyes, protects the heart and guards our faithfulness.
exp.30:2:
This verse is a question that Job answers with an implied yes: God does bring ruin upon the wicked, and sets apart, or turns away, those who practice evil, leaving them to a fate that is not their own.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. In this chapter he defends his integrity and lists sins he did not commit. He has just said that he made a covenant with his eyes not to look with lust at a young woman. His reasoning is that God sees everything and that evil has consequences. Scholars note that Job speaks with firmness, although later the book shows that his understanding of God's justice was incomplete.

For today: take care what you look at and what you think, because that is where decisions begin. Living with the awareness that God sees our ways should not produce paralyzing fear, but an honest life, even when no one is watching us.
exp.30:6:
Job says that if he has ever strayed from the right path, if he let his heart be led by what his eyes saw, or if his hands have been stained by anything wrong, then he is willing to be judged. The sentence about the old verb forms is not needed for the English reader, so it is left out. Job speaks of three things: his steps, his heart, and his hands.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly, and whose friends say his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. In this chapter he makes a solemn declaration of innocence. He places his life before God and asks to be weighed on the scales of justice. He does not claim to be perfect, but that he has not lived with deceit or with hidden wickedness.

For today: honestly examine what you look at and what you desire, because actions grow out of those. Before deciding something, ask yourself whether you could present it calmly before God.
exp.30:7:
It says Job accepts a punishment if he has done something wrong: that he sows and someone else eats the harvest, and that what he has planted is uprooted.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. Facing the accusations of his friends, he defends his innocence with a series of oaths: "if I have done such a thing, let such a punishment come upon me." He wants God to weigh him on fair scales. Some understand that he is referring to sins such as deceit, greed, or injustice. The text gives no further details.

For today: live with integrity even where no one sees you. Before claiming that you are righteous, ask God to examine your ways, your eyes, and your heart, and correct whatever He shows you.
exp.30:10:
It says that adultery is a wickedness and a iniquity, that is, a serious sin that deserves to be punished by the judges. "Iniquity" means injustice or deep wickedness. The judges were the authorities responsible for administering justice in the community.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. His friends accuse him of having sinned, and he answers with a series of oaths to defend his integrity. Here he says that if he had desired another man's wife or had lurked at his neighbor's door, he would accept a just punishment. Scholars understand the words about grinding and bowing down in different ways, but they usually see them as an image of humiliation or of being treated as a slave.

Today we can guard the heart before sin reaches our actions. Respecting our own marriage and that of others, and fleeing from thoughts and situations that would harm it, is living with integrity before God.
exp.30:11:
Job 31:12 describes adultery as a fire that burns without stopping, consuming everything until it reaches the place of ruin. The words used for that place of destruction carry the sense of devastation and loss. The fire would also uproot everything Job has. The word for possessions or harvest refers to goods and crops, and the idea of uprooting means pulling something out by its roots.

Job speaks as a man who is suffering and defends his integrity before his friends. In chapter 31 he declares with oaths that he has not committed certain sins. Here he says that if he had been unfaithful or had desired another man's wife, he would deserve to lose everything. He recognizes that adultery is a wickedness that even judges would punish.

For today: guard your heart from an early age. Hidden sins seem small, but they can destroy family, peace, and trust. Be faithful in your thoughts, your words, and your decisions, and ask God for help to remain firm.
exp.30:12:
He says that Job never looked down on the rights of his servants, both men and women, when they had a complaint against him. Looking down on something means giving it little importance. To bring a claim means to bring forward a complaint or a dispute. Job says he always listened to them with respect.

Job speaks in his last speech in his own defense. He feels treated unjustly and goes back over his life to show that he has been upright. Here he mentions how he treated his workers. In that time, a master had great power over his servants, and yet Job recognizes that they had rights. He says that God, who made us all, would one day call him to account.

For today: if you have authority, whether as a boss, a parent, or a leader, listen carefully to those who depend on you. Treat their complaints with justice and humility, remembering that we are all equal before God.
exp.30:16:
He says that Job did not eat his bread alone, but shared it with the fatherless. The word "morsel" is a piece of bread or food, and "fatherless" refers to the child who has lost a father, and often a mother too. Job states that if he had eaten alone and left the fatherless hungry, he would have done something wrong.

Job speaks in a long discourse in which he defends his integrity before God and before his friends, who had accused him of sinning in secret. Just before this verse he says that God made him and also the poor, so both have equal worth. Job gives examples of how he treated those in need: the widow, the fatherless, and the one who had no clothing.

Today we might ask ourselves: with whom can I share what God has given me? Perhaps a meal, time, or help with someone who lives alone or is in need.
exp.30:17:
Here Job says that from his youth the orphan grew up beside him as if he were his father. And since he was born, he was a guide to the widow. That is, caring for the weak has been part of his whole life. Some scholars think the phrase speaks of a care he felt almost as something natural, from the very beginning.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly and whose friends accuse him of having sinned. In chapter 31 he defends himself with a series of "if" statements: if he did wrong to the poor, may the punishment fall on him. This verse is set in parentheses because it is a declaration of what he actually did.

For today: let us not wait until we have much to help. Let us look for someone close to us who is alone or in need, a widower, a child without support, a neighbor, and accompany them with steadfastness and affection.
exp.30:20:
He says that Job never raised his hand against the fatherless, that is, he never threatened or mistreated them. He says this even though he knew that he would have help in the gate. The gate was the entrance of the city, where the elders and judges settled cases. Job says that, even though he would have had influence there and known he could win, he would not take advantage of the defenseless.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering, defending his integrity before his friends, who accuse him of being wicked. In this chapter he makes an oath: if he has done such a thing, he deserves punishment. Earlier he mentions that he clothed the needy, and then he says that he feared God.

For today: if you have authority, money, or good connections, do not use them to take advantage of someone who cannot defend themselves. Use them to protect and help the most vulnerable.
exp.30:21:
It says that, if Job had harmed the orphan, he would deserve to have his shoulder blade fall away and his arm broken from the bone. The explanation notes that the word for the bone of the arm, near the elbow, is an old term. Job speaks with strong language: if he raised his hand against the helpless, then that very hand and arm should be the ones punished.

Speaking in the middle of his suffering, Job defends his integrity before his friends and before God. In this chapter he makes a series of oaths: "if I did such a thing, let such punishment come upon me." Here he insists that he never abused his power or his influence in the court at the city gate. Some understand the punishment literally; others take it as a very intense way of speaking.

For today: use your strength, your money, or your position to protect the weak, never to take advantage of them. Think of someone vulnerable near you and ask how you can help them this week.
exp.30:29:
This verse says that Job did not let his mouth sin by asking for a curse to come upon the life of his enemy. The mouth here refers to his words, that is, what he said. Letting the mouth be used for evil is what it means to give it over to sin.

Job speaks, a man who suffers greatly. In this chapter he defends himself before his friends and before God, and he reviews how he has lived. He says that he did not rejoice when someone who hated him fared badly, and that he did not wish his ruin with words. For Job, doing so would have been to wrong God.

For today: when someone hurts you, guard your words. Before speaking badly of that person or wishing harm on them, pause and pray for them. Asking God to bless them protects your heart and honors the Lord.
exp.30:38:
It says Job wonders whether he ever took advantage of other people's land. Eating the produce of a field without paying for it means enjoying what grows there without giving anything in return. Making the owners of the land lose their lives means mistreating, oppressing, or causing suffering to those who owned or worked that land. The quoted wording is a list of the terms the verse uses, and it does not need separate explanation.

Job speaks near the end of his long defense. His friends tell him he suffers because of some hidden sin, and he answers with a series of oaths: if I have done such a thing, then let such a punishment fall on me. Here he declares himself innocent of exploitation and economic abuse. Then comes the curse he himself accepts, if he were guilty: that thorns should grow instead of wheat.

For today: check whether you pay fairly those who work for you or serve you. God sees the way we treat people in money matters, and he cares about the dignity of every person.
exp.31:1:
Here we are introduced to Elihu, a young man who becomes very angry with Job. He says that Job was making himself right rather than God, meaning he defended himself so strongly that it seemed he was putting his own rightness ahead of God's. The words that describe Elihu's family origin, from Buz, are in the verse's own name list, and his anger is the anger described in the verse itself.

Job's three friends had already stopped speaking, because Job would not give in. Elihu had waited in silence out of respect for his elders. Now he speaks up because he believes Job is wrong to defend his innocence in that way. Some think Elihu says useful things; others think he also speaks with pride. The Bible does not fully settle the question.

Today we can learn to defend ourselves with humility. Even when we suffer unjustly, it is wise to let God have the last word and not to speak as though He owes us explanations.
exp.31:7:
What it says: Elihu affirms that within every person there is a spirit, and that the breath or inspiration of God, the Almighty, is what gives understanding.

Context: Elihu is a young man who has waited in silence while Job and his three friends, all of them older, argued. Since they were unable to answer Job, Elihu dares to speak. He says that age does not guarantee wisdom. Scholars debate whether Elihu speaks with true wisdom or with some pride, since the book does not fully make this clear.

For today: Do not dismiss someone because they are young, and do not think yourself wise simply because of your years or experience. Listen to each person with respect, and ask God for understanding, because He is the one who gives it. Always compare what you hear with the Word of God.
exp.31:14:
The explanation says that Job's three friends were left astonished and without words. The first phrase means they were startled or amazed. The second phrase means their arguments ran out; they no longer had anything to say.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who has waited in silence while the older men argued with Job. Here he addresses the friends, or speaks about them, and notes that they stopped answering. Elihu feels ready to give his own view. Scholars do not agree on whether this verse is addressed to the friends or is a comment about them, but the general meaning is the same.

There are moments when our explanations run out, especially in the face of someone else's pain. Instead of forcing answers, we can be quiet, listen, and walk alongside others with humility, trusting that God knows more than we do.
exp.31:18:
He says that Elihu feels like wine shut in with no way out for its gas, or like new leather wineskins about to burst. "Belly" here speaks of the deepest part of a person, and the "vent" is an opening that lets the pressure escape. With this image, Elihu expresses that he can no longer keep quiet.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who listened in silence to the long debate between Job and his three friends. Out of respect for their age he waited, but now he is upset because none of them answered Job well. He believes he has something to say. Some readers see sincerity in his words; others notice a certain pride, and the Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: before speaking, examine your motives. Feeling the urge to give your opinion does not always mean you should. Ask God for wisdom to speak with truth, humility and love, at the right moment.
exp.31:20:
He says that Elihu will not show favoritism toward anyone because of their importance, nor will he flatter anyone with praising titles to win their approval. Showing favoritism means treating someone better because of their position or influence. Flattering titles are exaggerated names or praise given to please people.

Elihu is the young man who listened quietly to the debate between Job and his three friends. Now he feels full of words, like a wineskin about to burst, and he wants to respond. He says he will speak frankly, without flattering Job or the older friends, because he fears God. Some readers see healthy sincerity here; others notice that Elihu can also sound very sure of himself.

For today: let us seek to speak the truth with respect, without flattering anyone or showing favor to someone because of their position. Before speaking, let us ask God for humility and love, so that our honesty helps and does not wound.
exp.32:3:
This verse says that God is the one who made Elihu and gave him life. "Spirit of God" and "breath of the Almighty" are two ways of saying the same thing: the breath of God. "Breath" here means breath or puff of air, not a sudden idea.

Elihu speaks, a young man who steps in after the long speeches of Job and his three friends. He addresses Job and says he will speak with sincerity. By recalling that both of them were formed from clay by God, he wants to show that he does not place himself above Job. Some think his words carry a certain arrogance; others see in them a balanced voice. The Bible does not make this entirely clear.

For today: your life is a gift from God, not an accident. Remembering this helps you speak with humility and treat with respect even those who think differently.
exp.32:9:
This verse says that God has looked for occasions against Job. The word "occasions" in this verse means pretexts or excuses for accusing someone. According to this complaint, God treats him as his enemy.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the conversation at the end of the book. He quotes what Job had said: that he was clean and innocent, and that God pursued him without cause. Elihu does not agree with that view and wants to correct it. Interpreters debate whether his correction is fair or partial, since afterward God himself speaks and does not fully endorse anyone, although he does rebuke Job's friends.

For today: when you suffer, it is natural to feel that God is against you. Tell him honestly about your pain, but do not draw conclusions about his character only from what you feel. Trust that God is greater than your understanding.
exp.32:11:
Elihu tells Job that he is not right in what he has claimed. Job had said that God was looking for pretexts against him and treating him as an enemy. Elihu answers that God is greater than any human being, and that for this reason he cannot be judged as if he were an equal.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He quotes Job's complaints (verses 10 and 11) in order to correct them. Some readers see in Elihu a wise voice, and others think he speaks with too much certainty. The book does not make this entirely clear.

When we suffer, it is natural to pour out our hearts to God, and he allows it. But it is good to remember that his greatness goes beyond our understanding. We can trust him even without having all the answers.
exp.32:12:
Elihu asks Job why he sets himself to argue with God. He says that God does not have to give an account or explain everything he does.

Elihu is the one speaking, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He believes Job was wrong to insist that God was treating him unjustly. Shortly after, he claims that God does speak, even though human beings do not always understand it. Some think Elihu is partly right; others think he also speaks with arrogance. The Bible does not fully settle the question.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, you can bring your pain to him honestly, but without demanding explanations as if he were someone on trial before you. Trust that God is greater than your understanding, and stay attentive to listening to him.
exp.32:14:
This verse says that God can speak to people through a dream or a vision at night, just when deep sleep falls on them and they are lying in their beds, half asleep. Since this phrase is only in the original wording and not in your verse, it is not needed here.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who comes in at the end of the discussions between Job and his friends. He says that Job complains that God does not answer, but he claims that God does speak in several ways, although people do not always understand it. The verses that follow say that God seeks to correct people and turn them away from pride. This is Elihu's opinion, not a rule for every case.

For today: do not assume that God is silent. With humility, listen for his voice in the Bible, in prayer, and in wise counsel, and weigh everything in the light of his Word.
exp.32:18:
He is also corrected while lying in his own bed, that is, while he rests, through a strong pain that reaches down to his bones. Here "chastened" is understood as corrected or disciplined. It does not speak of a final judgment, but of an illness that makes him feel his weakness.

The one speaking is Elihu, the young man who intervenes near the end of the book of Job. He maintains that God uses suffering, just as he uses dreams, to warn a person, turn him away from pride, and save his life. Many believe Elihu exaggerates, because not every pain is the result of a fault, as Job himself shows.

For today: when an illness or a difficult night arrives, we can stop to pray and ask God whether he wants to teach us something, without assuming that all suffering is punishment.
exp.32:20:
He says that the body of this sick man wastes away so much that his flesh almost disappears, to the point that it can no longer be seen. His bones, which before were covered and not noticed, now show and stick out. It is an image of extreme thinness caused by suffering.

The one speaking is Elihu, the young man who intervenes at the end of the dialogues with Job. He is explaining that God sometimes speaks to human beings through pain and sickness, in order to turn them away from pride and draw them toward repentance. Interpreters debate whether Elihu is entirely right, because God afterward does not directly side with anyone, but his description of suffering is very vivid.

For today: when sickness or exhaustion weakens us, we do not have to pretend to be strong. We can stop, pray with sincerity, and ask God to speak to us and sustain us. We can also accompany someone who is suffering with tenderness, without judging them.
exp.32:21:
The explanation says the sick person is so weak that they feel they are almost reaching the grave. The word for the grave is the pit or tomb. The phrase about those who bring death is a difficult expression: some understand it as referring to angels or messengers of death, others to forces that bring death. The text does not fully clarify this.

Here Elihu speaks, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He describes how God can speak to a person through suffering. Elihu says that pain can bring someone to the edge of death, but that a faithful messenger can show them the way back to God. We should remember that Elihu does not fully explain everything Job is going through.

For today: when you are weak or afraid, do not shut yourself away. Seek God in prayer, and let someone you trust encourage you with the truth of his mercy.
exp.32:24:
It says that this man's flesh, once sick and close to death, will become tender and soft, fresher than a child's. That is, he will receive healing and renewed vitality. The word "youth" is also used here, so it also says he will again feel the strength of his younger years.

Elihu, the young man who answers Job, speaks. He explains that God sometimes uses suffering to call a person to repentance. If someone listens and recognizes their need, God is merciful and rescues them from the grave. Some understand this healing as literal, others as a picture of restoration in general. Be careful: Elihu does not always speak accurately about Job, so not everything applies to every kind of suffering.

For today: when you are tired or wounded, do not run from God. Come to Him with humility, because He knows how to renew your life and your hope.
exp.32:25:
The explanation says that the person who has been healed and forgiven will pray to God, will love Him, and will see His face with joy. "Face" is the meaning of the word here, and "joy" is great gladness, and "righteousness" here is understood as one's good name or one's right standing before God. God restores him.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He describes someone who suffers close to death, yet has a messenger who pleads on his behalf. Elihu holds that God uses pain to correct and to rescue. Some think his view is partial, because the book itself shows that Job's suffering was not a punishment for his sin.

For today: when God lifts you out of a difficult moment, respond with prayer and sincere thanksgiving. Draw near to Him with joy, knowing that He is able to restore you completely.
exp.32:29:
It says that God acts to deliver a person from death. "Pit" here means the grave, the place of the dead. "To be enlightened with the light of the living" means that God restores that person's life and lets them enjoy it again, with hope and clarity.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job and his three friends have finished arguing. Elihu explains that God corrects and rescues human beings in several ways, including through suffering. His idea is that pain can be a warning from God meant to save. However, the book shows that Job's suffering was not simply a punishment, so his words are only one part of the truth.

Today we can remember that God does not forget us in moments of crisis or sickness. We can ask him for help with confidence, and thank him for each new day as a gift of his mercy.
exp.32:30:
Elihu asks Job to pay close attention and listen carefully to what he is about to say. He also asks him to be quiet for a moment so that he can be heard. These words are an invitation to listen without interrupting.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who had waited while Job and his three friends argued. In this chapter he explains that God speaks to human beings in different ways, even through suffering, in order to rescue them from destruction and give them life. Some scholars see Elihu as a balanced wise man, and others see him as somewhat arrogant. The Bible does not fully settle the question.

For today: before answering in the middle of an argument or a pain, practice attentive silence. Truly listening, to people and to God, opens the door to wisdom and healing.
exp.33:1:
Elihu asks the wise men and those with understanding to hear him. Elihu is the young man who speaks after Job and his three friends have finished arguing. Here he addresses those who are listening, because he wants to correct what Job has said about God and justice. He speaks with confidence, although the Bible shows that his speech mixes truths with harsh judgments, which is why it is interpreted in different ways.

Today we can learn to listen carefully and to examine what we hear, without accepting everything or rejecting everything right away. Before forming an opinion, it is wise to think, to compare with the Word of God, and to ask Him for wisdom to distinguish what is good.
exp.33:7:
It says that Job keeps company with wicked people and walks with those who have bad intentions. Working iniquity means doing what is wrong and unjust. Those who have bad intent are people who seek to harm or deceive. It is an accusation: Job is said to share the life of the ungodly.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He quotes and criticizes Job's words, and he accuses Job of saying that it is useless to please God. Note: the book of Job shows that God calls Job blameless, so Elihu exaggerates or judges wrongly. How much right he has in the rest of his speech is debated.

For today: before accusing someone because of their suffering or their complaints, it is wise to listen with humility and not draw hasty conclusions. God sees the heart better than we do.
exp.33:12:
This verse asks two questions to make us think: who put God in charge of the earth? Who gave him the task of ordering and sustaining the whole world? The answer expected is no one: God did not receive his authority from anyone else, but is the Creator.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He argues that God is just and does not pervert justice. He says that if no one gave God the rule of the world, then no one has the authority to correct him or accuse him. Some think Elihu is partly right, although later God neither approves nor explicitly condemns what he says.

Today we can rest: the world is in no one's hands but God's. When we do not understand what is happening, we can trust that he governs with justice, instead of accusing him.
exp.33:18:
This verse says that God does not show partiality, that is, he has no favorites and does not treat someone better because of their position. He does not respect a prince more than a humble person, nor the rich more than the poor, because we are all the work of his hands.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the dialogue between Job and his three friends. He is upset because he believes Job is questioning God's justice. He argues that if a human king who acts wrongly can be called wicked, then it is even less appropriate to accuse God, who is completely just. Some think Elihu says true things, though he does not always apply them well to Job.

For today: treat everyone with the same respect and dignity, regardless of their money or position, because God created them and values them just as he values you.
exp.33:19:
It says that the powerful can die suddenly, in a moment. At midnight the peoples are shaken or stirred, and the great pass away, that is, they disappear. The most striking thing is that the mighty is taken away without hand, that is, without human force; it is not an army that brings him down, but God.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He argues that God is just and impartial: He does not favor kings or the rich, because He made them all. His point is that no one escapes His judgment.

For today: power, money or prestige do not make us more important before God, nor do they give us security. Live with humility, treat everyone with respect, and act with honesty, knowing that God sees everything.
exp.33:27:
It says that those who turned away from God caused the cry of the poor to rise up to him. "Cry" means a shout asking for help. "Afflicted" refers to those who are suffering and have no one to defend them. The verse shows that God hears those who suffer injustice.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's friends. He argues that God is just and does not tolerate wickedness. In this passage he speaks of the wicked who oppressed the weak and would not acknowledge the ways of God. Some readers think Elihu is right in general, but God does not mention him afterward in his verdict, so he should be read with caution.

Today we can remember that God pays attention to the pain of the poor. For that reason, we too should listen to those who suffer, help with whatever we have, and not ignore injustice close to us.
exp.33:34:
This verse says that Job speaks without knowledge, and that his words are without wisdom. That is, according to the one speaking, Job expresses himself foolishly, without fully understanding what he is saying.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He claims that wise men will agree with him. We must be careful: the Bible records his words, but that does not mean everything he says is correct. At the end of the book, God does not approve of Job's friends, and Elihu is neither clearly corrected nor clearly praised, so many interpret him in different ways.

For today: before judging another person's pain, listen with humility. You may not understand what God and that person are living through. Guard your words and accompany others with compassion.
exp.34:1:
Elihu is the young man who speaks after Job's three friends. He believes Job has spoken wrongly about God in defending his innocence so strongly. Some scholars think Elihu sums up what Job said in an exaggerated way; in other passages Job does not state exactly that, but rather says that God has treated him unjustly. For that reason it can be debated how faithful the accusation is.

For today: when we suffer, we can pour out our hearts to God, but we should take care that our pain does not lead us to place ourselves above Him. We can pray with honesty and also with humility, trusting that God is just even when we do not understand.
exp.34:4:
It says that Job should lift his eyes to the sky and notice that the clouds are far above him. The image invites us to see how small the human being is in comparison with the greatness of God.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job and his three friends have finished arguing. Elihu believes Job has suggested that he gains nothing by being righteous and loses nothing by sinning. So he invites Job to look upward to correct that idea. Some believe Elihu speaks with wisdom and others that he is partly mistaken, and in the end God neither explicitly approves nor rebukes him.

For today: when you feel confused by what you are going through, lift your eyes and remember that God is greater than your questions. Trust him, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.34:11:
There they cry out, but he gives no answer, because of the pride of evil men. This describes people who cry out for help, yet God does not answer them. The reason given is the pride of the wicked: that arrogance which does not acknowledge God. "There" refers to the situation of oppression mentioned just before it. "Cry out" means to shout for help.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the discussion between Job and his friends. He thinks people complain when they suffer, but do not truly seek God, the one who gives songs in the night, that is, comfort in dark moments. Be careful: Elihu is not the final voice of the book, and God himself does not always remain silent in the face of pain; other passages show that he hears the humble.

For today: when you suffer, do not seek only relief; draw near to God with humility and sincerity, recognizing him as your Maker, not merely as a resource for emergencies.
exp.35:4:
This verse says that God is great and powerful, yet he looks down on no one with contempt. His strength is not brutal or capricious, but is joined to his wisdom.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He wants to defend God's justice and correct Job, who feels he has been treated unfairly. His words contain truths about God, though their application to Job is limited, and the book itself shows that Job's suffering had reasons that none of them knew.

For today: when you feel small, forgotten, or unimportant, remember that God, being so great, does not despise you. You can trust that his power acts with wisdom, even when you do not understand what you are living through.
exp.35:7:
It says that some people, perhaps kings or important figures as in the previous verse, may be held fast in fetters, that is, bound with chains on their feet, and held in cords of affliction, meaning caught by suffering as if by ropes.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job's three friends. He argues that God is just and that He uses suffering to correct and awaken the heart. The following verses show that purpose. Note: Elihu does not always get it right, and in the end God does not treat him as the final answer. Even so, here he expresses an idea that the Bible also teaches in other places.

For today: if you are going through a trial, ask God to show you whether there is something He wants to teach you, without concluding that all suffering is punishment.
exp.35:8:
It says that God, when someone is suffering, shows them what they have done wrong. The phrase about God making known their work means that God lets them see their actions. And the one about their rebellions prevailing means that their defiance and pride grew strong and took control of them.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who tries to correct Job. He believes suffering can be a way God wakes up someone who has gone astray. Note well: not all suffering is punishment, and the book of Job itself shows that Job was not suffering because of such a fault. That is why Elihu's words should be read with care.

For today: when you go through a trial, ask God humbly to show you whether there is anything in your life that needs correcting. Do it without assuming that every difficulty is your own fault.
exp.35:10:
It says that if people listen to God and serve him, they will end their lives in well-being and with joy.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who comes in at the end of the dialogue between Job and his three friends. He holds that God corrects those who go astray so that they will repent. Here he presents two paths: listening and living well, or rejecting and perishing. Interpreters disagree about how right Elihu is, since God neither explicitly approves nor corrects him, and the book teaches that suffering is not always punishment.

For today: when something corrects you, whether the Bible, wise counsel or your conscience, do not harden yourself. Listen with humility and return to God. Even so, do not assume that every pain is punishment; trust that God is good.
exp.35:19:
He says not to long for "the night," that dark time when peoples are cut off from their place. It probably refers to a time of judgment or sudden death. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and scholars translate it in different ways.

The speaker is Elihu, Job's young friend. He believes that Job, in his pain, is tempting God to act harshly, and he warns him not to be carried away by impatience or bitterness. His idea that Job suffers because of his sin is debatable, since God later does not back it up in that way.

For today: when you suffer, do not ask that everything end in any way at all, and do not wish that God would act quickly and harshly. Instead, wait with humility, guard your heart, and seek God with patience.
exp.35:22:
It says that no one directs God in His way, and no one has the authority to accuse Him of doing wrong. Two rhetorical questions are asked, and the answer to both is: no one.

The speaker is Elihu, the young friend of Job, who speaks after the three older friends. He wants to defend God's justice and correct Job, who had questioned the way God was treating him. Elihu reminds Job that God is wise, powerful, and the best teacher. Some think Elihu is partly right, although in the end God does not hold him up as a model of a counselor.

When something hurts or we do not understand what God allows, we can be honest with Him in prayer, but without accusing Him. Trusting that His way is just, even when we cannot understand it, brings us rest and humility.
exp.35:23:
This verse calls us to remember and to acknowledge the greatness of what God does. "Magnify his work" means to praise it, to value it, and to speak well of it. It also says that men behold it, that is, everyone sees it and observes it.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in before Job and his three friends. He wants to defend God's justice and wisdom, while Job suffers and questions what is happening to him. Elihu insists that no one can correct God or teach Him. His speech leads into the topics of creation, rain, and storms. Some scholars see his words as wise, and others as incomplete, since God Himself speaks afterward.

For today: when it is hard to understand your situation, stop and look at what God does, such as in nature or in His help in your life, and give thanks to Him with humility.
exp.35:27:
This verse says that the clouds let the rain fall, drop by drop, and that the rain comes down in abundance upon people. The picture is of water falling steadily from the clouds, one drop after another.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the book of Job. After the long debates with Job's three friends, Elihu argues that God is just and great, and that we humans cannot grasp everything about him. He uses the rain as an example: it is an ordinary thing, yet it is full of mystery and of God's care.

For today: when you see it rain, or take a glass of water, give thanks to God. Everyday things are gifts from him, and remembering this teaches us humility and trust when we do not understand everything that happens.
exp.35:28:
This verse asks who can truly understand how the clouds spread out and what the loud noise of his dwelling place means. A dwelling place is a tent, meaning the place where God seems to live in the heavens. The thundering noise refers to thunder, which rumbles with great force.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the discussion with Job. He wants to show that God is great and just, and that his work in nature goes beyond what human beings can explain. He uses rain and storms as an example. Some scholars see here a foreshadowing of the answer God will give Job later on.

For today: when you do not understand something about life, remember that we do not fully understand even a cloud. You can trust God with humility, without needing all the answers.
exp.35:29:
He spreads his light all around himself, like someone unfolding a blanket, and with that same light he covers the deepest parts of the sea, the very bottom of the ocean. "Covers" means to cover or wrap up. "He" refers to God. The exact sense is debated: it may speak of the lightning that lights up the sky and the sea, or of the idea that nothing, not even the deepest places, escapes his power. Some translations read that God clothes himself in light and also covers the bottom of the sea.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He is defending the greatness and justice of God, showing that he governs the clouds, the rain, and the storm. He does this to call Job to humility.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, remember that his power and his care reach even to the deepest places. Rest in him and trust, even when you cannot see everything.
exp.36:5:
It says that God speaks to the snow and commands it to fall on the earth. He does the same with the light drizzle and with the heavy downpours, which are rains that fall with great strength, that is, with a great deal of force. The idea is that nature obeys the voice of God.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of Job's conversations with his friends. He is describing the power of God in storms, thunder, and weather. He wants Job to recognize that God does great things that humans cannot fully understand.

For today: when a change in the weather disrupts your plans, take it as an invitation to remember that God governs what you do not control. Rest in him and trust, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.36:6:
He says that God, through the weather, causes people to stop and set their work aside. The idea of being held back here suggests being kept indoors, unable to go out. The phrase about God making every man stop has also been translated in other ways: some versions say that God "seals up" the hand of every man, meaning that he halts their labor. The purpose is that everyone may recognize that this is the work of God.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks near the end of Job's conversations with his friends. He describes the snow, the rain, and the storms as signs of God's power. He wants Job to see that the Creator is great and that we humans do not understand everything.

For today: when something holds you back, such as an illness, the rain, or a change of plans, do not treat it only as an obstacle. Use it as a chance to stop, pray, and remember that God is still in charge.
exp.36:9:
It says that the ice is formed by the breath or blowing of God, and that the broad waters, that is, the lakes, rivers and wide seas, are hemmed in, that is, pressed together, trapped and hardened by the cold. Where the water once ran free, it now lies frozen.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the conversation with Job. He is describing the power of God in winter and in storms. His purpose is for Job to recognize that God governs nature with a wisdom that human beings do not fully grasp.

For today: when you find yourself in a "frozen" season, where everything seems to stand still, remember that God also governs those seasons. Rest in Him, trust His timing, and wait with patience.
exp.36:14:
It says that God orders the forces of nature with precision. The phrase about making the light of his cloud shine most likely refers to the flash of lightning that comes out of the cloud. The question is: do you know how God does all this?

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the book of Job after the three friends. He wants to show Job, who is suffering greatly, that God is so great that a human being cannot understand all his ways. His questions prepare the moment when God himself will speak.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God governs with wisdom things you do not control. You can rest and trust in him, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.36:16:
It says that when the south wind goes still and the air grows heavy over the land, the clothing feels warm.

Elihu, a young man who speaks near the end of Job's conversations, is the one speaking. He wants to show that God governs nature with a wisdom no one can reach. He uses something everyday, the warmth, to ask Job whether he understands how God does everything.

Today it reminds us that there are many things we do not control or fully understand. When you feel that warmth or that weight, you can pause, acknowledge the greatness of God, and entrust to him what you do not understand.
exp.36:19:
Elihu asks whether anyone should tell God that they want to speak with Him. He suggests not, because human reasoning ends up overwhelmed, confused and caught up in wonder. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and some translations understand it differently, as the fear of being swallowed up by speaking before God.

Elihu is speaking to Job and his friends. He has just described storms, wind and skies to show the greatness of God. He wants Job to see that no human can explain or question the Almighty with his own ideas.

Today, this verse invites us to humility. We can pray with confidence, but also with reverence, accepting that we do not understand everything. When something confuses us, instead of demanding explanations, we can rest in the fact that God is greater than our questions.
exp.37:3:
God asks Job where he was when God laid the foundations of the earth. He asks Job to answer, if he truly has understanding.

Here God speaks himself, out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and had asked for explanations, and his friends had talked at length without getting it right. God does not answer him with an explanation of his pain, but with questions about creation. Through them he shows Job that his wisdom and power are far greater than those of any human being. Interpreters debate how this should be understood, but almost all of them see a call to humility and trust.

For today: when you do not understand why certain things happen, remember that God is still wise and faithful. You can bring him your questions honestly and rest in the fact that he sustains the world, and your life as well.
exp.37:5:
This verse uses the image of a building. It asks what the foundations of the earth rest on, and who set its cornerstone, the main stone that holds up and aligns the whole structure. It is a question that no one can answer except God.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and asked for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons. Instead he shows Job his greatness as Creator, with questions that invite Job to see his own limits. Interpreters understand this language as poetic, not as a scientific description.

For today: when you do not understand why certain things happen, remember that the God who holds up the earth also holds you up. You can trust him even without having all the answers.
exp.37:6:
This verse describes a moment of celebration when God created the earth. The morning stars sang praises together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy. The verse says they were glad, meaning their hearts were filled with delight. Many understand the sons of God to be the angels, although the text does not explain this in detail.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and had asked for explanations. God does not give him direct answers, but invites him to remember that He is the Creator and that He was present when everything began, while Job was not.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God sustains the world with wisdom and joy. You can trust Him even when you do not have all the answers, and respond to Him with humble praise.
exp.37:7:
God asks who shut up the sea behind doors when it burst forth, as if it had come rushing out of the womb like a newborn child. "The sea" is simply the sea. "Burst forth" means to break out with force from the womb; the word is also used for something that overflows.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had asked for an explanation of his suffering. God does not give him a direct reason, but instead presents him with questions about creation (the earth, the stars, the sea) to show him his wisdom and power. The sea, which seems uncontrollable, has a boundary that God himself set for it.

For today: when you feel that your problems overflow like a sea, remember that God sets limits on what seems chaotic. Even when you do not understand everything, you can trust that he still governs and cares for you.
exp.37:12:
It says that the morning is ordered to reach the ends of the earth, and that the light of dawn, when it arrives, shakes the wicked out of it the way one shakes dust out of a blanket. The ends of the earth means the farthest edges. The wicked are those who live without reverence for God and do evil.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons, but asks him questions about creation to show him his wisdom and power. The dawn appears as an image of justice: many wrongs are done in the dark.

For today: when you see injustice and grow tired of waiting, remember that God governs even each sunrise. Trust that He knows when to bring hidden things to light, and in the meantime live with honesty.
exp.37:13:
It says the earth is transformed by the morning light, like clay when it is pressed with a seal and shows its pattern. At dawn, colors and shapes appear as if the earth were putting on a garment.

God speaks to Job from the whirlwind. He asks him questions to show that Job does not control creation, not even the dawn. God does not explain Job's suffering; he shows him his wisdom and power. Some understand that the seal speaks of how the light reveals the details of the earth, although the image is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when you do not understand what you are living through, remember that the same God who renews each morning also sustains your life. Trust in him, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.37:16:
It says that Job has never seen the gates of death. God asks him whether he has ever been able to see the way into that hidden world.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him one specific reason, but asks him questions about creation, the sea, light and death, to show him that he does not know everything, but that God does.

For today: you do not need to understand everything to trust God. When pain or death leave you without answers, you can rest in the fact that he knows what you cannot see, and remains wise and faithful.
exp.37:18:
This verse asks where the road is that leads to the place where light lives, and where the place of darkness is. It speaks of light and darkness as if they had houses or dwelling places, using poetic language.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a direct answer. Instead, he asks Job a series of questions about creation to show him how limited human knowledge is. The verses nearby speak of death, the earth, and Job's age.

For today: when you do not understand why certain things happen, remember that you do not see the whole picture. You can rest in the knowledge that God does see it all, and trust Him even in dark times.
exp.37:19:
This verse continues the earlier question about light and darkness. God asks Job whether he could take the light and the darkness to their boundaries, that is, to their limits or their place of origin, and whether he knows the paths that lead to the place where they dwell.

Here God himself speaks, out of the whirlwind. Job had asked for explanations of his suffering, and God answers with questions about creation. Through them he shows Job that his wisdom is immense and that Job knows only a very small part. It is poetic language, not a lesson in science.

Today we can learn humility. We will not understand everything that happens to us, but we can trust that God does know what he is doing. When there are questions without answers, we can rest in his care.
exp.37:24:
This verse asks who opened a channel for the heavy downpour and a path for the lightning and thunder. It is a poetic way of saying that rain and storms do not move at random: someone set their course. A "channel" is a watercourse or bed through which the water runs.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him an explanation, but asks him questions about creation to show that God's wisdom and power are far greater than ours.

For today: when a storm comes into your life and you do not understand why, remember that the God who directs even the lightning does not lose control. You can rest in his wisdom, even without having all the answers.
exp.37:27:
Here God asks questions full of poetic images: does the rain have a father? Who gave birth to the drops of dew? "Begotten" means to bring into being or give origin, as a father does with a child. God is not speaking of a literal family, but asking who stands behind the rain and the dew.

God himself speaks to Job out of the whirlwind, after Job had suffered greatly and asked for explanations. Instead of giving reasons for his pain, God shows him the greatness of creation through questions that Job cannot answer. The verses before this one say that God makes it rain even in the desert, where no one lives, so his care reaches further than what we can see.

For today: when you do not understand what you are going through, remember that the God who cares even for the dew of the desert has not forgotten you. You can trust him even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.37:29:
It says that the water becomes hard like a stone, and that the surface of the deep waters freezes over. It speaks of lakes or seas whose surface is covered with ice.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons; instead he asks him questions about creation: the rain, the ice, the stars. In this way he shows Job that his wisdom and power are far greater than what Job can understand.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that God sustains even the things we do not control. Rest in his wisdom, and pray with humility and trust, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.37:33:
What it says: God asks Job whether he can shout at the clouds and make them obey, so that a great quantity of water covers him. Speaking with authority is what the phrase about raising the voice conveys, and the phrase about a multitude of waters refers to heavy rain, like a downpour.

Context: Here God himself speaks, out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a direct answer, but instead asks him questions about creation, to show him how limited a human being is compared with God's wisdom and power.

For today: No one controls the rain, nor so many other things in life. When something has no explanation or is beyond your control, you can rest in the fact that God does govern. Take a moment today to hand over to him in prayer what you cannot manage, trusting in his wisdom.
exp.37:37:
This verse describes dry, hardened ground. The dust becomes firm like stone, and the clods, that is, the pieces of earth, stick together. It is an image of drought, when the rain has not come and the soil is packed hard. It is the final part of a question that begins in the previous verse, about who controls the rains from the sky.

God speaks to Job from the whirlwind. Job had questioned his suffering, and God does not give him explanations about his case, but asks him questions about creation. He wants to show him that wisdom and the order of the world come from him. The clouds heavy with water are described in poetic imagery as the waterskins of the heavens.

For today: when we do not understand what is happening in our lives, we can remember that God cares even for dry ground and sends the rain in its season. We can trust him even without having all the answers.
exp.37:39:
The text of the verse arrived empty, so I am relying on Job 38:39-40, which speaks of young lions when they lie down in their dens or hide in their lairs, waiting. To wait hidden in order to catch prey is what the verse describes. God asks whether Job could provide them with food.

God himself speaks, from the whirlwind, answering Job. After much suffering and many questions, God does not give Job explanations; instead he asks him questions about creation. He wants to show Job that he sustains even the most fearsome of the animals, and that his wisdom is far greater than Job's.

For today: if God cares for the hungry young lions, he can also care for you. When you do not understand what you are living through, let go of the need to control everything, and trust in his wisdom and his care.
exp.37:40:
Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God and wander about without anything to eat? (The text of the verse did not come through, so I am quoting it from memory.)

Here God himself is speaking, answering Job from the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons; instead he asks questions about creation. He wants to show Job that his wisdom and his care reach even to the smallest creatures, though no one else sees them.

For today: if God cares for the young of the raven, you can trust that he also cares for you. When you do not understand what you are going through, bring your need to him in prayer and rest in his care.
exp.38:1:
God asks about the lions: who looks after them when they lie down in their dens, or wait hidden in their hiding places, ready to pounce on their prey? This sentence continues the question before it. Note: in many Bibles this appears as Job 38:40.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons. Instead, through questions about the animals, He shows him that He sustains creation with wisdom and care, and that Job does not see the whole picture.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God cares even for the lion hidden in its den. You can trust that He also cares for you, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.38:3:
This verse asks two questions about wild animals. The mountain goats are the goats that live in the mountains and among the rocks, and the does are the females of the deer. God asks whether Job knows the exact time when they give birth, and whether he has watched them while they bring forth their young. The question assumes that the answer is no.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and had questioned the justice of God. God does not explain his reasons to him, but shows him the greatness of his care for creation, even in places where no one is watching. In this way Job can see how limited his knowledge is.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God takes care of details you cannot see. Trust him even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.38:4:
This verse asks whether a person has kept count of the months in which the mountain goats and the deer are with young, and whether he knows the exact time they will give birth. The question assumes the answer is no.

Here God is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. After Job's long debates with his friends, God shows him the creation: wild animals that no one looks after, yet which are born and grow under his care. With these questions, God is not humbling Job for its own sake; he is inviting him to see how great divine wisdom is and how limited human knowledge is.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that the God who cares for animals that no one sees also cares for you. Rest in him, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.38:5:
The explanation says that the wild goats and the deer bend low when they give birth, bring forth their young, and so bring their labor pains to an end. The verse here speaks of wild goats and deer in the wild places, where Job could not see their birth and care for their young.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him reasons for his pain, but asks him questions about creation. He wants to show Job that he cares for wild animals that no one watches over, and that his wisdom is far greater than Job's.

For today: when you go through hard times that you do not understand, remember that God cares even for what no one sees. Rest in his care, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.38:7:
This verse is a question: who set the wild donkey free and loosed the cords that bound it? The expected answer is that God did.

God himself is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He asks many questions about animals to show Job that he cares for all of creation, including creatures that no one tames or controls. Job had challenged God in his suffering, and these questions remind him how limited his understanding is.

For today: you do not need to understand everything or control everything to trust God. If he cares for the wild donkey in the desert, he also cares for you. Today, bring to him in prayer a situation you cannot resolve.
exp.38:9:
The explanation says that the wild donkey laughs at the noise of the city and pays no attention to the driver, that is, the one who leads and drives the pack animals. It is a free animal that does not obey human shouts. (This passage appears in most Bibles as Job 39:7, not 39:10.)

God speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He asks him questions about the wild animals to show him that He cares for creatures that no one controls. Job had questioned God, and so he learns that God's wisdom is far greater than ours.

For today: not everything God does has an explanation we can understand. When something in your life does not make sense, trust that God knows what He is doing, and rest in His care.
exp.38:16:
The explanation says that the ostrich lays its eggs on the ground and leaves them there, on the dust, where the heat of the sand and the sun helps to warm them. The image shows a bird that seems careless with its young.

God is the one speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He asks questions about the animals to show Job that creation is full of wisdom which Job does not control and does not fully understand. The ostrich seems clumsy, and the text says that God did not give it understanding (verse 17 in other versions expresses it this way). Even so, it lives under the design and care of the Creator. Some scholars explain in different ways how it actually looks after its nests.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows in your life, remember that He is still wise and present. Trust Him even when you do not see all the reasons.
