exp.38:18:
The passage says the ostrich treats its young harshly, as if they were not its own, and does not worry that all its effort may be lost.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He shows Job the creation with many animals, so that Job will see that God knows and cares for things that human beings do not understand. The ostrich is mentioned, and its lack of wisdom, which according to the text God did not give it. Some interpreters see here a careless bird, and others a poetic way of showing that each creature has a design of its own.

For today: we do not need to understand everything to trust God. If He cares even for the ostrich, He also cares for our lives, even when we do not see the reason why.
exp.38:25:
This verse describes the horse in the middle of battle. The quiver is the case where the arrows are kept, and it rattles when the warrior moves. The spear and the lance are long weapons with iron points. All that noise and threat sound around the horse, and yet it does not turn back.

Here God himself is speaking. From chapter 38 on, the Lord answers Job out of the whirlwind, asking him about creation. By showing him animals such as the horse, God reminds Job how much there is in the world that he did not create or control, and that God sustains with wisdom.

For today: we often face problems that sound threatening, and we would like to run away. Just as God gave the horse its courage, he can give us steadiness too. Trust that he cares for you, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.38:26:
This verse describes the war horse. It says he paws the ground with strength and eagerness, impatient to advance, and that not even the sound of the trumpet holds him back. Reading it slowly, you can also notice that some translations render the last part differently: some say he does not stand still when the trumpet sounds, others say he cannot believe the trumpet has already sounded. For that reason it is wise to compare translations.

Here God is speaking. From chapter 38 onward he answers Job with questions about creation, showing him animals that Job does not control and does not fully understand. The horse is an example of the strength and courage that God himself has given.

For today: if God cares for and equips each creature with such attention to detail, we can trust that he also knows our lives, even when we do not understand what we are going through.
exp.38:29:
What it says: God asks Job whether the eagle rises at his command and makes its nest on high. He describes how it lives among the rocks, from where it watches for its food with very sharp sight. Its young feed on blood, and wherever there are dead bodies, there it is. Then God challenges Job: can the one who argues with the Almighty be right? Job answers that he is small and unworthy, and covers his mouth to keep silent.

Context: Job suffered greatly and asked God for explanations. Now God himself speaks out of the storm and shows, through examples from the animal world, that his wisdom and care for creation are immense. Job acknowledges that he spoke without understanding. The verses mentioned span the end of chapter 39 and the beginning of chapter 40.

For today: When you do not understand what you are going through, pause and look at how much God cares for what he created. Trusting him does not require having all the answers, but humbly recognizing that he knows more than we do.
exp.39:2:
Here God asks Job two questions. The first phrase, which the reader will see in the translated text as the wording of his challenge, means to cancel or throw out what God has decided, as if it were unjust. The second describes accusing God of wrongdoing just to prove that oneself is right.

God Himself speaks here, out of the storm, after Job has repeatedly asked for an explanation of his suffering. Job kept insisting on his innocence, and now God reminds him that he cannot sit as judge over the Creator. Earlier, God had also told him to prepare himself like a man to answer.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, you have the right to cry out to God honestly. But guard your heart, so that you do not defend your own righteousness at the cost of accusing God. Trusting Him, even without having all the answers, is a sign of humility and faith.
exp.39:4:
God tells Job to adorn himself and clothe himself with greatness, dignity, and splendor, as a king would. Some Bibles render this verse as Job 40:10 instead.

God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned God's justice, and God answers him with irony: if you think you could correct my rule, then put on the majesty that belongs only to me and govern the world. This is not praise but a challenge that shows the limits of human power.

Today it reminds us that we do not have to understand everything or direct everything. When you doubt God, pause, acknowledge that He is God and you are not, and rest in His wisdom and His care.
exp.39:14:
The explanation says that the mountains provide food for this creature, and that the wild animals of the field play and leap near it. It is a picture of calm and abundance. (This text usually appears as Job 40:20.)

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He speaks of Behemoth, an enormous and powerful animal. It is not known with certainty what it is: some think of the hippopotamus, others of the elephant, and others of a symbolic creature. God wants to show Job that his wisdom and his care are far greater than anything Job can understand.

For today: God cares even for creatures that no one sees. If He sustains His creation in this way, you can entrust Him with your questions and your needs, even when you do not understand everything you are going through.
exp.39:16:
The verse describes a great creature resting peacefully under the shade of leafy trees, surrounded by willows that grow beside the stream. It is a scene of calm and protection in the midst of nature. The shade is thick and the branches close all around it.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He presents Behemoth, a powerful animal that tradition often identifies with the hippopotamus, although some scholars think of another creature, or even of a symbol. God wants Job to see how great and how carefully made his creation is, and how limited human understanding is.

For today: God cares even for the most powerful of the animals, giving it shade and rest. If he provides for his creatures, he can also sustain you. When you do not understand what is happening, trust his wisdom and rest in his care.
exp.39:18:
Does anyone catch this creature by looking at it directly, with traps, or pierce its nose with a hook? Snares are traps, and to pierce means to bore a hole through something. The question implies that no one can do it.

God himself speaks to Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Behemoth, an enormous and powerful creature. Some believe it is a hippopotamus or an elephant; others think it is a symbolic figure. God wants to show Job that there are things in creation that human beings cannot master, and that he can.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God governs what you cannot control. Rest in his wisdom, and speak to him with humility and trust.
exp.39:19:

I invite you to confirm this in your Bible.

What it says: the behemoth is an enormous and powerful animal. It is not frightened even when the river rises, because it feels secure, and no one can easily catch it in traps.

Context: God himself is speaking to Job out of the whirlwind. After so much suffering and so many questions from Job, God shows him his greatness in creation. Interpreters disagree about which animal the behemoth is, perhaps a hippopotamus or a symbolic creature.

For today: when you do not understand what you are living through, remember that the God who cares for creatures so immense also sustains your life. Trusting in him brings calm.
exp.39:20:
It seems the text of this verse did not come through in full, and I don't want to make up what it says. In many Bibles, Job 40:21 belongs to the description of the leviathan, but the numbering differs between versions, so I prefer not to assume the exact words.

exp.39:23:
1) What it says: The text of the verse did not come through to me, but Job 40:24 speaks of the behemoth, an enormous creature. It asks whether anyone could take it by the eyes or pierce its nose with snares or hooks, the way one handles a tamed animal. The implied answer is that no one can.

Context: God is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He shows Job the behemoth to remind him that there are creatures Job cannot control, and that God can. It is not known for certain which animal this is: some think of the hippopotamus, others of the elephant, and others of a symbolic creature.

For today: Not everything is under my control, and that is all right. When I do not understand what is happening, I can rest in the fact that God is wise and powerful, and entrust to him what is beyond me.
exp.40:7:
God tells Job that if he dares to lay a hand on this powerful creature, he will remember the battle and will not try it again. The idea is that confronting it is so dangerous that no one would repeat the experience.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a fearsome creature that many understand as a crocodile, others as a sea monster, and others as a symbolic picture of chaos. The Bible does not fully clarify it. God uses this creature to show that Job cannot master it, much less understand everything God governs.

For today: we do not need to control or understand everything. When life overwhelms us, we can rest in the knowledge that God does have control and is worthy of trust.
exp.40:10:
It says that no one has given God something first so that He would have to pay it back. God declares that everything under the heaven belongs to Him.

God Himself is speaking, answering Job from the whirlwind. He has just described Leviathan, a fearsome creature that no one dares to stir up. His point is this: if no one can stand against that creature, then surely no one can come before God and demand an account from Him. Scholars debate exactly what animal it was, but the argument is understood just the same.

For today: we can live with humility and gratitude. We have not given God anything that was not his before. So instead of making claims on him as creditors, we trust in him as the one who gives everything.
exp.40:16:
This verse continues describing the scales of Leviathan, the creature God presents in Job 41. It says they are so closely joined to one another, and so tightly fitted together, that nothing can pull them apart. The image is of a perfect armor, without gaps or cracks.

Here God is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. After Job's suffering and his many questions, God shows him His power in creation. Many think Leviathan is the crocodile or some other real animal, while others see a symbolic creature of chaos. There is no full agreement. The central idea is that if no one can subdue this creature, then how much less can the Creator be questioned.

For today: when you do not understand what you are living through, do not lean only on your own explanations. Rest in a God greater than your questions, and speak to Him with humility and trust.
exp.40:18:
Here the leviathan is described with images of fire. The phrase for the first image refers to lit torches, and the word for the second refers to sparks that leap out. It says that flames and sparks come out of its mouth, as if it carried a furnace inside.

God is the one speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He presents the leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature that some identify with the crocodile and others with a symbolic monster; it is not known for certain. Through this poetic language, God shows Job that Job cannot even control one of God's creatures, much less understand all the ways of the Creator.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God is greater than whatever frightens you or overwhelms you. Rest in his wisdom, even if you do not have all the answers, and speak to him with humility and trust.
exp.40:21:
It says that the strength of Leviathan is in his neck, that is, in his most powerful part, and that dismay, meaning fear and loss of courage, runs ahead of him. The neck is the back of the neck or the throat area. To dwell means to live or reside. To be scattered means to spread out or be poured forth. Thus, whoever confronts him is left without strength.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a fearsome creature whose identity is interpreted in various ways (perhaps a crocodile or a mythical animal). God is not seeking to frighten for the sake of frightening: he wants to show that if Job cannot face this creature, he is far less able to call the Creator to account.

For today: when you feel that problems overwhelm you, remember that God is greater than everything that frightens you. Rest in his wisdom and his care.
exp.40:22:
It says that the soft parts of this creature's body, which would normally be weak, are tightly joined together and firm. Nothing on it loosens or moves.

God himself speaks out of the whirlwind, addressing Job. He describes Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature. It is not certain which animal he has in mind: it has been thought to be the crocodile, or a symbolic being of chaos. God wants to show Job that there are things in creation that he cannot control or fully understand.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God governs even what seems unmanageable to you. Rest in his wisdom, and speak with him with humility and trust.
exp.40:25:
This verse says that if anyone tries to attack this creature, no weapon will harm it. Neither the sword, nor the spear, nor the dart (a small arrow that is thrown), nor the habergeon (a coat of armor that protects the chest) will be able to withstand it or stop it.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome animal. Some think it is a crocodile; others see a symbolic or mysterious creature. It is not known for certain. The purpose is to show Job that there are things he cannot control, but God can.

For today: when you feel small before problems you cannot overcome, remember that God governs what is beyond you. Trust in Him instead of depending only on your own strength.
exp.40:26:
He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood. For him, the hardest weapons of men are no more than dry straw that crumbles, and steel is like decayed wood. The idea is that the strongest weapons men make seem weak and worthless to him.

God speaks here, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature, which some identify with the crocodile and others with a symbolic monster. God shows that if man cannot master such a creature, much less can he call the Creator to account.

Today we can learn humility. We do not control everything, and there are things beyond our strength. Instead of demanding answers, we can trust God, whose wisdom and power are greater than our own.
exp.40:27:
The explanation says that the arrow does not make Leviathan flee, and that the slingstones turn against him like chaff, that is, like dry straw or light remnants of wheat. An "arrow" is a missile shot from a bow, and a "sling" is a cord used to hurl stones. What could wound others does him no harm at all.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature, which many connect with a crocodile or a sea monster; there is no single certain interpretation. God wants to show that Job cannot master this creature, and therefore cannot judge God's government of the world either.

For today: when you face problems you cannot control, remember that God is above them. Place your trust in Him, not in your own strength, and rest with humility.
exp.40:30:
This verse describes Leviathan, a powerful creature, moving through the water. It says he makes the deep boil like a pot set over the fire, and he makes the sea like a pot of thick ointment, meaning a thick, bubbling mixture.

Here God is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He presents Leviathan to show Job that there are forces in creation that human beings cannot master. Scholars debate whether it is a crocodile, a sea creature, or a symbolic figure of chaos.

For today: if we cannot control even one creature, we understand far less of everything God governs. When life confuses you, you can rest in the fact that God remains wise and strong. Trust in Him with humility.
exp.41:8:
The explanation says that Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite obeyed what God commanded them: to bring seven bulls and seven rams as an offering and to ask Job to pray for them. And God heard and accepted Job. Accepted here means that God received him with favor and answered his prayer.

Here the narrator tells the end of the story. God had rebuked the three friends because they had not spoken about Him rightly, while Job had. God gave them a way out: to acknowledge their mistake with an offering and let Job intercede for them. After this, God restored Job.

For today: when we go wrong, God offers forgiveness if we admit it with humility. Obeying without excuses opens the door to reconciliation, even with someone we may have hurt.
exp.41:11:
God blessed the last part of Job's life more than the first. Job received twice as much as he had before: fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen (pairs of oxen for plowing), and a thousand female donkeys.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling how the story turns out. Job had lost his property, his children, and his health, and he had argued with his friends. After God spoke to him, Job prayed for those friends, and then God changed his circumstances. Some see in this a restoration given as grace from God, not as payment for the suffering.

For today: not every pain is resolved in this life as it was for Job, and God does not promise riches. But we can trust that he sees our suffering and does not forget us. While you wait, pray for those who have hurt you, because that also heals the heart.
exp.41:12:
It says God gave Job a new family: seven sons and three daughters. These are the same numbers he had before his suffering (Job 1:2). The words "had" and "sons" are easy to understand today; what has changed is the older style of the time.

The narrator of the book tells the end of the story. After Job's long suffering and after God spoke to him, Job was restored. The verses before this show his relatives comforting him and God blessing the last stage of his life. The new children do not erase the pain of those who died; they show that God continues to bring life after loss. Some scholars debate how to understand this restoration, but the text presents it as a gift from God.

If you are going through a loss today, you do not have to pretend you have already healed. You can still trust that God is able to open a new chapter, in his time and in his way.
exp.41:15:
After all his suffering and his restoration, the explanation says, Job lived another one hundred and forty years. In that time he saw his children, his grandchildren, his great-grandchildren, and his great-great-grandchildren, that is, four generations.

The words that were once spelled with an accent mark and "á" are now simply written as the ordinary forms of those words, so the spelling changes are only matters of the old script and do not change the meaning.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not Job. He is closing the story after God gave Job back his well-being and gave him new children. Some think the one hundred and forty years count only the time after the trial; the text does not make this entirely clear. What it does show is a long and full life.

For today: God can bring blessing and hope after very hard seasons. He does not always remove pain at once or explain everything, but He is faithful. If you are going through a trial today, keep trusting Him and care for your family, because your faith can also leave fruit for generations to come.
exp.29:20:
It says that Job feels God as someone who has turned against him and is treating him harshly. The verse describes God's hand as strong and opposing him.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost his health, his position, and his respect, and he feels mocked by others. He cries out and feels that God is silent. It is his sincere complaint, spoken out of pain. The book shows that God is not cruel to Job, though Job feels that way, and his perspective is limited.

For today: when you suffer and feel God is distant, you can tell him honestly what you feel, as Job did. But do not stay only with your feelings; remember what God has revealed about himself: he is good and faithful, even when we do not understand.
exp.5:21:
Here Job asks his friends: "Have I ever said, 'Give me something; offer me a bribe from your wealth?'" The verse asks whether he ever asked them to hand him something or to pay for him out of their riches. Job says that he never asked them for gifts or for money from their own means.

Job speaks in the middle of his great suffering. His friends came to comfort him, but they judge him harshly. Job complains to them that he did not ask for money or grand solutions. He only hoped for sincere compassion, and he received reproaches. Earlier he compared them to streams that dry up just when the traveler needs them.

For today: when someone is suffering, often they do not need us to fix everything or to spend a lot. They need presence, listening, and kindness. Before giving advice or judgments, let us ask humbly: "How can I be with you?"
exp.30:26:
It says that Job, if his heart had been secretly drawn away by the sun or the moon, and he had thrown a kiss from his hand as a sign of worship, would have sinned. "Was secretly enticed" means that he was attracted or seduced. "My hand threw a kiss from my mouth" seems to describe a gesture of homage to the heavenly bodies, sending them a kiss with the hand. Some scholars understand it this way, although the gesture is not explained in detail.

Job speaks in his final defense before his friends. He is saying that he has lived with integrity, not only outwardly but also inwardly. In his time, worshiping the stars was a real temptation. He affirms that doing so would have been to deny the sovereign God, and that he would deserve to be judged.

Today we do not usually worship the sun, but we can still admire and love money, success, or beautiful things too much. Ask God to examine your heart in secret, and to be the one who takes first place.
exp.41:2:
Here Job repeats the question God asked him earlier: "Who is this who conceals My counsel without knowledge?" Job admits that he spoke about things he did not understand. The phrase "spoke of things I did not understand" describes words he said without grasping their meaning. Things "too wonderful for me to know" are things too great for him to comprehend.

Job speaks after God answered him out of the whirlwind and showed him his greatness in creation. Job had suffered greatly and questioned the ways of God. Now, when he meets God, he responds with humility and admits his limits. He does not deny his pain, but he acknowledges that he could not see the whole picture.

For today: when you do not understand why something difficult happens, you can bring your questions to God honestly, but also trust that he knows more than you do. Speaking with humility keeps us from drawing hasty conclusions about God.
exp.11:20:
He pours out contempt on nobles, meaning he causes people to look down on them so that they lose their honor. He also disarms the mighty: he takes away the strength of the strong and brave. Here the "mighty" are the powerful or valiant men, and "disarms" means he strips them of the strength they depended on.

Job speaks here in reply to his friends, who were saying that God punishes only the wicked. Job shows that God is sovereign over everyone: kings, judges, elders, and nations. Some read his tone as bitter complaint, and others as genuine praise of God's power. Probably there is a bit of both.

For today: do not place your security in power, reputation, or your own strength, because all of that is passing. Trust in God, who upholds or brings down according to his wisdom, and live with humility.
exp.7:14:
He says the godless person will lean on his web, meaning what he thinks holds him up, but that web will give way. He will grab hold of it, but it will not stay firm. The verse's wording here is the verb "lean" and the verb "hold fast": "He leans" and "he holds fast." The web represents his security, his possessions, and his family.

It is Bildad speaking, one of Job's three friends. He believes suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he hints that Job has forgotten God. Earlier he compared the confidence of the wicked to a spider's web, as fragile as a spider's house. Note: Bildad says something true in general, but he is wrong to apply it to Job, and the book itself shows that Job was blameless.

For today: check where you place your security. Money, success, or plans can fail. Trust God first, and treat those who suffer with compassion, without judging them hastily.
exp.33:3:
It says that we should choose together what is right and learn among ourselves what is good. "Let us choose" means to decide, and "right" here means a fair standard for weighing a matter. It is an invitation to examine carefully, not to offer opinions lightly.

It speaks of Elihu, a young man who spoke up after Job and his three friends had argued. He addresses the wise men present. He is upset because, as he understands it, Job said he was righteous and that God denied him his right. Elihu wants them to weigh Job's words with care. Some scholars see in Elihu a voice with valid points, and others see in him a harsh and presumptuous tone. The Bible does not fully make this clear.

Before we offer opinions or pass judgment on anyone, let us listen calmly, compare what is said with the truth of God, and seek together what is good, with humility.
exp.18:13:
The explanation says that Job's relatives stopped coming near him, and that his friends forgot him. The words "they stopped" mean they stopped visiting or helping. In today's language: they abandoned him when he needed them most.

Job speaks, a man who lost everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends accuse him of having sinned, and he complains that God seems to be against him. In this passage he describes his loneliness: his relatives have failed him, and his friends have forgotten him. Even so, Job continues to cry out to God.

For today: think of someone who is suffering and who may have been left alone. Call them, visit them, or write to them this week. You don't need grand words; often it is enough simply to be present and to listen with kindness.
exp.10:17:
It says that when a person turns back to God, they will trust again because there is hope. The phrase "look around" is worth noticing: it can mean that they will check that everything is well, or it can suggest settling into a safe place to camp. Either way, the idea is that they will lie down and sleep safely, without fear.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he promises that if Job repents, God will give him peace again. Note that the book of Job later shows that Zophar and his friends were wrong to explain Job's suffering this way. Even so, this picture of rest is beautiful.

For today: when anxiety takes away your sleep, bring your worries to God in prayer before going to bed. He cares for you, even when we do not always understand the reason for our trials.
exp.8:0:
This verse is a simple introduction. It says that Job took the floor to answer what his friend Bildad had just said. "Answered" means that Job speaks in reply, and the colon announces that his speech is coming.

Job is in the middle of great suffering: he has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends maintain that God punishes the wicked, so Job must have sinned. Here Job begins to acknowledge the greatness of God, but he also wonders how a human being could bring his case before Him. His words reflect pain and confusion, not always a complete view.

For today: before responding in the midst of pain or a dispute, we can speak honestly before God, without pretending. He hears our sincere questions, and He also invites us to listen to His answer.
exp.20:32:
He says that the clods of the valley, that is, the grave, are sweet or pleasant to the wicked after he dies. "Clods" are the pieces of earth that cover a tomb, so the word here refers to the soil that covers the grave. He then adds that everyone follows behind him, and that those who have gone before are without number. In other words, death is a path that everyone walks, and he will have a quiet burial.

Job speaks here in reply to his friends. They maintained that the wicked always suffer punishment in this life. Job points out that this is often not so: some live prosperously, no one makes any claim against them, and they even receive honors at their funeral. With this he shows that his friends' simple explanation does not hold, and that is why he ends up calling their answers a "fallacy."

For today: do not judge God's justice only by what you see now. Death comes to us all, so trust that God will judge with truth, and live today with humility and uprightness.
exp.15:11:
Job says that he used to live at peace and in comfort, but God shattered him, that is, he broke him apart. The word for the neck refers to the back of the neck. God seized him by the neck, crushed him, and set him up as a target, the mark that archers aim their arrows at.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. His friends accuse him of having sinned, and he, wounded and confused, feels that God himself has become his enemy. It is very strong language, of sincere pain. This is what Job feels, and the book later shows that God did not see him as an enemy.

For today: when pain makes you feel abandoned, you can speak to God with complete honesty, without pretending. Tell him your complaints and your confusion. He listens, and our feelings do not always describe everything that he is doing.
exp.5:4:
It says that a wild donkey does not bray when it has fresh grass, and an ox does not low when it has good pasture. "Groan" means complaining out of pain, and "wild donkey" means a donkey living freely in the wild. The idea is that animals cry out only when something is missing.

Job is speaking, answering his friend Eliphaz. Job has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and he feels an enormous pain. Eliphaz suggested that his complaint was exaggerated. Job replies that his lament has a reason, since he feels the arrows of the Almighty, that is, arrows of suffering. Some understand that Job is defending himself; others, that he is also expressing his despair.

For today: when someone suffers, do not demand that they be silent or downplay their pain. Listen to them with patience. And if you are the one suffering, you can bring your sincere complaint to God, without pretending that you are fine.
exp.35:13:
They die young, in the prime of their years, and their lives end among male shrine prostitutes. Here the explanation says that people who are false at heart die young, and that their lives end among men who sold themselves in pagan worship.

Elihu, the young friend of Job, speaks here, defending God's justice. He believes God corrects through suffering the one who listens, but punishes the one who, out of pride and deceit, does not cry out to Him.

It is worth noting that the book itself shows that Elihu does not explain Job's case well, since Job suffered without being a hypocrite.

For today: do not use the pain of others to judge anyone. Rather, when God corrects you, do not harden your heart or pretend; cry out to Him with sincerity, because He does hear and deliver.
exp.29:11:
At Job's right hand, a crowd rises up. In Job's world, the right hand was the place of a defender or of an accuser. This crowd works to knock his feet out from under him, making him stumble, and they lay snares for him just as someone builds siege ramps to break into a city, so they set up paths meant to crush him.

Job speaks as someone who has lost nearly everything: his children, his property, and his health. In this part of the chapter he painfully recalls that people of low standing, whom he once would not have bothered to consider, now mock and attack him. Job believes God has taken away his strength, and that is why they dare so much. That is his reading of events; the book itself shows that the reality was more complex.

For today: when someone is suffering, we should not trample them further or judge them. Let us come alongside them with respect and practical help, and if we ourselves are suffering, we can bring our honest pain before God.
exp.20:22:
Job says that some people die full of vigor, in the prime of their life, at their best. They die secure and at peace, without suffering or sudden alarm. The "buckets" mentioned in the following verses were containers, and the "marrow" is the substance inside the bones, a sign of good health.

Job is speaking in reply to Zophar. His friends held that the wicked always suffer and the righteous always prosper. Job contradicts them with what he sees: some live well and die in peace, while others die bitter. He says this because he does not accept that his suffering proves he is guilty. What Job describes is his own complaint, not a teaching from God about how life always works.

Today, let us not judge anyone by their health or their fortune. When life seems unfair, be honest with God and trust that He is the just judge.
exp.15:8:
Job says that someone's anger tore him apart. That person became his opponent, gnashed their teeth at him, and pierced him with their eyes.

Job speaks here in the middle of tremendous suffering. His friends accuse him, and he feels that God himself has attacked him. Many understand that the "adversary" is God, as Job perceives him; others think it also refers to those who attack him. Job expresses his pain, though he does not always understand what is happening. In the end, God does not treat him as an enemy.

When you suffer, you can tell God honestly what you feel, even your complaints. Job did not pretend to be fine. Praying with honesty is a way of continuing to draw near to God, not of moving away from him.
exp.5:25:
Job asks his friends whether they really intend to correct his words, when he is speaking in despair. To correct means to criticize or rebuke. He says that the cry of one in despair is "as wind," that is, it blows away and should not be taken as a cold and exact statement of what he believes.

Job is speaking in reply to Eliphaz. He is suffering greatly: he has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. Instead of comforting him, his friends point out his mistakes and accuse him. Job asks them first to understand his pain before they judge his words.

For today: when someone is hurt, listen before you correct. Words spoken in the middle of pain often express anguish, not a settled conviction. Offer presence, patience, and compassion first; correction, if it is needed, can wait for a calmer moment.
exp.3:17:
He says that God does not fully trust his servants, and that he charges his angels with error. "Noted" means that he saw or found. The Hebrew word for "error" is unclear, which is why it is translated in various ways.

Eliphaz speaks, one of Job's friends. He tells that a spirit appeared to him at night and said these words. Eliphaz uses them to hint that Job is suffering for some sin. Note: at the end of the book, God says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7), so not everything he says applies to Job.

For today: none of us can claim to be perfect before God. That invites us to humility and to trust in his grace, not in our merits. But it also warns us not to judge those who suffer, as if their pain were always a punishment.
exp.34:13:
It says that, although Job claims he cannot see God or be heard by him, the truth is that his case stands before the Lord. Therefore he should bring his concern before God with integrity and wait for him. "Look" here means to pay attention to or take into account. The phrase "your case is before him" means that Job's situation has already been placed before God's judgment.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who, after the three friends, answers Job. He believes Job complains too much and speaks as if God did not pay attention. Even so, this verse carries a good exhortation: to trust and to wait. Some think Elihu is partly right and partly wrong in judging Job so harshly; the book itself shows that tension.

Today, when you feel that God is slow or keeps silent, do not stay only in complaint. Bring your case to him with sincerity and wait on him patiently, trusting that he sees and knows what you cannot see.
exp.38:10:
The verse says that the wild animal roams the mountains searching for its food. "The hidden places of the mountains" are the secluded corners of the ranges, where no one goes. There it grazes, moving from one place to another in search of anything green. The verse does not name the animal, and it is not known with certainty which animal is meant.

God himself speaks out of the whirlwind. He asks Job questions about the wild animals to show him that He cares for creatures that no human being controls or feeds. Through this He wants Job to recognize His wisdom and His care.

Today we can rest in the knowledge that God provides even in places where we see nothing. If He cares for what is hidden in the mountains, He also cares for you, even when you do not understand your situation.
exp.33:26:
It says God judges the wicked because they turned aside from him and had no regard for any of his ways. "Turning aside" means no longer following him. "Having regard" means reflecting on something and paying attention to it. His "ways" are both the manner in which God acts and what he commands for living well.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his three friends. He wants to defend that God is just and does no wrong. Here he explains why God punishes the wicked: they turned aside from him and were indifferent, and they also oppressed the poor (v. 28). Some believe Elihu is partly right, but that he does not understand Job's case.

For today: do not live on autopilot. Stop each day to think about whether your decisions are moving in God's direction, and correct your course with humility. Also care for the needy, whom he hears.
exp.2:14:
Job says that if he had died at birth, he would now be resting with princes who had much gold and who filled their houses with silver. Here "filled" simply means "filled completely." It speaks of rich and powerful people who, in the end, also lie in the grave.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. He is in such pain that he wishes he had never been born. For him, death appears as a place of calm where there is no more suffering. It is a sincere expression of grief, not a teaching about how to view death. The Bible shows his complaint without hiding it.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, do not pretend to be strong; tell God honestly what you feel. And remember that wealth and power do not last forever. Seek support from people you trust and entrust your life to God.
exp.20:21:
Scripture says that no one can give lessons to God. He is the one who judges even the highest and most powerful, meaning those who are lifted up in position or in wealth. The question is rhetorical: the answer is no one. "Can anyone teach knowledge to God?" asks, in effect, whether anyone can teach God.

Job speaks here, answering Zophar and his other friends. They claimed that the wicked always suffer soon and the righteous always prosper. Job contradicts them: he sees that some wicked people live at ease and die in peace. Here he acknowledges that God is the one who judges and that his ways are not always understood. Some interpreters see a touch of irony toward his friends in this verse.

For today: when life seems unfair, do not hurry to tell God how he should act. Bring your pain to him honestly, but trust that he sees everything and judges with justice.
exp.17:3:
It says Job tears himself apart in his anger. Bildad asks him, with irony, whether the earth must be abandoned on Job's account, or the rocks moved from their place. The phrase "tear yourself" describes a person ripping themselves apart with rage, and the "rocks" here are great, massive stones.

The speaker is Bildad, Job's second friend. He feels offended because Job rejected their arguments. He believes Job complains too much and that his suffering must be punishment for some sin. The verses that follow show this, since he speaks of the light of the wicked being snuffed out. His view was partial, and at the end of the book God corrects him.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us listen patiently before offering quick explanations. And if our own anger is consuming us, let us bring that burden to God with honesty.
exp.30:4:
Here Job says: "If I have walked in falsehood or my foot has rushed to deceit." The phrase "walked in falsehood" means "lived" or "conducted myself" in what is false. "My foot has rushed" speaks of hurrying toward something wrong. "Deceit" is acting with trickery to gain an advantage.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly and whom his friends accuse of having sinned. In this chapter he makes a final defense and lists possible sins, saying that if he had committed them, he would deserve punishment. He believes God sees all his steps, and so he asks to be examined with justice.

For today: it is not enough to avoid the big lie; it is also wise to review the small shortcuts, such as exaggerating, hiding facts, or pretending to be what we are not. We can pray, "God, examine my ways," and decide today to be honest in one concrete matter.
exp.14:27:
He says the wicked man lived in ruined cities and in abandoned houses that were destined to become rubble. "Ruined" means destroyed, and "rubble" means broken pieces left behind after the collapse.

Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, is the speaker. He describes the wicked person as stubborn and defiant, someone who ends up in cursed or empty places. Some think this is a picture of his arrogance in living among ruins that were not meant for him; others think it announces his own fate of ruin. It is not entirely clear. We should remember that God later rebuked Eliphaz for speaking wrongly about Job (Job 42:7).

For today: let us be careful not to use another person's suffering to judge them. Someone who stands among ruins does not always deserve them. It is better to accompany others with humility and compassion.
exp.31:13:
This verse says that Job has not aimed his words against Elihu, the one who is speaking now. That is why Elihu states that he will not answer Job with the same arguments the three friends used. In the Berean Standard Bible, the words "directed" and "arguments" carry the sense of pointing at someone and of reasoned points made in debate.

Elihu is a young man who listened in silence while Job and his three friends argued. Now he grows angry because the friends were unable to answer Job. Elihu notices that they did not manage to convince him. He promises to speak in a different way, although scholars debate whether he really offers something new or repeats similar ideas.

For today: before correcting someone, ask yourself whether your words come from a personal and humble view, or whether you are only repeating worn-out arguments. Listening with patience and speaking with sincerity helps more than answering back with stock phrases.
exp.10:6:
This verse asks two questions: can a person fully grasp the deep things of God? Can a person discover the limits of the Almighty? The expected answer is no. The word "fathom" points to the depths of God, and "the Almighty" is another name for God.

It is Zophar, one of Job's three friends, who speaks. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and so he tells Job that God knows more than Job understands. His words about God's greatness are true, but the Bible later shows that his accusation against Job was mistaken (Job 42:7).

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, do not judge it, and do not judge others lightly. Trust God even when you cannot see everything, and be humble when you speak about the pain of others.
exp.35:18:
This verse asks whether a person's wealth or all their mighty effort can keep them from trouble. The question points to the limits of riches and personal strength when hardship comes. The phrase about "mighty effort" refers to the resources and influence a person is able to gather.

The speaker is Elihu, the young man who joins the conversation near the end of the book, after Job's three friends. He warns Job not to follow the path of the wicked and not to think that a great ransom will free him from God's judgment.

For today: do not place your security in money or in your position. Before God, what counts is humility, justice, and a sincere heart. Ask yourself today what you are really trusting in.
exp.36:20:
It says that no one can gaze at the sun when it shines brightly in the skies after the wind has swept the clouds clean. "Bright" describes a very brilliant light, and "swept clean" refers to the skies, which the wind leaves free of clouds.

The speaker is Elihu, Job's young friend, near the end of his speech. Before God answers, he describes God's power in nature. If we cannot even look at the sun, how much less can we understand or stand before God, whose majesty is greater still. Some think Elihu is right in this, although his view of Job's suffering is limited.

When you do not understand what God allows, remember that you cannot see everything. Trust in His justice and His goodness, and instead of demanding answers, come before Him with humility and respect.
exp.5:22:
Job asks his friends whether he ever asked them to rescue him from the hand of the enemy. "The hand of the enemy" and "the grasp of the ruthless" refer to people who mistreat others by force. "Redeem" here means to set free by paying a price. It is a rhetorical question: Job reminds them that he never asked them for that kind of help.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends accuse him of having sinned, but he answers that he did not ask them for money or a ransom, only compassion and sincere support. Some believe that "enemy" is a way of speaking about his pains; others, that it alludes to real people. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: when someone suffers, often they do not need us to solve everything or to judge them. They need us to listen with care. Ask them humbly what help they need, and accompany them with patience, without accusations.
exp.36:0:
The speaker says that his heart pounds and leaps at what he has just described, a reaction of amazement and fear. Stands "filled with awe" is how this reaction is best understood: he is startled and filled with reverent fear, and the image of his heart pounding and leaping from its place pictures a heart beating hard, as if it were jumping out of his chest.

The speaker is Elihu, the young man who speaks near the end of the dialogues in Job. He is speaking about God's power in the storm: the thunder and the lightning. He presents them as signs of divine greatness, and so he calls everyone to listen closely. Some scholars think his speech prepares the way for God's answer in chapter 38, although this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you feel small before nature or your problems, stop and recognize the greatness of God. A healthy sense of awe helps you trust Him and rest from wanting to control everything.
exp.28:24:
He said that Job chose the way the people should go and presided at the head as their leader. He lived like a king among his troops, and he was also a comforter to those who mourned. The word "dwelt" here means lived or stayed, and "troops" can be understood as a company or a crowd.

Job speaks in chapters 29 to 31, where he looks back with longing on his life before the suffering. He does this while defending his integrity against his friends. He remembered when people listened to him and sought his counsel. Some scholars see pride in this, while others see a simple, sincere memory of his service.

For today: if you have influence or authority, let it be used not only to direct others but also to comfort. Use your place to walk alongside those who grieve and to guide them with tenderness.
exp.38:20:
This verse describes the warhorse. It says that the horse paws the ground in the valley and takes joy in its own strength, and then it charges forward into battle. The picture is of a horse full of energy and eager for the fight, proud of its power and ready to face danger.

Here God speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He asks questions about the animals to show Job that creation is full of wisdom and power that Job cannot explain or control. The verses around this one describe the horse's strength and fearlessness, which help make the point that God alone made and governs such creatures.

For today: God gives each creature its own gifts and strengths. Instead of comparing ourselves with others or complaining about what we lack, we can be thankful for what God has given us and use it with humility.
exp.12:1:
Job tells his friends that what they know, he also knows. The phrase "I am not inferior to you" means that he is not less than they are. Job affirms that he has the same understanding as they do about God and his ways.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job has seen and heard the same things they have, but he does not accept their explanations. Shortly afterward he calls them "worthless physicians," that is, useless healers, and prefers to bring his case directly to God.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us avoid giving them easy answers or judging them from above. It is better to listen with humility and to accompany them. And if we ourselves suffer, we can bring our sincere questions directly to God.
exp.4:1:
It says that resentment destroys the foolish person, and that envy ends the one who lacks understanding. The word for "fool" refers to a person without wisdom who does not want to be corrected. Emotions left uncontrolled do harm from the inside.

Here Eliphaz, Job's friend, is speaking. He believes that suffering always results from sin, and he suggests to Job that his misfortune has that cause. But the book shows that Eliphaz is wrong to apply this to Job, because God himself declares Job blameless. The statement has some general truth, but it is misused here.

Today, when you feel anger or envy, do not let them grow in silence. Bring them to God in prayer and seek wise counsel, before they hurt you and others.
exp.4:23:
You will be assured that your home is secure and at peace. The "tent" is the house or dwelling where the family lives, and the "home" is the place you return to and look after. When you inspect your flocks and your goods, you will find nothing amiss, with no lack or loss, and the Hebrew word behind that sense carries the idea of something missing or falling short.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He believes that God blesses the person who accepts correction and trusts in Him. His words sound beautiful, but later in this book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. They applied this idea to Job unjustly, as if his suffering were always punishment.

For today: take care of the peace of your home with prayer, kind words, and trust in God. But never use these promises to judge someone who is suffering; walk alongside them with compassion.
exp.9:5:
Here Job asks God why he searches him so closely. The words "seek my iniquity" mean to look for or call to account, and "iniquity" means wickedness or guilt. "Search out my sin" is like tracking down every fault, as someone looks for something lost. It is a phrase that continues the question of the previous verse.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous pain. He feels that God treats him as a guilty man, although he knows he is not wicked. His questions about God's eyes and the days of man express that God is not limited as we are. Job does not say this calmly but with bitterness; the book shows his honest complaint, not necessarily that he is right in everything. There are several ways to understand his tone, but clearly it is a sincere lament.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand why, you can speak to God honestly, even with your hardest questions. But do so trusting that He knows you and is not like a limited human judge.
exp.6:10:
Job says he will not keep quiet. He will speak even though his spirit is anguished, and he will complain even though his soul is full of bitterness. The words "I will not restrain my mouth" mean that he will not hold back or hold in what he feels. The "bitterness" is a deep pain that turns into resentment or heavy sadness.

Job is speaking in the middle of his suffering. He has just said that life is brief, like a cloud that passes away, and that whoever dies does not return. So he feels he has nothing left to lose, and he speaks to God with complete honesty. His friends, by contrast, ask him to calm down and accept his situation.

For today: you do not have to pretend strength before God. You can tell him about your pain honestly, just as Job did. Praying sincerely, even with tears and questions, is a way of trusting that He listens and does not turn away from us.
exp.8:14:
It says that, even if Job were right, he would not be able to answer God. Instead, he would beg his Judge for mercy, that is, for God himself. "Even if I were right" means "even if I were in the right." "Beg for mercy" means asking with humility.

Job speaks in the middle of terrible suffering. His friends say he suffers because of his sin, and he answers that God is so great that no one can win a case against him. Job feels that God strikes him without explanation. Here he expresses his pain and confusion, not a complete teaching about God. Later on, God himself hears him and corrects him with love.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening, do not come before God demanding an account, but with humility and sincerity. You can tell him your pain and ask him for mercy, trusting that he hears you.
exp.22:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that Job now speaks to answer. "Answered" means that he speaks after someone else has already spoken, and the colon points forward to the words that follow.

Here Job speaks, a man who suffers greatly and has lost almost everything. In the previous chapter, his friend Eliphaz told him that he was suffering because of his sins. Now Job replies, and in the verses that follow he expresses his pain with sincerity. He says that his complaint is bitter and that he wishes to find God so that he can present his case.

For today: when you are going through pain, you do not need to hide it or pretend. Job spoke with frankness, and the Bible does not silence him. You can tell God what you feel, honestly and without embellishment. And before answering someone who is suffering, listen with patience, for Job needed comfort more than explanations.
exp.40:23:
Its chest is as hard as a rock, as hard as a lower millstone. The "lower millstone" is the fixed stone on which the upper one turns to grind the grain. It is the hardest of the two, since it bears all the weight and wear. The "chest" here speaks of its whole inner strength and courage.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes an imposing creature called Leviathan, which is sometimes identified with the crocodile or another sea animal, though this is not certain. God shows that Job cannot subdue it, and therefore cannot question divine rule.

For today: when life seems uncontrollable, remember that God governs even what overwhelms you. Rest in Him, without demanding explanations, and trust in His wisdom.
exp.21:10:
It says Job is surrounded by darkness so thick that he cannot see, and that a flood of water covers him. These are pictures of distress: not being able to see the way ahead and feeling overwhelmed by suffering. The word "or" here means "or else," offering another way of describing his situation.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he accuses Job, without any proof, of mistreating widows and orphans. Later, God will show that Eliphaz was wrong about this.

For today: let us not judge the pain of others as if we knew the cause. When someone suffers, it is better to stand beside them with kindness and listen, rather than offer harsh explanations. And if you are in the darkness, remember that God does see you.
exp.30:22:
This verse says that Job did not mistreat the weak because he feared God. "Calamity" here refers to the ruin or disaster that God can bring. "Splendor" means God's greatness and overwhelming power. Job recognizes that no one can stand against or escape a God so great.

Job speaks, in the middle of his suffering, defending his life before his friends and before God. In this chapter he lists sins that he says he has not committed, such as abusing the orphan or trusting in money. Here he explains his motive: he respected God as a just judge. Some understand this fear as deep reverence, and others emphasize dread of divine justice. It probably includes both senses.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat fairly those who cannot defend themselves: children, the elderly, employees, or poor people. Remembering that God sees and that we are accountable to Him helps us act with honesty and compassion, even when no one sees us or asks us to account for our actions.
exp.36:22:
It says that God is Almighty and that we cannot reach him fully, that is, we cannot understand him completely. He is exalted in power. It also says that, in his justice and great righteousness, he does not oppress, meaning he does not treat people with cruelty without cause.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in at the end of the speeches between Job and his friends. After describing the wind, the clouds, and the light of the sky, he concludes that God is majestic and far above us. Elihu tries to defend God's justice, although the book does not present him as the final word; God will speak afterward.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening, you do not have to have all the answers. You can rest in the fact that God is powerful and just, and draw near to him with humility and trust.
exp.27:9:
It describes a miner who hews out channels in the rocks and searches with sharp eyes until he spots every treasure hidden in the stone. "Crags" here means large rocks, and "channels" probably refers to passages or tunnels cut through the stone. With careful eyes, the miner uncovers precious stones and metals hidden away.

The speaker is Job, although some scholars think this chapter is a separate poem about wisdom. Job describes all that human beings achieve through skill and hard work. But he does so to arrive at a question: "Where shall wisdom be found?" Not even the most skilled mining can find it.

Today we can admire what human intelligence accomplishes, but without believing that this alone is enough to live well. True wisdom is not dug out by our own effort; it is sought with humility, by asking God for it and listening to his Word.
exp.8:1:
Job says he knows very well that what has been said is true, and he asks a question: how can a mortal be righteous before God? In other words, how can any person be recognized as innocent or right in God's eyes? Job feels that no human being can stand before God and win his case.

Job is speaking after his friend Bildad told him that God does not pervert justice and that his suffering must have a cause. Job is suffering greatly and does not understand why. He agrees that God is just, but he feels small before God's greatness. Some think Job speaks with sadness; others think he speaks with a certain bitterness. Even so, he expresses an important truth.

For today: we do not need to present God with a list of good deeds to feel accepted. We can come near with humility, trusting in his mercy, and not in our own righteousness.
exp.7:2:
Here Bildad asks a rhetorical question, that is, a question whose answer is taken for granted: "Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right?" The expected answer is no. "Pervert" means to twist or turn aside from what is right, and "justice" and "what is right" refer to what is fair and upright.

Bildad is one of Job's three friends. Job has just lamented his suffering, and Bildad believes Job is hinting that God is unjust. So he answers harshly, and in the verses that follow he suggests that Job's children died because of their sin. Note that the book itself shows Bildad is wrong to apply that idea to Job.

For today: we can trust that God is just, even when we do not understand our pain. But let us be careful not to explain the suffering of others with easy answers. Someone who suffers is better served by kind companionship than by a hasty verdict.
exp.30:14:
The explanation says that the same God who formed Job in his mother's womb also formed his servant. The word "them" refers to the male or female servant mentioned earlier. The phrase "the same One form us" means "made us" or "prepared us," and "womb" is the mother's belly. Job asks: did not God make us both in the same way?

Job speaks in defense of his integrity before his friends, who accuse him of sin. He says he never despised the complaints of his workers, because he knows he will give an account to God. For Job, master and servant share the same origin and the same dignity before the Creator.

For today: treat with respect those who work for you or depend on you. Listen to their complaints with humility, remembering that all of us are created by God and are equally worthy before Him.
exp.8:34:
Job says that if God were to take away his rod and his terror, he would speak without fear. The closing words of the verse, "But as it is, I am on my own," are not simple to read. They may mean that in his present state, with so much fear and pain, he does not feel in command of himself. Others take them to mean that he is not guilty in the way his friends think he is.

Job speaks as a man who suffers greatly and does not understand why. He answers his friend Bildad and longs for someone who would stand between him and God. He feels too small and frightened to bring his case before God.

Today, when suffering fills us with fear, we can be honest with God in prayer. He invites the weary to come near. In Christ we have a mediator, something Job longed for.
exp.40:2:
God asks: will the leviathan beg you for mercy? Will it speak to you softly? The implied answer is no: this creature does not give in or plead.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. After Job's suffering and his complaints, God shows him His power through questions about creation. The leviathan, a strong and fearsome creature (some think of the crocodile, others of a symbolic monster), shows that if a person cannot master it, he is even less able to argue with his Creator.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, do not rely only on your own strength or your own arguments. Come to Him with humility and trust, remembering that He is wise and sovereign.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that the person whom God corrects is blessed. "Blessed" here means fortunate and well off in God's favor. "Correct" and "discipline" refer to God's training or instruction, and "do not despise" means do not treat it lightly or with contempt. The Almighty is God.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to comfort Job by saying that God cares for the one who suffers and that, although he wounds, he also heals. Be careful, though: the book of Job shows that Eliphaz was not entirely right, because Job's suffering was not a punishment for his sin. So his words contain truth, but they do not apply to every case.

For today: when you go through a hardship, do not harden your heart or give up. Ask God humbly whether he wants to teach you something, without assuming that all suffering is punishment. He corrects out of love, and he wants to heal you.
exp.4:26:
Elifaz and his companions say they have examined carefully what they have just said, and that it is true. The verse says "we have investigated," which means they have looked into it and studied it thoroughly. Then he invites Job to listen to it and to know it for himself: "know for yourself" means judge it for yourself, in your own heart, for your own benefit.

The one speaking is Eliphaz the Temanite, the first of Job's three friends. He closes his first speech, in which he argues that God corrects those who need it and that, if Job turns back to Him, he will prosper again. Note, however, that at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). For that reason, their words should not be taken as the complete truth.

For today: listen to advice with humility, but do not accept it without testing it. Compare it with the Word of God, pray, and be compassionate when counseling someone who is suffering, without treating as certain what you do not know.
exp.8:25:
He says that Job's days passed very quickly, like boats of papyrus or like an eagle swooping down on its prey. The word for the boats is uncertain in the original, and some understand them as light boats made of reeds, which fits the picture of something fast and fragile moving over water.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering, replying to his friend Bildad. He feels worn out and believes his life is slipping away quickly, without joy. He uses three images of speed: a messenger, a boat, and an eagle. His pain makes him feel that God is very great and that he cannot defend himself before Him.

Today we can remember that time is short. Instead of waiting for better days, let us ask God for wisdom to live with gratitude and to love the people around us today. If we are suffering, we can speak with God honestly, as Job did.
exp.41:3:
Job asks God to listen: "Listen now, and I will speak," he says, and then, "I will question you, and you shall inform me." The opening words are a humble request. Here Job repeats, in his own words, what God had said to him out of the whirlwind: "I will question you, and you shall inform me" (Job 38:3; 40:7). Now Job takes these words as his own, accepting the role of a learner.

Job speaks after long chapters of complaint and argument with his friends. God has just shown him his greatness in creation, and Job admits that he had spoken about things he did not understand. His attitude changes: he no longer demands explanations but is ready to learn.

For today: when you go through a situation you do not understand, you can speak to God honestly, but also with humility. Ask, yes, but leave room to listen and to be taught.
exp.16:1:
Job says that all around him there are only mockers. "Mockers" are people who laugh at someone with contempt. "Rebellion" means open defiance and rejection of what is right, that is, hurtful words and attitudes. His eyes must keep gazing at that rebellion: he cannot look away from it, and he does not even find rest at night from it.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything and suffers from illness and pain. His friends, instead of comforting him, accuse him and pass judgment on him. He feels alone, with his life nearly spent, and so he cries out to God, whom he considers the only one who can defend him.

For today: when you feel misunderstood or mocked in the middle of a trial, you do not need to pretend you are fine. You can honestly tell God what you feel, as Job did. And if you are the one walking beside someone who is suffering, listen with tenderness before offering your opinion or criticism.
exp.30:37:
It says that if Job's land could bring a charge against him, and its furrows (the lines left by the plow) wept together over some wrong he had done, then he would have to answer for it. It is a picture: the land "cries out" and weeps like a witness against its owner.

Job speaks here, near the end of his long defense. He has already gone over many aspects of his life and declares that he is innocent. In this verse he refers to his fair dealing in the field and with the earlier owners of the land. The next verse makes clear that he says he did not use the land abusively or take advantage of anyone. Commentators see this as a final example of his integrity.

For today: our work, business and money should also be clean. Ask yourself whether what you have was obtained honestly and whether you pay what you owe, so that no one has a complaint against you before God.
exp.34:5:
It says that if a person sins, they accomplish nothing against God or weaken him. And if someone keeps multiplying their wrongs, they still cannot harm him. The words "sin" and "transgressions" in the verse above describe acts of disobedience against God, and the explanation here treats them as such.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who answers Job after the three friends. He wants to show that God is far above us, like the clouds in the sky. His argument is partly true, but it sets aside the fact that God does care about people. For this reason, the book does not present everything Elihu says as the final word.

For today: our sin does harm our own lives and the lives of others, even though God does not depend on us. So confess your faults with humility and seek his forgiveness, knowing that he hears you with love.
exp.7:11:
It says that the shoots of a plant, while they are still green and tender and nobody has cut them, dry up faster than grass. The word "shoots" refers to the young, fresh growth of the plant. The phrase "more quickly than grass" means these plants wither sooner than the grass around them. The image is of something that looks strong but has no firm root.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because he has done something wrong, and he uses examples from nature to say that whoever forgets God comes to a bad end. But the book shows that Bildad is not entirely right: Job's suffering was not punishment for some hidden wickedness.

For today: take care of the roots of your life with God, not just its appearance. Pray, read the Bible, and seek community. But avoid judging others who suffer, as Bildad did; accompany them with compassion.
exp.13:16:
He says that God keeps Job's wrongs the way someone puts something in a bag and seals it shut, so that nothing gets lost. The word "transgression" in the verse above carries a sense of a deliberate turning away from what is right, and the idea of gathering things together is what the verse expresses when it speaks of God covering over Job's iniquity. Job feels that God keeps a careful record of every mistake and adds it all up.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. In this chapter he reflects on how short and fragile human life is. He feels that God watches him closely and that his pain is a punishment for his sins. Interpreters debate whether Job speaks with complaint, with fear, or with a little hope, since just before this he mentions that God might long for "the work of his hands." Let us remember that his friends were not right about everything.

When you suffer and feel guilty, speak honestly to God, as Job did. In Christ, the believer finds forgiveness and not an accumulated list of faults (Colossians 2:14).
exp.24:3:
This verse asks two questions that already carry their own answer: how can a person be declared right before God? How can someone be pure who was born of a woman, that is, a mere human being? "Just" means being recognized as righteous, without fault. "Pure" speaks of moral cleanness.

Here Bildad, one of Job's friends, speaks in his last and shortest speech. He wants to show the greatness of God and the smallness of humanity. His idea is partly true, but he uses it to suggest that Job suffers because of his sin, and in the end God will say that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: acknowledge with humility that you cannot present yourself before God on the strength of your merits. Trust in his mercy, and avoid using truths about sin to judge someone who is suffering.
exp.30:34:
Job wishes that someone would truly listen to him. He longs for God himself to hear him and to speak up for his innocence, even though his accuser has brought charges against him in court.

The phrase "here is my signature" comes from a Hebrew word that can be understood as "my signed defense." Scholars interpret this detail in several ways.

Job speaks at the end of a long speech in his own defense. He has lost everything, his friends accuse him of having sinned in secret, and he insists that he lives with integrity. Here he closes his case and asks God to answer.

For today: when you feel misunderstood or unjustly judged, bring your heart to God with sincerity. He does listen, and he knows the truth. But also ask him to examine your life with humility, since only he judges perfectly.
exp.26:21:
He says that God will hurl his judgment against the wicked without mercy. The word for "hurl" means to throw something with force. The wicked person will run headlong to escape from God's power, but he will not be able to get away.

The speaker is Job, answering his friends, who said his suffering was punishment for some sin. Job insists that he is innocent, but he describes the end of the wicked. Some think he is repeating what his friends say, and others that he affirms it as his own. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not use this passage to judge the suffering of others, as Job's friends did. Rather, do not take lightly the justice of God. Seek his forgiveness today instead of fleeing from Him.
exp.19:13:
It says that what the wicked man enjoyed so eagerly will turn sour inside him. The word "sours" means that it will change and be transformed. The food that once tasted sweet turns in his stomach into the venom of cobras. It is a strong image: sin seemed delicious, but in the end it does harm.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He insists that the wicked always fall soon and that their unjust gain does not last. His words contain truths about God's justice, but he uses them to hint that Job is suffering for some hidden sin. The book itself shows that this conclusion was mistaken.

For today: do not let yourself be fooled by the momentary taste of what is wrong, such as lying or unjust gain. And be careful not to judge others by their suffering, as Zophar did with Job.
exp.5:12:
Job asks whether he still has any resource within his reach. He feels that his strength is gone, and nothing he can draw on seems to be left. The verse describes a man who has run out of his own resources.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. He is answering Eliphaz, one of his friends, who asked him for patience without understanding his pain. Job says he is not made of stone or of steel, and then complains that his friends do not give him the comfort he had hoped for.

Today it reminds us that admitting our weakness is not a lack of faith. If you are exhausted, tell God honestly, and look for someone who will stay with you without judging you.
exp.29:25:
Job says he hoped for good things, but bad things came instead. He looked for light, meaning joy and hope, and darkness fell on him, meaning sorrow and confusion. He expresses the pain of a hope that has been broken.

Job speaks here in the middle of his great suffering. He has just recalled that he wept with those who were in trouble and felt compassion for the poor. That is why he cannot understand why this is happening to him now. His friends tell him he suffers because of his sin, but Job protests and feels that God does not answer him. The book teaches that his suffering was not a punishment for something wrong, although he does not yet know this here.

When life does not turn out the way you hoped, you can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did. You do not have to pretend to be strong. And do not assume that all suffering is punishment; sometimes we do not understand why, but God remains close.
exp.19:1:
Zophar says he cannot keep quiet. His anxious thoughts push him to answer, and that is why he speaks in such a hurry. The verse itself shows this urgency, since the reader sees the phrase "because of the turmoil within me," and that inner unrest is what matters here. He feels a need to answer right away, without waiting or calming down.

Zophar is one of Job's three friends. He has just heard Job's reply, which he feels as a rebuke or an insult to his wisdom. Zophar had already accused Job of suffering because of some hidden sin. Now he feels wounded and answers in anger. His hurry shows more pride than patience, and God does not approve of it at the end of the book.

When something upsets us, it is wise to wait before we answer. Strong thoughts are not always correct. Breathe, pray, and listen first. James 1:19 advises us to be quick to hear and slow to speak.
exp.5:7:
Job says: "If only my request were granted and God would fulfill my hope." The wording is simple: "if only" expresses longing, and "fulfill my hope" means to bring about what he has been waiting for. What Job hopes for, according to the verses that follow, is that God will bring his life to an end.

Job speaks in the midst of enormous pain. He has lost his children, his property, and his health, and his friend Eliphaz has just given him a speech with little compassion. Job answers with raw honesty: his suffering is so great that he would rather die. Even so, he says he has not denied the words of God. His complaint is sincere, but it is not an abandonment of faith.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you can speak with God in complete honesty, without pretending to be strong. And if you are going through thoughts of giving up, seek out also someone you trust or a professional who can walk alongside you.
exp.32:10:
He says that God, according to Job, put his feet in the stocks and watches over every step he takes. The stocks were a block of wood with holes where a prisoner's feet were locked. Here "watches over" means that God kept close watch over him, like a jailer.

The one speaking now is Elihu, a young friend of Job. He quotes the words Job said earlier (Job 13:27) and repeats them to correct him. Job felt innocent and believed God was treating him like an enemy. Elihu says Job has not spoken with justice, because God is greater than man.
