Note: Elihu does not have the final word; later God himself speaks.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand why, you can be honest with God, but avoid accusing him. Trust that he sees more than you see.
exp.27:3:
This verse is difficult, and scholars translate it in several ways. In this rendering, the miner is the one who cuts a shaft far from where people live, in places where no one has ever walked. The verse pictures him hanging and swaying as he works in the depths, far from other human beings.

The speaker is Job, in a poem about wisdom. He describes the remarkable human skill for bringing metals and precious stones out of the darkest parts of the earth. But he does this to show afterward that true wisdom is not found that way; it comes from God (vv. 12-28).

For today: we can accomplish admirable things with our effort and our intelligence, but the wisdom to live well is received from God. Ask Him for it with humility and reverence.
exp.33:0:
It says that Elihu speaks again. The phrase "then Elihu continued" means he kept speaking or went on with what he was saying. It is just a transitional phrase: Elihu had already spoken before, and now he picks up his speech again.

Elihu is a young man who listened in silence to the long debate between Job and his three friends. He grew angry because he felt that no one was answering well: Job justified himself too much, and the friends did not convince him. Here begins his third speech, in which he argues that God is just. Scholars differ on how much right Elihu has, since God does not correct him afterward, yet God also does not explicitly approve of him.

For today: before accepting what we hear, it is wise to examine it calmly, as the palate tests food. Let us listen carefully, but compare everything with the Word of God and with humility.
exp.15:1:
Job says that he has already heard many times words like those of his friends. He calls them "miserable comforters," that is, people who say they want to console, but who in reality wear him out and make his pain heavier. The word "you" here is addressed to all three of them together.

Job is suffering greatly, after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, have come to help him, but they insist that his suffering must be punishment for some sin. Here Job responds with pain and weariness, because he feels that their speeches neither relieve him nor truly understand him.

For today: when someone is suffering, sometimes the best thing is not to offer quick explanations, but to listen, to accompany, and to show compassion. Before speaking, let us ask: does this help them, or does it only make me feel that I am helping?
exp.26:7:
He says that the godless person, even if he has piled up much wealth by unjust means, has no true hope when he is cut off by death. The "godless" is someone who turns away from God and lives without regard for what is right. Saying God "takes away his life" means that God brings his life to an end, suddenly and without warning. Everything he gained does him no good on that day.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. His friends tell him that he suffers because of some hidden sin, but he insists that he is innocent and will not give up his integrity. Here he affirms that someone who lives in ungodliness cannot have confidence before God. Some think Job answers his friends with irony, but the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: a sincere life is worth more than a good reputation or an unjust gain. Ask yourself whether what you show on the outside matches what you live on the inside, and ask God for help to be honest.
exp.39:0:
This verse says that the LORD speaks to Job again. The name here is the LORD, the personal name of God, and the verse opens with a word that links this moment to what came before. In this reading, the earlier speech from the whirlwind is still in view, and now God addresses Job directly once more.

Job had suffered greatly and had asked God for an explanation. God had already spoken to him earlier, showing his power and wisdom in creation. Now he speaks again, and his questions aim to help Job see that God governs the world with a wisdom greater than his own.

For today: when we do not understand what is happening to us, we can bring our questions to God, but also bring humility, trusting that He knows and cares more than we can see.
exp.33:30:
It says that the right thing is to speak to God with humility and to acknowledge: "I have endured my punishment; I will offend no more." "Suppose someone says" frames this as a fitting words for a person to speak to God. "I have endured my punishment" means that the person has suffered the correction and accepts it. "Offend no more" refers to not doing wrong again.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He thinks Job should respond to his suffering with repentance rather than complaints. Note: the book shows that Job was not suffering because of a specific sin, so Elihu's words do not explain his whole case. Even so, his idea of humility before God has value.

For today: when life corrects you or hurts you, do not defend yourself right away. Speak to God honestly, ask him to show you what you should change, and trust in his care.
exp.16:9:
Job tells his friends to come back and try again, all of them, and to make another attempt at speaking to him. But he has already reached his conclusion: he will not find a wise man among them. The word "But" marks this contrast, and "come back and try again" simply invites them to return and speak once more.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. His friends insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin, and he feels that their advice has neither true wisdom nor comfort. His tone is one of weariness and rebuke. Some readers take it with a certain irony; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Before offering advice to someone who is suffering, it is wise to listen with humility. Wisdom does not consist in having quick explanations, but in keeping someone company with compassion, and in recognizing that we do not always understand what God allows.
exp.35:14:
God rescues the afflicted through their own suffering. "Rescues" means to save or bring someone out of danger. "Opens their ears" means that God opens the person's ability to hear and understand. Affliction, then, can become a way in which God speaks to us.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who answers Job after the other friends. He holds that God corrects and saves the humble who listen to him, while the arrogant harden themselves and do not cry out. Many interpreters think that Elihu speaks wisely in part, but there is debate about whether he is right to apply this to Job.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, ask God to open your ears. Before asking only "why?", ask "what do you want to teach me?" And do not judge others who suffer as if their pain were always punishment.
exp.0:4:
He says that, when the days of feasting ended, Job would send for his children and purify them, making them clean before God. Early the next morning he would offer burnt offerings, one for each of them. He was afraid that his children might have sinned and cursed God in their hearts. This was Job's regular practice.

The speaker is the narrator of the book, who shows us Job's character before his suffering. After describing his wealth and his family, he stresses that Job was a careful man in his relationship with God. His reverence was sincere and constant, not only for himself but also for his children.

Today we can pray steadily for our family, without living in fear, but with an attentive heart. Interceding for those we love is a real way of caring for them before God.
exp.18:10:
The explanation says that God's anger burned against Job and that God counted him among his enemies. The phrase "His anger burns against me" means that God's anger felt like a fire. The phrase "He counts me among His enemies" means that God placed Job on the list of those he opposed.

Job speaks here. He is a righteous man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends tell him he suffers because of his sin. Job does not understand, and he feels that God is against him. This is what he feels, not what God thinks. At the end of the book, God himself says that Job was his servant (Job 42:7-8).

For today: when pain makes you feel that God is far away or angry with you, do not keep it silent. Job spoke honestly to God. Bring him your questions and your complaint, and remember that what you feel is not always the whole truth.
exp.29:3:
They plucked mallow leaves from among the shrubs, because they were so hungry. They also ate the roots of the broom tree, a desert shrub. Some translators understand that these roots were their food, and others that they were firewood or charcoal. The Hebrew text allows both ideas.

Job is speaking. He is recalling what his life was like before and how it is now. He describes outcast men, younger than he is, who now mock him. His extreme poverty serves to show how far he has fallen, he who was once respected.

For today: Job reminds us that extreme poverty is painful and real. Let us ask God for compassionate eyes so that we do not despise those in need, and look for a concrete way to help someone near us.
exp.33:36:
It says that Elihu thinks Job adds one more fault to his sin: rebellion. The word "rebellion" here points to a refusal to submit to God. Elihu claims that Job claps his hands, a gesture that can express mockery or scorn, among the people, and that he speaks much against God.

The one speaking is Elihu, the young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He believes that Job, by defending his innocence so insistently, is speaking without understanding and accusing God of injustice. Note: this is Elihu's opinion, and the book shows that Job was not a wicked man; in the end God himself corrects both Job and the friends. Elihu is right about some things concerning the greatness of God, but he goes too far in judging Job.

For today: when you suffer, be honest with God and pour out your heart to him, but guard your words so that you do not accuse him or harden your heart. And when you speak with someone who is suffering, avoid judging them; instead, listen with humility.
exp.21:11:
He says that God is high above, in the highest part of the heavens. Eliphaz invites Job to look up at the stars: they are very far away and very high, and God is higher still. The Hebrew word that stands behind this picture points to something lifted up or raised high, a picture of God's greatness.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He is accusing Job of sins that are not mentioned anywhere else, and he believes Job's sufferings are a punishment. In the verses that follow, he says that Job thinks God cannot see from so far away. Note that Eliphaz is the one attributing that thought to Job, and that God later says the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: God's greatness is true, but it does not mean that He is far away or blind to our pain. Before judging someone who is suffering, it is better to walk alongside them with humility and compassion.
exp.6:19:
If I have sinned, I have failed or done wrong, so Job asks God what he could have done to harm him. He calls God "the watcher of mankind," someone who sees over people and keeps a close eye on them. Then he complains: why have you made me your target, and why have I become a burden to you? The image is of a target that is singled out and hit again and again. "Burden" means a weight that is hard to carry.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He feels that God watches him closely and gives him no relief. Here he does not admit to a specific guilt; rather, he acknowledges that he is human and asks what sense there is in so much pain. His friends insist that he suffers because of his sin, but he struggles to understand.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you can speak to God honestly, even with hard questions. He is not frightened by your complaint. Bring him your weariness and ask him for forgiveness and comfort.
exp.4:5:
Job 5:6 says that distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground. In other words, hardship and suffering do not appear on their own, as if they grew out of the earth without cause. Here "distress" means harm or misfortune, and "trouble" means pain or affliction. The point is that problems have an origin and do not arise by chance.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes that suffering comes as a consequence of sin, and so he hints that Job is suffering because of something he did. However, the book itself shows that this explanation was incomplete and mistaken in Job's case. What Eliphaz says about suffering does not always apply.

For today: when you suffer, or see someone else suffering, do not rush to look for someone to blame. Some afflictions have causes we do not understand. It is better to accompany others with compassion and seek God with humility.
exp.38:0:
God asks Job: "Can you hunt food for the lion and satisfy the hunger of its young?" The verse in your Bible reads: "Do you know when mountain goats give birth? Have you watched the doe bear her fawn?" Note: in most Bibles this text appears in Job 38:39.

God is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons. Instead, He shows Job His care for creation, even for the lion and the raven, so that Job can see the limits of his own knowledge and power.

For today: if God cares for the animals that no one sees, you can trust that He also cares for you, even when you do not understand what you are going through. Today, bring one worry to God in prayer and rest in the fact that He knows more than you do.
exp.35:15:
This verse says that God would draw you out of the jaws of distress, that is, out of a situation that seems to swallow you up, and lead you to a spacious, open place. The image of a table full of richness speaks of abundant provision and blessing.

Here Elihu speaks, a young man who steps in near the end of the book. He tells Job that God corrects those who suffer, but also rescues them if they listen. Elihu suggests that Job was in danger of falling into the judgment of the wicked. His view of suffering is partial, since the book shows that Job was not suffering because of wickedness.

For today: when you are in tight places, do not just stay looking at the problem. Ask God to teach you and trust that He can open a wide path, even if you do not know how or when.
exp.20:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that Job takes up the word to answer what his friend has just said to him. "Answered" means that he replies to an earlier speech, and the colon announces that he is about to speak.

Here speaks Job, a man who suffers greatly and has lost his possessions, his children, and his health. Earlier, Zophar, one of his three friends, spoke and hinted that Job suffers because he is wicked. Job now begins his reply by asking that they listen closely. In the verses that follow he asks them to let him speak, and then, if they wish, to mock him.

For today: before giving advice to someone who suffers, let us learn to truly listen to them. Often the best comfort is to be silent, pay attention, and not rush to judge.
exp.5:17:
The explanation says that the caravans searching for water leave their route and wander into the wasteland, where they are lost and die. "Caravans turn aside from their routes" describes travelers who step off the course they were following; "go into the wasteland" means they head out into the empty desert; "perish" means they die there.

Job speaks, answering his friend Eliphaz. Job compares his friends to winter streams: they seem to promise comfort, but when he most needs them, they give him nothing. The travelers of Teman and Sheba, places far away and known for their caravans, came with hope and were left disappointed. Some scholars see a somewhat different picture of the watercourse here, but the central idea of disappointment is clear.

For today: let us strive to be dependable people in the pain of others. Before offering explanations or advice, let us accompany them with presence, listening, and compassion, and let us seek God, who never runs dry.
exp.41:4:
In this verse Job says that before, he knew God only through what others had told him, like someone repeating what he had heard. Now, after hearing God's voice, he feels that he knows Him directly and truly. "My eyes have seen You" expresses a personal encounter, not necessarily that Job saw a physical form.

Job speaks here after suffering many losses and after a long argument with his friends. God answered him out of the whirlwind and showed him His greatness and wisdom. Job recognizes that he spoke about things he did not understand. Then he humbles himself and repents. Afterward God vindicates Job before his friends, because they had not spoken rightly about Him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith rests only on what we have heard from others. God invites us to seek Him personally in prayer and in His Word, especially in times of trial, trusting Him even when we do not have all the answers.
exp.30:9:
Job says that if he had been unfaithful, then his own wife should grind grain for another man, and other men should sleep with her. Grinding grain was the work of servant women, and many believe that here it also suggests sexual relations; scholars understand it in several ways. The second image, of other men sleeping with her, shows the same kind of harm, and it is a curse that Job accepts if he were found guilty.

Job, a long-suffering man whom his friends accuse of being a sinner, speaks in this chapter and makes an oath of innocence. He says that his heart was not deceived by another woman, nor did he lie in wait at his neighbor's house. For him, adultery is a serious wrong, and he recognizes it as something that God and the judges punish.

For today: guard your faithfulness from the heart, not only from your actions. Turn away quickly from thoughts and glances that harm your marriage or someone else's, and ask God for help to be upright in private too.
exp.29:18:
He says that Job feels thrown into the mud, as if God had thrown him down there. The idea of being knocked down or thrown to the ground is what the original language conveys here, and it is rendered in your Bible as "He throws me into the mud." When Job says he has become "like dust and ashes," he expresses that he feels worthless, fragile, and humbled. It is language of deep pain, not a calm explanation.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his body aches at night. In this chapter he contrasts his former honor with the present contempt. He addresses God with complaint, because he feels that God does not hear him. Some readers see this being thrown down as the work of God according to Job; the book shows that this is his perception, not the whole truth.

Today, if you feel fallen and without strength, you can speak to God honestly, even with your complaints. Job did not pretend to be well, and you are not alone in your pain.
exp.34:2:
Here Elihu reminds Job of something he asked: "What does it profit me, and what benefit do I gain apart from sin?" The idea behind the question is this: "What good does it do me to live rightly, if things end up for me just as they do for the one who sins?" It is a complaint about whether it is worth obeying God.

Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job's three friends, corrects him. He believes Job went too far in feeling more righteous than God. Some scholars think Elihu summarizes what Job said poorly, and others think he interprets it rightly. Even so, Elihu wants to defend God's justice and to have Job see God as greater than his suffering.

For today: when you suffer, avoid measuring your faith only by what you gain. Obeying God is not a business transaction aimed at benefits, but a relationship of trust. Speak to Him honestly, but let Him be God.
exp.41:13:
Job gave names to his three daughters born after his suffering. The names are written here as Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch. Many understand them to mean "dove," "cassia" (a fragrant spice), and "horn of paint" (an eye cosmetic), though some of these meanings are uncertain.

The narrator of the book tells the end of the story. After the trial, God restored Job. That the daughters are named, and not the sons, stands out, and the next verse says that Job gave them an inheritance along with their brothers, something uncommon in that time. It seems to show the care and dignity Job gave them.

For today: God can bring new life and blessing after pain. Value and bless the people God gives you, without making distinctions, and recognize their goodness with gratitude.
exp.28:19:
He says that Job's honor and good name stayed new within him, as if fresh each day. Here "glory" means respect, standing, or reputation. "My bow is renewed in my hand" means that his bow, a symbol of strength and ability, kept being strengthened and made firm again.

Job speaks here in his lament. He looks back with longing at how his life was before the suffering: he had health, respect, and the expectation of dying peacefully in his home. He says this while he is in ruin, to show how much he has lost and that his former life had been whole. Some see in the bow a symbol of strength or of readiness to act; the text does not clarify this further.

For today: thank God for good seasons as a gift, not as something guaranteed. And if you are going through a hard stage today, you can speak to God honestly about what you miss, as Job did.
exp.30:18:
He asks Job to consider whether he ever saw anyone die of cold for lack of clothing, or a needy man without a cloak, and did nothing. "Perish" means to die or come to an end; "needy" means someone in want; a "cloak" is a warm outer covering. It is a question left open, and the implied answer is that Job did not stand by indifferently.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, defending his integrity before his friends, who accuse him of having sinned. In this chapter he makes a series of oaths: "if I have done such a thing, let the punishment fall on me." Here he points to his care for the poor, the orphans, and the widows as proof of an honest life before God.

For today: check your closet and your surroundings. Donate or hand over a garment or blanket in good condition to someone who needs it, perhaps through your church or a trustworthy organization. Faith is shown in concrete acts of care.
exp.32:2:
Here, Elihu says that when he speaks he promises to say what he really thinks. His "words" are the points he makes, and the claim that his lips "speak sincerely what I know" means that he will say only what he truly understands. He claims that his heart is upright and that what he says will be sound wisdom, with no trace of deceit.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who had not joined in until now. He addresses Job after Job's three friends stopped answering him. Elihu believes he can make clear what they could not. His confidence is very great, and the book does not say that God approves of it; later God corrects Job but does not mention Elihu, and interpreters evaluate him in different ways.

For today: before advising someone who is suffering, examine your own heart. Speak with humility, without presuming that you are entirely right, and let God be the one who has the final word.
exp.31:9:
Elihu asks them to listen to him, and he says that he too will declare what he knows. "Declare" and "what I know" capture the sense of the verse's wording for his telling what he understands, and "my wisdom" refers to his way of understanding the matter. "Listen to me" is the same request as the verse's opening words.

Elihu is the young man who speaks after Job and his three friends, who are older than he is, finish their debate without reaching any conclusion. He had kept quiet out of respect for their age, but now he feels he must speak. He says that understanding comes from the spirit God gives, not only from years. Some scholars see in him a sincere young man, and others see him as somewhat conceited; the text leaves room for both readings.

Today we can learn to listen to everyone, young and old, because God can give light through anyone. And if we speak, let us do so with humility and after having listened well.
exp.29:30:
Job says that his joyful music has turned into weeping. The "harp" and the "flute" were instruments of celebration and praise, and the flute is the instrument the Berean verse names. "Mourning" is sorrow over a loss, and "weeping" is crying out in grief.

Job speaks in his last great speech of complaint (chapters 29 to 31). He remembers how he was respected before, and now he describes his pain: sickness, mockery, and loneliness. Here he closes his lament by saying that there is no more song in his life, only grief. God has not yet answered him.

For today: if you are going through a time when you feel no desire to sing, do not pretend to be joyful. You can bring your sincere sorrow to God, as Job did, and look for someone you trust who can stand with you in that pain.
exp.38:22:
This verse describes the war horse. The question is whether anyone could startle it like a locust, making it leap and run away with ease. But the horse does not scare easily. The snorting of its nostrils commands respect. The word "terrifying" here means that it causes fear or awe.

The speaker is God, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was questioning God. Then God asks him a series of questions about creation and the animals, to show him that God made them and sustains them. That is why he asks: "Did you give the horse its strength?"

For today: when we do not understand what is happening in our lives, we can look at the strength and order of what has been created and remember that God knows what He is doing. Trusting Him is wiser than demanding explanations from Him.
exp.6:11:
Job asks God whether he is the sea, or the monster of the deep, that God must keep him under guard. The word "guard" in the verse above refers to close observation, like a guard who keeps a prisoner under constant eye. Job asks: "Am I some dangerous monster, that you keep me under guard?"

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He feels that God watches him and hems him in, even at night, with dreams that frighten him. In the ancient world, the sea and sea monsters sometimes symbolized chaos that had to be restrained. Job exaggerates and complains honestly. His words express his pain, not necessarily a truth about God, and the book itself shows that his view was limited.

When you suffer, you can speak to God with sincerity, even with complaints. He is not frightened by your pain. Bring him your questions in prayer, and let him hear them and hold you up.
exp.25:12:
By his breath he made the skies clear and bright. Some understand this as his breath. The "fleeing serpent" is a creature that slips away and writhes. Some believe it is a constellation, and others think it is a sea monster that symbolizes chaos. It is not known for certain.

Job is speaking, replying to Bildad, who had said that God is great and that human beings are insignificant. Job shows that he too knows the power of God, but he acknowledges that what we see of Him is only a small part.

For today: when life feels disordered or threatening, remember that God governs even what we fear most. Take a moment to look at the sky and trust in Him, even though you do not understand everything.
exp.0:0:
This verse introduces Job, a man who lived in the land of Uz. It describes him with four traits: "blameless" means whole and sincere, with no double life; "upright" means he was just and honest with others; "fearing God" means he held God in reverence and took him seriously; and "shunning evil" means he deliberately turned away from what was wrong.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and he does not identify himself. No one knows for certain who wrote it or when, and it is not known exactly where Uz was, though it is usually placed to the east of Israel. The author wants us to know from the start that Job was an exemplary man, so that we see his later suffering was not a punishment for some hidden sin.

For today: let your faith show in your daily life, in your work, your family and your decisions, not only at church. A whole life will not spare you from trials, but it gives you firm roots when they come.
exp.26:1:
Job begins with an oath: "As surely as God lives." He says that God "has deprived me of justice," meaning that God has denied him a fair hearing and has not defended his case. He also calls him "the Almighty," the All-powerful, who "has embittered my soul," that is, who has filled his life with pain and sorrow.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends insist that he suffers for some hidden sin, and he denies it. Even while feeling unjustly treated, he swears by God himself. His words are sincere and painful, not a calculated accusation. The verses that follow show that he will keep speaking with integrity.

For today: you can be honest with God about your pain, even when you do not understand what is happening. Bringing him your bitterness is better than turning away from him. And even in trial, you can choose to keep your words and your conduct clean.
exp.37:35:
Job 38:36 asks a question: who has placed wisdom in the heart, and who has given understanding to the mind? The wording here refers to the heart and mind, the seat of thinking and knowing. The Hebrew word behind this verse is hard to pin down. Some scholars take it to mean the heart or the mind, while others suggest it may refer to the clouds, or even to a bird, the ibis. That is why translations differ, and there is no full agreement on the exact sense.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned God about his suffering. God does not explain his reasons to him, but asks him questions about creation: clouds, lightning, the heavens. In this way he shows Job that his wisdom surpasses that of any human being.

For today: recognize that all your intelligence is a gift from God. When you do not understand what you are living through, rest in the knowledge that He knows more than you do, and ask Him for wisdom with humility.
exp.0:12:
This verse tells us that one day, while Job's sons and daughters were gathered together, eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother, the firstborn. The sentence simply begins with "one day," so the wording stays close to the plain telling of a particular day.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Just before this, God allowed Satan to test Job, but with a limit: he could not touch Job himself. The verse describes a common, peaceful family scene, and it lets us see that what follows strikes without warning. The text does not say that the children were doing anything wrong at that gathering.

For today: we do not know when a trial will come, so it is wise to value and care for family now. Thank God for your loved ones, show them your affection, and trust that God remains with you even when everything changes suddenly.
exp.38:12:
God asks Job whether he could tie the wild ox to his yoke so that it would pull the plow and break open furrows in the valleys. The yoke here is the wooden frame or harness that joins working animals together. In Hebrew the animal is called the reem, which was probably a large, strong wild bull, now extinct, though scholars are not entirely certain. It was not the horse with a horn of the fairy tales.

God himself speaks out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not answer with reasons, but with questions about creation, showing that there are creatures no human being can master or fully understand.

For us today, this means we do not need to control or comprehend everything that happens. We can rest in the knowledge that God holds what we cannot manage, and entrust to him what we do not understand.
exp.6:5:
The explanation says that Job's days pass more quickly than the shuttle of a weaver, the piece that moves back and forth swiftly between the threads of the loom. And "they come to an end" means that they run out. Job feels that his life is slipping away and that he has no hope left that things will improve.

Job is the one speaking, a man who lost almost everything: children, possessions and health. He is sick, suffers at night and feels worn out. Here he answers his friends and speaks to God with sincerity, without disguising his pain. Some scholars see in "without hope" an expression of the moment rather than his final word, since later Job again puts his trust in God.

When pain makes you feel that life is passing without meaning, you can speak to God with complete honesty, as Job did. He is not frightened by your complaints. Tell him what you feel, and also seek the support of people you trust.
exp.14:30:
He says that a person who deceives himself should not rely on what is empty, because emptiness is all he will receive in return.

The word translated as "deceive" here refers to someone who has been fooled and believes something false. Here "emptiness" means something without worth or lasting substance, like smoke. "Reward" is what a person harvests in the end.

The one speaking is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's three friends. He describes what he believes happens to the wicked, and he uses it to suggest that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. But the book shows that Eliphaz was wrong to apply this to Job, and God himself corrects him at the end.

For today: let us examine what we rest our security on. Money, fame, or appearances may look firm, but they cannot sustain the soul. And when we see someone suffering, let us not judge them quickly; rather, let us walk alongside them with humility.
exp.1:5:
God tells Satan that Job is in his hands, meaning that he allows Satan to test Job with suffering. But he sets a clear limit: "you must spare his life," that is, Satan may not take Job's life.

God speaks, answering Satan, who has just suggested that Job is faithful only because he has not suffered in his own body. God had presented Job as a man of integrity, and now he allows a new test. Even so, Satan acts only as far as God permits.

For today: in moments of pain, it can seem that everything is out of control. This verse reminds us that suffering has limits that God knows. We will not always understand the why, but we can trust that we are not abandoned and keep seeking him sincerely.
exp.29:14:
Here Job says that terrors have been turned loose against him. They drive away his dignity as if by the wind, and his prosperity has passed like a cloud. His dignity and his sense of who he is are being blown away, and what he once had has vanished quickly, like a cloud that drifts off and disappears.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. In this chapter he contrasts his former honor with the present contempt: people who once respected him now mock him. He feels unsupported and without direction, and he expresses this with raw, sincere pain.

For today: when everything seems to fall apart and you feel your peace has slipped away, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God your anguish honestly, as Job did, and look for someone you trust who will stand with you.
exp.22:14:
Job is overcome with dread before God. The phrase "I am terrified in his presence" describes the fear and distress he feels when he stands before him. The words "when I consider this" mean that he thinks deeply about all of it, and "I fear him" means that he is afraid of God.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. He has lost everything, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He wants to bring his case before God, but he cannot find him. Now he thinks that God does what he decides and that no one can stop him. That is why he feels overwhelmed, unable to understand what is happening. It is an honest lament, not a final conclusion; Job will go on to trust.

Today, when you do not understand what God allows, you can be honest with him, as Job was. Bringing your fear and your questions to him in prayer is healthier than keeping them silent. And remember that a feeling is not the whole truth about God.
exp.17:17:
This verse says that the wicked person will be taken from the light and driven into darkness, and that he will be chased from the inhabited world. The words "driven" and "chased" match the wording of your verse, so you can see them there. Light stands for life, well-being and favor; darkness stands for ruin and death.

Here Bildad, Job's friend, is speaking. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he describes the end of the wicked with harsh images. But at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. So their words describe a partial idea, not the whole truth about Job.

For today: do not judge the pain of others as if it were certain punishment. Accompany them with compassion, listen, and let God be the judge.
exp.22:12:
However, he is unchangeable, and no one can oppose him. He does what he desires.

This means that when God has made a decision, no one can make him change his mind. "However" introduces the contrast with what Job has just said. "He is unchangeable" means that God's purpose stands firm. The phrase "what he desires" simply says that whatever God wants, that is exactly what he does. In other words, God acts freely, and no one can stop him.

Job speaks here, a man who suffers greatly without understanding why. He has just said that he has been faithful to God and that he valued God's word more than food. Now he acknowledges that God is sovereign, but this fills him with fear, because he cannot bring his case before God or change what God has decided. There are different ways to understand his tone: some read it as confidence, others as complaint or anguish.

When you do not understand what you are going through, you can remain faithful and rest in the knowledge that God does not act without purpose. Bring your pain to him honestly, while still showing him respect.
exp.32:8:
This verse repeats what Elihu says Job claimed: "I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, with no iniquity in me." These are four ways of saying that Job felt he bore no guilt. The word "pure" speaks of having no stain, and "without transgression" speaks of having committed no wrong.

Here Elihu is the speaker, a young man who steps in after Job's friends. He quotes what he believes Job said and corrects it. Job did defend his innocence, but Elihu thinks that by doing so he was accusing God of being unjust (v. 10). Some readers see here an exaggeration by Elihu; others see a fair criticism. The book leaves this open.

For today: we can be honest with God about our pain, but with humility. Even when we feel treated unjustly, let us avoid defending ourselves so much that we end up judging God. Let us trust that He sees more than we do.
exp.37:9:
God says that he set a limit for the sea. "I fixed its boundaries" means that he established a command or boundary that the sea must respect, and "set in place its bars and doors" is an image: God treats the sea like a prisoner or a wild force that he keeps behind a closed gate.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. After Job suffered greatly and asked for explanations, God asks him questions to show him his wisdom and his power over creation. The sea, which for the ancients was a symbol of chaos and fear, is under his complete control.

For today: when you feel that your life is like a stormy sea, remember that God sets limits on what seems ready to overflow. We will not always understand everything, but we can rest in the knowledge that he still governs.
exp.30:24:
Here Job says that he did not rejoice in a wrong way when his possessions grew. He speaks of his great wealth, and the phrase about his hand having gained so much refers to the many gains his hands had earned. It is the language of a solemn "if": "If I did this, I deserve punishment."

Job speaks as a rich man who is suffering and whom his friends accuse of being wicked. In chapter 31 he makes a final defense of his life. He declares that his riches were not his god or his security. Many understand that he does not condemn having possessions, but condemns placing the heart on them instead of on God.

For today: give thanks for what God gives us, but do not depend on it. We can ask ourselves whether our peace comes from money or from God, and practice generosity as a way of remembering who our true trust is.
exp.18:22:
Job wishes that his words were recorded and inscribed in a book. The phrase "I wish that" expresses the longing of a man who wants his testimony not to be lost or forgotten.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends accuse him and do not comfort him, and he feels wounded by God and abandoned by everyone. Since no one believes him, he wants his words to be engraved forever. A few verses later, from that longing comes a great confidence: "I know that my redeemer lives."

When no one understands you, do not fall silent before God. You can tell him honestly what you feel, and you can also hold on to the hope that he lives and has the last word.
exp.10:5:
Here it is said that God has deep secrets of wisdom, and that true wisdom has two sides. The phrase "secrets of wisdom" refers to hidden things, mysteries that God has not fully made known. The idea of two sides means that God's wisdom is far greater than it first appears. Zophar wishes that God would speak and reveal this wisdom to Job, and show him that the punishment he has received is less than his wrongdoing deserves.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job suffers because of some hidden sin, and he accuses him of claiming to be innocent. It should be noted that the book of Job later shows that Zophar was wrong to judge him this way; his belief that all suffering comes from personal sin was not correct.

For today: let us be humble before the mystery of God and not judge harshly those who suffer. When someone is going through pain, it is better to stand beside them with kindness than to explain their reasons to them.
exp.27:20:
This verse says that wisdom is hidden. No human being, and not even the birds, which fly high and see from far away, can discover it on their own. "Hidden" means covered or concealed, and "every living thing" refers to every creature that has life.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of his suffering. In this chapter, which many read as a poem about wisdom, Job describes how people know how to bring silver and gold out of the earth, but cannot find true wisdom. Neither gold nor precious stones can buy it. The verses that follow say that only God knows its path.

Today it reminds us that intelligence and money are not enough to live wisely. We can ask God to give it to us, with humility, instead of relying only on our own strength.
exp.39:15:
Behemoth, a huge creature, lies down to rest in the shade, hidden among the reeds and the marshes. The verse itself shows its strength in its loins and the power in the muscles of its belly, so here we picture a powerful animal living calmly and securely in its surroundings.

Here God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind. He shows Job powerful creatures that Job cannot control, to remind him that God governs creation with wisdom. Scholars do not agree on which animal Behemoth is: some think of a hippopotamus or an elephant, and others think of a symbolic or legendary creature.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, look at how God cares even for the greatest creature. You can rest in his wisdom and entrust to him what you cannot control, with humility and peace.
exp.9:10:
God says that he formed Job's body with care: first he clothed him with skin and flesh, and then he knit him together with bones and sinews. The verbs "clothed" and "knit together" are the only ones in this line that need explaining, and in this verse they simply describe how God built the body, as if God were a craftsman weaving with great care.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering, after losing his children, his possessions and his health. He addresses God with pain and complaint, reminding him that Job himself is the work of God's hands. He wonders why God watches over him so closely and yet seems to let him suffer. Interpreters debate the exact tone: some hear a complaint, others a confident plea.

For today: when you feel fragile or worthless, remember that God made you with purpose and care. You can bring him your doubts and your pain honestly, because he knows your life from its beginning.
exp.33:5:
Job says he cannot lie about his own case, that is, about what he knows to be true about himself. He describes his wound as incurable and painful, even though he is not aware of having done wrong.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job's three friends. Here he repeats and sums up what Job has said, and he does so to accuse him. Some understand that Elihu misreads or exaggerates Job's words, since Job never fully denied being a sinner. What he did maintain was that his suffering had no obvious cause.

For today: before judging someone who suffers, let us listen carefully and not repeat their words harshly. Let us ask God for humility to accompany, not to condemn.
exp.9:21:
It says that death is like a very dark land, so gloomy that it seems like night itself. "Gloomy" means sad, dark and frightening. "Deep shadow and disorder" can be understood as a confused place, where nothing can be made out. The last sentence repeats the idea to emphasize that there even the light seems no different from darkness.

Job is speaking, a man who lost everything: his children, his possessions and his health. He is hurting and speaks to God with honesty, asking for a little relief before he dies. He describes the afterlife according to his pain at that moment, not as a complete teaching about death. Later the Bible speaks with more hope.

For today: if you are going through a dark time, you can speak with God with complete honesty, as Job did. You do not need to hide your sadness. And seek the support of trusted people as well.
exp.12:5:
Job asks his friends to listen to him closely. "Argument" and "plea" refer to his defense, to what he is about to explain in his own words. Listen here means pay attention. Job does not want more quick speeches; he wants to be truly heard.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job calls them forgers of lies and worthless physicians, meaning that they invent false explanations and heal nothing. He wants to bring his case directly before God, and first he asks them to stop defending God with crooked arguments.

Today, when someone suffers, we sometimes help more by keeping quiet and listening than by giving quick explanations. Before you offer an opinion on another person's pain, ask yourself: am I really listening, or do I just want to be right?
exp.21:18:
It says that when God judges the wicked, the righteous will see it and be glad. The innocent will mock them and say what follows in verse 20. "To mock" means to laugh at someone with contempt. "Will be glad" means they will feel joy.

Here Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He accuses Job of being wicked and reminds him of the end of the ungodly, who told God to leave them alone. Eliphaz is wrong to apply this to Job, since God himself says at the end of the book that the friends did not speak rightly about him. Even so, his description of judgment against evil reflects something the Bible teaches elsewhere.

For today: do not use this text to judge others or to mock anyone. Instead, trust that God will do justice, and keep a humble heart, knowing that all of us need his mercy.
exp.32:32:
Here Elihu tells Job: "But if you have nothing to say, listen to me, be quiet, and I will teach you wisdom." The words "listen to me" and "be quiet" are kind but firm instructions: to hear and to keep silent. The phrase "I will teach you" is a direct promise of instruction.

Elihu is a young man who speaks after Job and his three friends had argued at length about Job's suffering. He believes Job has justified himself too much before God and wants to correct him. His tone is confident, though the Bible does not present him as the final word: later God himself speaks and corrects everyone. Some readers see in Elihu a useful voice, others a limited one.

For today: learn to listen before you respond. When you are suffering or arguing, be silent for a moment and pray. But examine with humility what you hear, comparing it with Scripture, because not every confident voice speaks with full wisdom.
exp.17:4:
This verse says that the life of the wicked will be snuffed out like a lamp. The wicked are those who live without reverence for God. A flame is the light that a lamp gives off, and not even a small glow from their fire will continue.

Here Bildad, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He feels offended because Job has criticized his speeches. Bildad believes that suffering is always punishment for wickedness, and so he describes Job as someone walking the path of the wicked. The book itself shows that Bildad is wrong to apply this to Job, although some of what he says about the wicked sounds true.

For today: do not use general truths to judge another person's pain. When someone is suffering, stand with them in compassion and listen, rather than looking for someone to blame.
exp.16:5:
Job says that God has made him a byword among the people, a figure whose misfortune others repeat and mock when they speak of hardship. In his reader's verse, the people treat him with open contempt, and the picture of a man in whose face they spit shows how deep that scorn runs. Job is describing a humiliation that is public and personal.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends accuse him of having sinned, and he feels disgraced before everyone, unable to understand why God allows this. He is exhausted and nearly without hope.

For today: when someone suffers, let us avoid judging them or mocking them. Better to accompany them with respect, patience, and prayer, as Job's friends should have done.
exp.7:12:
Those who forget God are headed toward a future that goes nowhere. Anyone who lives without reverence for God is living on borrowed time, and their hope will come to an end and be lost. It may look healthy and green for a while, but it has no root to keep it alive.

Bildad, a friend of Job, is the one speaking here. He wants to explain Job's suffering with a simple idea: bad things happen to the wicked, and good things happen to the good. He uses the picture of a reed that withers when there is no water. But at the end of this book, God says that Bildad and his companions did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So this general truth is wrongly applied to Job.

For today, check where you place your hope. If it depends on your work, your money, or your own strength, it is fragile. Seek God every day in prayer and in His Word. And do not judge the one who suffers, as Bildad did. Come alongside them with compassion.
exp.35:9:
God opens the ears of people so that they will listen to correction. "Opens" here means making someone pay attention. "Iniquity" means wickedness or wrongdoing. "Turn" means to turn back. God does not only correct people; he also calls them to turn away from what is wrong.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks at the end of Job's conversations with his friends. He maintains that God uses suffering, pictured as chains and cords, to reveal sin and call people to change their hearts and lives. Many scholars think Elihu oversimplifies, since the book teaches that Job was not suffering because of a particular sin. Even so, this sentence reflects something true: God corrects in order to heal.

Today, when something troubles you or holds you back, ask God humbly whether he wants to teach you something. Listen to his Word, and if he shows you something to change, take a concrete step to correct it.
exp.26:20:
The east wind carries him away, and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place. The east wind, a strong and hot wind from the east, will carry off the wicked person. The word "carries" means that it will push or drag him ahead of itself. So the unjust rich man will leave, and the wind will sweep him out of his place. It is an image of sudden loss: what seemed firm disappears.

Job is speaking, answering his friends, who insist that he suffers because of some sin. Here Job describes the fate of the wicked. Some think Job really affirms this; others think he repeats what his friends say with irony. It is not certain. In any case, Job insists that he is innocent.

For today: do not envy unjust wealth, and do not trust in your possessions. Trust in the justice of God. But do not judge others: suffering is not always punishment, as Job himself shows.
exp.7:19:
Behold, God does not reject the blameless, and He does not strengthen the hand of evildoers. It says that God does not turn away from the person who lives with integrity and sincerity. Nor does God strengthen the hands of those who do evil; he does not support or help them as one who rescues someone. "Reject" here means to refuse or cast off. "Blameless" does not mean without any sin, but sincere and whole in one's way.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, so he implies that Job or his children did something wrong. But take note: at the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. His sentence has some truth in it, yet they misuse it.

For today: trust that God cares for the sincere, but do not use this verse to judge someone who is suffering. Pain is not always the consequence of a sin. Accompany others with compassion, not with accusations.
exp.15:10:
It says that God has left him in the power of wicked people. The words "has delivered me" mean that God has handed him over, giving him up to others. Here "unjust men" refers to people who act without fairness or mercy, and "the wicked" are those who do not honor God. The phrase "thrown me to the clutches" paints a picture of being flung into the grip of those who seize and hold on, leaving him helpless and without defense.

Job speaks in the middle of his great suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He feels attacked by everyone and, in his pain, believes that God himself has let him fall into cruel hands. This is his honest complaint, not a complete explanation of what God does. The book will later show that Job did not understand everything that was happening.

For today: when you suffer and feel that everything is against you, you can tell God what you feel with honesty, as Job did. Praying frankly is not a lack of faith; it is continuing to seek him even without understanding.
exp.14:7:
Here Eliphaz asks Job, with irony, whether he was present in God's council. "Listen in on the council of God" refers to God's private plans and thoughts, and "limit wisdom to yourself" means keeping wisdom for oneself and not sharing it. In other words: do you think you are the only one who has wisdom, so that no one else could teach you?

Eliphaz the Temanite is one of Job's three friends. He is upset because Job maintains his innocence in the midst of suffering, and he accuses him of arrogance. His questions aim to humiliate him. Note that Eliphaz is wrong to judge Job, since at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. Even so, the question about the limits of our knowledge is valid.

For today: nobody knows everything. Before speaking with firmness about the pain of others, let us listen with humility and accept that God understands what we cannot see.
exp.37:11:
Here God asks Job whether he has ever in his life given orders to the morning, or shown the dawn the place where it should rise. The question does not expect a "yes." It aims at having Job admit that he has not done this.

God speaks out of the whirlwind, after Job has suffered greatly and asked for explanations. Instead of answering each doubt, God shows him his power over creation: the sea, the light, the earth. The next verse says that the light of morning reaches the ends of the earth and shakes the wicked out of it, which can be understood in several ways, but suggests that God brings order and justice.

Every sunrise reminds us that we do not control everything, but God does. When you do not understand your situation, rest in the fact that He governs time and sustains you.
exp.29:29:
He says that Job's skin has turned black and is peeling, and that his bones burn with fever. The word "black" here describes skin that has grown dark and is coming away, and "burn" describes an intense, scorching heat. It describes an illness that shows on the outside and burns on the inside.

Job speaks here, a man who lost nearly everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. In this chapter he complains before God and before his friends, because he went from being respected to being despised. Earlier he mentioned that his skin did not darken from the sun, but from suffering. Some think this was a skin disease, but the text does not say what it was.

Today it teaches us that we can speak to God honestly about pain, without pretending to be strong. If you are going through an illness or a loss, tell God how you truly feel, and also seek the support of people who will walk with you patiently.
exp.11:3:
He says Job is the object of ridicule from his own friends. He prays to God, and God has answered him, yet even though he is righteous and upright, they make him a laughingstock. The phrase "a laughingstock" means someone people make fun of and hold in contempt.

Job speaks here, answering his friend Zophar and his other friends with irony. They maintain that suffering is always punishment for sin. Job rejects that idea: he is hurt because his faith and his honest life have not spared him from pain or from ridicule. Some scholars understand that "I called on God, and He answered" refers to past answers, and others that he says it with bitterness.

For today: do not judge a person who suffers as if they were guilty. Accompany them with patience and compassion, and if you go through ridicule while remaining faithful, keep praying; God hears you even when others do not understand you.
exp.24:4:
It says that even the moon, which gives light, does not shine in the eyes of God, and that the stars are not pure to Him either. "Does not shine" means that the moon gives no light of its own, and "pure" means clean and without stain. It is a comparison: if the brightest things in the sky are not bright enough before God, how much less so are we ourselves.

Bildad speaks, one of Job's three friends. This is his last speech, and it is very short. He wants to convince Job that no human being can be righteous before God. Although his words about the greatness of God are true, the book shows that Bildad misapplies that idea to Job's suffering.

For today: approach God with humility, without boasting of your goodness. But remember that God does not despise us; in Christ He offers us forgiveness and cleansing. And when someone suffers, let us avoid judging them with harsh words.
exp.28:1:
Job says he longs for the months gone by, for the days when God watched over him. "How I long for" simply means "I wish I could return to." "Watched over" means that God kept him safe and cared for him.

Job speaks after losing his possessions, his children, and his health. In this chapter he looks back with longing on his former life, when he felt the favor of God close to him. His friends have told him that his suffering is a punishment, but he seeks to be heard and understood. Here he does not accuse God; he expresses his pain and his longing.

For today: It is normal to miss better times when we suffer. You can tell God honestly what you feel, without pretending. Remembering how he cared for you before can give you hope, but do not forget that God is still with you, even when you do not feel him so close.
exp.21:28:
The explanation says that when others are brought low, you may confidently say, "Lift them up!" and God will raise them. And God will save the lowly, the one who is humble and not proud. The phrase "brought low" means brought down or humbled. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some translations understand it a little differently.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He advises Job to return to God, thinking that Job suffers because of some sin. His words contain truths about God, but in the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly of Him, so they must be read with care.

For today: when you feel brought low, do not fill yourself with pride or bitterness. Come to God with humility and trust that He knows how to lift up in His time. Remember also that suffering is not always punishment for a sin.
exp.22:3:
Here Job says that, if he could come before God, he would lay out his case as if in a court. The phrase "plead my case" means to present his side in a clear and organized way, and "fill my mouth with arguments" means he would fill his mouth with reasons to defend himself.

Job is a man who suffers greatly and does not understand why. His friends tell him he is suffering because of some sin, but he maintains that he is innocent. He feels far from God and wishes he could find him to speak face to face. Later he acknowledges that God would not crush him, but would listen to him.

For today: when you do not understand your pain, you can bring your honest questions to God in prayer. He is not offended by your candor. Speak frankly, but also leave room to listen and to trust that he is just.
exp.40:28:
He says that Leviathan is not frightened by men's weapons. To him, a club is worth no more than straw, dry and light. When someone swings a lance, he only laughs at the sound of it. He describes a creature that fears nothing.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He is describing Leviathan, a powerful creature that some understand as a crocodile and others as a mythical or symbolic animal. God uses this image to show Job that there are things in creation that human beings cannot master, and that God alone rules over all.

For today: when you feel that the forces of life are overwhelming you, remember that God is greater than what you cannot control. Trust Him with humility and rest in His care.
exp.27:0:
Verse 1 says that there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined. The author begins with mining, something people know how to do very well.

These words are part of a poem about wisdom in the book of Job. Traditionally Job is understood to be the speaker, though some scholars think the author is pausing to reflect. The idea is that people can dig deep into the earth to bring out metals, but they cannot find wisdom by their own strength. In the end, the chapter says that wisdom is to fear the Lord.

For today: we put great effort into getting money and valuable things. Devote that same determination to seeking God's wisdom in his Word and in prayer.
exp.18:6:
Here Job says that he cries out, "Violence!" and gets no response, and that when he calls for help, there is no justice. He feels ignored, even by God.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends tell him he suffers because of some hidden sin. Job answers in pain, convinced that God has treated him badly, even though he knows himself to be innocent. That is his feeling, and the book itself shows that he did not understand everything that was happening.

For today: when you feel that no one hears you, do not keep your pain silent. Job spoke with frankness, and the Bible does not hide it. Bring your complaints to God honestly, and seek out people who will stand with you without judging you, as Job's friends failed to do.
exp.19:26:
What it says: The verse says that heaven and earth will together expose the wicked person's wrongdoing. Nothing he did wrong will stay hidden. "Wickedness" means evil or injustice, and "expose" means to uncover it so that everyone can see it.

Context: This is spoken by Zophar, one of Job's friends. He insists that the wicked always fall and that their joy does not last long. However, he applies this to Job as if his suffering proved that he was guilty. At the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so their ideas should be read with care.

For today: It is certainly true that God sees all injustice and that nothing stays hidden forever. But we should not judge others by their sufferings. Instead, let us examine our own hearts, live with honesty, and trust that God will do justice.
exp.31:2:
Elihu was filled with anger against Job's three friends. The reason is that they had run out of things to say to Job, since they had failed to refute him, yet they still insisted that he was guilty. In this context, "burned with anger" means that his anger was intense, and it is the strength of his feeling that the verse emphasizes. "Condemned" here means that they had judged Job to be guilty.

Elihu is a young man who had listened in silence to the debate between Job and his friends. The friends kept insisting that Job was suffering because of some hidden sin, but they could not prove it. Elihu is indignant because he sees an unjust conclusion without any basis. Keep in mind that the account shows his anger, but it does not guarantee that everything he says afterward is correct.

For today: before judging someone who is suffering, avoid drawing quick conclusions. Listen, accompany them with humility, and recognize that we do not always understand the reason for another person's pain.
exp.11:15:
He says that God has true wisdom and power, and that he uses them to carry out what he intends. The word "existence" here is understood as effective wisdom, or the ability to get things done. Some versions speak of "wisdom" or "success." He also says that both the one who is deceived and the one who deceives others belong to God and are under his rule.

Job is speaking and answering his friends, especially Zophar. They believed they knew exactly how God acts. Job replies that God's power is enormous and that at times he brings down, imprisons, or confuses leaders and judges. There are different ways of understanding how far God controls human error, and the text does not fully explain it.

For today: you do not need to understand everything in order to trust God. When you see injustice or confusion, pray with humility and remember that his power and wisdom are greater than those of any person.
exp.30:39:
He says that if Job has done something unjust to his land or to his workers, he would rather have briers grow instead of wheat, and stinkweed instead of barley. In other words, he accepts that his harvest should fail if he is guilty. The closing words, "Thus conclude the words of Job," show that his defense comes to an end.

Job speaks here at the last point of his long defense. His friends accuse him of being punished for some hidden sin. That is why in chapter 31 Job swears that he is innocent in several matters, such as honesty, purity, and justice toward others. Here he speaks of not having abused the land or those who worked it.

For today: check whether your work, your business, or the way you treat others is fair. Pay what is owed, treat with respect the one who helps you, and ask God to show you any hidden injustice.
exp.6:9:
It says that when a person dies, they never return to their home, and the place where they lived no longer remembers them. The words "never returns" mean that death is a final departure with no coming back, and "his place remembers him no more" means that the familiar setting has no lasting trace of them. Job speaks of death as a farewell with no return.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. Here he speaks to God with sadness and weariness, and he feels that his life is brief, like a cloud that fades away. He says this out of pain, and not as a complete teaching about death. Later in the book, Job also expresses hope.

For today: life is brief, so value the people and the moments God gives you. And if you are suffering, you can be honest with God, as Job was. He listens to your complaints and does not turn away from you.
exp.20:9:
The explanation says that the livestock of the wicked reproduce without problems. The bulls breed without fail, the cows bear calves, and the cows do not miscarry. The verse describes healthy, successful births, with no losses along the way.

Job speaks, answering his friends. They claimed that God always punishes the wicked with misfortunes. Job contradicts them with what he sees: some who live without reverence for God prosper, they have families and well-being. Job suffers and does not understand why, and he rejects easy answers.

Today it reminds us not to measure anyone's faith by their success or their pain. If someone suffers, walk alongside them without judging. If another prospers, do not assume God approves of them. Trust that God is just, even though we do not yet see everything.
exp.37:36:
This verse asks who has the wisdom to count the clouds, and who can tilt the water jars of the heavens. A water jar was a container used to hold liquid. Here it is a poetic picture of clouds heavy with water, which pour it out the way a jar is emptied when it is tipped over. The question of counting the clouds points to a kind of exact knowledge that no one but God possesses.

God is speaking, answering Job from the whirlwind. Job had questioned the suffering that had come to him, and God asks him many questions about creation. He does not do this simply to humiliate him, but to show him that God's wisdom and power surpass everything a human being can understand.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God cares even for the clouds and the rain. You can rest in the knowledge that He knows what He is doing, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.33:28:
The verse says that when God keeps silent, no one can bring charges against him, and when he hides his face, no one can see him. Yet he watches over both people and nations. "Hides his face" means that God turns away from someone, so that they cannot sense his presence or help. The verse applies this to a whole nation and to one person alike.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He argues that God is just and that he rules over all. Earlier he mentions those who turned away from God and brought about the cry of the poor. Some interpret that Elihu is right about God's sovereignty, though he misapplies that idea to Job's suffering.

Today we can remember that our peace depends on God, not only on circumstances. When all is calm, let us thank him; when we feel him far away, let us seek him with humility and trust.
exp.30:36:
Job says that, if God gave him the chance, he would give a full account of his life, the way someone accounts for every step he has taken. The word "him" refers to God, or to his accuser, depending on how the passage is understood. And the phrase "like a prince" means with his head held high, without fear or shame.

Job speaks after losing everything and being accused by his friends of having sinned in secret. In this chapter he makes his final defense and lists his acts of integrity. He wants a fair hearing before God. Some see here a sincere confidence; others see a somewhat bold tone, which God will correct later on.

For today: living with a clear conscience gives us freedom to approach God with sincerity. Even so, let us do this with humility, acknowledging that only God's grace sustains us. Today you can examine your steps honestly and ask God to correct and guide you.
exp.7:15:
He is described as a plant that is well watered and thriving in the sunshine, with its shoots spreading over the garden. "Spreading its shoots" refers to the new growth reaching outward, and "garden" is the plot where it grows. On the outside, everything appears to be flourishing.

It is Bildad, Job's friend, who speaks, and he believes that God punishes the wicked and blesses the good. For that reason he suggests that Job suffers because of his sin. Here he describes someone who trusts in something other than God: he seems prosperous, but his roots are tangled among stones, and when he is uprooted, no one recognizes him. Watch out: the book shows that Bildad is wrong to apply this to Job.

For today: do not judge anyone only by their appearance or by their troubles. And take care of your own roots; seek to place your trust in God, not in what looks good on the outside.
exp.33:4:
Here Elihu repeats what Job has said: that he is righteous and that God has deprived him of justice, meaning that God has not treated him fairly. The word "justice" here means the fair treatment that someone deserves.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He is angry because Job defended himself by saying he was innocent. Elihu sums up Job's words in order to accuse him of doubting God's justice. Note: Job did say something similar, but God himself, at the end of the book, says that Job spoke rightly about Him, while the friends did not. For that reason, Elihu's words should be read with care.

For today: when you suffer, you can tell God your pain honestly, but do not stop trusting that He is just, even when you do not understand what is happening. And when you correct others, listen carefully before you judge.
exp.38:2:
This verse asks who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God. The chicks cry out, moving restlessly because they are hungry.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job from the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him an explanation, but instead asks him questions about nature to show him his wisdom and his care for every creature, even the smallest.

For today: if God takes care of the ravens' chicks, we can entrust our needs to him even when we do not understand everything we are going through. Today you can pray honestly, ask him for what you need, and rest in the knowledge that he is wise and faithful.
exp.4:7:
In this verse, Eliphaz says that if he were in Job's place, he would turn to God and lay his cause before Him. Turning to God means going to Him with confidence. Laying one's cause before Him means placing one's situation, one's case, and one's concerns in His hands.

Eliphaz is one of Job's three friends. Job is suffering greatly, and Eliphaz urges him to turn to God. The advice itself is good, but the thinking behind it is mistaken: it assumes Job is suffering because of some sin. Later, God Himself corrects Eliphaz and his companions for not having spoken rightly about Him.

For today: when something weighs on you, do not carry it alone. Tell God honestly what troubles you and leave it in His hands. And take care not to explain another person's pain with easy answers; sometimes it helps more to walk alongside them with respect.
exp.3:16:
It says that no human being can be more righteous or more pure than God, who made him. It is a rhetorical question: the obvious answer is "no." The word "mortal" here refers to a human being who will die, and "pure" means clean, without guilt.

It is spoken by Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He recounts a mysterious experience at night, when a spirit spoke to him. He uses it to suggest that Job is suffering for some sin. Note that the book itself shows Eliphaz was wrong to apply this to Job, since God declares him blameless from the beginning. The statement is true in itself, but it is misused.

It is true that before God all of us need humility and his grace. But do not use that truth to judge someone who is suffering. Accompany them with compassion, without assuming that their pain is a punishment.
exp.20:12:
This verse says that the wicked spend their days prospering, without suffering, and at the end they die peacefully, without a long agony. The phrase "spend their days in prosperity" means that they live in comfort and well-being. The phrase "go down to Sheol in peace" means that they die; Sheol is the place of the dead, and the peace describes a calm, untroubled death.

Here Job is speaking, answering his friends. They maintained that the wicked always suffer and the righteous prosper. Job contradicts them with what he sees: people who live without respecting God and yet enjoy happy children, celebrations, and a peaceful death. Job is suffering, and this apparent injustice grieves him.

For today: do not measure your life or your faith by the comfort of others. If you see that someone without faith is doing well, do not become bitter; trust that God is just and that earthly life is not the end of the story.
exp.19:18:
It says that this man crushed and abandoned the poor, and seized houses that he did not build. "Crushed" means that he oppressed them or left them broken. "Abandoned" means that he left them without help. It is an accusation of injustice and abuse against the weakest.

The one speaking is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He describes what, in his view, happens to the wicked: their riches do not last, and God makes them give back what they took. Zophar believes that all suffering comes from a specific sin, and so he hints that Job is guilty. The book itself shows that this conclusion was mistaken.

Today, this invites us to examine how we treat those who have less power: employees, neighbors, or needy family members. Paying fairly, keeping our promises, and not taking advantage of anyone honors God. But we should not judge others for their hardships, as Zophar did.
exp.40:1:
He says that no one can tame Leviathan the way one controls a beast of burden. A "cord" is a rope or line that was put through the nose of an animal to control it. To "pierce" means to pass a sharp point through, and a "hook" here refers to a barbed or spiked tool that would be driven through the jaw. The question expects a "no": no human being can subdue this creature.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. He shows Leviathan, a powerful and frightening creature, to remind Job how limited human beings are. There is discussion about which animal is meant: some think of a crocodile, others of a symbolic creature of chaos. The central point is the message of God's greatness.

For today: when life seems out of control, remember that you do not have to master everything. Trust in God, who does have control, and rest in his wisdom.
exp.32:19:
