It says that the person who suffers in bed no longer wants even bread. Even their favorite food causes them disgust. "He detests his bread" and "his soul loathes" refer to the person himself, and they describe a deep sense of revulsion and distaste.

It is Elihu, a young man who speaks near the end of the book. He tries to explain to Job that God sometimes uses pain and sickness to get people's attention and turn them away from ruin. This is one of his ideas; the book itself shows that it does not explain all of Job's suffering.

Today, when someone goes through an illness, we do not need to give them quick explanations. We can accompany them, bring them simple food, pray with them, and be present. And if we are the ones suffering, we can ask God to sustain us.
exp.31:8:
This verse tells us that being great in age, position, or fame does not guarantee being wise. The "great" are those of high standing or importance, and the "elderly" are those who have lived many years. "Justice" means what is fair and right. In other words, having many years does not always bring good judgment, and the older are not automatically the wisest.

The speaker is Elihu, a younger man who had stayed silent out of respect while Job and his three friends, who were older than he was, argued. Seeing that they were getting nowhere, he takes courage and speaks. He says that understanding comes from God, not simply from age. Some scholars regard his voice as sound, while others think he is also partly mistaken.

Today we can listen to everyone with humility, neither despising the young nor assuming that only the older person is wise. Let us seek wisdom in God and weigh advice by its truth, not by who is giving it.
exp.18:27:
Here Job tells his friends that, rather than accusing him, they should ask themselves: "Why are we going after him?" The phrase "the root of the matter" is the part to notice. The word "matter" means the cause or issue at stake, and "root" is the heart of the problem. Job claims that the heart of his case is a cause he can defend with a clear conscience.

Job speaks as one who suffers and has lost everything. His friends insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Just before this, Job expresses his hope of seeing God. Afterward he warns his friends that their unjust judgments have consequences, because God judges.

For today: before pointing out or criticizing someone who is suffering, pause and ask yourself whether you truly know the root of their situation. Sometimes the wisest thing is to offer compassion, listen, and leave the final judgment in God's hands.
exp.9:6:
Job says to God: "Though You know that I am not guilty, there is no deliverance from Your hand."

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends tell him he suffers because of some hidden sin. Job protests his innocence and speaks directly to God, with pain and confusion. He acknowledges that God is all-powerful, but he does not understand why God treats him this way. Some readers see here a brave complaint; others, a plea that shows little understanding of God's purpose.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, you do not have to pretend or stay silent. You can bring your pain to God honestly, as Job did, trusting that he listens and remains greater than your questions.
exp.14:22:
He wanders about as food for vultures, always alert for the next meal. "Restless" means without peace, unable to settle down. "Hand" here means nearness, at close range. "Day of darkness" refers to a time of gloom: ruin, misfortune, or death. He knows that day is already close at hand.

Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. Here he describes, in his view, the fate of the wicked: they live in fear and have no true peace. But notice that Eliphaz uses this to hint that Job is suffering because of his sin, and at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. So these words do not apply to all suffering.

For today: do not judge someone who is suffering by assuming it is God's punishment. Instead, stand beside them with compassion, and seek for yourself the peace that comes from trusting God.
exp.11:1:
Job speaks to his three friends with irony. He tells them: "Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!" He does not mean it seriously; he is mocking how much they pride themselves on knowing. Here, "the people" means something like "the only ones who count." The word "understanding" in the next verse refers to the same kind of knowing.

Job is answering Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, who have insisted that his suffering is punishment for some sin. Job feels hurt and judged without cause. So he replies with sarcasm: they speak as if they had the whole truth, but he understands these things too.

Today we can learn not to speak with an air of superiority toward someone who is suffering. Before offering explanations or advice, it is good to listen with humility, to accompany with compassion, and to remember that no one knows everything about the ways of God.
exp.25:0:
This verse is a simple introduction. It says that Job took the floor and began to reply. "Answered" means that he speaks in response to someone who had spoken to him before, and "then" marks the moment his words begin, which come in the next verse.

Job, a man who suffers greatly, speaks after hearing the speech of his friend Bildad (chapter 25). Bildad spoke of the greatness of God, but he did not comfort Job. So Job responds with irony, pointing out that those speeches did not help him in his pain.

For today: before speaking with someone who is suffering, let us truly listen. Correct statements about God do not replace compassion. An attentive ear and a kind word can help more than a long speech.
exp.32:1:
He says that Elihu is about to begin speaking. "Behold, I will open my mouth; my address is on the tip of my tongue" is a plain way of saying: "I am now going to speak, and I will do it with care and seriousness." It works like a formal introduction before giving his argument.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who listened in silence to Job and his three friends. He is upset because Job kept justifying himself and the friends could not answer him. Here he asks Job to listen closely. He claims to speak with sincerity, though God, at the end of the book, neither approves nor directly corrects Elihu, so his words should be read with caution.

For today: before speaking, especially in a conflict or in front of someone who is suffering, it is good to pause, listen well, and ask ourselves whether what we are about to say is sincere, helpful, and humble.
exp.19:9:
It says that the children of the wicked man will fall into poverty and will have to seek the favor of those he harmed. Also, his own hands must return what he gained unjustly. The phrase "seek the favor" means they will try to win the goodwill of the poor, and "return" means to give back.

Here the speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He believes God always punishes the wicked quickly, and so he implies that Job must have done something wrong. His words describe injustice well, but they do not apply to Job, and in the end God corrects the friends (Job 42:7). Some understand that the children give back what was stolen; others, that the wicked man himself does it.

For today: do not profit from what is not yours, and if you have taken something improperly, make it right with honesty. Also, do not judge others by their suffering.
exp.21:27:
It says that if you make a decision, it will be carried out and succeed. It also says that light will shine on your path. The words "decree" and "established" in the old wording meant "decide" and "held firm," so the idea is that a decision made in faith will hold and be achieved.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he promises that if Job turns back to God, everything will get better. However, at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. So this promise is true only in part: suffering is not always punishment.

For today: when you make decisions, bring them to prayer and ask God to guide your steps. Trust that He gives light for the way, but do not judge anyone who suffers as if their pain were always their own fault.
exp.3:13:
Elifaz says that a great fear suddenly came over him, along with a trembling that made all his bones shudder. "Came over him" means that it overtook him all at once. "Fear" is a deep fright, and "shudder" means that it made him shake strongly.

The speaker is Elifaz, one of Job's three friends. He is describing a night experience, during a dream or vision, which he uses to support what he tells Job. Then a voice asks whether a man can be more righteous than God. It is worth noticing that Elifaz presents this as a revelation, but at the end of the book God says that he and his friends did not speak rightly about Him (42:7). Therefore, his experience does not guarantee that his application to Job was correct.

Today: a strong experience, even when it feels very real, is not enough to decide what is true. Let us compare what we feel or hear with Scripture, and speak with humility and compassion to those who are suffering.
exp.34:15:
The verse's wording comes through as "So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge." Here "in vain" means without profit, so Elihu is saying that Job's many words accomplish nothing. The phrase about knowledge points to speech that is not grounded in understanding. The exact sense of the closing phrase in the Hebrew is uncertain.

Elihu speaks next, a young man who intervenes after Job's three friends. He believes that Job, in his grief, has spoken without good sense and has doubted the justice of God. His accusation is harsh, and the book does not say that he is entirely right. God later answers Job, but in a different way.

When we suffer, it is good to speak honestly before God, but also with humility. Before complaining or judging others, let us ask for wisdom and remember that God sees more than we can understand.
exp.25:4:
This verse is difficult. The Hebrew word here refers to the dead, or to the shades of the underworld, and the picture is of the dead trembling beneath the waters, along with those who dwell there.

Job speaks, answering his friend Bildad. First he rebukes him with irony for his unhelpful advice. Then he shows that he does know the greatness of God: God's power reaches to the deepest and most hidden places, even the realm of the dead, which lies open before Him.

For today: nothing in your life is outside the sight and power of God, not even what is most hidden or deep. You can trust Him in the middle of your pain, even when you do not understand everything, as Job did.
exp.15:5:
Job says that his pain is not eased in any way. If he speaks and tells what he feels, the suffering stays just the same. If he holds back and stays silent, it does not go away either. The words "relieved" and "go away" are the verse's own words for this, and "is not relieved" means the pain is not lessened.

Job is speaking, a man who has lost everything and suffers greatly. His friends have given him long speeches telling him that his pain is the result of some sin. Job answers that he could do the same if they were in his place, but that he would rather comfort them. Now he feels worn out and without support, and he admits that neither speaking nor keeping silent brings him relief.

For today: if you are suffering and nothing seems to ease you, do not judge yourself for it. Keep speaking with God honestly, as Job did, and look for someone who will stay with you patiently, without offering easy explanations.
exp.0:21:
This verse says that, although Job lost everything, he did not sin or accuse God of wrongdoing. The phrase "charge God with wrongdoing" means that he blamed God or held God responsible for something unjust. Job did not speak against God or treat him as acting unjustly.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not Job. He summarizes Job's reaction after he lost his possessions and his children in a single day. Job responded with grief, tearing his robe and shaving his head, but he also worshiped. The narrator wants the reader to see that his faith remained firm.

For today: when a loss comes or something you do not understand, you can weep and feel pain without accusing God of wrongdoing. Bring your questions to him honestly, and keep trusting that he is good.
exp.36:15:
This verse asks Job a question: do you understand how the clouds float? The phrase "those wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge" refers to God, whose understanding has no flaws. Here the clouds are presented as one of the wonders that show how wise God is.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in at the end of the speeches of Job and his friends. He uses wonders of nature, such as the clouds, the wind, and the light, to show that God is great and that Job cannot grasp everything. In this way he prepares the way for the answer God himself will give later.

Today, when we do not understand what we are going through, we can look at the sky and remember that God knows more than we can see. Trusting Him does not require having all the answers, but resting in his perfect wisdom.
exp.16:13:
Here Job says he speaks to the "pit", which is the grave or burial place, and calls it "father". To the worms he says "mother" and "sister". In other words, he feels that the grave and decay are now his only family, the closest thing he has left.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He is sick, his friends accuse him without cause, and he feels that God is not answering him. That is why he sees death as his home and has almost no hope left. It is language full of pain, not a teaching about how to view death.

For today: when pain makes you feel alone and without a way out, you do not have to hide it. Job spoke honestly to God, and the Bible records it. You can pray with honesty, and seek out someone you trust who can walk with you and listen.
exp.19:17:
What it says: The wicked man must give back the fruit of his labor, meaning what he gained through his work, and he will not be allowed to consume it. The verse says he cannot enjoy the profits of his trading. "Labor" here means the effort he put in, and "profits" refers to what he earned from trade.

Context: Zophar, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. He holds that the wicked always end badly and that gains made by injustice do not last. For this reason he suggests that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. The verses that follow describe how this man oppressed the poor. Although Zophar describes something that is partly true, the book shows that his application to Job is mistaken.

For today: Gains taken through injustice do not bring true peace. If you have taken something that was not yours, try to make it right and give it back. But do not judge someone who is suffering, as Zophar did, for not all pain is punishment.
exp.20:14:
Here the words of people who live without taking God into account are quoted. They ask with contempt, "Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him?" and they wonder what they would gain by praying to Him. "Gain" means "benefit" or "help," and "to Him" simply refers to God.

Job speaks, answering his friends. They were saying that the wicked always end up badly. Job shows them that many who reject God spend their days in prosperity. Then he makes clear that he does not share their way of thinking: "the counsel of the wicked is far from me." Some understand the end of the passage as a warning that their well-being is neither secure nor lasting.

For today: be careful about measuring God only by what he gives us. Prayer is not a business deal but a relationship with the One who created us. Serve Him for who He is, not only for what you receive.
exp.11:8:
It says that all created things, the animals, the birds, the earth, and the fish, recognize that the hand of the LORD made them. It is a rhetorical question: the expected answer is "everyone knows it." The name "LORD" is the name of God, and "the hand" speaks of his power and his work.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly. His friends tell him his pain is punishment for some sin. Job answers them with some irony: what they say is not so special, since even nature knows that God governs everything. Some scholars point out that this is the only place in Job where the divine name appears within a speech like this, while others see it as a detail of how the text was copied over time, and there is no full agreement.

For today: when you feel confused or tired, go out and look at the sky, the plants, or the animals. You will remember that God is still in control, even when you do not understand your situation.
exp.27:2:
People go deep into the earth to find what is hidden. Man puts an end to the darkness, carrying his lamp into the dark places and marking how far the gloom reaches. He probes the farthest recesses, examining every corner with care, and he searches out ore in the deepest darkness.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of his conversation with his friends, while he suffers greatly. In this chapter he describes human skill in extracting silver, gold, and iron from the earth. But he does so to make a contrast: the human being reaches the deepest places, and yet true wisdom cannot be found with that same skill.

For today: value your effort and your intelligence, but remember that the most important thing, the wisdom for living, must be asked of God with humility.
exp.32:26:
He sings before men, and when someone says, "I have sinned and perverted what was right, yet I did not get what I deserved," the verse describes a person who admits his wrongdoing and says the outcome was not what his actions earned. In the Berean Standard Bible, God is the one who sings before men, and the speaker's words carry both a confession and a complaint about what he received.

Elihu, a young man who rebukes Job, speaks these words. He explains that God uses suffering to bring people to repentance and to save them from death. This is a fair reading within Elihu's speech, although the book shows that Job's suffering was not the result of one specific sin.

For today: do not hide your mistakes. Confess to God honestly, without excuses. He sees you, but not in order to condemn you; He invites you to return and to begin again.
exp.0:6:
God asks Satan where he has come from, and Satan replies that he has been roaming through the earth and walking back and forth in it. Going around the earth means traveling through it from one place to another.

God speaks first, and then Satan. Job has just been introduced as a man who cares about the spiritual life of his children. Here the scene moves to heaven, where Satan presents himself before God. His answer shows that he is watching people. Many believe God's question is not because he lacks knowledge, but to open the conversation that follows about Job. The text does not explain every detail of this scene.

For today: you can trust that nothing escapes the sight of God, not even what you do not understand. Even in difficult times, keep seeking him sincerely, as Job did.
exp.33:23:
He shatters the powerful without needing to inquire into their cases, and he sets up others in their place. The phrase "without inquiry" means God does not need to search or question, because He already knows everything.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who tries to correct Job and his three friends. He argues that God is just and that no wicked person can hide from Him. Elihu is partly right about God's justice, but in the end the book shows that God does not blame Job for wrongdoing, so not all suffering is punishment.

For today: do not despair in the face of abuse by powerful people. God sees everything and is just. Trust in Him, do what is right, and avoid judging others by their troubles as if they were always punishment.
exp.3:7:
The explanation says that those who cultivate evil and plant harm or injustice will, in the end, gather that same crop. The words "plow," "sow," and "reap" in the verse above name the work of preparing the ground, scattering seed, and gathering the harvest. "Trouble" here means harm, injustice, or affliction.

Elifaz, Job's friend, speaks in the first discourse. He wants to explain Job's suffering by saying that, according to what he has seen, only the wicked fall. His idea sounds logical, but God later says that Elifaz and his friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). The principle of sowing and reaping is real, but applying it to Job was a mistake.

Today, be careful about what you sow with your words and decisions. But do not judge others by saying that their pain is always punishment. In the face of another person's suffering, accompany them with compassion and humility.
exp.19:19:
The person who got rich at the expense of others, Zophar says, will not have peace within. "Appetite" here refers to a restless hunger that is never satisfied, and the verse describes a person who cannot hold on to what they have gained. Moreover, he cannot escape with his treasure, meaning whatever he has grabbed by greed will not stay with him.

The one speaking is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He maintains that the wicked always end badly, and he hints to Job that his suffering comes from some hidden sin. His words describe well how injustice tends to go, but the book shows that Zophar is wrong to apply them to Job, who was innocent.

For today: unchecked ambition steals peace, even when a person has a great deal. Ask yourself whether there is something you desire so much that it would lead you to trample over others. Learn to give thanks for what you have, and to work with honesty. And do not judge another person's pain as punishment.
exp.31:5:
Elihu begins his speech by saying that he is young in years and that Job and his three friends are old. For that reason he felt timid and afraid, and did not dare to tell them what he knows. Here "what I know" refers to what he understands about the matter. The verse names his father, Barachel, and his family or place of origin, the Buzite, which indicates where he came from.

Elihu appears suddenly after the three friends stopped answering Job. He had waited silently out of respect for their age. But now he becomes angry, because it seems to him that no one has given a good answer. Scholars debate how to evaluate his speech, but his initial attitude shows courtesy.

For today: respect those who have more experience, but do not stay silent if you have something wise and useful to offer. Do it with humility, at the right moment, and without letting anger take control.
exp.8:17:
He says that Job feels God does not even let him catch his breath. Catching his breath means getting air back, resting for a moment. In your verse, the phrase is "overwhelms me with bitterness," and the picture is of Job feeling that his pain is crushing him and gives him no relief.

Job is speaking in reply to his friend Bildad. He has lost children, possessions, and health, and he does not understand why. At this point he is expressing what he feels, not teaching about what God is like. He thinks God is so powerful that there is no way to argue with Him. Later in the book, it shows that God does listen to Job, though He does not explain everything to him.

When pain leaves you without breath, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how you feel, as Job did, and keep seeking Him even when you do not understand.
exp.16:11:
The explanation says that some people turn night into day, so that the light seems too near to be overcome by the darkness. In other words, things are turned upside down: what is dark is presented as if it were bright, and hope feels far away.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly. His friends tell him that everything will soon be put right if he repents, but Job sees none of that. To him their advice makes no sense, and his pain is so great that hope seems far away. Some understand that the friends make night into day with empty words; others see it as Job's complaint about his own darkness.

When someone is suffering, let us avoid saying easy phrases that deny their pain. It is better to stay with them with patience and truth. And if you are in the night, you can speak with God honestly, as Job did.
exp.20:18:
This verse says that God stores up the punishment for a wicked man's wrongdoing for his children. Here "violence" refers to his wickedness or injustice, and "payment" is the consequence he deserves. The final request is that the guilty person himself be repaid and so come to know what he has done, that is, realize it.

Job is speaking to his friends, who insisted that the wicked always suffer quickly. Job answers that wicked people often prosper. In this verse he repeats one of his ideas, and in the next he asks that the punishment fall on the guilty person himself, not on his children. Some take it as a quotation of what his friends say, others as Job's own voice.

For today: do not judge the lives of others by what they appear to be. Trust that God is just, and live with integrity without expecting everything to be resolved right away.
exp.37:21:
Here God asks Job whether he has ever entered the storehouses of the snow, or seen the storehouses of the hail, that is, the places where God keeps them. It is a poetic way of saying that Job does not know where they come from or how they are kept.

God speaks out of the storm. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him an account of his pain; instead he asks Job questions about creation to show him that God governs everything with wisdom, even what Job cannot grasp. The next verse says that God keeps snow and hail for times of distress and battle, and the Bible sometimes shows hail as an instrument of God (Joshua 10:11).

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that your view is limited. Trusting God does not require having all the answers, but resting in the fact that He does have them and is good.
exp.32:16:
This verse says that God speaks to man in dreams and visions to turn him away from wrongdoing, that is, from wrong choices and the harm they bring, and to keep him from pride, which is arrogance.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He explains that God does communicate with people, sometimes at night, to warn them and correct them. His idea is that God wants to stop a person before pride destroys them. Some scholars think Elihu is partly right, but that he is mistaken in applying this to Job.

For today: ask God to show you whether there is any proud plan or attitude in your life, and listen for his correction in the Bible, in prayer, and in wise counsel.
exp.28:8:
The princes, that is, the important men who held authority, would stop speaking when Job arrived. Covering their mouths with their hands was a gesture of respect and silence. In this verse, the phrase "refrained from speaking" means that they fell silent in order to listen to him.

The one speaking is Job. He is recalling with sadness what his life was like before he lost everything. In those days he would sit at the city gate, the place where judgments were made and decisions were taken. The young, the elders, and the leaders honored him for his wisdom and his justice.

Today we can learn that true respect is earned through a just life and kind treatment of others, not by demanding it. Let us ask God for help to live with integrity, so that our words and actions deserve trust.
exp.5:2:
Job says that his suffering, if it were placed on a scale, would weigh more than all the sand of the seas. "Then" points back to his complaint and his torment from the previous verse. That is why he admits his words have been rash: the Hebrew wording here is uncertain, and some read it as words spoken in a hurry, without restraint, out of bewilderment.

Job speaks after his friend Eliphaz suggested that his suffering came from some sin. Job has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and he feels that no one grasps the depth of his pain. He asks that his suffering be weighed fairly.

For today: when someone is suffering, listening is worth more than explaining. And if you are the one suffering, you can speak to God honestly, even when your words come out rash or broken. He knows how heavy what you carry is.
exp.23:15:
He says that certain wicked people work in the dark. At night they dig through houses, that is, they break through the walls (which were made of mud) in order to steal. During the day they shut themselves in, keeping away from the light. They seem to want nothing to do with it.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. He is answering his friends, who said that God punishes the wicked quickly. Job shows that many wicked people seem to get away with it: they steal, kill, and deceive, and injustice continues in the world. He complains to God that he does not bring order right away.

For today: God sees what we do in secret. Ask yourself whether there is something you do in secret that you would not do in front of others. Bring it into the light of Christ, confess it, and ask for his help to live with sincerity.
exp.33:16:
The explanation says that someone who hates justice could not govern. The verse asks whether a person who hates justice could rule, and it asks Job whether he will condemn the just and mighty One. The words "govern" and "justice" in this explanation are the words the verse uses. Elihu asks Job whether he will condemn God, who is both just and mighty.

Elihu speaks next, the young friend of Job, after the three older friends have fallen silent. He believes that Job, in defending his innocence, has suggested that God is unjust. His argument is that if God hated justice, the world could not hold together. Although Elihu is right that God is just, the book shows that he does not really understand Job's suffering.

For today: when something hurts and has no explanation, we can ask God honest questions without accusing him. And it is wise to be careful when explaining another person's pain, because we do not always know what God is doing.
exp.12:24:
Job asks God whether he really means to frighten a leaf the wind is already tossing about, or to chase after dry chaff. The first image is a thin, light scrap of dried plant, something weightless and without strength. "Frighten" here means to terrify. Job compares himself to something fragile and worthless, and he asks why God would spend such force against him.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends tell him that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin, but he cannot find any such sin, and he asks God to show him what it is. He feels treated like an enemy, even though he is very weak. It is a sincere lament, and the book itself makes clear that his suffering was not caused by any particular sin.

For today: when you feel fragile and confused, you can bring your questions to God honestly, without pretending. He hears a sincere lament, and you do not need to have all the answers in order to keep trusting Him.
exp.27:17:
The verse says that coral and quartz are not even worth mentioning in the same breath as wisdom. "Unworthy of mention" means that comparing them is not appropriate, because wisdom is worth far more than any precious object. The verse adds that wisdom's price is beyond rubies, meaning no gem can match its value.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his dialogue with his friends, while he suffers greatly. In this chapter he describes how human beings know how to search for and bring out metals and stones from deep within the earth, but cannot find wisdom or buy it. Then he asks where it comes from. Later the chapter answers that only God knows it, and that fearing Him is wisdom.

Today we can ask ourselves what we seek most: money or things, or judgment to live well. Let us ask God for wisdom each day, before making important decisions.
exp.15:6:
He says Job feels worn out. The phrase "exhausted me" means that it left him with no strength left. "Devastated" means laid waste or destroyed. "Family" refers to his children and the people closest to him. Some read "you" as God, and others read it as the pain itself; the text does not fully make this clear.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His three friends came to comfort him, but they accuse him of having sinned and give him long, cold speeches. Job feels that God has struck him and that he has been left alone, without children, without possessions, and without real support. That is why he expresses his pain with complete honesty.

For today: if you are exhausted and alone, you can tell God what you feel without disguising it. And when someone is suffering, stand with them through presence and listening, not with easy explanations or judgments.
exp.36:21:
The verse says that out of the north comes a golden splendor, a light that shines like gold. It affirms that God is surrounded by awesome majesty, a greatness so immense and admirable that it produces deep respect and reverent awe, not that He is cruel.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in before Job and his friends. He describes storms and skies that clear to show that God is vast and that we do not fully grasp Him. What "the north" refers to exactly is understood in several ways, but the central idea is clear: the glory of God surpasses our understanding.

Today we can pause before creation and the sky with humility and wonder. When you do not understand what God allows, remember that His greatness is beyond your questions, and trust Him with reverence.
exp.34:10:
This verse continues a question: "Where is God my Maker... who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the air?" It says that God gave human beings understanding and wisdom that animals do not have.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in near the end of the book of Job. He responds to Job and to his friends. He says that people suffer and cry out, but do not seek God as their maker and source of comfort, nor do they think about what he has given them. Some understand that Elihu exaggerates or oversimplifies Job's suffering; the Bible does not present him as an infallible voice.

For today: when trials come, do not only ask for the pain to end. Also ask: "Where is God?" Remember that he gave you a mind and a heart to know him, and seek him with confidence, even in the night.
exp.19:23:
He says the wicked man will try to escape from an iron weapon, but a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him. The word here is usually understood as bronze or copper, and the image is that there is no escape: if he flees one danger, he falls into another.

Zophar, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. With this speech he means that the wicked always end badly, and he implies that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. But the book shows that Zophar is wrong to apply this idea to Job, who was an upright man.

For today: trust that God is just, but do not judge the suffering of others as if it were always a punishment. Accompany them with compassion, listen with humility, and leave the final word to God.
exp.27:14:
It says that wisdom cannot be bought with gold, and that its price cannot be weighed out in silver. "Cannot be bought with gold" means it cannot be purchased with gold. "Weighed out in silver" refers to silver being measured on a scale to make a payment, since back then there were no paper bills as there are today.

This is Job's poem about wisdom, within his reply to his friends. Job explains that people know how to bring metals out of the earth, but they do not know where true wisdom is found. Neither the deep nor the sea has it. He ends by saying that the fear of the Lord is wisdom (v. 28).

For today: do not seek wisdom for life only through money, studies, or success. Ask God for it with humility, honor him, and let his Word guide your daily decisions.
exp.33:22:
God does not need to examine a man any further or have him come forward for judgment. So no one has grounds to bring God to trial as if He had acted unjustly. The phrase "have him approach for judgment" means to summon a person to stand before a court to argue or dispute a case, and the verse itself is difficult in the original Hebrew, so its exact sense is debated.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's friends. He argues that God is just and sees everything. His point is that God does not make mistakes and does not need further proof. Even so, Elihu does not always get it right, for the book itself shows that Job's suffering was not punishment for some hidden wickedness.

For today: when life feels unfair, express your pain to God honestly, but without accusing Him. Trust that He sees everything clearly and acts justly, even when you do not yet understand.
exp.28:22:
They waited for me as for rain, and they drank in my words like spring showers. The verse pictures people longing for Job's advice the way farmers long for rain in a dry season. Their eagerness is shown by how they took in what he said, as if his words were something they badly needed.

Here Job is speaking. He is suffering greatly, and he remembers with longing when he was a respected man in his city. His counsel was listened to closely, and people left helped and encouraged. Job describes his past life to show how much everything has changed.

For today: let us seek to make our words like good rain, words that refresh and encourage others. Before we speak, let us ask ourselves whether what we are about to say will help, comfort, or give direction with humility.
exp.6:18:
Job asks God how long he will keep his eyes on him so closely, giving him no relief at all. The image of not being allowed to swallow his spit means not even a moment to catch his breath. Job is asking for a break from the pressure he feels.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He suffers greatly and feels that God watches and tests him without rest. His complaint is sincere and somewhat exaggerated by pain; his friends do not understand him, and he does not yet know the reason for his suffering. Even so, he keeps speaking to God and does not abandon him.

For today: when pain weighs heavily on you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, including your complaints. He listens and does not reject someone who speaks to him sincerely.
exp.20:5:
It says that Job is stunned and his body shakes when he recalls what he is about to say. "When I remember, terror takes hold" means that he is struck with dread and left without words. "My body trembles in horror" means that his whole frame shakes with fear or deep shock. The line "When I remember" shows that his own thought startles him.

Job speaks in the middle of his argument with his friends. They hold that God always punishes the wicked and blesses the good. Job, who suffers without understanding why, answers them with an uncomfortable question: why do many wicked people live long years and prosper? His trembling comes from facing that mystery.

For today: do not be afraid to bring your hard questions about injustice or pain to God. Do so with honesty and reverence, without offering easy answers to someone who is suffering.
exp.40:17:
When the Leviathan sneezes, its snorting flashes with light, as though it throws off sparks. Its eyes are compared to the rays of dawn, a poetic image for the first reddish light of sunrise appearing on the horizon.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes the Leviathan, a powerful creature that no one can subdue. Some believe it is a crocodile, others a symbolic monster of chaos; there is no certain agreement. God does not intend to frighten for its own sake, but to show that He rules over what human beings cannot control.

For today: when life feels out of control, remember that nothing escapes the power of God. You can rest in the fact that He sustains what you do not understand and cannot manage, and trust Him even without having all the answers.
exp.5:11:
Job asks whether his strength is like that of stone, or whether his flesh is made of bronze. The original word for "strength" simply means strength, and the word for "flesh" refers to his body. It is a rhetorical question, and the answer is "no." Job is not made of stone or metal, and he has no more endurance left.

The one speaking is Job, in the midst of great suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. His friend Eliphaz has just advised him to be patient, but Job feels he has no strength left to keep waiting. He says he has not denied the words of God, but he is exhausted and needs compassion, not reproach.

Today, this verse reminds us that it is good to acknowledge our limits. We do not have to pretend to be strong. We can be honest with God about our weariness, and we can also be gentler with those who suffer, staying with them without rushing or judging them.
exp.39:5:
God tells Job to release the full force of his anger and to look at every proud person and bring them low. Plain words are enough here: "pour out" means to let something spill or be released, "anger" means strong displeasure, "the proud" means the arrogant person, and "bring down" means to lower or knock down.

The one speaking is the LORD, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned God's justice, and God responds with irony: if Job thinks he could govern the world better, let him try. The point is to show that Job has neither the power nor the wisdom for such a task. Many understand that God does not intend to mock him, but to teach him humility.

Today we can remember that it is not ours to take God's place as judge of the world. When something seems unjust to us, we can express our pain honestly, while trusting that the LORD governs with perfect justice.
exp.35:11:
It says that those who do not obey God's correction will "perish by the sword," that is, they will die in a violent or sudden way. It also says they "die without knowledge," meaning without having understood what God wanted to teach them.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who tries to explain to Job why people suffer. He holds that God uses suffering to correct people and call them to repentance. Many scholars think Elihu is not entirely right in Job's case, since the book itself shows that Job was not suffering because of some specific sin. Even so, the general principle of listening to God is wise.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to God when he corrects us, whether through his Word or through sincere counsel. Being humble and willing to change guards our hearts and leads us to a wiser life.
exp.25:2:
Job asks his friend ironically: "How have you counseled the unwise?" Here "unwise" points to someone who lacks understanding, and "provided fully sound insight" shows the same mocking tone. The words sound like praise, as if to say, "How wise you have shown yourself to be!", but Job means the opposite.

Job speaks in answer to Bildad, who had just described the greatness of God without offering any comfort to Job in his suffering. Job feels that his friends have neither helped nor strengthened him. For that reason he reproaches them, saying that their words, though they may sound wise, do not serve someone who is suffering.

For today: before advising someone who is suffering, listen with patience. Often they do not need great speeches, but companionship, tenderness, and words that truly lift their spirits.
exp.8:19:
He says that even if Job were righteous and wanted to declare himself innocent, his own words would end up condemning him. And if he claimed to be blameless, that very claim would declare him guilty. The phrase "declare himself righteous" means claiming to be in the right; "guilty" means deserving blame or punishment; "blameless" speaks of someone with no fault.

Job is speaking, answering his friend Bildad. He is suffering greatly and feels he cannot win a case against God, because God is very powerful and no one can summon him to court. Job expresses his distress and his helplessness. Some readers see humility here; others see a complaint from someone who does not yet understand God. Both readings are possible.

For today: we do not need to boast of being blameless or to build a defense before God. We can come to him with sincerity and humility, trusting in his mercy and not in our merits.
exp.0:7:
In this verse God asks Satan whether he has considered Job, his servant. God describes him as someone without equal on the earth: "blameless" means whole-hearted and sincere, not without flaws; "upright" means honest; "fears God" means he respects and honors God; and "shuns evil" means he turns away from doing wrong.

God is speaking in a scene where the sons of God present themselves before Him and Satan comes among them. God mentions Job first, and not as a meaningless provocation. Satan then answers that Job serves God for the benefits he receives. This begins a test that shows what Job's faith is really like. How this heavenly scene should be understood is explained in several ways, but the text highlights Job's integrity.

For today: try to make sure your faith does not depend only on blessings. Live with honesty and reverence toward God, including when everything is going well.
exp.1:3:
Satan answers God with a saying: "Skin for skin." It means that a person will give up everything he owns in exchange for his own life. The explanation applies this idea to Job's situation and the sincerity of his faith.

Satan, the accuser, speaks. God has just praised Job because he stayed faithful even after losing his possessions and his children. Satan does not give up and says that Job endured because his own body was kept safe. That is why he asks to touch Job's health. Scholars explain the saying "skin for skin" in several ways, but the central idea is clear: Satan doubts that Job's faith is sincere.

Today we can remember that true faith does not depend on everything going well for us. When trials come, we can keep trusting God, even when we do not understand what is happening, because he remains good and worthy of trust.
exp.8:27:
Job says that he dreads all his pains and sufferings. The word "dread" in the verse means that his sorrows frighten him and fill him with fear. Job adds that he knows God will not acquit him or let him go free from guilt.

Here Job speaks in the midst of his great suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He has said that his days pass quickly and that, although he tries to forget his complaint and cheer himself up, the pain returns. He feels that God is so great that he cannot defend himself before Him. His fear comes from his suffering, and we should remember that he does not always have it right in what he thinks about God.

When pain fills you with fear and doubt, do not hide it: bring it to God honestly, as Job did. And remember that, in Christ, God does declare us righteous and receives us.
exp.8:22:
It says that when a sudden disaster brings death, God seems to mock the despair of the innocent. A "scourge" is a calamity or a blow; "sudden" means all at once; "despair" is the deep hopelessness of someone in anguish. It is a harsh line, and it is worth noting that it expresses what Job feels, not an exact description of God's character.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous pain. He feels that God treats the righteous and the wicked alike, and he cannot find an explanation. Later God himself corrects his words, and elsewhere the Bible shows a God who is compassionate toward those who suffer.

For today: when pain leads you to think bitter things about God, do not hide them; tell him honestly, as Job did. Then seek the support of people of faith, and remember that what you feel is not always the whole truth about God.
exp.13:12:
Job asks God to hide him in Sheol, the place of the dead, and to conceal him there until God's anger has passed. He wants God to appoint a set time for him and then to remember him. The words "hide" and "conceal" carry the sense of covering and protecting him, and "until Your anger has passed" describes waiting for the anger to ease.

Job speaks as a man who suffers greatly and does not understand why. He feels that God is angry with him. He has just said that human life is brief and fragile, and that death seems final. Even so, he dares here to imagine that God would not forget him and that there would be a meeting again. Some see here a hope of resurrection; others see only a wish that Job barely dares to think.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, speak to God honestly, even if you understand nothing. You can tell him your deepest wishes, trusting that he remembers you.
exp.8:2:
If one wished to contend with God, he could not answer Him one time out of a thousand. This means that a person who wanted to argue his case against God, or bring a lawsuit against Him, would be unable to answer even one of the countless things God might ask. "Contend" means to argue or bring a case, as in a court of law.

Job speaks as a man who suffers greatly and feels that God is treating him unjustly. He is answering his friend Bildad, who says that God does not pervert justice. Job agrees that God is just, but he wonders how a human being could defend himself before someone so great and wise. Some understand that Job speaks with bitterness; others see him honestly acknowledging his smallness.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, you can be sincere in prayer, but with humility. God is wise, and you do not have to have all the answers; you can trust Him.
exp.9:1:
Job tells God not to condemn him and asks to be told why God is prosecuting him. The word "prosecute" here means accusing or bringing charges, as in a legal case. Job is asking not only for relief but for an understanding of the reason behind his pain.

Job is a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is weary of living and decides to pour out his bitterness. He feels that God treats him as guilty, even though he does not know what wrong he has done. Later, the book shows that his suffering was not a punishment for a specific sin, though Job does not yet know this.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, you can be honest with God. Bringing him your questions and your pain, instead of keeping them silent or turning away, is also a way of trusting that he hears you.
exp.13:0:
Job 14:1 says that man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble. The phrase "short of days" means that life is brief. The phrase "full of trouble" means filled with sorrows, grief, and hardships. It is a simple way of describing how fragile our existence is.

The speaker is Job, a man who lost nearly everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He answers his friends and speaks with God, pouring out his pain. The verses that follow compare life to a flower that is cut down and to a shadow that passes away. Job complains and asks why God would fix his attention on someone so frail. Interpreters see this as honest prayer, not as a lack of faith.

Today we too can speak to God with sincerity about our weariness and pain, without pretending. Recognizing that life is brief also helps us value each day and trust in God.
exp.25:3:
Here Job asks his friend: "To whom have you uttered these words? And whose spirit spoke through you?" Job questions where what Bildad has just said comes from.

Job speaks, answering Bildad. His friends give him long speeches that bring no comfort, as if his suffering were the result of some hidden sin. Job is being sarcastic: such words do not help a weak man. Some interpret this as suggesting that Bildad does not speak with inspiration from God, but out of pride or by repeating what is already known.

Before speaking to someone who is suffering, it is good to ask ourselves whether our words come from love and truth, or only from our pride. Sometimes keeping quiet and listening to someone helps more than giving long explanations.
exp.9:11:
He says that God gave Job life and also loving devotion, meaning a kind treatment Job did not deserve. The word "care" in the verse describes God's attentive concern for him, like someone who comes close to see how we are doing. That is why Job says this care "preserved" his spirit, meaning it protected and sustained him.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of terrible suffering. Earlier he recalls how God formed him in the womb, and then he complains that God seems to watch closely for his faults. This verse is a moment of gratitude within a painful complaint. Job mixes faith and confusion, and the Bible does not hide this.

For today: even when you are going through a trial and do not understand God, you can remember his past goodness. Today, write down three ways God has cared for you, and thank him sincerely, even if you also bring him your questions.
exp.40:8:
This verse says that anyone who hopes to overcome Leviathan will be let down: that hope is false and will come to nothing. Simply seeing him is enough to make a person fall, that is, to lose strength and courage out of fear. The verse puts it as a question: is not the sight of him overwhelming?

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful creature that no one can tame. It has been understood as a crocodile or as a monster of chaos; scholars do not agree. God wants to show that if Job cannot face this creature, he is even less able to call his Creator to account.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, remember that He is greater than everything that frightens you. Rest in his wisdom and trust in Him, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.23:11:
In the city people groan with pain, and the wounded cry out for help. But God does not seem to charge anyone with wrongdoing or act against this injustice. Some versions present this as God not paying attention to their cries. The original Hebrew can be understood in more than one way.

Job speaks in the middle of his debate with his friends. They say that wicked people always end up suffering. Job answers with examples from real life: there are oppressors who seem to get away with it, while the poor suffer. Job complains and does not understand God's silence.

Today we can do what God has not yet asked us to stay silent about: we can refuse to ignore those who suffer. If God seems silent, we can be his hands: help someone in need, support someone who is hurt, and pray sincerely, even with questions.
exp.31:6:
Elihu says that he thought age should speak and that many years should teach wisdom. "Age should speak" means that older people, because of their long lives, ought to speak first. "Many years should teach wisdom" means they will show wisdom through their words.

Elihu is a young man who has listened quietly to Job and his three friends, who are older. They could no longer answer Job, and Elihu becomes angry. Out of respect for their age he waited, and that is why he says he was afraid to speak. But in the verses that follow he makes clear that wisdom does not depend only on years, but on the spirit that God gives.

Respecting older people is good, since their experience often teaches a great deal. But let us not assume that whoever has more years is always right. Let us listen to everyone with humility and compare what they say with what God teaches. And if you are young, speak with respect and without pride.
exp.0:9:
Here Satan says that God has placed a protective hedge on every side around Job, his household, and all that he owns. He also says that God has blessed the work of Job's hands, and so his possessions have increased in the land. A "hedge" is the wall or fence that surrounds something and keeps it safe. The word "possessions" refers to Job's property and livestock, and "on every side" means all around him.

Satan answers God, who has just praised Job as a blameless and upright man who fears God. Satan suggests that Job serves God only for what he gets, because he receives benefits. In this way he questions the motive behind Job's faith. The Bible does not explain everything about how this episode works, but it shows that God allows the test.

For today: examine why you love God. Thank him for his blessings, but try to trust him also when they are missing, because he deserves to be loved for who he is.
exp.29:24:
Job asks whether he has not wept for the person who was in distress, and whether his heart has not grieved for the needy. The phrase "in distress" refers to someone going through pain or misfortune. The word "needy" refers to a person who lacks what is necessary. The question expects the answer "yes, of course I wept."

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He feels treated unfairly by God and by his friends. Before losing everything, he cared for the needy and felt compassion. That is why he does not understand why evil came to him now, when he expected good. Some think he seeks to defend his integrity; others also see a sincere pain at having been abandoned.

For today: compassion is part of a life faithful to God. This week, notice someone near you who is suffering, and weep with them: listen to them, pray for them, and help them in something concrete. And if you are suffering, you can tell God your pain honestly, as Job did.
exp.23:7:
They are left exposed to the rain that falls from the mountains. They get soaked through, and with no roof or covering over them, they huddle against the rocks looking for any kind of shelter. The "flash floods" here are simply the heavy, rushing rains, and the "crags" are the large rocks.

Job speaks in the middle of his debate with his friends. They maintained that wicked people soon suffer misfortune. Job replies that in real life the wicked often abuse the poor and seem to get away with it. That is why he describes here the suffering of the exploited and expresses his grief over that injustice.

For today: let us not ignore the needs of the most vulnerable. We can help with clothing, food, or support for those who suffer near us, and speak up with respect for those who have no voice.
exp.20:30:
It says that no one dares to confront the wicked to his face about his conduct, and that no one makes him pay for what he has done. Here "denounce" means to openly point out or rebuke, and "repay" means the deserved payment or punishment. It seems the wicked man lives on without anyone calling him to account.

Job is speaking, answering his friends, who held that the wicked always suffer soon. Job replies that the wicked often prosper and die in peace, honored at their funeral. Some understand the verse itself as a rhetorical question about people; others think it also points to God. The text does not fully settle this.

For today: do not measure God or people only by what you see. When injustice seems to go unanswered, trust that God sees, and try yourself to act with truth and gentle courage.
exp.17:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that Bildad, a man from Shuah, takes up the word to reply to what Job has just said. Here "replied" means that he continues the conversation. The phrase "the Shuhite" indicates that he came from the land or the family line of Shuah.

Bildad is one of the three friends who came to comfort Job in his suffering. This is his second speech. Job has just defended himself, and Bildad is annoyed that he does not accept his explanation, so he begins with rebuke and little patience, as the following verses show.

For today: when someone is suffering, it is better to listen with patience than to rush to correct or to give explanations. Bildad spoke without tenderness and ended up wounding. Let us ask God for kind words and an attentive heart before we respond.
exp.23:6:
They spend the night without clothes, with no blanket to protect them from the cold. The word "covering" refers to a cloak or blanket. The verses around this one show that the cause is the cruelty of unjust people.

Job is speaking, answering his friends. They were saying that wicked people always end up suffering. Job replies that in real life many people oppress the weak, and it seems nothing happens to them. Some scholars debate who the "wild donkeys" in the context refers to, but in this verse the suffering of the poor is clear.

For today: let us not ignore the cold of others. We can give a blanket, clothing in good condition, or help to a family in need. We should also avoid taking advantage of those who have less.
exp.37:15:
God asks Job whether he has ever journeyed to the vents of the sea, the places where its waters rise from below, or walked through the trenches of the deep. The word "trenches" points to the deep, hidden parts of the ocean, a place of mystery to the ancient world.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give Job reasons for his pain. Instead he asks him questions about creation, to show him how great his wisdom is and how limited human knowledge is.

Today we can learn humility. We will not always understand why things happen, but we can trust that God, who knows even the deepest places, also knows our lives and cares for them.
exp.31:17:
Elihu says he is so full of words that he can no longer stay silent. "Belly" refers to his inner self, the deepest part of his being. "Compels" means it presses on him, as if something within him were pushing him to speak. He feels an inner pressure that needs to come out.

Elihu is a young man who listened quietly to Job and his three friends. Out of respect for his elders he waited, but they stopped answering and Job remained unconvinced. Elihu feels obliged to give his own view. Although he speaks sincerely, the book does not present him as a perfect voice, and in the end it is God who answers Job.

For today: it is good to know how to wait and listen before speaking. But when you do speak, do it with humility, and check whether what you feel is wisdom or just the urge to give your opinion. Ask God to guide you in what you say.
exp.12:14:
Job says that even if God kills him, he will still hope in Him. Even so, he wants to present and defend his conduct to God's face. "Though He slay me" means "even if He takes my life." The "I" in "I will still defend my ways" is the same speaker who declares his hope, so his trust and his honesty stand side by side.

Job speaks as a righteous man who has lost everything and suffers greatly. His friends say his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job denies this, and for that reason he asks to speak directly with God, risking everything, because he believes that only the guilty fear to stand before Him.

When you suffer without understanding why, you can be honest with God, bring Him your doubts and complaints, and still keep trusting in Him. Faith is not keeping silent about pain, but holding on to God in the middle of it.
exp.21:3:
He says that God does not rebuke you or bring you into judgment because you revere him. The question "Is it for your reverence that He rebukes you?" asks whether God would rebuke you because of your reverence, and "enters into judgment against you" means he brings a charge against you in a legal proceeding. The word "reverence" refers to deep respect and awe toward God. Eliphaz poses a rhetorical question: does God act against Job because of Job's reverence for him? The expected answer is no.

Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He believes that suffering is always the consequence of sin. For that reason, in the verses that follow, he accuses Job of great wickedness without offering any proof. His argument is unjust, and the book of Job itself shows that God does not agree with him.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us avoid giving them quick explanations or accusing them. Better to walk alongside them with compassion, listen, and let God be the judge.
exp.31:10:
It says that Elihu waited patiently while Job's friends were speaking. He listened closely as they were searching for words. "Reasons" refers to their explanations and defenses. The phrase "as you searched for words" suggests that at times they seemed to be looking for how to answer, without having a clear answer.

Elihu speaks now, a young man who had kept silent out of respect for his elders: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. Now he sees that they had not been able to answer Job, and so he takes courage to speak. He says that wisdom does not depend only on age. Some interpreters see in Elihu a balanced voice; others note that he also speaks with a great deal of self-confidence.

For today: let us learn to listen well before we speak. If we have something to say, let us consider whether it will help, whether it is true, and whether we say it with humility and respect, especially when someone is suffering.
exp.24:2:
He says that God's troops cannot be numbered, and that his light rises over everyone. "Troops" may refer to the angels, to the stars, or to all the forces of heaven; interpreters understand it in different ways. "His light" speaks of his care, his presence, and his watchful eye, which shines over everything. Both questions expect the same answer: no one can count them, and no one is outside his light.

Bildad, one of Job's three friends, is the speaker. This is his last speech, and it is very short. He wants to show that God is so great and so pure that no human being can claim to be righteous before him. Yet the book itself shows that Bildad is not entirely right about Job's suffering.

For today: since God's light reaches everyone, there is no need to pretend before him. We can live with sincerity and humility, trusting in his mercy, and treat others with respect.
exp.27:26:
It says that God, when he created the world and set order over the wind, the water, the rain and the lightning, looked at wisdom and appraised it. He established it and searched it out. Wisdom appears almost as the plan God had in mind when he created.

Job speaks in a poem about wisdom. Before this, he says that human beings can dig mines and find treasures, but they do not know where wisdom is and cannot buy it. Only God knows it. Some understand that God used it as a guide in creating; others, that he simply recognized it as his own.

For today: do not rely only on your own understanding. Ask God for wisdom, who knows the origin of all things, and live with reverence toward him, as the next verse says.
exp.39:9:
Look at Behemoth, a huge creature that God made just as He made you. "With you" means that both of them are creatures of God. Although it is so strong, it eats only grass, like an ox. "Behemoth" sounds like "great beasts." No one knows for certain which animal it is: some think of a hippopotamus or an elephant, others of a legendary creature.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had asked for explanations of his suffering. God does not give them to him directly, but shows him His power and wisdom in creation. Earlier He asked Job whether he could humble the proud and save himself. Behemoth shows that there are enormous things that only God controls.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that the God who sustains everything created also cares for you. Trust in Him even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.5:16:
It says that the streams Job speaks of dry up in the heat. In other words, the water they hold stops flowing in the dry season and disappears from its channels. "Ceasing" means the water stops running, and "vanishing from their channels" shows that the streams are gone from the very places where they had been.

Job speaks here while suffering greatly and hurt by his friends. Earlier he compared his companions, meaning his friends, to seasonal streams: they look full of water, but when the heat comes they disappear. So they failed him just when he most needed comfort. The travelers of Tema and Sheba, who searched for water, were left disappointed.

For today: let us be steady people who do not vanish when someone is suffering. Sometimes great words are not needed, but rather staying present, listening, and accompanying with patience, especially when the difficult time goes on.
exp.23:4:
The verse compares the poor to wild donkeys that go out into the desert early in the morning to find something to eat. In the Berean Standard Bible, "their work" is described as foraging for food, which is what they must do simply to survive. The wasteland itself provides food for their children.

Scholars debate whether this verse describes poor people who are exploited and survive as best they can, or wicked people who live by plunder. The surrounding verses point more strongly toward exploited poor people.

Job is speaking here, answering his friends, who insist that God quickly punishes the wicked. Job protests that he sees the poor suffering while abusers prosper, and he asks why God does not act.

Today we can open our eyes to those who work hard and barely get by, and help them with generosity and justice in whatever way is within our reach.
exp.36:7:
This verse says that wild animals go into their lairs and settle down in their dens. A "lair" is a place where an animal rests or hides, and a "den" is the shelter where it lives.

The one speaking is Elihu, the young man who speaks near the end of the book of Job. He is describing winter, with its snow and heavy rains. He says that God sends those storms, and that even animals and people come to a stop. His purpose is to lead Job to recognize God's power and greatness.

For today: when times of storm come and you have to stop, do not see it only as an obstacle. You can use that pause to pray, to rest, and to remember that God is still great and cares for you.
exp.14:3:
According to his accuser, Job's words undermine reverent fear of God and hinder meditation before Him. The phrase "undermine the fear of God" means weakening respect for God. To "hinder meditation" means to get in the way of quiet, thoughtful devotion. The idea is that by speaking this way, Job would be getting in the way of genuine devotion.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He believes that Job, in defending his innocence and complaining about his suffering, speaks with pride and without wisdom. We should remember that God later said the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so this accusation is Eliphaz's opinion, not God's judgment.

For today: before correcting someone who is suffering, let us listen with humility. And when we suffer, we can pray honestly, without losing our reverence for God.
exp.40:9:
No one is so fierce as to rouse Leviathan. If no one dares to stir up this creature, then how much less can anyone stand against God, that is, resist Him or present himself to Him as an equal.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. In this chapter He describes Leviathan, a powerful creature that some understand as a crocodile and others as a monster of chaos; scholars interpret it in several ways. God uses this image to show Job that He is the Creator, and that no one can claim anything from God.

When we do not understand what God allows, we can rest in the fact that He is greater than everything that frightens us. Trusting in His power and wisdom gives us peace, even without having all the answers.
exp.8:4:
He says God has such great power that he can uproot the mountains from their place. He does it "in his anger," meaning with his wrath or righteous anger. And the mountains do not even notice who moved them: it happens suddenly, without warning.

The phrase "overturns them" means that he turns them over or flips them upside down.

Job speaks, a man who suffers greatly. He answers his friend Bildad and acknowledges that God is wise and strong. But he feels that he cannot argue with God or present his case before him. He uses images from nature to describe the greatness of God. Some think Job exaggerates because of his pain, since God has not yet given him an explanation.

For today: when life shakes you as if mountains were moving, remember that God is still in control. You can draw near to him with humility and trust, even without understanding everything.
exp.14:26:
It says the wicked man was covered with fat on his face and that his waistline bulged with flesh. The image is of someone who lives in plenty and comfort. Fat on the face and a bulging waist are signs of wealth and ease.

It is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, who speaks. He is describing the wicked person and his fate. According to him, whoever defies God, even if he seems prosperous and free of worry, ends badly. With this he hints that Job is suffering because of some sin. Note that the book later shows that Eliphaz was wrong to apply this to Job. Many understand that the fatness suggests pride and self-sufficiency, though this is an interpretation.

Today we can ask ourselves whether comfort is making us forget God. Giving thanks, being generous, and staying humble helps us. And let us also be careful not to judge the suffering of others as if it were always a punishment.
exp.25:5:
He says that nothing is hidden from God. The word translated "Sheol" is the Hebrew name for the place of the dead, and "Abaddon" means destruction or the place of death. A covering is a veil or lid. So even the world of the dead lies open and in full view of God.

Job speaks here in reply to his friend Bildad. Bildad had spoken of God's power, but Job reminds him, with irony, that he too knows that greatness. Job describes God as Creator who rules over both the visible and the unseen: the seas, death, the heavens, and the earth. Some see in this poetic language rather than a scientific explanation.

For today: if God sees even the most hidden things, you can bring Him your pain, your doubts, and your secrets. You need not hide from Him; you can come to Him with sincerity and rest in His care.
exp.21:1:
It says that a human being gives God no benefit, even if he is wise and things go well for him because he lives wisely. "Be of use to God" means bring Him gain or advantage. The question expects a "no": God does not need anything from us.

Elifaz of Teman, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. He is accusing Job of suffering because of some hidden sin. Although this idea about God is partly true, Elifaz misuses it, since he suggests that Job's integrity does not matter to God. Later God Himself says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: serve God with gratitude, not to earn His favor or to show off. And be careful about using biblical truths to judge someone who is suffering.
exp.6:8:
The verse says that human life is brief and fragile, like a cloud that vanishes and is gone from the sky. In the same way, the one who goes down to Sheol, the place of the dead, does not come back up, meaning does not return to this life. "Vanishes and is gone" describes the cloud slowly passing away until nothing of it remains.

The speaker is Job, who has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. In the middle of his pain, he speaks to God honestly and tells him that his life passes like a breath. Here he speaks out of anguish, with not much hope. Some scholars see in his words a human outpouring of grief rather than a teaching about what happens after death.

For today: life is short, so we can value each day and the people we love. And when we suffer, we can speak to God with honesty, as Job did, without pretending to be strong.
exp.18:26:
Job says that he himself will see God, with his own eyes and not those of someone else. In the Berean Standard Bible, the verse reads "I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger," so the comment can refer to that wording. The phrase "How my heart yearns within me!" shows the depth of his longing. Job holds on to this hope even as his body and strength are wasting away.

Job speaks while suffering from illness, loss, and the unjust accusations of his friends, who believe his pain is a punishment for some sin. Abandoned by everyone, he affirms his hope in a living Redeemer. Some understand that he speaks of seeing God after death; others, of seeing God defend his cause in this life. The text allows for both readings.

For today: when pain leaves you without strength and no one understands you, hold on to God honestly. You may weep, ask questions, and still hope that He will see you and defend you.
exp.33:6:
What man is like Job, who drinks up derision like water? Elihu asks whether there is anyone like Job, who "drinks up derision like water." This means that Job, in Elihu's view, swallows mockery and irreverent words as naturally as someone who drinks water without thinking about it.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in near the end of the book, after the three friends have run out of answers to Job. He is upset because he believes that Job, by insisting on his innocence, is accusing God of injustice. Note that this is Elihu's opinion, and later God himself will say that Job spoke rightly in what matters most (Job 42:7).

For today: before judging someone who is suffering, let us listen with humility. It is easy to accuse the hurting person without knowing all that God is doing in their life.
exp.36:11:
This verse says that the clouds swirl and move in every direction at God's direction. They carry out, across the whole surface of the earth, everything he commands.

The word "direction" in the verse points to guidance or instruction. "All the earth" refers to the whole surface of the globe. "Swirl about" describes clouds moving and turning all around.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in near the end of the book of Job. He tries to comfort and correct Job, who is suffering greatly. Elihu speaks about the weather to show that God governs nature with wisdom. The verses that follow say that the clouds can bring punishment, rain, or mercy. Many think Elihu is right to speak of the greatness of God, although not everything he says about Job's suffering is correct.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God still governs with wisdom. Pause for a moment, look at the sky, and trust him.
exp.28:20:
They listened to me with expectation. They waited for me to speak, and when I gave my counsel, they stayed silent to receive it. The idea of listening to me is the same as the idea of waiting for my words, and the picture of silence at my counsel means that they remained quiet before what I advised.

Job speaks here as a man who has lost nearly everything. In chapter 29 he looks back with longing on his days of blessing, when God watched over him and the community respected him. He does not say this out of empty pride, but because he suffers to see how much his situation has changed. The verses that follow compare his words to the rain that people waited for.

For today: if others listen to you, take care that your words give life, like rain. And when someone advises you with wisdom, learn to be quiet and to truly listen.
exp.20:20:
