It says that when a person dies, he no longer cares about the household he leaves behind. If his months of life run out, he does not care or rejoice about what happens to his home afterward. "Run out" means ended, and "care" means concern or delight in what is left behind.

Job speaks, answering his friend Zophar. Zophar had said that God punishes the wicked by making their children suffer. Job replies that this is not enough as justice: the wicked person will not feel that punishment after he dies. Therefore, he says, God should punish him himself, not his children. Scholars understand the passage in somewhat different ways, but this is the most common sense.

For today: let us not judge the suffering of others quickly or give easy answers. Let us live with humility and responsibility, knowing that our time is short and that God is the just judge.
exp.18:25:
Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God. This verse says that, even though Job's skin is destroyed, he expects to see God. "Even after my skin has been destroyed" speaks of the body wearing away or dying. "Yet in my flesh I will see God" can be understood as seeing God with a restored body, or from his own person. The original text is difficult, and scholars interpret it in several ways.

Job speaks while he is sick, struck by pain and unjustly accused by his friends. He feels abandoned, but in the middle of his anguish he expresses a deep confidence: his Redeemer lives and in the end will stand upon the earth. Job wants that hope to be engraved forever.

For today: when suffering makes you feel that everything is coming to an end, remember that your hope does not depend on your strength or your health. You can keep trusting that God lives and has the final word.
exp.19:20:
He says this man consumed everything and left nothing behind. For that reason, his prosperity will not endure. The word "consume" here means to eat up, to use everything up, or to take it all for himself without leaving anything for others. The word "endure" means to last for a long time.

It is Zophar, one of Job's friends, who speaks. He describes what he believes happens to the wicked person who oppresses the poor. Zophar insists that injustice always ends badly. But notice that the book shows his idea is incomplete, because Job was suffering without being a wicked person as Zophar was implying.

Today this invites us to examine greed in the heart. If we have more, we can ask ourselves how to help those who have less, instead of hoarding everything for ourselves. But we should not use this verse to judge the one who suffers.
exp.26:10:
Here Job says he will teach his friends plainly and in order about the power of God. He promises not to hide the ways of the Almighty. "Almighty" refers to the Almighty, and "the power of God" points to God's strength and to the way he acts.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his argument with his friends. They accuse him of being a wicked man because he suffers so much. Job defends his innocence and now tells them that he too understands how God deals with the wicked. Some scholars think Job answers here with irony or repeats what they themselves maintain; the text allows several readings.

For today: before speaking about God, especially with someone who is suffering, let us speak with honesty and humility. Let us not use God to give quick answers, but share sincerely what we really know of him.
exp.21:5:
This verse accuses someone of taking advantage of the weakest people. "Needlessly demanded security" means asking for an item that someone gives as a guarantee on a loan, when there was no good reason to ask for it. The verse also says that the man deprived the naked of their clothing, meaning he took away even the most basic clothing that poor people had to keep warm.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, so he accuses Job of serious wrongdoing. The Bible does not show that Job did any of this; the book itself presents him as a man of integrity. For that reason, these words are a false accusation, not a reliable account of Job.

For today: the Bible does care about those who have little. Ask yourself whether, in your work, your debts, or your business dealings, you treat the most vulnerable with justice and compassion. And avoid judging others for their suffering without knowing their story.
exp.35:20:
Be careful not to turn to wrongdoing, for you have preferred it to suffering. The words here are "turn," "wrongdoing," and "suffering." Elihu is not speaking here; it is Elihu who warns Job not to turn his patience in suffering into the path of wrongdoing.

Elihu, the young man who speaks near the end of the book, tries to correct Job. He thinks suffering can be a lesson from God and that Job could fall into unjust complaint against Him. Some understand that Elihu accuses Job of having chosen rebellion; others see only a warning. Moreover, the book itself does not fully side with Elihu.

For today: when you suffer, do not look for crooked ways out or accuse God. Ask Him for strength to remain honest and faithful, even if the pain continues.
exp.30:35:
This verse says that Job would carry the written charge his accuser brings against him proudly on his shoulder, and would wear it like a crown. Job is not afraid of that charge. He is ready to face it openly and to show that he has nothing to hide.

Job speaks near the end of his defense. He is suffering greatly, and his friends tell him that his pain is punishment for some sin. Job maintains that he is innocent and wants God himself to hear him and answer him. In the verse before, the one who accuses him is the accuser, and Job asks that the accusation be put in writing. Some scholars think Job speaks with courage and others that he speaks with a certain arrogance; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when you feel unjustly accused, come before God honestly. But remember that only He judges with perfect justice, and that we also need his mercy.
exp.39:11:
He says that Behemoth moves its tail with the strength and stiffness of a cedar, a large and firm tree. The "sinews of its genitals" are the tendons in that area, tightly interwoven. Some translations say "thighs." Scholars are not sure what animal it is: some think of the hippopotamus, others of the elephant, and others of a symbolic creature.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons, but shows him his power in creation. Behemoth is a creature that Job cannot control, but God made it.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that God knows more than you do and cares for his creation. Rest in his wisdom, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.8:6:
It says that God has power over the sun: if He commands it not to shine, it does not shine. It also says He seals off the stars, meaning He shuts their light away so that it cannot be seen, much like closing a door.

The speaker is Job, answering his friend Bildad. Job is suffering greatly and acknowledges that God is wise and strong, but he feels he cannot defend himself before Him. That is why he describes how God rules over mountains, earth, sun, and stars. Some think he speaks with respect; others also notice a tone of complaint.

For today: when you feel that your life is dark or out of control, remember that the God who governs the sun and the stars also cares for you. You can speak to Him honestly and trust Him, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.22:11:
He says that Job never turned away from what God commanded. "Command of His lips" and "words of His mouth" refer to what God has said. "Treasured" means that he held it dear and obeyed it. And "more than my daily bread" means that he valued God's word above his daily food, which is something necessary for life.

Job speaks in the midst of enormous suffering, while his friends accuse him of having sinned. He does not understand why he suffers and longs to present himself before God. Even so, he trusts that God knows his path and that, after being tested, he will come out "like gold," that is, purified and firm. This verse is part of his defense: his life has been faithful.

For today: if you are going through a trial, do not let go of God's Word. Set aside time for it each day, as you set aside your food, and let it sustain you even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.37:4:
God asks who set the measurements of the earth and who stretched a measuring line across it. The "line" was a measuring cord, like the one builders use. God speaks of the earth as though it were a carefully planned building. The question "Surely you know!" is an invitation for Job to answer honestly.

Here God himself speaks, out of a whirlwind, after Job had suffered greatly and asked for explanations. God does not give Job a reason for his pain; instead he asks questions that show his wisdom and power as Creator. Job was not present when the world was founded.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that God designed and sustains all things with wisdom. You can trust him even when you do not have all the answers, and you can pray with humility and sincerity.
exp.39:8:
Job 40:9 asks Job whether he has an arm like God's and can thunder with a voice like His. The verse is a challenge. If Job could do what God does, then God would admit that Job's own strength could save him. The "arm" stands for power and strength, and the "voice" stands for the authority to command.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned God's justice and asked for explanations. God responds with questions that show His own greatness: Job cannot govern the world or judge the wicked as God does. There is irony here. If Job could do all this, he would not need God to save him. But clearly he cannot.

For today: humbly recognize that you cannot save yourself or control everything by your own strength. When you do not understand what is happening, rest in the fact that God still governs with wisdom and justice.
exp.14:31:
The verse says that the wicked person will see his life cut short before his time, like a tree whose branch is struck down. His new shoots, which would bring hope, will never grow green again. It pictures a tree that does not recover.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, so he describes the downfall of the wicked, implying that Job is one of them. At the end of the book, God says that Eliphaz and his friends did not speak rightly (Job 42:7). So this passage is not a correct judgment about Job.

For today: do not use the Bible to accuse someone who is suffering. Not all pain is punishment. Instead, walk alongside them with humility, and examine your own heart before God.
exp.35:2:
Elihu says he will get his knowledge from afar, meaning he will speak from a wide view, not only from what he can see right away. The word "knowledge" here means understanding or learning. His words "I will ascribe justice to my Maker" mean that he will affirm that God, his Creator, is just.

Elihu is the young man who spoke after Job and his three friends finished their debate. He is upset because Job seemed to justify himself more than God. He asks for patience and says he still has something to say in defense of God. Some think that "from afar" points to his general view of creation; the text does not make this entirely clear.

When we suffer or do not understand something, it helps to look beyond the present moment. We can keep our trust that God is just, even when we do not see all the answers, and speak of Him with humility and respect.
exp.38:27:
The passage in view here is about the eagle, not the war horse. Job 39:28 describes it as making its home on a cliff and staying there, with its stronghold on a rocky crag. Some Bibles number this passage a little differently, but it speaks of the eagle.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons, but shows him animals that He created and cares for, such as the horse and the eagle, so that Job may see His wisdom and power.

For today: we do not need to understand everything to trust God. If He cares for the eagle on its high rock, He can also care for you. When you do not understand what you are living through, pause and trust in Him.
exp.33:11:
He says that God never acts with wrongdoing. "Almighty" means All-powerful. "Does not pervert justice" means God does not twist what is right, make what is right look wrong, or give a false verdict. The verse repeats the same idea in two ways to state it strongly.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job and his three friends have argued. Job had said that God was treating him unfairly. Elihu answers that God is just and that he rules over the whole world without anyone putting him in his place. His words contain truth, but in the end God himself corrects Job and the friends, so not everything they say applies to every situation.

When we suffer or do not understand what is happening, we can still trust that God is just, even when we do not see all the answers. We can bring our questions to him honestly, without accusing him or turning away from him.
exp.26:11:
Here Job says to his friends: "Surely all of you have seen it for yourselves. Why then do you keep up this empty talk?" The phrase "empty talk" refers to words with no real substance behind them.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends insist that he suffers because he is wicked. Job reminds them that they themselves have seen how God acts, and that their conclusions do not fit reality. Right afterward, he himself explains the fate of the wicked. Some scholars think Job here repeats what his friends say, and others that he actually agrees with them on this point; the text allows both readings.

Before explaining another person's pain, it is wise to pause. It is easy to repeat ideas that sound correct but do not fit what the one who suffers is living. Today we can accompany others with listening and compassion, not with easy answers.
exp.32:28:
This verse says that God acts more than once in a person's life. "All these things" refers to what has just been described: warnings, corrections, and rescue. "Two or even three times" is not an exact count; it is a way of saying that God does this again and again. "Redeem" means to rescue, and "the pit" speaks of death or ruin.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who comes in at the end of the dialogue between Job and his friends. He wants to argue that God is not silent or unjust, but speaks to people to guide and save them. Some scholars think Elihu is partly right, but that he does not understand Job's case, since Job was suffering without having sinned in the way his friends assumed.

For today: if God has given you another chance, do not despise it. Acknowledge your mistakes honestly and return to Him with humility.
exp.16:10:
What it says: Job says his days have passed quickly and that his plans and the desires of his heart have been broken off. The image of being "uprooted" is like pulling a plant up by the root: what he had hoped to do with his life was cut off all at once. The "desires of his heart" are the projects and longings he once held.

Context: Job speaks here, and he is suffering greatly. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and his friends accuse him instead of comforting him. He feels that death is drawing near. Even so, shortly before this he said that the righteous will hold to their way. In other words, he mixes deep pain with a flicker of faith.

For today: When your plans fall apart, do not pretend you are fine. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did. Then take the next small step of faithfulness, trusting that God is still with you even when you do not understand.
exp.34:14:
Elihu says that Job speaks without understanding. In his view, since God has not punished wickedness or taken much notice of folly, Job takes the opportunity to complain at length and without wisdom. "Punished" here means that God has not called folly to account; "taken much notice" means that God has not paid close attention to it. The Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, and some translations understand it differently.

Here Elihu speaks, the young man who intervenes almost at the end of the book. He is upset because Job has said that serving God does not seem to bring any benefit. Elihu believes Job is mistaken, although the book itself shows that his understanding of suffering is also incomplete.

Today it reminds us to be careful with our words when we suffer. We may pour out our hearts before God, as Job did, but it is good to do so with humility and without accusing him. Before we speak, let us ask for wisdom and trust in his justice even when we do not understand.
exp.20:28:
Job asks his friends whether they have never talked with travelers, with the people who go along the roads. He also asks whether they do not accept the reports those travelers give. Job says that anyone who has listened to such people already knows what they have seen.

Job speaks to his friends, who insist that the wicked always come to a bad end and that his suffering must be punishment for some sin. Job answers that the experience of many people shows something else: sometimes the wicked prosper. The next phrase is difficult, and it can be understood in different ways.

Today, before judging someone who suffers, it is good to listen humbly to what real life shows us. Not all pain is punishment, and God is greater than our formulas.
exp.37:30:
God asks Job whether he can bind the chains of the Pleiades, that cluster of stars bunched together, or loosen the belt of Orion, another famous constellation. The meaning of some of the Hebrew words here is uncertain, so the picture is best read as a bold image of the heavens and their arrangement rather than a precise claim about how the stars are held in place.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a reason for his pain, but shows him his greatness as Creator through questions Job cannot answer. Earlier he spoke of the ice and the frost, and now of the starry sky.

For today: when you do not understand what you are living through, remember that God holds the universe together with order and wisdom. You can rest in the fact that he is greater than your questions and entrust to him what you cannot control.
exp.12:16:
Job asks his friends to listen to him closely. The phrase "my words" in this verse refers to his defense, the case he wants to make with his reasons. The phrase "my declaration" is what he wants them to clearly understand. "Ring in your ears" points to the need for them to really take it in, not just half-hear it.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends tell him he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job disagrees and wants to present his case before God. A little earlier he said that, even if God kills him, he will still wait for him. Now he asks to be heard before they keep judging him.

For today: when someone is suffering, before giving advice or judgments, let us listen with patience and attention. And if we are the ones who suffer, we can speak honestly before God, trusting that he hears us.
exp.8:24:
He says that Job's days pass more quickly than a runner, someone who hurries along carrying a message. His days go by without him being able to see anything good. It is a complaint about how short and painful life feels to him.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He has lost children, possessions and health, and feels that God acts in ways he cannot understand. His words are a sincere lament, not a complete teaching about God. The book itself later shows that God listens to him.

For today: when you feel that time is slipping away in pain, do not hide what you feel. Speak with God honestly, as Job did, and seek the support of people you trust. God is not frightened by our sincere complaints.
exp.5:9:
He says that Job would still find comfort, even if God kept striking him with pain and gave him no relief, because he has not denied the words of the Holy One. The phrase "I would still have comfort" means he would still have some peace left. The phrase "unrelenting pain" means pain that never lets up, with no pause or ease. "The Holy One" is God.

Job speaks here, answering his friend Eliphaz. He is suffering greatly and wishes that God would end his life. Even so, he wants it to be clear that he has not abandoned his faithfulness. Some understand "the words of the Holy One" to mean God's commandments; others, more broadly, everything God has said. In either case, Job relies on his clear conscience.

For today: in the middle of pain, you can find comfort if you remain faithful to God, even when you do not understand what is happening. Tell him honestly what you feel, but do not let go of his Word.
exp.41:0:
This verse says that Job replied to the LORD. The sentence is short and simply introduces Job's words that follow.

Before this, God spoke to Job out of the whirlwind and asked him many questions about creation and his wisdom. Job had suffered greatly and had questioned God. Now, for the first time since God's speeches, Job speaks again. What follows shows a humble heart: he acknowledges God's power and his own limits.

For today: when you do not understand why something painful is happening, before accusing or doubting, stop and listen to God. Answering Him with humility, and not with pride, opens the door to trusting Him even without having all the answers.
exp.22:8:
Job says he searches for God in every direction and cannot find him. When God is at work in the north, Job cannot behold him; when God turns to the south, Job cannot see him. Together with the east and west mentioned in the previous verse, these make up all four directions of the compass.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends accuse him of having sinned, but he knows he is innocent and wants to present his case before God. He feels that God is absent and cannot manage to find him. Even so, in the following verse he affirms that God knows his way and that he will come out "as gold," that is, purified.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, do not conclude that he has abandoned you. Job did not see God, but he remained faithful and trusted that God did see him. Keep praying and obeying, even when you feel nothing.
exp.21:22:
If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored. If you remove injustice from your tents, you will be restored again and live at peace in your home and family. The explanation's point about the word "tent" still holds: the tent stands for the home and the family. The idea of being "restored" can also mean being raised up or rebuilt, and the word for "injustice" can also mean wickedness.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and so he urges him to repent. His idea that all suffering comes from personal sin was mistaken, and God corrects him at the end of the book (Job 42:7). Even so, returning to God does bring restoration and peace.

For today: draw near to God with sincerity, not using him as a formula to obtain blessings. If you are suffering, do not judge yourself or judge others harshly; seek his presence and his Word, and trust that he cares for you.
exp.10:18:
It says that if the person turns back to God, they will be able to lie down to sleep without fear, and no one will frighten them. Also, many will come to seek their favor.

The words about being scared and the phrase about people seeking favor are the ones that mean to frighten someone or to win their goodwill.

The one speaking is Zophar, one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he promises that if Job repents, everything will get better. Be aware: the book later shows that Zophar was wrong to judge Job, even though his words about the peace God gives sound beautiful. God himself rebukes the friends at the end of the book.

For today: true peace comes from trusting God, but we should not judge someone who suffers as if they were always guilty. Today, instead of explaining another person's pain, accompany someone who is suffering with your presence, your listening, and your prayer.
exp.4:18:
He says that God will rescue the person again and again in the midst of many difficulties. The numbers "six" and "seven" are a Hebrew way of saying "many times, and always." The phrase "no harm will touch you" means that evil will not have the last word or destroy you. The word "rescue" here means delivering someone from trouble, and "touch" means reach or harm.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to comfort Job by saying that God corrects, but also heals. However, Eliphaz assumes that Job's suffering comes from some sin, and at the end of this book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. So his words contain truths, but they do not apply to every case.

For today: when you go through trials, trust that God can sustain and heal you. But do not use this verse to judge others who are suffering; instead, walk alongside them with care and patience.
exp.17:18:
The explanation says that the wicked person the text speaks of will be left without descendants: no offspring or posterity among his people, and no survivor in the place where he once lived. The word "posterity" here means the people who come after a person, his future family line. Its closing phrase is about no one remaining where he once lived. In that culture, having no descendants was seen as losing one's future and the memory of one's name.

Here Bildad, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He describes the fate of the wicked harshly, and he does so with Job in mind, though he says Job is suffering because of his wickedness. The book shows that Bildad was wrong to apply this to Job, since God declares him blameless. His words are not a rule for judging everyone who suffers.

For today: do not use someone else's pain as proof of sin. Instead, accompany them with compassion, and entrust your life and your legacy to God, not only to what you leave behind.
exp.36:23:
It says that people should respect God with awe, because he does not show favor to those who think they are wise on their own. "Therefore, men fear Him" means that people will fear him, or stand in awe of him. "The wise in heart" refers to those who consider themselves wise in their own minds and in their pride.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who closes his speech in the book of Job. He tries to explain that God is great, powerful, and just, and that we cannot fully grasp him. After Elihu, God himself answers Job. Some think Elihu is partly right and others think he is mistaken, so his speech should be read with care.

Today we can practice humility before God. When we do not understand what we are going through, instead of demanding answers or relying only on our own intelligence, we can say to him: "Lord, you are greater than my understanding, and I trust you."
exp.33:10:
It says that God repays each person according to their deeds. "Repays" means giving the fair reward or consequence; "according to his deeds" means in keeping with what he has done; "brings consequences according to his ways" means each person meets the results of the way they live.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in when the speeches of Job's three friends come to an end. He quotes a statement attributed to Job, that it is useless to try to please God, and rejects it. He argues that God is always just. Other passages in the book show that his arguments do not explain everything, since Job suffered without being punished for sin.

Today we can trust that God is just and sees everything clearly. That encourages us to live with honesty, without becoming bitter over injustices, and not to judge others' suffering as if it were always a punishment.
exp.40:6:
He says that no one can wound Leviathan with ordinary weapons. The phrase about filling his hide refers to trying to pierce his skin, and the fisherman's weapons are harpoons and fishing spears, with "head" showing that even aiming at the most vital part achieves nothing. The question expects a "no." The words "hide" and "spears" are the key terms here: the hide is the skin, and the fishing spears are the tools fishermen use to catch their prey.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful and untamable creature. It is not known with certainty what animal this is: some think of the crocodile, others of a symbolic monster. God wants to show that Job cannot master or subdue that creature, and that for this reason he must trust the Creator.

Today, this invites us to humility. We do not control everything, and that is fine. When something overwhelms you, rest in God, who does have control.
exp.34:8:
It says that when there is great oppression, people cry out for help and plead for relief from the power of the mighty. "Men cry out under great oppression" means people shout for help when they are crushed by injustice, and "they plead for relief from the arm of the mighty" describes people begging to be freed from the force of those in power.

Elihu, a young man, speaks up in the debate between Job and his friends. He wants to correct Job, because he believes Job complains against God without reason. Here he notes that the oppressed cry out in their pain, but, according to Elihu, they do not truly seek God (v. 10). Some interpreters think his criticism is too harsh, because God himself does not rebuke him at the end as he does the other friends.

For today: when you suffer or see injustice, do not stop at complaint alone. Bring your pain to God honestly, ask him "where are you?", and trust that he hears even in the night.
exp.30:33:
Job continues a sentence that begins in the previous verse: "If I have hidden my sin... for fear of the crowd." The Berean Standard Bible reads "I greatly feared the crowds and the contempt of the clans," so the fear is of the crowds and of the scorn of the clans. "Contempt" means scorn, and "terrified me" means it frightened me. Job says that he did not stay silent or stay inside, keeping away from the door, out of fear of what people thought.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends accuse him of being a hidden sinner. He answers with an oath, reviewing his life and saying he has nothing to conceal. That is why he asks to speak with God.

For today: do not live hiding your failures out of fear of what others will say. A sincere life before God brings freedom. If there is something hidden, confess it to God and, if needed, to a trusted person.
exp.38:6:
The verse speaks of the young of the wild goats and the deer. "Healthy" means strong and sturdy. "They grow up in the open field" means they develop out in the wide countryside, feeding on what the land provides. When they are grown, they go off and do not return to their mother.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the storm. After Job's long complaints, God asks him a series of questions about the wild animals. Through them he shows Job that he sustains all of creation, including what no one sees or controls.

For today: God takes care of what you cannot keep watch over. If you have children or loved ones who have already moved beyond your care, you can entrust them to God, for he sustains them where you cannot reach.
exp.3:14:
This verse describes how a spirit glided past Eliphaz's face and caused him such fear that the hair on his body bristled. The hair on the body bristling is the kind of reaction we have when we get chills. It was an experience at night, while others were sleeping.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to explain why Job is suffering and says he received a message in a night vision. That message suggests that no one is pure before God.

Note: later God says that Job's friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so not everything they say should be taken as safe teaching.

For today: let's not base our faith on impressive experiences or on someone who says "I had a vision." Let's test everything against what the Bible teaches about God, and comfort those who suffer with humility, without judging them.
exp.23:10:
It says that the poor who are exploited work at producing wealth for others, yet they enjoy none of it. The phrase about "crushing olives" refers to pressing oil out of olives, and the phrase about "treading the winepresses" means stepping on grapes to make wine. The words "within their walls" most likely speak of the walls of the rich people's estates, though some understand it differently. Despite this labor, the workers go thirsty, that is, they go without.

Job speaks in the middle of his debate with his friends. They were saying that wicked people always end up badly. Job answers that in real life there are often oppressors who seem to get away with it, while the weak suffer. With this he voices his complaint before God.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we pay fair treatment to those who work for us, or whether we buy things without thinking about who produced them. God cares about humble workers, and we too should care about them.
exp.10:10:
God knows the deceit of people well, meaning those who are false, hollow, or without true worth before Him. He also sees iniquity, which is wickedness or injustice. The closing question, "does He not take note?", means: will He not pay attention? The expected answer is yes.

The one speaking is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He is responding to Job and implies that Job's suffering is due to some sin. He speaks rightly of God's greatness, but he errs in applying it to Job, because the book itself shows that Job was not suffering for that reason.

For today: God sees everything, even what others overlook. This invites us to live with sincerity before Him. It also warns us not to judge the pain of others lightly; rather, let us accompany them with humility and compassion.
exp.29:1:
Job asks: "What use to me was the strength of their hands, since their vigor had left them?" The men he means are the younger men who now mock him, and he says their help was worth nothing to him. The last part of the verse is not entirely clear. It may mean that their strength had already been used up, or that they were people worn out by hardship.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. Before, he was respected, but now even men of low standing look down on him. His pain mixes with bitterness and a wounded pride. The Bible does not hide his harsh words, and God listens to them with patience.

For today: when you feel humiliated, tell God honestly about your pain, but guard your heart so that you do not despise others. All of us have worth before God.
exp.21:2:
The verse asks whether God takes delight in your being righteous, and whether He gains anything when your ways are blameless. The words "delight" and "profit" are what the question really turns on. The question expects the answer "no": God does not need our goodness to be complete.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, so he accuses Job without any proof. His idea that God does not need man has some truth in it, but he uses it badly, as if God did not care about Job's righteousness. In the end, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: obey God out of love and gratitude, not to earn His favor. And be careful not to judge others by their pain, since we do not always know what God is doing.
exp.19:12:
The verse says the wicked person savors his sin as if it were a sweet food. He cannot bear to let it go, so he keeps it in his mouth, rolling it over his tongue to taste its flavor for as long as he can. "Seems good to him" means that it is pleasant to him. "Keeps it" means that, instead of letting it go, he holds on to it.

This is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He argues that the wicked person may enjoy a little, but in the end comes to ruin. He uses the image of a meal that later turns bitter in the stomach. Here he applies this idea to Job, although the book shows that Zophar was wrong to think Job suffered for this reason.

For today: we need to be honest about what we secretly savor, such as pride, envy, or a vice. If we hold on to it, it will end up harming us. Confessing it to God and letting it go in time brings freedom.
exp.20:33:
Job tells his friends that their comfort is of no use. "Empty words" means words without real substance. Job holds that what they answer does not help, because what they say does not match reality. "Full of falsehood" means full of what is untrue. The final comment, that their answers "come to nothing," means they end up accomplishing nothing.

Job speaks at the end of his reply to Zophar, in the third round of speeches. His friends maintain that God always punishes the wicked and blesses the righteous. Job answers that many wicked people live well and die with honor, as he described earlier. For this reason he considers his friends' explanations of his suffering false.

When someone suffers, they do not need easy answers or stock phrases. Before advising, listen with patience and humility. Accompanying a person sincerely, and admitting that we do not understand everything, comforts more than explaining a pain with words that are not true.
exp.33:32:
This verse is difficult and can be understood in several ways. Elihu asks whether God should repay a person on that person's own terms. He says that God is the one who decides, whether Job has disavowed Him or not, and that the choice is Job's, not Elihu's. Then he challenges Job: tell me what you know. "Repay" means that God will give each person what is due; "disavowed" means to reject or deny.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate at the end. He is angry with Job because he believes Job justifies himself and questions God. So he asks Job to humble himself and say to God: "Teach me." Note: at the end of the book, God himself shows that Elihu's analysis does not explain everything.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, do not demand that he conform to your measure. Pray with humility: "Teach me what I cannot see," and trust that he is just.
exp.14:23:
It says that distress and anguish will terrify the wicked man, overwhelming him like a king poised to attack. Here the word for "terrify" means to frighten or fill with dread. These evils will come against him with force, like an army king ready to strike.

Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He describes what he believes happens to the wicked: they live in fear and without peace. He says this with Job in mind, whom he believes is guilty of some hidden sin. But at the end of the book, God says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So this speech contains general truths, but it is wrongly applied to Job.

For today: we should be careful when explaining the suffering of others. Not all suffering is punishment. Let us accompany people with compassion instead of judging them.
exp.23:22:
It says that the wicked and powerful man is given a sense of security, and he feels firm and at ease. The wording here suggests that he is granted confidence. But God's eyes are on his ways: he sees everything. Some scholars read it as God being the one who grants him this calm; others understand that people give it to him. The text leaves this somewhat open.

Job is speaking, answering his friends. They maintain that God punishes the wicked right away. Job replies that many oppressors, who mistreat the widow and the barren woman, seem to live secure and prosper. Even so, he affirms that God is not blind: he sees, and their end will come.

For today: when you see injustice seem to get its way, do not lose hope or fill yourself with bitterness. God sees everything. Trust in his justice, and seek to live yourself with honesty and compassion.
exp.35:21:
God is exalted and raised high above all things because of His power. The verse says that God is lifted up in His power, and it asks, "Who is a teacher like Him?" The point is that no one teaches as God does, and no one compares with Him in wisdom.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the discussion at the end of the conversations between Job and his friends. He wants to defend God's justice and warn Job not to harden his heart in the middle of his suffering. Many readers find useful things in his words, but in the end God does not approve of him or correct him directly, so his speech is best read with care.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not rush to judge God. Ask Him to teach you, and keep your heart open to learning, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.33:8:
According to Elihu, Job has said that it does a person no good to delight in God. The phrase "conform one's will to God" is rendered here as delighting in God, meaning to seek what God wants and to live in line with it.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the debate with Job's friends. He sums up what he believes Job has said and accuses him of siding with the wicked. Job never said those exact words, so Elihu exaggerates or interprets Job's complaint. Afterward, Elihu argues that God is just.

For today: when you suffer and feel that doing what is right gets you nothing, do not jump to hasty conclusions about God. Bring your pain to Him honestly, but keep trusting that He is just, even when you do not yet understand.
exp.13:5:
Here "look away from him" means to look away or leave someone alone. Job asks God to let the man be, so that he can rest. The word used in this verse describes a hired hand, a worker paid by the day, who looks forward to the end of the workday and his pay. The verse says "look away from him and let him rest, so he can enjoy his day as a hired hand."

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly. He speaks with God and tells him that human life is brief, fragile, and full of weariness. His words are a sincere outpouring, not a complete teaching about God.

For today: when life wears you down, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how you feel, and remember that he knows your limits and cares for you.
exp.11:9:
This verse says that the life of every living creature is in God's hand, and so is the breath of all people. "Life" here refers to the life that each living thing has, and "breath" points to the breath that keeps every person alive. "Every human being" means all people.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of his suffering. His friends, especially Zophar, have told him that his pain is punishment for some sin. Job answers that this is not something only they know: even the animals and the natural world show that God is the Creator and that everything is under his power. Job believes in God, even though he does not understand what is happening to him.

For today: when your life feels fragile or confusing, remember that you and your loved ones are in God's hands. You can rest in him and ask him for wisdom, without having to explain everything.
exp.35:3:
Here Elihu assures Job that what he is about to say is true and free of deceit. When he speaks of "one perfect in knowledge," he means someone whose knowledge is sincere and complete. Many understand that Elihu is speaking of himself; others think he means God. The Bible does not fully clarify this.

Elihu is the young man who speaks after Job and his three friends finish their discussion. He is angry because he believes Job justified himself more than God. Now he asks for a little more patience and promises to speak in defense of the justice of the Creator. Although his tone is confident, we should not forget that in the end God does not present him as the final voice.

For today: before speaking with firmness about God or about the suffering of others, examine your heart. Seek to speak with truth, humility and compassion, and let the Word of God correct your opinions.
exp.32:6:
Elihu says that he does not want to frighten Job or weigh him down. "Surely no fear of me should terrify you" describes a strong, overwhelming dread. The image of a hand that is not heavy upon you means that he will not press down on Job or treat him harshly. Elihu offers Job a conversation without threats.

Elihu, a young man who listened in silence to Job and his three friends, now speaks to Job. He says that he stands in God's place in the sense that, like Job, he is also human, formed from clay. Job had felt that God was too terrible for him to be able to defend himself before Him. Elihu assures him that with him he will not have that fear. Many scholars see in Elihu a wise voice; others see a somewhat presumptuous one. He is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when we must correct or advise someone who is suffering, let us do it with tenderness and humility, without intimidating. Truth is received better when it is spoken with respect.
exp.9:17:
Job asks why God let him be born. The "womb" is the belly of his mother. The phrase "Oh, that I had died" means he wishes he had died, and "no eye had seen me" means no one would have seen him live or suffer. It is a lament: Job wishes he had never known so much pain.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. He has lost children, possessions and health, and he feels that God is hunting him down like a lion. His friends accuse him, and he, not understanding what is happening, pours out his anguish before God. Notice that he does not curse God, but speaks to him with frankness.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, even your darkest questions. He listens to those who cry out. And if someone near you suffers this way, accompany them with patience, without rushing or judging them.
exp.20:23:
He says this prosperous man is full of life and health. The Hebrew wording behind his body being well nourished and his bones being rich with marrow points to abundance and vigor, the picture of someone who lacks nothing. The image of a body well fed and bones full of strength is a way of saying he has good health right up to the end.

Job is speaking, answering his friends, who said that wicked people always end up badly. Job replies that the wicked often live long and in comfort, and die in peace. With this he argues that life cannot be explained by such a simple formula. In the end, he says, both the rich and the poor wind up in the dust.

For today: do not measure people, or yourself, only by how well or badly things go for them. Prosperity does not prove that someone is good, and suffering does not prove that someone is guilty. Trust that God is just, even when you do not yet see the answer.
exp.20:29:
It says that the wicked person is spared from the day of disaster and kept safe from the day of anger. The word "spared" means held back or kept from something. The word "wrath" means anger or punishment.

Job is speaking, responding to his friends. They were saying that the wicked always fall and lose their homes. Job answers that those who travel and have seen the world know that many wicked people live without visible punishment. Here he recalls that, in the end, the wicked does face a day of judgment. Some scholars understand the verse as a statement by Job; others take it as an idea he quotes in order to refute it.

For today: do not lose heart if you see injustice seem to go unpunished. Trust that God sees everything, leave judgment in his hands, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.25:7:
It says God wraps up the waters in His clouds, and the clouds do not burst under their own weight. "Wraps up" means He gathers and holds the water securely. "Yet the clouds do not burst under their own weight" means the clouds carry all that water without breaking apart and without releasing it all at once.

The one speaking is Job, responding to his friend Bildad. Job acknowledges God's great power over the earth, the heavens, and even the place of the dead. Before and after this verse he mentions things that God sustains or limits. Here he uses the image of the clouds to show God's order and control over creation.

If God cares for something as ordinary as the water in the clouds, He can also sustain your life when you feel great weight. Today you can pray with confidence, giving Him your burdens and remembering that He works with wisdom and care.
exp.18:24:
Here Job says firmly that he is sure his redeemer lives. The Hebrew word behind "redeemer" describes the close relative who would defend and rescue a family member in trouble, so the explanation can speak of that kinsman's role in general terms. The phrase "in the end" can be understood as "at last" or "after me," and the phrase about standing upon the earth may mean that he will appear on the earth, or upon the dust of the grave. Scholars interpret this in several ways.

Job speaks here as a man who has lost everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends accuse him of having sinned, and he feels alone and misunderstood. He wants his words to be engraved in stone, because he trusts that someone will defend him and vindicate him.

For today: when you feel alone, unjustly judged, or without answers, you can hold on to the fact that God lives and knows you. Tell him so in prayer, honestly, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.6:7:
The verse says that the eye that now sees Job will see him no longer. Then Job addresses God directly: "You will look for me, but I will be no more." This means God will look for him, but Job will be gone, and he will no longer be there. "I will be no more" means he will cease to exist in this life. It is a poetic way of speaking about approaching death.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering, answering his friend Eliphaz. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and he feels that his life is brief and without hope. He does not speak like someone teaching doctrine, but like someone pouring out his pain before God. Scholars debate how much Job knew about life after death; here he looks only at what he sees: his end.

When pain overwhelms you, you can speak to God honestly, without pretending to strength. Job did not hide his anguish, and the Bible records it. Praying this way is also an act of faith.
exp.33:17:
The explanation asks whether anyone would dare call a king "worthless" or nobles "wicked." The question is whether one should speak to such people with that kind of contempt at all. The kings and nobles here are the powerful people of the time. The idea is that people usually treat those in power with respect, and no one insults them lightly.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He argues that God is just and cannot be accused of injustice. His point is this: if one does not speak with such contempt even to a king, then how much less should God, who rules over all, be condemned. Many scholars think Elihu is partly right, but that he does not fully understand Job's actual case.

For today: before judging or criticizing God, or any authority, it is wise to speak with humility, to think carefully about what we say, and to remember that our view is limited.
exp.14:2:
This verse is a rhetorical question. Eliphaz means that a wise man would not argue with words that are useless or with speeches that serve no purpose. The word "argue" means to debate or dispute. "Useless words" refers to arguments that help no one.

Eliphaz, from Teman, is one of Job's three friends. In this second speech, he is upset because Job defends his innocence in the middle of his suffering. Eliphaz thinks Job speaks without sense and with pride. Yet the book itself later shows that Eliphaz was wrong to accuse Job in that way.

Before we answer in an argument, it is good to ask ourselves whether our words help or only wound. But we must also be careful not to judge someone who is suffering harshly, as Eliphaz did. Sometimes the best help is to listen with patience and speak with kindness.
exp.36:1:
It says to listen very closely to the thunder of God's voice, which is impressive and awe-inspiring, and to the rumbling that comes from his mouth. The word "dreadful" here does not mean "evil" but rather that it inspires reverence and wonder.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks near the end of the book of Job. He is describing a storm, with its thunder and lightning, as a sign of God's power. His heart trembles at it, and he wants Job and those present to stop and listen too. Some understand the thunder to be God's voice in a poetic sense; others see it as a preparation for the voice that God himself will speak afterward.

For today: pause in the middle of life's noise and listen to God with humility. You can do this by reading his Word quietly, or by looking at creation and remembering that he is great and cares for you.
exp.26:15:
Job 27:16 says that even if the wicked person heaps up silver like dust and piles up a wardrobe like clay, that brings him no real security. The words "heaps up" and "piles up" are plain enough on their own, and they mean what they say: to gather a large amount and stack it high. The comparison with dust and clay shows that he has a great deal, but that what he has is passing.

Job is speaking to his friends, who were saying that he suffered because he was a wicked man. He answers them by describing what happens in the end to the ungodly: their riches do not save them, and others will enjoy them, as the next verse says. Some scholars think Job is taking up his friends' ideas here, and others think he uses them to defend his own integrity.

For today: do not place your security in what you accumulate. Try to live with justice and generosity, because possessions pass away, but an honest life before God endures.
exp.23:14:
The adulterer watches eagerly for evening to fall. He tells himself, "No eye will see me," and covers his face so that no one will recognize him. Watching for twilight means waiting for dusk, and covering his face means hiding himself so he cannot be identified.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of his debate with his friends. They were saying that God punishes the wicked quickly, but Job observes that many do wrong in secret and seem to get away with it. Here he describes those who hate the light: the murderer, the thief, and the adulterer, all sheltered by darkness. Job does not justify their actions; he shows that God's justice is not always seen immediately.

For today: if there is something you would only do "if no one could see you," examine it honestly. God sees everything, and living in the light, with openness and repentance, brings true freedom.
exp.28:23:
It says that when Job smiled at people, they hardly believed it, as if it were too good a favor to be true. The light of his face was precious to them, and they treasured his cheerful look. The Hebrew here is difficult, and some understand the line differently, taking it to mean that his good spirit would not let itself be discouraged.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He remembers with longing the days when God blessed him, when people respected him and sought his counsel. With this memory he prepares his defense, because he feels unjustly brought low and wants to show how he lived.

For today: your kind treatment of others may encourage more than you imagine. Use your influence, great or small, to comfort and lift up others, as Job did, the one who comforted those who mourned.
exp.12:11:
Job says that what his friends remember and defend, their sayings and arguments, is worth as much as ashes, which the wind scatters. Their defenses are as fragile as clay. Here "maxims" and "proverbs" name the wise-sounding sayings they keep repeating, and the image is of words that look solid but crumble under pressure.

Job speaks to his friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. They insist that his suffering is punishment for some hidden sin. Job tells them that by defending God with false arguments and with partiality, they do not honor him; their fine words do not withstand God's gaze.

For today: before explaining another person's pain with quick answers, it is good to accompany them with humility and truth. Speaking on behalf of God requires care, and sometimes the most faithful thing is to listen, not to judge.
exp.15:3:
Here Job tells his friends that he could speak as they do if they were in his place. He could heap up words against them and shake his head at them. Shaking the head was a gesture of mockery or disapproval. And "if you were in my place" means: if you were in my situation.

Job speaks as one who suffers greatly after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar have given him long speeches, claiming that his pain is punishment for some sin. Job calls them miserable comforters, because instead of comforting him they judge him.

For today: when someone suffers, listening with tenderness helps more than offering quick explanations. Let us accompany others with presence, patience, and gentle words, without accusing or assuming that we know why pain comes.
exp.31:0:
So these three friends of Job, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, stopped answering him. The reason given is that Job seemed righteous in his own eyes, that is, he was convinced of his innocence, and they could not get him to change his mind.

The word "stopped" means they quit speaking.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking here. After three rounds of speeches, the friends kept insisting that Job was suffering because of some hidden sin, but Job denied it. This verse marks a turning point: the debate ends, and Elihu enters, a young man who will become angry. Some think that "righteous in his own eyes" is a criticism of Job; others see it only as a description of his conviction.

For today: when a discussion goes nowhere, it is worth pausing and listening with humility. We must be careful that defending our own reasoning does not make us forget that God is always more just and wise than we are.
exp.33:31:
It says that a person asks God to teach them what they cannot see. "Teach me what I cannot see" is a humble request for correction. The second part is a promise: if I find out that I have done wrong, I will not do it again. The words "I will not do it again" express repentance and a desire to change.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job's three friends. Here he offers what would be a good prayer and presents it to Job, because he believes Job has defended himself too much and has not accepted being corrected. Some think Elihu is partly right and others think he is harsh with Job; the book itself does not fully clarify this.

For today: ask God to show you your blind spots. Pray with sincerity, listen to his Word and to the voice of wise people, and decide to correct whatever he reveals to you.
exp.22:5:
Job asks whether God would use his great power to contend with him in a trial. He answers his own question: "No." Instead, God would take note of him, that is, pay close attention to him and care for him.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends accuse him of having sinned, but he knows himself to be innocent and wants to make his case before God. Here he expresses confidence that God is just and would not misuse his power. Some understand that God would give Job the strength he needs to speak; others understand that God would simply give him careful attention. Both readings agree on the central idea.

For today: when you suffer and have questions, you can come to God with sincerity. He does not crush you with his power; he notices you and gives you what you need to keep going.
exp.16:3:
He says that God has closed the minds of Job's friends, so they have not grasped his suffering. For that reason Job concludes that God will not lift them up or let them stand above him. "To exalt" means to lift up, honor, or give victory. "Closed their minds to understanding" means that God did not let them see the truth.

Job speaks here in great pain. His friends accuse him of having sinned and treat him with mockery instead of comforting him. Job feels that no one is defending him, so he asks God for a pledge (a "surety") so that he can present his case. Scholars understand in different ways whether Job speaks with bitterness or with faith, but it is clear that he feels misunderstood.

Today we can learn not to offer easy explanations to someone who suffers. Before passing judgment, it is wise to listen, to accompany, and to admit that we do not know everything.
exp.21:25:
This verse says that when someone turns back to God, they find joy in Him and can come before Him with confidence. "You will delight in the Almighty" means you will take pleasure in God, and "lift up your face to God" means you no longer feel shame or fear in facing Him. The Almighty is God, the all-powerful one.

The speaker is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and so he promises that if Job repents, God will restore him. Note that the book later shows Eliphaz was wrong in explaining Job's suffering (Job 42:7). Even so, this picture of delighting in God and lifting up your face to Him is beautiful and resembles other teachings in the Bible.

For today: do not treat God as a means to obtain things. Seek Him for Himself. Spend a few minutes speaking to Him honestly, giving thanks and trusting in His love.
exp.17:1:
Bildad asks Job how long it will be before he stops making so many speeches. He tells Job to show some sense first, meaning to think carefully and pause to reflect, and then they can talk together. The question is pointed and impatient, and it reflects how much Bildad has been unsettled by what Job has said.

The one speaking is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. Job has just insisted on his innocence and complained bitterly about his suffering. Bildad feels offended and answers harshly, because he believes Job is speaking without good sense. Later on, God will show that the friends also did not speak well about Him.

For today: before speaking with someone who is suffering, let us listen with patience and humility. Showing some sense first keeps us from words that wound and do not help.
exp.8:30:
Job says that even if he washes himself as thoroughly as he can, God would plunge him into the pit, a mire of mud or a grave, and he would be so filthy that even his own clothes would turn against him in disgust. The word "despise" means to look down on with scorn or strong dislike. It is a vivid picture: nothing Job does can make him truly clean before God.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He feels he cannot win a case against God, because God is far greater and there is no one to judge between the two. Job exaggerates out of his pain; some see here a longing for a mediator, and Christians often think of Christ.

For today: do not trust in your own efforts to feel clean before God. Come before him with sincerity and receive his forgiveness through Jesus, the mediator Job longed for.
exp.40:3:
It says it is impossible to make a deal with Leviathan so that it becomes your slave for life. The question "will he make a covenant with you" asks whether this creature would agree to a binding arrangement with a person, and "take him as a slave for life" means taking it on as a servant for the rest of its life. The question expects a "no": this creature does not yield or submit to any agreement with man.

The speaker is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. He asks Job questions about Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature. Some think it is the crocodile; others see a mythical or symbolic beast of chaos. It is not known for certain. God wants Job to see the limits of human power.

For today: recognize that you do not control everything. There are things that exceed your strength, and you can rest in the fact that God does govern. Hand over to Him what you cannot manage, with humility and trust.
exp.12:7:
This verse has Job rebuke his friends with two questions. Job asks whether they really intend to show God partiality and argue on his behalf, as if God needed to be defended with crooked arguments.

The one speaking is Job, who is suffering greatly. His friends insist that he is suffering because of some hidden sin, and they keep saying that God always punishes in this way. Job feels that they speak falsely in order to look good before God. So he tells them that they cannot defend God with lies or with a half-truth about justice.

Today we can learn not to use harsh or inaccurate words to "defend" God. When someone is suffering, it is better to listen with humility and to speak with truth and love, without offering easy explanations that we do not actually know.
exp.5:24:
He says that honest words, sincere and true, can be painful and reach deep into the heart. But Job asks, "What does your argument prove?" That is, what do his friends' criticisms actually establish? For him, their rebukes prove nothing and point to no specific mistake.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous pain. His friends, above all Eliphaz, have told him that he suffers because of some sin. Job has already asked them to show him where he went wrong, and he would be silent. But he feels that he receives only vague accusations, without proof, while he suffers.

For today: when someone is suffering, before correcting them, let us listen and accompany them. If something difficult must be said, let it be said with truth, clarity and love, not with hasty judgments. And if we are corrected, let us humbly ask that they show us clearly where we have failed.
exp.17:9:
The verse says that hidden traps surround the wicked person. The "noose" is a rope with a loop for catching, hidden in the ground. The "trap" is a word that is hard to pin down. Some believe it refers to another kind of trap or noose, which is why the verse places it in his path, on the very road where he is about to walk.

Bildad, one of Job's friends, speaks in his second speech. He describes how the wicked person comes to an end, using pictures of nets, nooses, and traps. Bildad believes that all suffering is punishment for wickedness, so he hints that Job must be guilty. At the end of the book, God shows that this view was mistaken (Job 42:7).

For today: be careful about explaining another person's pain with easy answers. Before judging someone who is suffering, it is better to walk alongside them with patience, listening, and prayer. Also remember that sin does have consequences, and it is wise to walk humbly before God.
exp.7:21:
Those who oppose you will be covered in shame, wearing their disgrace like a garment. The verse also says that the tent of the wicked will be gone for good. The word "tent" points to where they live, and it can also stand for their family and their future. The "wicked" are people who live with no regard for God.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He believes that God always rewards the good and punishes the wicked in a direct way. For this reason he hints that Job is suffering because of some sin. At the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so their words are not a complete teaching.

Today we can trust that God is just, but without judging anyone by their suffering. When someone is going through pain, it is better to accompany them with kindness than to give them harsh explanations.
exp.28:11:
It says that Job helped those who had no one to defend them. "Rescued" means pulled out of danger or injustice. The "poor who cried out" were people who called for help, and the "fatherless" were children without parents. "The fatherless who had no helper" describes a child with no one to come to their aid.

Here Job speaks. He is sadly recalling the days when his life went well and people respected him. The verses before this one show that even the leading men kept silent before him. Job explains that this honor did not come from his wealth, but from how he treated those in need. He says this while he suffers and his friends accuse him, to defend that his life had been upright.

For today: open your eyes and your ears to the one who is alone and needs support. You can accompany a vulnerable person, help a child, or stand up for someone treated unjustly. One concrete act of help is worth more than good intentions.
exp.39:22:
1) What it says: The verse speaks of the behemoth. Even when the river rages, the animal is unafraid and stays secure, though the Jordan surges up to its mouth. The point is its calm in the face of a powerful flood.

2) Context: God speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He shows Job the behemoth, a powerful creature. There is debate over whether it was a hippopotamus, an elephant, or another animal, and there is no certainty. God wants Job to see his own smallness and the greatness of the Creator, who sustains all things with wisdom.

3) For today: If God cares for and sustains a creature so strong, He can also sustain you. When the floods of life come, trust in Him and rest. You do not understand everything, but He does.
exp.35:31:
He fills his hands with lightning and commands it to strike its mark. He gathers the lightning in his hands and sends it exactly where he chooses. Some scholars think the verse is describing lightning, because the Hebrew of this verse is difficult and has been understood in several ways.

Elihu speaks, the young man who comes in at the end of the book, after Job and his three friends. He wants to show that God is just and powerful, and he uses the storm as an example: God holds the lightning in his hands and directs it with perfect aim, just as he rules the rain and the clouds.

For today: when you go through stormy days, when you see no way out and do not understand what is happening, do not conclude that God has gone away. The storms are also under his command. Trust in him, pray with sincerity, and take the next step with patience.
exp.20:3:
Job asks whether his complaint is against a man. He implies that it is not, because his pain goes deeper than a debate with his friends. Then he asks: why should I not be impatient? In this verse, "impatient" means grieved, restless, or full of distress. Some readers take Job to be complaining before God rather than before people; others take him to be speaking of himself with irony.

Job is speaking in reply to Zophar, one of his three friends. They insist that he suffers because of some hidden sin. Job asks them to listen carefully and to let that be their comfort, since until now their words have only added to his pain. He wants to be heard before being judged.

For today: when someone is suffering, sometimes the best thing we can do is be quiet and listen without rushing to offer explanations. And if you are suffering, you can express your distress honestly before God; he is not offended by your candor.
exp.14:18:
He says the land was given only to the ancestors of those wise men, and that no foreigner mixed among them. "Was given" means "was handed over to them," and "foreigner" means someone from outside. The phrase closes a thought that began in verse 18.

Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He tries to convince Job that he is suffering because of some sin. He claims that his teaching comes from ancient wise men whose tradition was kept pure, free from outside influences. The verses that follow say the wicked always suffer. But the book shows that Eliphaz is wrong to apply this to Job.

For today: value the wisdom of those who came before us, but do not use it to judge the one who suffers. Tradition helps, but it does not replace compassion and humility before God.
exp.4:24:
This verse says that the person will see their family grow greatly. The words "offspring" and "descendants" mean children and later generations. The comparison with grass shows a large family line that springs up and spreads everywhere.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He describes the blessings that, in his view, come to someone who turns to God and accepts his correction. Be careful: later on God says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about Him, so his words cannot be taken as a sure rule. Besides, Job had already lost his children, and this comfort must have hurt.

For today: thank God for the family you have and pray for them, but do not assume that blessings prove someone's faithfulness, or that suffering proves the opposite. Walk alongside those who are suffering with compassion, not with formulas.
exp.10:4:
Zophar wishes that God himself would speak. The BSB says "if only God would speak," which expresses the same longing. "Open His lips against you" means that God would speak to you directly, face to face. Zophar thinks that if God spoke, Job would be silent.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He is upset because Job keeps insisting that he is innocent. Zophar assumes that Job's suffering is punishment for some sin. Later in the same book, it becomes clear that Zophar and his friends were wrong in their judgment of Job.

For today: before speaking on God's behalf about another person's pain, it is wise to be humble. It is easy to assume that we know what God thinks. Sometimes the wisest thing is to offer compassion and listen, rather than judge.
exp.4:17:
He says that God is the one who allows the wound and also the one who binds it up. A "wound" is an injury, and "binds up" means He will tend to it until it heals. "Strikes" speaks of a painful blow, and "His hands also heal" shows that God Himself restores. The verse presents God as one who corrects, but also as one who heals.

Here Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He tries to comfort Job by saying that suffering can be a correction from God. His words contain truths about God's care, but later God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). For that reason, Eliphaz does not explain all of Job's suffering.

Today, when you go through pain, you can bring it to God with confidence, without assuming that all suffering is punishment. He is compassionate and able to heal. Ask Him for help and comfort.
exp.26:16:
He may gather up clothing and riches, but he will not enjoy them. What he lays up, the righteous will wear, and his silver will be divided by the innocent. In other words, what the wicked person piled up will pass into the hands of upright people.

Job is speaking, responding to his friends. They were saying that Job was suffering because he was wicked. In this chapter, Job describes the fate of the wicked, using words similar to those of his friends. Some scholars think Job is quoting what they believe; others think he is expressing his own conviction that God is just. This is debated.

For today: piling up more than we need does not give us security. We can live generously, trust God, and use what we have to help others, knowing that we cannot take any of it with us.
exp.2:1:
This verse is only an introductory phrase. It says that Job spoke and began to say what he felt. The phrase "this is what he said" introduces his words, which come out of very deep pain. Although no one had asked him anything, it is as if he were answering everything that had happened to him.

Job is a righteous man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. For seven days he sat in silence with his friends. Now he breaks the silence and expresses his anguish. He does not curse God here, but he does speak about the day of his birth.

For today: you do not have to hide your pain before God. Job spoke honestly, and the Bible preserved his words. You can tell God what you feel, even when it is hard, and keep trusting that He hears you.
exp.23:20:
They prey on the barren and childless, and show no kindness to the widow. The word "afflicted" means that he oppressed or made her suffer. These are people without protection, and he takes advantage of them.

Job is speaking, answering his friends. He complains that God seems to let the wicked abuse the weak, and that they sometimes prosper for a time. The verses before this one speak of their downfall, and some scholars debate whether Job says all of that himself or is quoting his friends' ideas. What is clear is that Job cares about the helpless.

For today: look at who around you is alone or without support, like a widow, a single mother, or someone who is hurting. Help them with one concrete act: visit them, keep them company, or reach out a hand.
exp.29:4:
This verse says that those men were banished from among the people. Whenever they appeared, others shouted at them as one shouts at a thief. "Banished" means cast out or rejected, and "shouted at like thieves" means calling out to them to drive them away and shame them.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. People once respected him, but now he complains that even people of very low standing, described in the verses before, mock him. He describes how society despised them and treated them as dangerous. Some scholars think Job uses them to show how far he has fallen.

For today: let us not judge or reject the poor or the marginalized because of their condition. God calls us to treat with dignity and compassion those whom others despise, and to draw near to them with help and respect.
exp.36:2:
It says that God unleashes, beneath the whole sky, something that comes from Him: according to the context, His thunder-voice. "Unleashes" means He sends it out and guides it along its course. His lightning, which here probably refers to the lightning bolt, reaches to the ends of the earth, that is, to every corner of the world.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the book, after the long dialogues between Job and his three friends. He describes a storm to show the greatness of God and the smallness of humanity. Some think he prepares the way for God's answer in chapter 38. His speech has its strengths, but it is not the final word of the book.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, remember that His power and His care reach every place. You can trust Him, even without having all the answers.
exp.21:21:
Receive instruction from his mouth, and keep his words close to your heart. This means accepting God's teaching and letting it sink deep into who you are. "Instruction" here means teaching or guidance. "Heart" is the center of the person: what they think, feel, and decide.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he advises him to return to God to recover peace and prosperity. Note: at the end of the book, God says that Eliphaz and his friends did not speak rightly, so his view of suffering is mistaken. Even so, this advice itself is wise.

For today: spend a few minutes each day reading a passage of the Bible and choose one phrase to repeat during the day, so that you not only hear it but let it guide your decisions.
exp.28:3:
