Job looks back with longing to the years when he was in his prime. He remembers a time when, as he puts it, the friendship of God rested on his tent, meaning that he enjoyed a close bond and trust with God. The Hebrew word behind "friendship" can also be understood as intimate fellowship or closeness, so it carries the sense of a warm and personal relationship.

The speaker is Job, who has already lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. In this chapter he looks back and longs for the time when he felt God's care, his light in the darkness, and his family united. He does not say that God has stopped loving him, but that is how he feels.

For today: when you go through hard times, remember with gratitude the moments when God felt near, but do not rely on those memories alone. Keep praying sincerely, even in silence, because God has not gone away.
exp.2:4:
Job asks that the day of his birth be swallowed up in darkness. "Reclaim" here means to take back, as if the day were something that belonged to the night; "gloom" is a deep, heavy darkness; "a cloud settle over it" pictures a dark cloud coming down and covering the day; "overwhelm" means to be crushed and flooded with blackness. Job wishes that day to be so dark and frightening that no one would want to remember it.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. After seven days of silence with his friends, he opens his mouth and expresses his pain. He does not curse God, but the day he was born. His language is poetic and raw, and the Bible presents it honestly, without softening it.

For today: when you suffer greatly, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, even if the words are raw. Job kept speaking with God, and that opens the way for Him to respond.
exp.6:3:
He says that when Job lies down, he thinks, "When will I get up?" He wants the morning to come already. The night feels endless, as if his heart were counting it hour by hour. The BSB says he "tosses and turns," which means he is tired of lying still, restless, unable to rest. So it drags on until dawn.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering: he has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. He answers his friend Eliphaz and compares his life to that of the servant and the hired worker, who wait for rest, but he receives only nights of anguish. Here he does not speak calmly, but with sincere pain.

For today: if you live through difficult nights, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can bring God your sleeplessness, your fear, and your weariness with honesty. The Bible shows that prayer can also sound like a lament.
exp.4:8:
He says that God does things so great that we cannot fully understand them. "Unsearchable" means they cannot be fully examined or understood. "Wonders without number" means there are so many that they cannot be counted.

Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, speaks. He tries to comfort Job and advises him to seek God in the middle of his pain. Note: although this verse is true, God later says that Job's friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). For that reason, it is wise to read their words with care, without applying them blindly to every suffering.

When you cannot understand what you are living through, remember that God is greater than your questions. You can bring Him your burdens with sincerity and trust that He is still at work, even when you cannot see how.
exp.11:18:
He leads priests away barefoot, and overthrows the established. "Barefoot" means stripped of what they had, and it can also mean led away as captives. "Overthrows" means that he brings them down or knocks them from their place.

Job speaks in reply to his friend Zophar and the other friends. They were telling him that God punishes only the wicked. Job answers that God is sovereign and that he also changes the fortune of religious leaders and established figures, without it always being clear why. Interpreters debate how much of this is praise and how much is Job's complaint.

For today: do not place your security in power, money, or position, because all of that can change. Trust in God, who remains in control, and live with humility.
exp.15:12:
God, like a warrior, surrounds Job with his archers. The archers are those who shoot arrows. Job feels he was struck without mercy: the image of his kidneys being pierced speaks of a blow to the deepest part of the body, and the words "without mercy" mean that God showed him no pity. The image of his gall spilled on the ground describes a pain so strong that his insides were left undone.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. He has lost children, possessions and health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He feels attacked by God, though he does not understand why. This is his sincere complaint, not a complete explanation of what God does. The book itself later shows that Job did not see the whole picture.

For today: you can be honest with God when you suffer. Job did not pretend to be fine; he cried out frankly. Bring your pain to God with sincerity, without pretending to understand everything.
exp.8:16:
What it says: Job says that God would crush him with a tempest and multiply his wounds without cause, that is, without a reason he can see. To crush means to break something badly. The image is that of someone swept away by a violent storm.

Context: Job is speaking in the midst of his suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and he feels he cannot defend himself before God, because God is too powerful. Note that Job speaks from his pain and his limited perspective. At the end of the book, God himself shows that Job did not see the whole picture, though he also recognizes Job as someone who spoke with sincerity.

For today: When pain has no explanation, you can bring your questions and your complaint to God honestly, without pretending. He is not frightened by your sincerity. And in the meantime, trust that his character is good even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.25:13:
Job says that what we see of God's works is only a small part of his ways. We barely hear a whisper of him. The thunder of his power is the phrase that refers to his strength, and the question of who can understand it means that no one can fully grasp him. The "twisting serpent" mentioned in the previous verse is a poetic image, and scholars understand it in different ways.

Job speaks here in reply to his friend Bildad. He is suffering greatly, yet he acknowledges that God rules the sea, the heavens, and all that has been created. He admits that his knowledge of God is limited, though he does not stop trusting him.

Today we can live with humility before what we do not understand. When suffering leaves us without answers, we can rest in the fact that God is greater than our questions, and keep trusting him.
exp.32:0:
Here, Elihu asks Job to listen closely. "Speeches" means arguments, or what someone explains, and "hear" and "listen" repeat the same idea to add force to the call. The speaker wants Job not only to hear, but to take in everything he is about to say.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who had waited in silence while Job and his three friends argued. He is angry with all of them and now takes the floor. He says he speaks with uprightness and wisdom, but the book does not present him as a perfect teacher, and God later speaks to Job without mentioning Elihu. So his words contain some truth, but they must be read with care.

For today: learn to truly listen, especially to someone who is suffering, and examine what you hear in the light of God's Word.
exp.35:16:
He says that Job has behaved like the wicked: he has "filled up" the judgment of the wicked man, that is, he has spoken and judged as they do, instead of upholding justice and right. To "uphold" means to maintain or defend. Some translations understand it this way: the judgment that the wicked deserves has overtaken you, and now you must uphold justice.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He believes God corrects through suffering, and he accuses Job of accusing God. This is Elihu's view; the book itself later shows that his understanding was incomplete.

For today: when you suffer, watch your words. You may express your pain to God with sincerity, but take care not to accuse him or to stop doing what is right. And be careful not to judge others by their suffering.
exp.21:19:
Here "excess" means what remains of their wealth or possessions. The speaker is glad over the wicked: "Our foes are destroyed, and fire has consumed their excess." The Hebrew here is difficult and can be understood in more than one way, so the exact sense of the last words is not fully certain.

Eliphaz, a friend of Job, speaks. He believes Job is suffering for some hidden sin, and he compares him with the wicked whom God judged. But the book shows that Eliphaz is mistaken: Job was not suffering for being wicked. After this verse, Eliphaz invites him to return to God and find peace.

For today: let us not judge others by their trials, as if all suffering were punishment. Rather, let us walk alongside them with humility, and examine our own hearts before God.
exp.18:3:
Job says that even if he had truly gone wrong, that error would concern him alone and not the friends who are pressing him. The word "error" here means a mistake or fault. The phrase "concerns me alone" means he would carry that responsibility himself, without others having to judge him or punish him with their words.

Job speaks here in the midst of his enormous suffering. His friends insist that he suffers because of some hidden sin, and they accuse him again and again. Job feels wounded and worn out by their speeches. He does not claim to be perfect; rather, he sets a limit: if there is a fault, it lies between him and God, and that does not justify such harshness.

For today: when you accompany someone who is suffering, do not give them quick explanations or accuse them of things you do not know. Listen, accompany with tenderness, and let God be the one who examines the heart. And if you are the one who is suffering, you can be honest with God about your failures and your pain.
exp.13:9:
This verse says that a human being dies and is laid low, meaning his life comes to an end. Job's phrase "is laid low" means that his existence here is over. Then Job asks: "and where is he?", a question that expresses sorrow and doubt before the mystery of death.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. Earlier he compared a person to a tree that, though cut down, can sprout again with water. Now he contrasts: a person, once he breathes his last, seems not to rise again. It is the lament of a wounded man, not a complete teaching about life after death. The Bible later reveals the hope of the resurrection.

For today: when you feel pain or fear about how fragile life is, you can be honest with God, as Job was. And remember that the Christian hope rests in Christ, who rose again.
exp.34:12:
Surely God does not listen to empty pleas, and the Almighty does not take note of them. "Almighty" is another name for God, the All-Powerful. "Does not take note of it" means that he gives such a cry no attention or approval.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who rebukes Job. He thinks Job complains that serving God is worthless. Elihu says that many cry out in pain, but with pride, without seeking God as their Creator. Note: not all interpreters agree that Elihu is right, and in the end God himself corrects everyone.

For today: when you pray, do not limit yourself to complaining. Come near with humility and confidence, acknowledging who God is, and wait on him with patience.
exp.10:13:
It says that if there is some sin in your hand, that is, in what you do, you should put it far away from you. It also says that you should not let injustice live in your home and your daily life. The note about "consent" is no longer needed, since your verse does not use that word.

Here Zophar, one of Job's three friends, speaks. He assumes that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he urges him to repent so that God will restore him. Be aware, though: at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so their advice does not apply to all suffering. Even so, the principle of leaving evil behind is sound.

For today: honestly examine what harmful habit or attitude you are tolerating at home or in your heart. Bring it before God with humility, ask for His forgiveness, and make a concrete decision to leave it behind.
exp.37:14:
The explanation says that the wicked are deprived of their light, meaning whatever lets them act in the dark or enjoy their power. Their upraised arm is an arm raised to strike, a symbol of violence and pride, and in the end it is broken, that is, shattered. Some understand the light that is withheld to be the darkness of the night, which is their favorite time, and that the dawn takes it away from them.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He asks him questions about creation, and here he mentions how the dawn shakes the earth and exposes the evildoers. God wants Job to see that He governs the world and justice as well.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that violence and pride do not have the last word. Even if you do not understand everything, trust that God sees, and He will set a limit on evil in His time.
exp.31:16:
Here Elihu says that he too is going to answer, meaning that he will give his share and state what he knows. The word "judgment" does not mean a court sentence but what he thinks or knows about the matter. "Declare" means "make known."

Elihu is a young man who has listened in silence to the long debate between Job and his three friends. The friends stopped answering, and Elihu feels free to speak. He says he is full of words and cannot hold himself back any longer. Scholars disagree about how right Elihu is; God does not correct him directly afterward, but He also does not expressly approve of him.

For today: before speaking, it is wise to listen patiently and to examine whether our words help or merely release our own feelings. Speaking with humility is wise, especially when there is pain.
exp.15:4:
This verse says that Job, if he were in the place of his friends, would encourage them with his words. "Encourage" means giving courage, and "bring relief" means easing pain. Job says that his words would bring comfort and ease their suffering, instead of adding to it.

Job is speaking, and he is suffering greatly. His friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, have come to comfort him, but they only accuse him and give him long speeches. Job answers them with pain and a certain irony: he could speak as they do, but he would choose another way, the way of compassion. Some think it also shows how much it hurts him to feel alone.

For today: when someone is suffering, there is no need to give explanations or correct them. Listen to them, stay with them, and use words that encourage. Sometimes saying "I am with you" comforts more than a long speech.
exp.37:8:
It says that God dressed the sea with clouds, as one dresses a newborn baby, and wrapped it in darkness, as with a blanket. The clouds are described as the sea's garment, and the thick darkness as its blanket.

It is God himself who speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons, but asks him questions about creation to show him his wisdom and power. Here he presents the sea as something he cared for and set limits on from the beginning.

For today: when your life feels dark or out of control, remember that God governs even what seems to you immense and threatening. You can trust him even when you do not understand everything.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that God is the one who made the constellations. The Bear and Orion are well-known groups of stars, and the Pleiades is a cluster of stars that many people can spot in the night sky. "The constellations of the south" probably refers to the patterns of stars in the southern sky, which could not be seen well from where Job lived. Scholars are not sure exactly which stars the original Hebrew names.

Job is speaking, answering his friend Bildad. Job is suffering greatly and has lost nearly everything. He acknowledges that God is so great and powerful that no human being can easily argue with him or call him to account.

For today: when you look at the sky at night, let its vastness remind you that God is greater than your problems and your questions. Even when you do not understand what is happening to you, you can trust that the One who made the stars also holds you up.
exp.0:17:
This verse introduces the fourth messenger who comes to Job. While the third was still speaking, another came in with news that was even more painful. He reports that Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother.

The one speaking is a servant of Job, who brings the final blow in a series of disasters. In a single day Job has lost his possessions, and now he is about to learn that he has lost his children. The text goes on to say that a strong wind knocked down the house. The Bible presents this as a trial, and Job still does not know what is happening behind it.

For today: when bad news arrives one after another, you do not have to understand everything in order to return to God. Job responded with grief, but also with worship.
exp.16:4:
Flattery is false praise, pleasant words that are not sincere. The verse says that a person who denounces friends for personal gain will see their children suffer, with the eyes of those children growing dim from sorrow or need. The Hebrew is difficult, and some read it differently, as a person who betrays friends for profit.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. His friends claim to comfort him, but they accuse him without reason. Job asks God to stand as his guarantor, because no one else defends him. This verse sounds like a complaint against their falsehood and against its consequences.

For today: do not use pretty words to look good or to get ahead. Speak with truth and love, because your words also affect your family and those around you.
exp.19:5:
It says that even if a person is full of arrogance and their pride reaches the heavens, with their head touching the clouds, they will not stay there. The word "arrogance" in the verse means pride, the sense of thinking oneself better than others. It is a picture of someone who seems to have reached enormous power or success.

It is Zophar, one of Job's three friends, who speaks. He believes the wicked always fare badly, and so he hints that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. His words contain truth about how brief pride is, but the Bible shows that applying them to Job was a mistake, since God said that his friends had not spoken rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: be wary of pride and of success that does not rest on God. And do not judge someone who is suffering by assuming they must have done something wrong; stand with them in humility and compassion.
exp.20:4:
He tells his friends to look at him closely and be appalled, so much so that they cannot say anything. "Being appalled" means being shocked or deeply disturbed. The gesture of putting the hand over the mouth is a sign of silence, of staying quiet out of horror or respect.

Job speaks, a man who suffers greatly. His friends tell him that his pain is punishment for some sin. Job asks them to listen with patience before mocking him. He proposes that they look at reality: the wicked often prosper, and this itself causes him trembling and confusion.

For today: when someone suffers, let us listen before explaining or judging. Often pain has no simple answer. A quiet and attentive presence can help more than a hasty piece of advice, and we can bring our sincere questions to God.
exp.35:17:
Be careful, because God's anger could carry you off in one sudden blow, and no huge payment could buy your way out. In this verse, "beware" is a warning: be watchful and careful. "Carried off" here means taken away suddenly. A "ransom" is the price paid to save someone.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He believes that Job, in his suffering, is speaking badly of God and judging as the wicked do. His warning is sincere, but the Bible does not present Elihu as an infallible teacher, and interpreters understand him in different ways. Moreover, Elihu assumes that Job suffers because of something wrong he did.

For today: do not trust your money or your own resources to make you right with God. Be humble, listen to his correction, and do not judge the pain of others too quickly.
exp.32:22:
It says that if someone is very sick and close to death, a special messenger may stand beside him. A "mediator" is someone who stands between two parties to help bring them together; "one in a thousand" means one among a thousand, as the text said before. His task is to tell the man what is right for him, that is, what he is responsible for before God.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He holds that God, in grace, sometimes speaks to the suffering person through pain and through a messenger to rescue him from death. Some understand that this messenger is an angel; others, a person who gives counsel. The text does not make this clear.

Today, when someone suffers, they need wise and kind words that point them toward God. We can be that kind of voice for others, and also humbly accept correction from those who speak to us with truth and care.
exp.26:9:
This question says that the hypocrite does not find true joy in God, nor does he call on Him at all times. The word "delight" is used here in the sense of taking pleasure in God and finding joy in Him. The Almighty is God, the All-Powerful. To "call on" God means to cry out to Him or to speak to Him in prayer. It is a rhetorical question: the expected answer is "no."

Job speaks in the middle of his debate with his friends. They say that his suffering is punishment for some hidden sin. Job maintains that he is sincere, and that the one who only pretends to be devout does not draw near to God out of love, but out of convenience, and turns to Him only when distress arrives.

For today: examine why you pray. Do you seek God only when there are problems, or also to enjoy His company? Set aside a moment today to speak with Him without asking for anything, only to thank Him and to be in His presence.
exp.13:21:
The verse says that while a man lives, his body feels its own pain and his heart grieves for himself alone. The words "his body" and "feels only the pain" describe suffering felt within the person, and "mourns only for himself" describes sorrow turned inward on his own condition. Some understand this as speaking of the dying person who suffers; others, of the dead who somehow feel pain, and scholars debate this.

Job speaks here in the midst of his enormous suffering. In this chapter he reflects on how brief and fragile human life is. He feels that God is stronger than man, that death comes, and that the dead no longer know anything about their children. It is a sincere lament, not a final teaching.

For today: you do not have to hide your pain before God. Job spoke with frankness, and God heard him. When you suffer, pray honestly and seek support from other believers.
exp.14:12:
It says that Job is turning his spirit against God and pouring out harsh words from his mouth. The phrase "turn your spirit against God" means setting yourself against Him and opposing Him. "Spirit" here refers to his inner mood or his anger. It is a question that sounds like a rebuke.

It is spoken by Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He believes that Job, with his complaints, offends God and speaks with pride. For this reason, he soon reminds him that no human being is clean before God. Note: in the book, God will say at the end that these friends did not speak rightly of Him, so their speech is not a safe teaching in everything.

When we suffer, we can pour out our hearts to God with sincerity, as Job did. But we should also avoid judging harshly the one who suffers. Before correcting someone, let us listen with compassion.
exp.37:2:
God speaks to Job with firmness. "Brace yourself like a man" is a call to get ready and stand firm, the way someone would prepare for hard work or a struggle. God says he will question Job, and Job will have to answer. "Inform Me" means "explain it to Me, tell Me what you know."

God speaks to Job out of a storm, after Job, in the midst of his great suffering, had many times asked for an explanation. His friends had also spoken at length. God does not give him an explanation of his pain, but leads him to look at the greatness of creation. The questions that follow about the earth show how much Job does not know.

For today: when you do not understand what you are going through, do not stop trusting God. Prepare yourself with humility, pray with sincerity, and remember that He holds up the world and also holds you up.
exp.36:17:
Can you help God spread out the skies, which are as strong as a mirror of bronze? This verse asks Job whether he could join God in stretching out the heavens. The sky is pictured as sturdy and gleaming, like a polished mirror made of bronze. The question is meant to be answered with "no."

Elihu, the young friend of Job, is speaking here, near the end of his long speech. He describes God's power over the weather: clouds, wind, and heat. He wants to show that Job does not understand or control creation, so he should not demand explanations from God. Some believe Elihu is preparing the way for the voice of God that comes afterward.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, look at the sky and remember that He holds up what you cannot control. Trust His wisdom and rest.
exp.4:19:
The verse says that God can rescue a person when food runs short and keep them from dying. It also says He can protect a person in battle, freeing them from the stroke of the sword. "Redeem" here means rescue or deliver, not so much paying a price.

The speaker is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's friends. He believes suffering comes as God's correction, and he advises Job to trust Him. Be careful: although his words sound beautiful, God later says that Eliphaz and his friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So his advice does not apply to every case.

For today: when you go through a crisis of money or health, pray and trust that God sustains you. But do not use this verse to judge someone who is suffering, as Eliphaz did.
exp.17:5:
It says that the light inside the wicked person's home will gradually grow dark. The "tent" is his household, and the "lamp" is what gives light, life, and prosperity to a family. "Grows dark" and "goes out" are images of darkness settling over his life.

Bildad, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He is responding to Job and describing what, in his view, always happens to the wicked. His idea is that suffering comes as punishment for wickedness. Here there is a mistake: the book shows that Job suffers without being punished for some hidden sin. So Bildad's words may sound true in general, but they are wrongly applied to Job.

Today it reminds us that living far from God leaves the heart in darkness. But it also teaches us not to judge harshly someone who is suffering. Let us accompany them with compassion, not with accusations.
exp.2:11:
Job asks why there were arms to receive him when he was born, and why there were breasts that nursed him. The idea behind the words "knees to receive me" is that someone welcomed him at birth, most likely by taking him onto their lap, and scholars disagree about whether these were his mother's knees or his father's. The breasts are the mother's, which provided milk.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. After seven days of silence with his friends, he finally opens his mouth and expresses his deepest pain. He wishes he had never been born, because all he sees now is suffering and he longs for rest. This is not a plan, but a cry of anguish.

For today: if you are suffering greatly, you can tell God honestly what you feel. The Bible does not hide these cries. And if the pain becomes overwhelming, seek out someone you trust who can walk alongside you.
exp.9:8:
He says that Job asks God to remember something: that God molded him like clay, the way a potter shapes it. Then Job asks, in pain, "Would You now return me to dust?", that is, whether God is now going to send him back to the dust, to death. The word "return" here means to send him back.

Job speaks in the middle of very great suffering. His friends accuse him of being guilty, but he insists that he is not wicked. Here he does not address them, but God, and he speaks with frankness and complaint. He struggles to understand why God, who formed him with such care, now seems to undo him. It is an honest prayer, not a mockery.

For today: when you are in pain and do not understand God, you can speak to him with sincerity, as Job did. Remind him, and remind yourself, that he made you and knows you.
exp.6:16:
Job asks what a human being is that God should exalt him and give him such close attention. "Exalt" here means treating him as someone of great importance, and "set your heart upon him" means fixing on him your attention and concern. The words that follow add that God visits him every morning and tests him every moment.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He is worn out and wishes to die. This question recalls Psalm 8:4, but there it is a wonder full of gratitude. Here Job uses it with complaint, as if God's attention were a heavy watch. Some interpreters read it as bitter irony.

When you suffer, you can tell God honestly what you feel, including your doubts and your weariness. He does not turn away from someone who cries out with sincerity. And remember that his attention toward you springs from love, even when you do not feel it that way.
exp.21:4:
This verse says that Job's wickedness is very great and that his sins have no end. The word "wickedness" here means evil, and "endless" means that they cannot be counted. It is a very harsh accusation.

Here Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. He believes that suffering is always punishment for some sin, so, without any proof, he invents a list of supposed faults: failing to help the poor, the weary, and the hungry. At the end of the book, God Himself shows that the friends did not speak rightly about Him or about Job (Job 42:7). So this verse is not a teaching from God about Job, but a human mistake.

For today: before judging someone who is suffering, let us avoid assuming their guilt. It is better to walk alongside them, listen to them, and help them with humility and compassion.
exp.33:24:
He says that God recognizes everything the wicked do. "He recognizes their deeds" means that he knows what they have done and sees it clearly, so nothing stays hidden. "He overthrows them" means that he brings them down or reverses their situation, and "in the night" suggests that it can happen suddenly, when they least expect it. "They are crushed" means that they will be destroyed or broken.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job's three friends. He argues that God is just and never acts with wickedness. Here he insists that God sees everything and that no powerful person escapes his judgment. Note: in the book, God later shows that Elihu does not explain everything, so his words should be read with care.

For today: live with sincerity, knowing that nothing is hidden from God. This comforts those who suffer injustice and also invites us to correct what we do in secret.
exp.8:20:
Job says that even if he were blameless (honest and without fault), he still would not truly know his own soul. The phrase "I despise my own life" means that he would have no regard for his life and would hold it in contempt.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He feels powerless before God: God is so great that no one can bring him to trial and win. Job knows he has not been a wicked man, yet he feels that defending himself does no good. He is worn out, confused, and speaking out of pain, not as someone teaching perfect doctrine.

For today: you do not need to have everything clear or believe yourself perfect in order to draw near to God. Acknowledge your limits with humility, be honest about your pain, and place your life in the hands of the One who knows you completely.
exp.29:21:
He says that God snatched him up into the wind and drove him before it, so that he had no control and no firm footing. Then he describes being tossed about in the storm, as if everything he had was being broken down. The word "substance" in the older translations can refer to his possessions, his security, or his strength. Here the picture is of a storm that breaks everything down.

Job speaks in the midst of enormous suffering. He feels that God does not answer his cry and that God has become his enemy. His words express his pain and his confusion, not necessarily the complete truth about God. At the end of the book, God himself corrects Job's limited view.

For today: when you feel that life is slipping away like the wind, you can tell God honestly what you feel, without pretending. The Bible shows that God allows that honest prayer and does not abandon the one who cries out.
exp.38:24:
The verse describes the war horse. At the blast of the horn, he snorts with eagerness. He picks up the scent of battle from far away, and he loves the shouts of commanders and the cry of war. He is not held back by fear or danger.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He asks Job questions about creation to show him His wisdom and power. The horse, strong and brave, is an example of God's work, something Job could not have made or directed by himself.

For today: God sustains all things, even when we do not understand what we are going through. When you face a difficulty, do not let fear take control of you. Trust the God who knows more than you do, and ask Him for courage to keep going forward in faith.
exp.40:33:
It describes Leviathan, the great creature God describes, as looking down on everything that seems lofty or powerful. Where the source says it "looks with contempt," that refers to not giving such things importance or fearing them. The phrase "the haughty" refers to whatever is great and proud, and "the proud" are the arrogant. It is said to be "king" over them because none of them can overcome it.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. He presents Leviathan to Job so that Job will see his own smallness. Scholars do not agree on which animal is meant: some think of a crocodile, others of a symbolic creature of chaos. If God made something so awe-inspiring, then He is even greater.

For today: when pride tempts you to think you are invincible, remember that there is Someone greater. Before God, trust and stay humble.
exp.20:13:
The wicked say to God: "Leave us alone! We have no desire to know your ways." That is, they do not merely ignore God, but openly push him away. Here, "your ways" refers to how God wants people to live, and knowing them means living in line with what he asks.

Job speaks, replying to his friends, who claimed that the wicked always suffer soon. Job says that sometimes the wicked live joyful and at peace, even though they reject God. This causes him pain and confusion. Even so, at the end of this part he turns away from his own way of thinking. Scholars debate whether verse 16 is Job's own words or a quotation of the wicked.

Today: sometimes we tell God "leave us alone" through our actions rather than our words, when we ignore what we know pleases him. Ask him today to teach you his ways, and obey him in one concrete matter.
exp.15:13:
He says that God, as Job experiences it, strikes him again and again, giving him no rest. The phrase "he breaks me with wound upon wound" means that one wound comes right on top of another, one blow after another. "He rushes me like a mighty warrior" paints a powerful fighter charging into battle, and Job feels small and defenseless.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering. Answering his friends, who accuse him of having sinned, he describes his pain with very strong images. He is convinced that God is the one attacking him. This is how he feels at that moment; at the end of the book, God himself hears him and answers him.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you do not have to disguise what you feel. You can tell God with complete honesty that it hurts and that you do not understand. Job spoke plainly and did not turn away from God; seek him too, even with questions.
exp.7:17:
He says that if the plant is uprooted from the place where it stood, that very place will disown it and say, "I never saw you." The verse's word "uprooted" stands for being pulled out of the ground, and "disown" is the word for the place rejecting it. It is an image of someone who seemed well planted but, when he falls, is forgotten even by the place that watched him grow.

Bildad, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He compares the wicked person to a plant that looks strong but can vanish. With this he implies that Job is suffering because of some sin. Later God will show that Bildad was wrong to judge Job this way (Job 42:7).

For today: do not measure your life or the lives of others only by visible success or by the pain that is passing. Put down roots in God, and avoid judging someone who suffers, for suffering is not always punishment.
exp.40:11:
God says he cannot keep silent about Leviathan: he will speak of its limbs, of its power, and of its graceful form. "Limbs" refers to the creature's body parts, and the phrase about its graceful form refers to the harmony of its shape.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He has described Leviathan, a powerful creature that no one dares to provoke. Many think it is a crocodile or some other real animal; others see a symbolic creature. God uses this image to show that if no one can stand against that creature, much less can anyone call the Creator to account.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, remember that he is the wise and powerful Creator. Rest in his character, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.20:2:
Job asks his friends to be patient with him and let him speak. The words "Bear with me" mean "be patient with me" or "put up with me for a while." Job tells them: let me finish, and then, if you wish, go on mocking me.

Job speaks as one who is suffering greatly. His friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, have told him that his pain is punishment for some sin. Job does not feel heard but judged. That is why he asks that they at least listen carefully before condemning him. His complaint, moreover, is mainly directed toward God, not toward them.

For today: when someone suffers, the first thing they need is to be heard. Before giving advice or explanations, let us learn to be silent, listen with patience, and accompany others with respect and tenderness.
exp.33:15:
This verse is an invitation to listen carefully. Elihu says to Job: "If you have understanding, hear this; listen to my words." The words "hear" and "listen" ask Job not to answer quickly, but to think calmly.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who had waited for the three older friends to finish speaking with Job. He is upset because Job seemed to say that God was unjust. For this reason Elihu defends that God rules with justice, that he sustains all life, and that no one can accuse him of wrongdoing. Some scholars see wisdom in his words, and others notice that he also speaks harshly.

For today: before you complain or judge, practice listening. When you suffer or do not understand something about God, stop, pray, and let his Word and wise people speak to you before you draw conclusions.
exp.4:4:
The explanation says that the harvest of the fool, that is, of the person who lives without wisdom or fear of God, will be eaten by others: the hungry. They will take it even from among the thorns, and the thirsty will pant after their wealth. "Harvest" is the crop, and "wealth" is their possessions. Some words in this verse in Hebrew are difficult, and the translations vary.

It is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, who speaks. He tries to explain to Job that suffering comes as a consequence of wickedness. Later, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). For this reason, their words are useful for reflection, but they are not a rule for judging everyone.

For today: do not judge someone who is suffering by assuming they surely did something wrong. Instead, approach them with compassion and help, and entrust your own life to God with humility.
exp.39:10:
God describes the strength of Behemoth. The "loins" are the waist and the lower part of the back, and "the navel of its belly" refers to the muscles of the abdomen. In other words, this animal is powerful from head to toe, and its strength is found throughout its whole body.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned God in his suffering. Now God shows him Behemoth, a creature that He Himself made. It is not known with certainty which animal it is: some think of the hippopotamus, others of the elephant, and others see a symbolic figure. The point is that Job cannot subdue this creature, much less govern the world.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God sustains what you cannot control. Rest in Him with humility and trust.
exp.16:8:
It says that, despite all the bad things that happen, the righteous person does not give up. He keeps walking his path, and the one with clean hands, that is, the one who lives with integrity, grows stronger. The phrase "grows stronger" means that he becomes firmer and more courageous over time.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His eyes are dim from sorrow, and his friends accuse him of being guilty. Just before this verse he says that upright people are astonished at what is happening to him. Afterward, however, he turns to his friends and says that he finds no wisdom among them. Some believe this verse expresses his hope that God keeps the righteous firm.

Today, when you feel tired or misunderstood, keep doing what is right, even though no one notices. Every faithful step, however small, strengthens your heart.
exp.11:11:
The explanation says that the elderly usually have knowledge, and that whoever has lived many years usually has good understanding. Here "knowledge" means knowing things, and "a long life" is a life of many years. "Understanding" means insight or good judgment.

The one speaking is Job, answering his friends, who were giving him advice as if they knew everything. Some believe Job repeats, with a certain irony, what they think about age. Others think he says it in earnest. What is clear is that he soon says that true wisdom and strength are with God.

For today: listen with respect to those who are older, because their experience can help you. But remember that age does not replace God. Ask him for wisdom and measure all advice against what he teaches.
exp.26:4:
Job tells his friends that he will never agree with them. The verse says he will never say they are right. Here "right" means declaring that someone is in the right. "Integrity" means living with honesty and without deceit. Job promises that, until he dies, he will keep his integrity.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends insist that he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job does not claim to be flawless, for elsewhere he admits his need for God, but he refuses to confess a false guilt just to fit their explanation. He chooses to stay faithful to the truth and to his conscience before God.

For today: when you are pressured to say something that is not true, whether to calm others or to avoid trouble, stay firm with humility. Be honest, acknowledge your real mistakes, but do not trade the truth for comfort.
exp.9:12:
Job says that God kept "these things" in his heart, which means God had hidden purposes. He then adds: "I know that this was in Your mind," meaning Job is sure that all of this was in God's thinking. Job had remembered that God formed him and cared for him, but now he suspects that God was also planning his suffering.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous pain. He is answering his friends and addressing God with complaint and confusion. His words express what he feels, but they are not necessarily the complete truth about God. At the end of the book, God himself shows that Job did not understand everything.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, you can speak with God honestly, even with your doubts. But do not conclude that God is cruel just because you cannot see his purpose. Remember also his past care, and trust in him.
exp.15:7:
He says that God (or the pain Job feels as coming from God) has bound him, and that his suffering has become a witness against him. His frail body, wasted and weak, rises up like a witness who stands in court and testifies against him to his own face, as if proving that God is against him.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. His friends have accused him of sin, and he feels worn out, alone, and without answers. He reads his illness as evidence against him. Note: this is how things look to him in his pain; the book itself later shows that his conclusion was not entirely right.

When we suffer, we may believe that our body or our circumstances "prove" that God rejects us. Job teaches us to be honest with God in our complaint, without silencing our pain. But let us also remember that suffering is not always a verdict of guilt.
exp.2:24:
The explanation says that what Job feared so deeply actually happened to him. The verse uses plain language to make this clear: the thing he feared has overtaken him, and what he dreaded has befallen him. The fear that had followed him became a reality.

The speaker is Job, a righteous man who lost his children, his possessions, and his health. In this chapter, after seven days of silence, he expresses his grief and wishes he had never been born. The verses that follow show that he felt no peace or rest. The text does not explain in detail what he feared; it only shows his anguish.

For today: when fear or sorrow overwhelm you, do not keep them silent. Job spoke honestly before God, and the Bible records it without censorship. You can bring your fears to God just as they are, trusting that he listens to you.
exp.6:2:
Job says he has been allotted months of futility, meaning months without purpose or lasting result. He also says that nights of misery have been appointed to him, nights of suffering and exhaustion. The idea of being allotted these things suggests that they were given to him as a fixed share, much like a portion handed out to someone.

Job speaks here in the midst of his great pain, answering his friend Eliphaz. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. He compares his life to that of a hired laborer who only waits for the workday to end. He feels that his suffering has no end, especially when night comes and he cannot sleep.

For today: if you are going through months of futility or long nights of anguish, you can tell God so with complete honesty, as Job did. The Bible does not hide human pain. Speaking with God and with trusted people can be a first step toward not carrying so much weight alone.
exp.28:2:
Job says that in the past God used to make his lamp shine above his head. The word "lamp" in this verse refers to a light, and "shone" means gave light. With that light from God, Job could walk safely even when everything around him was dark, that is, in hard or uncertain times.

The one speaking is Job, a man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. In this chapter he looks back with longing on the months gone by, when he felt God's care and guidance close at hand. He is not explaining a doctrine; he is pouring out his pain and his desire to feel that closeness again.

For today: when you go through a dark night, remember how God has guided you before. You can tell him honestly what you feel, as Job did, and ask him for light to take the next step, even if you cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.34:6:
He says that even if you are righteous, you give God nothing he needs. "If you are" means if you are, and "what does he receive from your hand" asks what gain you bring him. The point is that God does not depend on our goodness.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who answers Job after the three friends have fallen silent. He is correcting what Job had said, which seemed to suggest that serving God brought no benefit. Elihu holds that our righteousness and our sin affect other people, not God. Some readers think his ideas are partial, since the book does not fully confirm them at the end.

For today: do good without believing that in this way you are doing God a favor. Your righteousness does help those around you. Serve them with humility and gratitude, not to bargain with God.
exp.9:19:
Job tells God that his life is already very short and asks: "Are my days not few?" Then he asks God to withdraw from him and leave him alone, so that he can have a little comfort, meaning a bit of relief or consolation before he dies.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost family, health and possessions, and he feels watched and struck down by God. In this chapter he expresses his bitterness with complete honesty, even wishing he had never been born. Scholars agree that this is a painful complaint, not a teaching about how God acts. The book itself later shows that God hears him.

Today, if you are exhausted or wounded, you can speak to God honestly, even with tears and questions. You do not have to pretend to be strong. And seek out trusted people too, who can walk alongside you with care and without judging you.
exp.32:7:
Here Elihu tells Job that he listened to him carefully. "Surely" means "truly," and "in my hearing" means that Job said it while Elihu was present, so Elihu is not repeating rumors. He is about to repeat Job's exact words in order to answer him.

Elihu is a young man who has waited for Job's friends to finish speaking. Now he addresses Job directly. Before correcting him, he wants to repeat exactly what Job claimed, and then he cites phrases such as "I am clean" and "God counts me as his enemy." Some understand that Elihu summarizes Job well, while others think he exaggerates a little what Job said.

For today: before correcting or criticizing someone, listen carefully and understand what they actually said. This way we avoid judging by assumptions, and our words will be fairer and wiser.
exp.9:2:
Job asks God whether it pleases Him to oppress him, to reject the work of His own hands, and to favor the schemes of the wicked. The word "reject" in this verse means to turn away from or cast aside, and "favor the schemes of the wicked" means that God seems to approve of what the wicked plan.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything and is suffering greatly. He is weary of living and decides to pour out his complaint in bitterness. He does not understand why God seems to be against him, and he says so with complete frankness. This is his pain speaking, not a complete account of what God is like. Later, God Himself will correct his view, though He will also accept him.

For today: when you are hurt and confused, you can be honest with God in prayer. Tell Him what you feel, without disguise, and keep seeking Him even when you do not yet have answers.
exp.26:0:
It says that Job spoke again. The verse only marks that Job goes on speaking, so there is no special word to explain here. His speech is calm and carries weight, like a serious statement made in front of others.

Job is a man who suffers greatly and who has had long arguments with his three friends, who insist that his pain is punishment for some sin. In the previous chapter he had already answered Bildad. Now, since the friends are silent, Job continues defending his integrity before God, without ceasing to believe in Him, even though he does not understand what is happening to him.

When you are in the middle of a trial, do not be afraid to speak honestly. You can keep expressing what you feel and, at the same time, remain firm in your trust in God.
exp.2:25:
Job says he has no peace, no ease, and no rest, and that trouble has come upon him anyway. When he says he is not at ease, he means he does not feel calm or settled inside. "Rest" here simply means he is not able to relax. "Trouble" describes deep anguish, a turmoil that is both inward and outward. Job feels that his whole life has become suffering.

Job is speaking as a righteous man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. This is the close of his opening lament, and the verses before it show that he was already living in dread of disaster. Now he pours out his pain before his friends. The Bible does not present this as a lack of faith, but as honesty before God.

For today: when you suffer, do not pretend you are fine. You can tell God sincerely how you feel, and look for someone you trust who will listen to you and stay with you.
exp.1:11:
It says that Job's three friends saw him from a distance and could barely recognize him, because his illness had changed him so much. Then they began to weep aloud. Each one tore his robe, and they threw dust into the air over their heads. These were gestures of deep mourning in that culture.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Job had lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends had agreed to visit him to keep him company and to comfort him. On seeing him, they understood that his suffering was enormous, and they expressed their grief without elaborate words. Later on, their speeches will be a different story, but here their attitude is noble.

For today: when someone is suffering, sometimes the best thing is to be present, to weep with them, and to be silent. There is no need to have explanations; it is enough to accompany them with affection and respect, as Romans 12:15 says: "Weep with those who weep."
exp.30:19:
He says that the heart of the needy man blessed Job because Job warmed him with the wool of his sheep. "Heart" here means the person's inner self, the part that feels gratitude, and "fleece" is the wool that has been sheared off. Job affirms that the one who was cold was warmed thanks to him, and for that reason he blessed him.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends tell him that he suffers because of some hidden sin. In chapter 31 he defends himself with a series of oaths, and here he shows that he always helped the poor. He says the same as in the previous verse: he did not let anyone perish without clothing.

For today: look at what you have that could relieve someone, such as clothing, food, or time. Giving generously, without much fuss, lets someone receive a little warmth and blessing through you.
exp.26:13:
This verse says that, even if the wicked person has many children, they are destined for the sword. And his offspring will never have enough food. Having enough food means eating until you are fully satisfied.

The speaker is Job, answering his friends, who were accusing him of being a wicked man because of his suffering. Here Job describes what, in his view, God has in store for the wicked. Some scholars believe Job is repeating the position of his friends, while others think he uses it ironically to show that he is not that kind of person. There is no single certain interpretation.

For today: let us not judge others by what they suffer, as Job's friends did. Instead, let us seek to live uprightly and trust that God is just, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.41:5:
He says that Job, after seeing God, realizes how small he is and humbles himself. "I despise myself" means that he rejects himself, or takes back what he said before. "I repent" means changing one's attitude, and "dust and ashes" is an image of humility and mourning. Some readings say that Job takes back his words, and others say that he finds comfort. The original text allows several readings.

Job speaks at the end of the book. After suffering greatly and asking for explanations, God spoke to him from the storm and showed him his greatness and wisdom. Job no longer argues. God later says that Job spoke what was right, and that his friends did not. Job is not condemned but restored, and he intercedes for them.

For today: when you do not understand your suffering, do not rest only on what you have heard about God. Come to Him with honesty and humility, trusting that He is greater than your questions.
exp.7:4:
This verse says: "But if you would earnestly seek God and ask the Almighty for mercy." The phrase "earnestly seek" means looking for God with real eagerness and without delay. The phrase "ask the Almighty for mercy" means pleading with humility, admitting that you depend on his kindness.

Here Bildad, one of Job's three friends, is speaking. He answers Job after his great suffering and assumes that the suffering comes from some sin. So he hints that Job's children died because of their own fault. Note this: God himself says at the end of the book that the friends did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7). Their advice sounds pious, but their basic idea is mistaken.

For today: seek God promptly and humbly, especially when you are suffering. But do not use this truth to judge others, for pain is not always punishment.
exp.2:7:
Job wishes that night, the night of his birth, would be cursed by those who are known for cursing days. The verse speaks of those who are prepared or ready to rouse Leviathan, the sea monster. Some scholars understand this to mean people skilled in spells who could stir up that creature of chaos. The exact meaning is not entirely certain.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends have been sitting silently beside him for seven days. Now, broken by grief, he opens his mouth and curses the day he was born. He does not curse God; he expresses his anguish in very strong words.

Today, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can tell God honestly what hurts, even in raw words. Job did, and God did not reject him.
exp.20:8:
The explanation says that the homes of the wicked are free from fear, and that no punishment from God falls on them, meaning no corrective blow of judgment. The phrase "safe from fear" means that they live in peace, without alarm or threat.

Job speaks here, answering Zophar and his friends. They held that bad people always suffer and that suffering is a sign of sin. Job, who suffers without understanding why, answers them with what he observes: sometimes the wicked prosper and do not seem to receive punishment. His complaint is sincere, and the book presents it without hiding it. Later God himself corrects both Job and the friends.

For today: do not measure your life or the lives of others only by comfort or hardship. Prosperity does not prove that someone pleases God, nor does pain prove the opposite. Trust God, and be honest with him when you do not understand.
exp.9:0:
He says Job is sick of his own life. Here the word for "weary" points to a deep exhaustion, the kind someone feels when they can no longer bear living with their pain. "I will express my complaint" means he will not keep his suffering locked inside but will let it out. "In the bitterness of my soul" shows that he will speak from a deep and raw pain.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends have insisted that his suffering is a punishment, but he does not accept this. So instead of speaking to them, he addresses God with honesty. It is a cry of pain, not a teaching to imitate in every way.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, do not pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel. If discouragement is very great, also seek out someone you trust who can listen to you and stand with you.
exp.8:28:
Job says: "Since I am already found guilty, why should I labor in vain?" The phrase "labor in vain" means working hard and getting no benefit from it. In the verse before, the weariness he describes refers to his sorrow and dejection.

Job speaks to his friends, but in reality he is speaking to God. He is suffering and feels that God will not declare him innocent, no matter how hard he tries. Here he does not confess any real wrongdoing, since elsewhere in the book he insists that he is blameless. Rather, he expresses his hopelessness: he feels that God has already condemned him. Some understand that he speaks bitterly, others that he speaks with irony.

When pain makes you think that nothing helps, do not conclude that God is against you. Tell him honestly what you feel, as Job did. And remember that our hope is not in cleansing ourselves alone, but in the grace of Christ.
exp.30:30:
The verse says that the people of Job's household, his servants and workers, had not been saying: "Who is there who has not had his fill of Job's food and kindness?" The word "house" means the people who live and work under his roof. The idea of having one's fill means having had enough and being completely satisfied. The meaning of Job's words is clear enough from this, though some readers take the phrase to mean that his people loved him so much that they never tired of his company, while others think of it differently. The text allows both readings.

Job speaks and defends his life before his friends and before God. He is declaring his innocence: he did not rejoice at his enemy's misfortune, nor was he harsh with anyone. The people of his household could bear witness to his kind and generous treatment, and that is why his hospitality was well known.

Today, ask yourself what those who live or work with you would say about you. Try to treat the people of your household and your employees with such kindness and justice that your testimony holds up in everyday life.
exp.9:7:
Job says that God's hands shaped him and formed him completely. Then he asks in pain, "Would You now turn and destroy me?" The explanation notes that the word for "shaped" and "formed" carries the sense of God arranging and fashioning him with care, and that "altogether" points to the whole of his being. The word for "destroy" means to tear down or ruin.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly and feels confused. He is addressing God, not his friends. He believes he is not wicked, yet he feels that God treats him like an enemy. That is why he reminds God that he is the work of God's hands. His complaint is sincere, although not everything he says in his pain is complete or correct.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, you can speak to God honestly, without pretending. Remember too that He made you with care and that your life matters to Him. Bring Him your questions with humility, and keep trusting even when you do not yet see answers.
exp.29:2:
The explanation says that some people, gaunt from poverty and hunger, went out alone to dry, desolate and barren land by night. "Desolate" means destroyed or laid waste, and "dry" means parched and lacking water.

Job speaks, a man who has lost his health, his possessions and his standing. In this chapter he complains that young people, the sons of outcasts and despised men, now mock him. He describes his own parents as people rejected by society. Job contrasts the honor he once had with the humiliation he now endures.

For today: poverty and hunger often lead to isolation and shame. We can seek out someone who lives alone or in need, offer them food, company or concrete help, and treat them with dignity, without mocking or despising them.
exp.7:5:
It says that if Job is pure and upright, God will rise up on his behalf and restore his righteous estate. "If you are" means the condition is stated plainly, as something Bildad is asking Job to consider. "Even now" means God would act right away, even in the middle of this trouble. "Rouse Himself" is an image: God would act like someone who wakes up to come to Job's aid.

Bildad, a friend of Job, speaks here and wants to explain his suffering. He believes God always punishes sin and rewards righteousness, so he implies that Job is suffering because of something wrong. But the book shows that Bildad is mistaken: Job was not suffering for that reason. His words sound pious, but they are harsh and unjust.

For today: when someone is suffering, do not judge them with quick answers. Walk alongside them with humility and compassion, and remember that we do not always understand God's ways.
exp.27:7:
It says that the place where the metals and precious stones are is so hidden and hard to reach that no wild animals have ever walked through there. The phrase "proud beasts" points to the animals of the wild; in the original Hebrew, the expression refers to proud or majestic creatures. The idea of treading means walking over that ground.

Job is speaking. This chapter is a poem about wisdom. It describes how human beings reach deep mines that no animal knows, yet still cannot find wisdom by their own means. Some understand these words as part of Job's speech; others note that the tone is different from his earlier complaints.

For today: if people work so hard to gain riches, how much more should we seek the wisdom of God? Spend time today reading the Bible and asking God for direction, with the same eagerness with which others seek money.
exp.23:1:
Some people, he says, are wicked and "move boundary stones," that is, they shift the markers that set the limits of a piece of land, in order to take ground that belongs to others. They also steal flocks and then "pasture" them as if they were their own, without any remorse.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. His friends tell him that God always punishes the wicked and blesses the righteous. Job does not agree: he sees many unjust people prosper while the poor suffer. So he asks why God seems not to act, even though nothing is hidden from him. This is an honest complaint, not a final explanation.

For today: do not get used to injustice or ignore it. Be honest in what belongs to others, and if you can, defend the one who is weaker. And when you do not understand why God delays, bring him your complaint with sincerity, as Job did.
exp.35:5:
This verse says that God does not let the wicked person keep his life, meaning he does not allow the godless to prosper without end. Instead, for the afflicted, those who suffer, he brings about justice and grants them what is rightly theirs. The words "grant" and "justice" in the verse are the ones that matter here: to grant means to give or bestow, and justice means what is fair and right.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks near the end of the book, after the long dialogues between Job and his three friends. Elihu wants to defend the justice of God and affirms that God is great and wise, and that he does not despise anyone. Some scholars believe his words have much merit, although they do not explain all of Job's suffering, and God later answers Job directly.

For today: if you are suffering or see injustice, you can bring your pain to God with confidence, trusting that he sees and does not despise you. In the meantime, avoid judging other people's suffering as if it were always punishment.
exp.25:8:
God covers the face of the full moon and spreads his cloud over it. The phrase "covers the face" in this verse means to block the view, so God hides the moon behind a cloud and we cannot see it clearly. The Berean Standard Bible says the moon is covered, and the reading that fits the wider context best is that God is concealed behind a veil of cloud.

Here Job is speaking, responding to his friend Bildad. Job acknowledges the great power of God over creation: he hangs the earth over nothing and binds the waters in the clouds. Job admits that what we see of God is only a small part of his greatness (see v. 14).

For today: you do not need to understand everything to trust God. If there are things about his ways that you do not grasp, rest in the fact that he is great, wise, and faithful, even when at times his path is covered by a cloud.
exp.11:19:
He can silence those who speak truthfully and take away the discernment of elders.

The phrase "He deprives the trusted of speech" in this verse means he silences those whose words can be relied on, and "the discernment of elders" refers to the good judgment of older people. Here the verse speaks of those whose speech is trustworthy and of the elders' ability to judge well.

Job speaks, answering his friends, who insisted that God always rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked. Job replies that God is sovereign over everyone, even over kings and wise men, and that his ways are not always understood. Here he describes God's power with a tone of complaint and wonder. This is what Job says, not necessarily the complete teaching of the book.

For today: do not boast of your wisdom or your experience. Ask God each day for humility and guidance, and listen with respect, even when you do not understand what He allows.
exp.22:6:
It says that, if Job could come before God, an upright man could lay out his case and reason with him there. And so Job would be set free forever from the one who judges him. "Reason" here means to argue a case with evidence and arguments, and "be set free" means to be released from the judgment that weighs on him.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends tell him that he suffers because of some hidden sin, but he maintains that this is not so. He longs for a fair hearing before God, convinced that God would listen to him with attention and would not crush him. Yet in the verses that follow he confesses that he cannot find him, neither to the east nor to the west. Some think Job speaks with faith; others, that he expresses his anguish.

For today: when you suffer and feel that God is far away, you can speak to him honestly, bring him your questions and your pain, without pretending. He invites an honest heart.
exp.18:12:
He has removed my brothers from me, and my acquaintances have abandoned me. Job is describing how completely he has been left alone, with family and friends stepping away from him.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He feels that God is behind his loneliness, although the book shows that the reality was more complex and that Job did not see everything that was happening. Here he expresses his pain with sincerity.

When someone suffers, others sometimes pull away out of discomfort or because they do not know what to say. Today you can reach out to a person going through a hard time: visit them, listen to them, and stay with them, without judging them or offering quick explanations.
exp.29:10:
Job says that God "unstrung my bow", that is, took away the strength and protection that kept him standing. Some understand the bow image as one of defense (he can no longer protect himself), and the wording itself does not settle the point further. God afflicted him, and for that reason people "cast off restraint in my presence": they lost all respect and treated him without shame to his face.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. He was once respected, but now young people mock him, despise him, and spit at him. Job attributes his fall to God, although the book shows that his understanding is limited; he does not know what happened in heaven (chapters 1 and 2).

For today: when pain leaves you weak and others treat you badly, you can bring your complaint to God honestly. You do not have to pretend to be strong. And treat with compassion someone who is suffering, instead of taking advantage of their weakness.
exp.12:10:
The explanation says that God's greatness should fill Job's friends with fear. The words "majesty" and "dread" in your verse are described here plainly: "majesty" refers to God's greatness and splendor, and "dread" is a deep, reverent fear. "Terrify" means to make someone tremble, not merely to frighten them. Job asks them whether they are truly not moved by speaking about God so carelessly.

Job speaks to Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. They insist that his suffering is punishment for some hidden sin. Job tells them that they defend God with crooked arguments and partiality. He reminds them that God will examine them, and that one cannot deceive the Lord the way one deceives a person.

For today: before we speak on behalf of God or explain someone else's pain, let us do so with humility and reverent fear. Sometimes it is better to accompany someone in silence than to give answers that God never gave us.
exp.17:2:
Bildad asks Job why they are treated like stupid cattle and seen as worthless in his eyes. The word "stupid" points to animals that are dull and do not reason. Cattle are used here as a picture of people who are thought to lack understanding and worth.

Here Bildad speaks, one of Job's three friends. He feels offended because Job had questioned his wisdom in his earlier replies. Bildad no longer listens with patience: he defends his pride and his position. Then he goes on with a harsh description of the fate of the wicked, implying that Job suffers because of his wickedness. The Bible does not support that conclusion, for God himself contradicts it at the end of the book.

When someone contradicts us, it is easy to feel offended and answer harshly. Before defending ourselves, let us ask God for humility to listen, especially to someone who is suffering.
exp.19:3:
This verse is a question that Zophar puts to Job: "Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth." Zophar appeals to the experience of all humanity, as if he were saying that this is something very ancient and well known.

Zophar is one of Job's three friends. He feels offended by Job's words and answers in haste. What follows is that the joy of the wicked lasts only a short time. Zophar takes for granted that Job suffers because he is wicked. The Bible later shows that this conclusion was mistaken, since God himself says that Job was blameless.

For today: a general truth may be true, but applying it wrongly wounds others. Before explaining another person's pain, let us listen with humility and compassion, without hurrying to judge.
exp.9:3:
Job asks God whether He has eyes like ours, that is, whether He sees things with the limited sight of a human being. The question "Do You see as man sees?" means judging by outward appearances, without knowing what is in the heart. It is a rhetorical question, not a doctrinal statement.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He feels that God treats him as guilty and asks Him to explain why. His friends tell him he suffers because of his sin, but he feels misunderstood. Here he speaks with bitterness and confusion, and some of his complaints will later be corrected by God Himself. Even so, Job still brings his pain to God and not somewhere else.

For today: when you do not understand your pain, bring it to God with sincerity. He is not shocked by your questions. But remember that His sight is greater than ours, and that we can trust Him even when we do not see everything.
exp.1:8:
Here his wife speaks to him out of pain and despair. "Integrity" means his honest life and his sincere faith in God. She asks him whether he still holds on to that, and she tells him to curse God and die.

Job has lost his children, his possessions, and now his health. She has suffered those losses too. She speaks from grief, perhaps without seeing what was happening in heaven. Job answers her firmly but without hatred, and the Bible says he did not sin with his lips. Interpreters see her in different ways: some harshly, others with compassion.

When we are suffering, let us be careful with what we say and what we listen to. Advice born of pain can sound reasonable and still pull us away from God. Let us seek to remain faithful, even with doubts and tears.
exp.13:8:
It says that a tree that has been cut down will sprout again at the scent of water and put out twigs like a young sapling. "Scent" here means the moisture it senses, and "put out twigs" means it sends up new shoots and growth. Even when the root is old and the trunk looks dead, there is still hidden life in it.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. He is comparing trees with human beings. For him, the tree has hope of coming back to life, but the man, as he sees it at this moment, dies and does not return. It is a sincere complaint, not a final teaching about death. Later in the book, Job expresses hope in a Redeemer (19:25).

For today: if you feel cut down or worn out, do not judge yourself by what you see on the outside. Come near to God honestly, even with doubts, and let Him renew little by little what seems dry.
exp.38:13:
Can you trust the wild ox? God asks Job this question. The animal is very strong; in Hebrew it is called "reem," a fierce wild animal, probably a wild bull, and some translators render it as "buffalo." Though it has great strength, would you leave your field work to it? Here "trust" means to entrust or hand over a task. The implied answer is no: it cannot be tamed or made to serve human plans.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned the way God governs the world. God gives him no explanations, but shows him creation: wild animals that live beyond human control, yet under God's care. In this way he teaches Job how limited his understanding is.

For today: there are things we cannot control or fully understand. Instead of demanding answers, let us learn to trust God, who sustains all creation with wisdom.
exp.26:8:
This verse asks a question: will God hear the cry of the hypocrite when distress comes upon him? Job implies the answer is no. "Distress" means deep pain or great hardship, and "cry" is a shout asking for help.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends tell him he suffers because he is wicked, but he insists that he is sincere. Here he describes the end of the hypocrite: though he may accumulate riches, he has no true hope, because his heart is not with God. Some think Job is also asking whether God hears him, but he affirms that he is not a hypocrite.

For today: do not seek God only when everything falls apart. Cultivate a sincere relationship with Him every day, so that in the trial your prayer springs from real trust and not from despair.
exp.8:23:
The explanation says that the earth seems to be in the hands of wicked people, and that God "blindfolds" its judges, meaning it seems he blinds them so they neither see the truth nor do justice. Job ends with a forceful question: if it is not God who allows this, then who is it? The words that appear nearby, "swiftly" and "messenger," are not needed here.
