The speaker is Job, in the middle of his pain. He has lost everything, and his friends tell him he is suffering because of his sin. He answers from his anguish and confusion, and he accuses God of injustice. Note: this is what Job feels and says, not necessarily what God teaches. At the end of the book, God himself corrects that limited view.

Today, if you see injustice and do not understand it, you can bring your questions to God honestly, as Job did, without ceasing to trust that he sees more than you do.
exp.20:19:
It says that the wicked person will see his own ruin with his own eyes, and that he will take in God's punishment for himself. The word for "ruin" here means destruction or downfall, which is the same word the verse uses. The image of drinking God's anger pictures receiving the full force of divine judgment, like someone who drinks a cup all the way to the bottom. "The Almighty" is a title for God.

Job is speaking here, answering his friends. They had said that bad people always end up suffering. Job replies that many wicked people prosper, and he argues that the punishment should fall on the wicked themselves and not only on their children. He is not stating a complete doctrine here but arguing with his friends, so the passage must be read within the whole book.

For today: do not be quick to judge others or to explain other people's suffering with easy answers. Trust that God is just, and leave in his hands what you cannot resolve.
exp.29:6:
The verse says that these rejected people cried out among the shrubs and huddled beneath the nettles. They called out in distress, and they crowded together under the prickly plants for shelter. "Among the shrubs" refers to the wild growth where they sought cover.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. He was once respected, but now he describes with pain how even people on the margins, whom he once never bothered with, mock him. His complaint shows how far his honor has fallen. Job's harsh words reflect his pain, and not necessarily the heart of God toward the marginalized.

For today: when you suffer humiliation, you can bring your pain to God with honesty, as Job did. And remember that no person is worth less before God; treat with respect and compassion those whom society sets aside.
exp.39:3:
God asks Job two questions: whether he has an arm like God's, that is, power like God's, and whether he can thunder with a voice like His. The "arm" stands for the strength to act, and the "thunder" stands for the authority that makes all creation tremble. The obvious answer is no.

Here the Lord speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and had questioned God's justice. Now God confronts him, not to humiliate him without reason, but to show him the difference between the Creator and the creature. The verses that follow challenge him to do what only God can do.

For today: when we do not understand the pain or the decisions of God, let us remember that we cannot see everything He sees. Trusting in His power and His wisdom gives us rest, even without having all the answers.
exp.36:8:
The verse says the storm comes out of its chamber, and the cold comes from the driving north winds. A tempest is a violent wind that churns the air. Job describes how the weather shifts depending on where the wind blows from. Some scholars link the storm's chamber to a hidden store where storms are kept, but the main idea stays the same.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins the conversation between Job and his friends near the end. He is describing storms and seasons as signs of God's power. His purpose is to lead Job to recognize that God governs nature with a wisdom that human beings do not fully grasp.

For today: when the weather gets in the way of your plans, remember that you do not control everything. Use it to pause, to trust God, and to thank him for sustaining the world, even the parts we do not understand.
exp.14:29:
This verse describes the wicked person using images from nature. "He will not escape from the darkness" speaks of a darkness he cannot get out of, that is, ruin and calamity. He is like a tree whose shoots are withered by fire. "The breath of God's mouth will carry him away" pictures God himself removing him, with a breath.

Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's friends, is speaking here. He is describing what, in his view, happens to every evil person, and he says it in a way that implies Job suffers because of his sin. But the book shows that Eliphaz is wrong to apply this to Job, since God himself corrects him at the end.

For today: the Bible teaches that evil has consequences, but we should not judge others by their suffering. When we face the pain of others, it is better to accompany them with humility than to accuse them.
exp.40:15:
It says that the scales of Leviathan are pressed so tightly together that not even air can pass between them. The phrase "one scale is so near to another" means that they are joined; the word "air" here simply means air. It is an image of a perfect armor, with no gap at all.

The speaker is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful creature, to show Job that there are things in creation that Job cannot master or fully understand. Interpreters disagree about whether it is a crocodile, a mythical animal, or a symbol of chaos; the text does not make this clear. The point is that if Job cannot stand against this creature, neither can he question his Creator.

For today: trust God even when you do not understand everything that happens. Recognizing that He is greater than what we do not control helps us rest in His care and wisdom.
exp.40:19:
Smoke billows from his nostrils, like the rising steam from a boiling pot set over burning reeds. The picture is of a fierce inner heat so strong that it pours out where everyone can see.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes the leviathan, a powerful creature. It is not known for certain what animal this is: some think of the crocodile, others of a mythical or symbolic creature. God uses it to show Job that there are things in creation he cannot master, and that God can.

For today: when life seems too large or confusing, remember that God governs what you cannot control. Hand over your fears and rest in his wisdom, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.38:15:
The verse asks whether Job was the one who gave wings to the ostrich. The word "peacock" is a doubtful translation: the original Hebrew is uncertain, and many scholars think it refers to a bird that sings or flutters with joy, while the ostrich is clear. Here the point is that its wings are showy, but they do not help it fly.

The one speaking is God, answering Job from the whirlwind. He asks many questions about the animals to show Job that the world is far greater and more mysterious than Job can understand. The ostrich seems clumsy and careless with its eggs, but God made it that way.

For today: trust God even when you do not understand his ways. He cares for his creation, even for what seems strange or senseless to us, and he cares for you too.
exp.40:12:
What it says: Job 41:13 asks who could strip off this creature's outer coat. It also asks who would dare to approach it with a bridle. The expected answer is: no one. Some translators understand the outer coat as its skin, and others as its armor of scales; the Hebrew allows several readings.

Context: God is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful creature that no human being can subdue. Many believe it refers to a real animal, such as the crocodile, and others also see a symbol of chaos. God wants to show that He is the Creator and that everything belongs to Him (v. 11).

For today: If we cannot control even one creature, we will certainly not control everything that happens in life. Today you can hand over to God what you cannot manage and trust that He does govern.
exp.25:11:
By his power he stirs the sea, and by his understanding he shatters Rahab. Rahab is a poetic name for a monster of the sea's chaos. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning, but the idea is clear: God rules the forces that seem most frightening.

Job is speaking, answering his friend Bildad. Job suffers greatly, yet he does not doubt the power of God. In this chapter he describes in poetry the greatness of the Creator over the sea, the heavens, and the earth, and he ends by acknowledging that what we know of God is only a small part.

For today: when your problems feel like a churning sea, remember that God governs them with power and wisdom. Bring your fear to him with confidence, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.21:7:
The explanation says that the mighty man held the land, and that the man of honor lived on it. "Mighty" means powerful or wealthy, with great influence. "Honorable" refers to someone of high standing, who is held in regard. The text can also be read as an accusation: the powerful claim the land for themselves while others go in need.

Here Eliphaz speaks, one of Job's friends. He is accusing Job of serious wrongs, such as oppressing the poor, and says that this is why his sufferings have come upon him. But the book shows that Eliphaz is mistaken: Job was an upright man, and his pain was not a punishment for those sins. This verse serves to show how Eliphaz thinks, not as an exact description of Job.

For today: do not use your position or your resources only for your own comfort. Think about how you can help someone who has less. And be careful not to judge the suffering of others harshly.
exp.18:8:
He has stripped me of my honor and removed the crown from my head. The word "stripped" means that what covered him was torn away, and "honor" refers to his good name and the respect he had. The image of the crown being removed from his head pictures losing his place of honor, the way a king loses his crown.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He feels that God treats him as an enemy and that he receives no justice. The verses before and after show his sense of being trapped, with no way out and no hope. This is his honest complaint, not a complete explanation of what God is doing.

For today: when you feel you have lost your dignity or your place, do not pretend that you are fine. Job spoke frankly before God, and the Bible records his complaint. Bring your pain to God honestly, and look for people who will stay with you without judging you.
exp.8:7:
It says that God alone stretches out the heavens, like someone spreading out a great cloth or tent, and that he treads on the waves of the sea. The verse shows God with a power that no one shares, one that rules even over what seems to us humans to be beyond control.

Job speaks here in the midst of his suffering, answering his friend Bildad. Job acknowledges that God is wise and strong, but he wonders how a human being could defend himself before someone so great. His tone mixes admiration with pain and confusion.

For today: when you feel that your life is like a restless sea, remember that God treads on the waves. We will not always understand what is happening, but we can rest in the knowledge that He is greater than our storm and entrust to Him what we cannot control.
exp.34:0:
Elihu went on speaking. The phrase in your verse means he kept on with his speech, without stopping, and moved on to a new point. It is simply a transitional phrase that introduces what follows.

Elihu is the young man who spoke after Job's three friends stopped answering him. He is explaining his view of Job's suffering. In the verses that follow, he confronts Job, because he understands that Job has implied that he is more righteous than God and that obeying God does him no good. Some scholars think Elihu is partly right and others think he exaggerates; the book does not correct him directly.

For today: when someone speaks to us honestly, let us listen until the end. Also, when we suffer, let us take care with our words so that we do not accuse God of being unjust.
exp.18:11:
His troops advance together, building a ramp against me and camping around my tent. The picture is of an army laying siege to an enemy, closing in from every side.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends insist he must be suffering because of some sin. Job feels that God himself has become his adversary, and he uses images of war to describe his pain. Interpreters see here his sincere complaint, not necessarily the whole truth about God.

For today: when you feel that everything is coming down on you, you can tell God honestly what you feel, without pretending. He hears the sincere cry, and you can also seek out someone you trust who will stand with you.
exp.20:10:
The explanation says that the little children of the wicked go out to play like a flock of sheep, and that their young ones skip about with joy. "Little ones" means the children; "flock" means a group of animals that run together; "skipping" means to leap about or move about happily.

Job speaks, answering his friends, who said that wicked people always end up badly. Job disagrees: he sees that some who live without God have peace, family, and well-being. He is hurt because he suffers without understanding why. Later on, Job also acknowledges that this prosperity does not last forever (v. 13), though here he is only describing what he observes.

When you see that an unjust person is doing well, do not become bitter or doubt God. Life does not always look fair right now. Trust that God sees everything, and guard your own heart so that you live with honesty and gratitude.
exp.13:11:
The explanation says that a man who dies lies down and does not rise again. The phrase about rising again means "does not rise" in the sense of not getting up once more. Job uses the image of sleep to speak of death, and he says this will last in a way that seems endless, until the heavens are no more.

Job is a man who suffers greatly and feels that God has left him alone. He compares human life to a river that dries up and asks what hope there is. Here he expresses his pain and his limits, not a complete teaching about the resurrection. A few verses later he asks whether a man will live again and says he will wait for his change, or renewal.

For today: if you are tired or without hope, you can speak to God with complete honesty, as Job did. He is not frightened by your questions, and the Bible later shows more light about hope in Christ.
exp.31:3:
Elihu had stayed quiet, waiting for Job and his three friends to finish speaking. He did this because the others were older than he was. The phrase "old in days" means they had more years of life. And "waited for Job in the debate" means he waited for his turn in the discussion.

Elihu is a young man who suddenly appears in the book. He had listened to the whole debate in silence. Now he becomes angry, because Job justified himself rather than God, and because the three friends could not answer Job, even though they kept condemning him. His anger is strong, but earlier he showed respect for the age of the others.

For today: before speaking, learn to listen with patience and respect, even when you have something to say. But when you do speak, be careful to speak with humility and not only with anger, seeking to honor God.
exp.1:0:
On another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came with them to present himself before Him. The phrase "sons of God" is usually understood to refer to angelic beings, although some scholars interpret it differently.

The narrator of the book shows us a scene in heaven, similar to the one in chapter 1. Job had already lost his possessions and his children, but he remained faithful. That is why the LORD speaks to Satan about Job. It is important to notice that Satan appears as someone who must answer to God and cannot act without His permission.

For today: when you suffer, remember that God is still in control, even when you do not understand what is happening. Trust in Him and remain faithful, as Job did.
exp.0:10:
Satan makes a challenge to God: stretch out your hand and strike everything Job has, and then Job will curse you openly, right to your face. The phrase means Job would do this in plain sight, not in secret.

The one speaking is Satan, the accuser, standing before God. He has just said that Job obeys only because God protects and blesses him. He questions whether Job's faith is sincere. God accepts the test, but with a limit: Satan may not touch Job himself. The text does not explain every mystery of suffering, and that is why the book moves forward.

For today: examine why you trust God. A mature faith loves him for who he is, not only for his gifts. When hard times come, hold on to him with sincerity and honesty.
exp.37:25:
It says God makes rain fall on lands where no one lives: the desert, a place without people. "Uninhabited" means without inhabitants, and the wording about a barren land where no one lives reinforces it. The verse continues in the next one: that rain satisfies the dry ground and makes the tender grass sprout.

God himself speaks here, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him an argument but a series of questions about creation, to show that his wisdom and care exceed what Job can see. This rain falls even though no one sees it or uses it.

For today: God cares for things we neither notice nor understand. When something in your life seems to make no sense, you can trust that his attention does not depend on our seeing it. Rest in his care, even in your deserts.
exp.15:17:
Here Job speaks to the earth and asks it not to hide his blood, that is, not to conceal the injustice he is suffering. He also asks that his cry for help never be laid to rest, meaning that it should not be silenced or left unanswered until it is heard.

Job is a man who suffers greatly and feels accused by his friends, who think his pain is punishment for some sin. Job insists that his hands are clean and that his prayer was sincere. His words recall innocent blood crying out from the ground, as in Genesis 4:10. Some understand that Job feels he is close to death.

When you suffer without understanding why, do not hide your pain or fall silent. Bring it honestly to God, as Job did, trusting that he sees what others cannot understand.
exp.0:1:
It says that Job had seven sons and three daughters. This is a simple detail, but an important one: Job appears as a man with a complete and large family.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and does not identify himself; we do not know with certainty who wrote it. After presenting Job as a man of integrity who respected God, the account shows his blessing: children, riches, and a good name. The numbers seven and three are usually understood as a sign of completeness, although the text does not explain this. This prepares the contrast with the trial that comes later.

For today: value your family as a gift from God, not as something secure forever. Pray for your loved ones and care for them with love, trusting God in the good times and in the difficult ones.
exp.26:18:
The explanation says that the rich man lies down to sleep, but he will not be the same when he wakes. He lies down wealthy, yet when he opens his eyes, all is gone. The verse does not say how this loss comes about, only that it happens at once, with no time to prepare. Some readers take the verse to mean that his wealth vanishes overnight, while others take it to mean that he is no longer alive at all. The text allows both readings.

The speaker is Job, responding to his friends, who were telling him that God punishes the wicked and that this was why he was suffering. Here Job describes the fate of the wicked person: his riches pass into the hands of the righteous, and his house is fragile like that of a moth.

For today: do not place your security in what you have, because everything can change suddenly. Live with generosity and trust in God, not in your possessions.
exp.23:24:
Job says: "If this is not so, then who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?" The words "prove me a liar" and "reduce my words to nothing" mean showing that someone has said something false and overturning what they said. Job issues a challenge: if anyone can show that he is wrong, let them do it.

Job speaks in the middle of his debate with his friends. They maintain that God always punishes the wicked quickly. Job replies that sometimes the wicked seem to prosper and live at ease, yet in the end they die like everyone else. With this challenge he closes his argument. Some scholars see here sincere confidence; others see also pain and frustration.

For today: let us not reduce the suffering of others to easy explanations. Let us be honest with God about our questions, and trust that his justice is greater than what we see.
exp.21:0:
This verse only introduces who is going to speak. Eliphaz, from Teman, takes up the word for the third time to answer Job. "Replied" means the same as "answered." The name Eliphaz is written the same way today.

Context: Job has lost his possessions and his children, and he is sick. Three friends come to comfort him, but they end up accusing him of having sinned. Eliphaz speaks first in each round, and here his third speech begins. His tone becomes harsher, and he even accuses Job without evidence. At the end of the book, God corrects these friends for not having spoken well about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: before answering someone who is suffering, it is wise to listen with humility. Having good theology is not enough if we speak without compassion or understanding. Sometimes the best comfort is to be present with someone, not to explain or judge.
exp.15:16:
Job says that he suffers and weeps although he has committed no violence or wickedness. The phrase about his hands being free of violence means that there is no wrong or harm in his actions. And the phrase about his prayer being pure means that he prays with sincerity, without deceit. The word "although" here marks the contrast: his pain does not match his conduct.

Job speaks in the middle of his trial. His friends insist that he suffers for some hidden sin, but he defends himself. He weeps, clothes himself in sackcloth, and calls on God as witness to his innocence. Some understand that he does not consider himself perfect, but rather that he denies being guilty of what they accuse him of.

When you suffer without understanding why, you do not have to pretend or keep silent about your pain. You can pray with sincerity and give your heart to God. And take care not to judge others who suffer, as Job's friends did; sometimes the best thing is to accompany them with humility and compassion.
exp.6:17:
God attends to the human being every morning and tests him at every moment. "Attend to" here means to pay close attention to someone. "Test" means to examine, the way gold is tested to see what it is made of. The verse is part of a question that comes from the verse before it: "What is man, that you should make so much of him?"

Job speaks in the middle of very great suffering. He feels watched without rest and without relief. He seems to use, with sadness, words similar to those of Psalm 8, where God's attention is an honor. Job, however, feels it as a burden. Some believe he speaks with irony; others, that he is pouring out his pain without understanding what is happening.

For today: when pain makes you feel that God only watches you in order to demand something from you, you can speak to him with honesty, as Job did. God is not frightened by your complaints. Tell him what you feel and keep seeking him, trusting that his care is real, even when you do not understand it.
exp.7:13:
His confidence is fragile, and the one who forgets God has security that is no stronger than a spider's web. It looks solid for a moment, but it holds nothing up and breaks at the slightest touch.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he hints that Job has forgotten God. But notice that at the end of the book, God says the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So the general principle about trusting in what is fragile holds true, but Bildad applies it wrongly to Job.

For today: examine what your security rests on. Money, success, or plans can fail. Trusting in God gives us a firm foundation, and we should not judge others by their trials.
exp.35:6:
God does not stop watching over the righteous with care. He even seats them alongside kings, enthroned with them, and honors them forever. "Exalted" means lifted up and honored.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who answers Job and his friends. He wants to argue that God is just, great, and wise, and that He does not despise anyone. Be careful, though: Elihu assumes that suffering is always punishment or correction. The book of Job shows that reality is more complex, since Job was righteous and yet still suffered. His words about God's care, however, are encouraging.

Today, if you feel overlooked, remember that God sees you. His care does not depend on your success or on your understanding everything. Keep doing what is right, and pray with confidence.
exp.14:25:
He rushes headlong at God with a thick, studded shield. "Rushing headlong" means charging straight at someone, without care for the danger. The "thick, studded shield" is a heavy shield with raised knobs or studs on its surface. The "He" can sound confusing, but the verse is describing the wicked man attacking God, not God attacking him.

Eliphaz, Job's friend, speaks in his second speech. He describes how the one who defies God comes to an end. He suggests that Job is like this, but he is mistaken: in the end God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: examine whether in some way you are becoming stubborn or defensive before God, and return to Him with humility. And do not use this text to judge the one who suffers, as Eliphaz did.
exp.19:4:
This verse says that the triumph of the wicked is brief, and that the joy of the godless lasts only a moment. "Wicked" refers to those who live without respect for God, and "godless" refers to people who do not honor God in how they live. The verse is framed as a question that expects a yes as its answer: Zophar believes this has always been the case.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He feels offended by Job's rebuke and answers firmly. His view is that the wicked always fall and that Job suffers because of something hidden. Note: at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so his rule does not apply to every case.

For today: do not envy the apparent success of someone who lives badly, nor judge others for their suffering. Seek sincere joy in God, one that does not depend on appearances.
exp.38:19:
The verse says that God did not give the ostrich wisdom or understanding. In plain modern terms: the ostrich does not reason the way other animals do. It leaves its eggs in the ground, without thinking that someone might step on them, and treats its young harshly, as if they were not its own. The word "deprived" means that God did not grant it that capacity.

The one speaking is God. He answers Job out of the whirlwind and shows him creation: wild animals that Job neither controls nor understands. God does not explain Job's suffering; He reminds him that He governs the world with a wisdom far greater than human wisdom, even when something seems strange to us.

For today: when you do not understand why certain things happen, remember that your understanding is limited, but God's is not. Trust Him instead of demanding explanations.
exp.32:5:
Elihu says to Job: "I am just like you before God; I was also formed from clay." His words show that he speaks to Job as an equal, not from above.

Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job's three friends, wants to answer him. Job had longed for God himself to reply. Elihu says he is just like Job before God, and he makes clear that he is just a man, the same as Job. For this reason he asks Job not to be afraid. Some think Elihu speaks with humility; others notice in him a certain presumption.

For today: when we advise or correct someone, let us do it remembering that we too are made of clay. Humility and tenderness open the other person's heart far more than superiority does.
exp.20:27:
Here Job quotes what his friends say: "Where now is the nobleman's house, and where are the tents in which the wicked dwell?" They believe that the home of the unjust rich man always ends up destroyed. A "nobleman" is a powerful man, and the "tents" are the place where the wicked live.

Job speaks in reply to his friends, especially Zophar and Eliphaz. They held that God punishes the wicked quickly, and so Job must have sinned. Job shows them that real life is not always like this: many wicked people prosper and die in peace. He knows that they accuse him unjustly.

For today: let us not judge anyone by their trials or by their success. Suffering does not prove that someone is guilty. Let us accompany those who suffer with humility, and trust that God will judge with justice, even when we do not see everything now.
exp.38:17:
The passage says that the ostrich leaves her eggs on the ground and forgets that a foot may crush them or that a wild animal may trample them. The phrase about a foot trampling them describes a passerby who crushes the eggs. A "wild animal of the field" is a creature living in the open country. The ostrich does not seem to take care of the danger her nest is in.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the storm. He asks Job many questions about creation to show him that God's wisdom is greater than human wisdom. The next verse says that God did not give the ostrich that wisdom, and yet this bird runs swiftly. Some scholars debate how much of this describes the ostrich's actual behavior.

For today: we do not need to understand everything in order to trust God. He governs even what seems strange to us, and we can rest in his wisdom when life has no explanation.
exp.14:33:
For the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery. This verse says that the group of godless people will be left empty and ruined. It also says that fire will destroy the tents of those who get rich through bribes and trickery. The word "barren" means empty and without fruit, and "company" here refers to a gathering or household of people who live without God.

The speaker is Eliphaz, a friend of Job. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he hints that Job is a wicked man. But the book later shows that Eliphaz was wrong to judge Job this way (Job 42:7). Still, the idea that injustice ends badly appears in other parts of the Bible as well.

For today: do not use this text to judge others for their pain. Instead, examine your own heart, leave behind double standards and dishonest gain, and trust that God is just.
exp.8:31:
Job says that God is not a man like him, so he cannot answer Him or take Him to court as two equals in a trial would. The phrase "that we can take each other to court" is the picture Job is painting, a legal dispute with God as the other party.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, responding to his friend Bildad. He feels powerless: although he declares himself innocent, he believes God is so great that he could never win a case against Him. For this reason, in the following verse, he longs for someone to stand as an arbiter between God and him. It is the sincere cry of a wounded man, not necessarily a complete truth about God.

Today we can bring our complaints to God honestly, without pretending. And as Christians, we see that Job's longing for a mediator finds its answer in Jesus Christ (1 Timothy 2:5), who allows us to draw near to God with confidence.
exp.2:10:
Job asks why he did not perish before he was born, or why he did not die the moment he came from his mother's womb. In the Berean Standard Bible wording, "perish at birth" and "die as I came from the womb" both describe the same wish: that his life had ended before it truly began.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. After seven days of silence with his friends, he finally opens his mouth and expresses his pain. What he says is not a plan from God, but a sincere outpouring of grief. The Bible records it honestly, without hiding his anguish.

When you are suffering deeply, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God your pain just as it is, and also seek out someone you trust who will listen without judging you. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, ask for help today from someone close to you or from a professional.
exp.14:19:
A wicked person is described as living every day in pain and inner distress. "Writhes in pain" pictures constant suffering, a restlessness that gives him no peace. "Ruthless" refers to the one who harms others without mercy, and the verse says that only a few years are kept for him, so his end is uncertain and not in his control.

Eliphaz the Temanite speaks here, one of Job's friends. He believes the wicked always suffer in this life, and so he suggests that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. He appeals to the tradition of the ancient wise men. Note this: at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So this verse does not apply to every kind of suffering.

For today: do not judge others for their pain; walk alongside them with compassion. And examine your own heart, for living without God unsettles the soul, and He offers peace.
exp.30:32:
Job asks: "Have I covered my wrongdoings, the way others do, keeping my guilt hidden in my heart?" The word "transgressions" here means serious wrongs or faults, and "heart" refers to the inner self, the hidden place where a person keeps private thoughts and secrets. The phrase "like Adam" is hard to pin down, and scholars do not agree on exactly whom or what is meant.

Job speaks in his final defense. He suffers greatly, and his friends accuse him of hidden sins. Here he affirms that he lives openly: he opened his home to the stranger and did not conceal his sin out of fear of people. He says he has had nothing to hide, and for that reason he expects God to hear him.

For today: do not disguise your failings, either out of shame or out of fear of what others will say. Acknowledge them before God and, if needed, before someone you trust. Living in the light brings peace and freedom.
exp.24:0:
This verse only introduces the next speaker. Bildad the Shuhite, from the region of Shuah, speaks for the third and last time in the dialogue with Job. "Replied" means that he responds to what Job has just said.

We are in the debate between Job and his three friends about why he is suffering. Bildad speaks very briefly, only six verses, and does not really answer Job's complaints. He insists that God is great and human beings are small. Some think his speech appears short because the friends were already running out of arguments, although the text does not explain this.

For today: before responding to someone who is suffering, truly listen. Bildad says things that are true about God, but he does not comfort Job. Ask God for wisdom to speak with love and not only with correct words.
exp.32:15:
It says that God, in those moments of deep sleep, opens the ears of people, that is, he speaks to them directly and closely. The warnings that come with this are meant to frighten people into paying attention, so God's message lands with force.

Here Elihu speaks, the young man who intervenes at the end of the book. He answers Job and his friends. He maintains that God does speak, even though people do not notice it. According to him, the purpose is to correct, to turn people away from pride, and to save them from ruin. This is his point of view; God himself will speak later.

For today: ask God to speak to you, and listen with humility. Compare what you feel with the Bible, and if it shows you an error, correct it quickly.
exp.21:23:
He says that if the person returns to God, they will have so much gold that it will be like dust on the ground, and the gold of Ophir will be as common as the stones of the ravines. Ophir was a place famous for its fine gold; no one knows for certain where it was. The phrase "You will have more gold than earth" is an exaggerated image to speak of great abundance.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some sin, and he invites him to repent in order to recover his wealth. At the end of the book, God says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about Him. For that reason, this advice should not be taken as a general promise.

For today: seek God for who He is, not as a path to becoming rich. And when someone suffers, accompany them with compassion, without accusing them.
exp.16:14:
Here Job asks, "Where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?" It is a painful question, close to a lament. Job feels that hope has disappeared from view altogether.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his friends accuse him instead of comforting him. For this reason he speaks of the grave as his home, and even of the worms as his family. Some think that at this point Job doubts all hope; others see in his complaint an honesty that still seeks God.

For today: when pain makes you feel without hope, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did, and ask someone you trust to walk with you.
exp.8:11:
He says that when God takes something away, no one can stop Him or make Him give it back. "Takes away" means to remove something from someone's life or possession. No one has the right to step in and ask Him, "What are You doing?"

The one speaking is Job, in the midst of his great suffering. He has lost his children, his property, and his health, and he is answering his friend Bildad. Job admits that God is so great and mysterious that he cannot argue with Him or understand everything He does. His words express pain and confusion; not everything Job says is a complete teaching about God, and at the end of the book God Himself corrects him.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, you can be honest with Him in prayer, without pretending. Acknowledge that His wisdom surpasses yours, and trust that He is good even when you cannot see the reason.
exp.11:10:
Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food? He says that just as the ear can tell apart the words it hears, and the tongue can recognize the taste of food, so we too should examine and test what we are told. "Food" here means what we eat, and "tastes" is the sense by which the tongue judges flavor.

Job speaks in reply to his friend Zophar and the others, who gave him harsh advice as if they knew everything. Job answers that he too has understanding and does not need lessons about the power of God. So he uses an everyday example: we all know how to judge what we hear. Some understand that Job is also suggesting that his own words deserve to be weighed fairly.

For today: before accepting a piece of advice, a teaching, or an opinion, test it calmly, in prayer, and in the light of the Bible. Listening carefully and discerning is not a lack of humility; it is wisdom.
exp.7:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It tells us that Bildad, who is described as a Shuhite, now speaks to Job. The word "replied" does not always mean that he is answering a question; here it means that he continues the conversation and gives his opinion.

Bildad is the second of the three friends who visit Job after his great losses. Job has just expressed his pain and his complaints (chapters 6 and 7). Bildad feels that Job speaks too harshly against God, so he steps in. Scholars do not know for certain where Shuah was, although it is usually linked with a region east of Canaan. Later on, God will show that the friends did not speak rightly about Him.

For today: before responding to someone who is suffering, listen with patience. Correcting quickly can wound. Sometimes the best thing is to stand with them, pray, and speak with tenderness.
exp.29:5:
It says that those people lived in harsh, remote places: on the slopes of dry streambeds, among the rocks, and in holes in the ground. The phrase "the slopes of the wadis" refers to the steep banks of dry riverbeds that fill with water only in the rainy season, and "holes in the ground" describes shelters dug out of the earth. They had no home and no safe place.

Job, who is suffering greatly, is the one speaking. In chapter 30 he tells how he is now mocked by people whom he would not earlier have placed among the dogs of his flock. He describes these men as outcasts, pushed out of society. Some understand that Job exaggerates because of his pain; the text shows more of his wound than a fair judgment of them.

For today: when you suffer, take care not to despise anyone, not even when they have humiliated you. Every human being, even the most forgotten, has dignity before God. Ask God for help to treat the marginalized with compassion.
exp.12:20:
Job asks God to lift his heavy hand off him, that is, to stop the suffering that God has allowed to come upon him. He also begs that God's terror not frighten him or leave him frozen with fear. The word "frighten" in the verse means to be startled or filled with dread.

The one speaking is Job, a man who has lost nearly everything and suffers greatly. His friends tell him that his pain is punishment for some sin, but he does not accept this. That is why he wants to speak directly with God. He asks for two things: relief, and the ability to come before God without fear. Then he proposes that God call him or answer him, and he asks God to show him where he has failed.

For today: when you suffer and feel confused, you can speak to God honestly, without pretending. Tell him what you feel, ask him for help, and seek to understand, trusting that he hears you.
exp.30:28:
Job says that if he had ever rejoiced when ruin came upon his enemy, or felt exultation when disaster befell him, that would be a serious sin. "Ruin" means downfall; "rejoiced" means he felt joy; and "befell" means a misfortune happened to him.

The speaker is Job, in his final defense. He is listing possible sins to declare that his conscience is clear before God. Here he says he did not give in to a vengeful heart, not even toward an enemy. The verses that follow add that he also never asked for a curse upon anyone.

Today, we can examine our hearts when someone who has hurt us fails. It is easy to feel secret satisfaction. Instead, let us ask God for compassion, pray for that person, and leave justice in His hands.
exp.31:12:
Elihu warns Job's friends not to hide behind an excuse. The word "refute" means "prove wrong" or "overturn." They might say: "We have already found wisdom; only God can prove Job wrong, not a man."

Elihu, a young man who had waited in silence, speaks to Job's three friends. They no longer knew how to answer him. Elihu thinks they should not cover up their failure by saying the matter belongs only to God. Some scholars understand the verse this way. Others see it as a warning against the pride of thinking oneself wise.

Today, when we do not have good answers, let us not use God's name to cover our lack of humility. It is better to listen, to admit what we do not know, and to speak with love and truth.
exp.31:4:
This verse says that Elihu saw that Job's three friends had no more to say, and then his anger was stirred up. The word "But" marks a turn in the story, and "anger" here means a strong feeling of displeasure. "Was kindled" means that his anger grew, like a fire catching and spreading.

Elihu is a young man who has been silent, listening to the long argument between Job and his three friends. He waited out of respect, because they were older than he was. Now he sees that the friends have run out of answers, even though they had condemned Job. This irritates him, and he prepares to speak. The Bible does not say whether his anger is just or unjust; each reader interprets it in their own way.

When something stirs our indignation, it is good to stop before we speak. We can ask ourselves whether our anger seeks the truth and the good of the other person, or only defends our own opinion. Let us ask God for humility and patience to speak with love.
exp.4:13:
They say that the cunning, those who think themselves very clever, run into darkness even in broad daylight. Even though there is light, they stumble around aimlessly, like someone walking in the night. "They encounter darkness by day" describes running into the dark in the middle of the day, and "grope at noon" describes feeling their way along, unable to see the path clearly.

The speaker is Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's friends. He praises God because He frustrates the plans of the wicked and helps the poor. Note: the Bible later shows that Eliphaz misapplied these ideas to Job's suffering, so not all of his words are correct. Even so, this passage about the limits of human cleverness agrees with other biblical texts, such as Proverbs 21:30.

For today: do not rely only on your own intelligence or your tricks. Ask God for wisdom and act with honesty, because He sees clearly when we cannot.
exp.14:15:
He says that if God finds no one pure, not even his holy ones or the heavens, then how much less will he find clean someone who is "vile and corrupt." "Vile" describes someone who disgusts God because of his wickedness. "Corrupt" describes someone who has been ruined by sin. Drinking injustice "like water" describes one who does wrong as naturally as thirst is satisfied, without thinking twice.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to convince Job that he is suffering because of his sin. His idea that no one is clean before God has some truth in it, but Eliphaz misuses it, because he accuses Job without cause. The same book says Job was blameless (Job 1:1). For that reason, it is not wise to take everything the friends say as the word of God.

For today: recognize with humility that you need God's grace, but do not use that truth to judge someone who is suffering. Stand with them in compassion, not with accusations.
exp.27:13:
This verse says that wisdom cannot be found in the depths of the ocean. "The ocean depths" refers to the waters far below, and "the sea" is the open ocean. Both are presented as if they were speaking and answering: "It is not in me" and "It is not with me." In other words, neither the deepest nor the widest parts of creation hold wisdom.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his long dialogue with his friends. This chapter is a poem about the search for wisdom. Job shows that people can dig mines and uncover treasures, but they cannot find wisdom by their own means. Later in the same chapter, the poem says that only God knows its way.

For today: do not look for wisdom only in money, success, or human knowledge. When you need direction, ask God humbly, and He will give it to you.
exp.17:16:
It says the wicked person will be forgotten. The phrase "the memory of him perishes from the earth" means that no one will remember him after he dies. "He has no name in the land" means that his name will not be spoken in the places where people gather and talk. It is the idea of vanishing without leaving a trace.

Here Bildad speaks, one of Job's three friends. He describes the fate of the wicked with harsh images, and he does so to convince Job that his suffering must be punishment for some sin. But the book shows that Bildad was mistaken: Job was an upright man, and God himself corrects the friends at the end.

For today: do not use your fame as the measure of your worth, nor other people's suffering as proof of their guilt. Instead, live with faith and honesty, trusting that God does know your name.
exp.37:28:
From whose womb does the ice emerge? The verse asks this in poetic language, pictturing ice as if it were born from a mother. The "frost from heaven" is the fine white ice that covers everything on cold mornings. The question "Who gives birth to the frost?" asks who is the source of the ice and the frost.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the storm. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons. Instead, he leads Job to look at creation: the rain, the dew, the ice, the stars. With these questions he shows Job that he does not know or control everything, but that God does care with wisdom even for what seems useless or hidden.

For today: when you do not understand what you are going through, look at creation and remember that God sustains everything with wisdom. You can rest in the knowledge that his care is greater than your answers.
exp.13:15:
Job says that God "counts my steps," meaning he keeps track of every single thing he does. He also says that God would not keep track of his sin. He feels closely examined.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. In this chapter he reflects on how brief life is and longs for God to hide him until his anger passes and call him back. Some translations read this verse as a hope: "then you would not keep track of my sin." That is why it is understood in more than one way.

For today: when you feel judged or worn out by your mistakes, speak honestly with God, as Job did. He can hear your complaints, and in Christ there is forgiveness and rest for anyone who trusts in him.
exp.17:6:
The wicked person, who once walked with power and confidence, will find his stride shortened, like someone who can no longer move forward freely. The word "vigorous" in the verse describes his energy and force. The image of "schemes" tripping him up means that his own plans and decisions will end up bringing him down.

Bildad, Job's friend, speaks here in his second speech. He wants to prove that the wicked always end badly, and he implies that Job is suffering because of some hidden wrongdoing. Note: the book shows that Bildad was mistaken in applying this idea to Job. What he says about the wicked has some general truth, but it does not explain all suffering.

For today: before making a decision, ask yourself whether it is wise and just, not only whether it benefits you. Crooked plans can trap us. And do not judge another person's pain as punishment; come alongside them with humility.
exp.38:23:
The explanation says that the war horse paws the ground, rejoices in its own strength, and rushes into battle without fear. The phrase "devours the distance" matches its pawing and eager rush. The horse's pawing and its boldness are described in the same spirit.

Here God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind. He asks him questions about the animals to show him his wisdom and power in creation. The horse is an example of strength and courage that Job did not give it. God wants Job to acknowledge that He governs everything, even what Job does not understand.

For today: when you face something difficult, remember that strength and courage come from God. Trust in Him, and move forward with humility and firmness, without letting fear stop you.
exp.18:2:
Job tells his friends that they have already insulted and humiliated him many times, and he asks them whether they are not ashamed to treat him this way. The word for the insults here means reproached harshly. The number ten probably stands for "many times" rather than an exact count.

Job is speaking, a man who has lost everything and suffers greatly. Instead of comforting him, his friends insist that he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job feels wounded and tired of so many harsh words, and he asks them to treat him with more respect.

For today: when someone is suffering, listening and staying with them is worth more than giving explanations or passing judgment. Before we speak, let us ask whether our words help to heal or wound even more someone who is already hurting.
exp.19:21:
It says that when the wicked person is in the midst of plenty, distress will come upon him right then. The "full force of misery" will fall on him, and it is not clear exactly who or what brings it, though some understand it as hard and violent people who rise up against him, while others see it as any kind of calamity.

The one speaking is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He believes that the wicked always fall and that their prosperity does not last. By this he implies that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. In the end, God Himself says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so his view does not apply to every case.

For today: do not use someone's suffering as proof of their guilt. And examine your own heart: having more does not give true peace. Learn to trust God and to be generous, instead of living anxious to accumulate.
exp.41:16:
He says Job died old and "full of years." This means that he had a long, complete, and satisfying life, lacking nothing essential. It was a way of saying that he died at peace, having lived his years well.

This is the last sentence of the book of Job. Here the narrator speaks and closes the story after Job's long suffering and his restoration. The text mentions that he lived 140 years and saw four generations of his descendants. Some scholars think that this long life shows God's blessing at the end; others stress that the book does not explain all the suffering, but shows God's faithfulness.

Today we can learn that a full life is not a life without pain, but a life where God remains faithful. If you are going through a trial today, trust that God can sustain you and give meaning to your whole story.
exp.17:12:
It says that a terrible disease, called "the firstborn of death," will devour the body of the wicked. "Patches of his skin" and "his limbs" are poetic ways of speaking of the wicked person's body. Scholars are not sure which disease is meant; perhaps it was an expression for the deadliest of all.

Bildad, one of Job's friends, is speaking. He wants to prove that the wicked end badly, and he implies that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. But at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). Their words contain general truths, but they apply them wrongly to Job.

For today: when someone suffers, do not judge them or offer easy explanations. Instead, stand beside them with compassion, listen, and pray for them. God is greater than our conclusions.
exp.21:8:
He says that you sent widows away empty-handed, giving them no help, and that you crushed the strength of the fatherless. Being crushed in strength is a figure of speech: it means taking away their power, their support, or their protection. Widows and orphans were the most defenseless people in society.

Eliphaz speaks, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because he has sinned, so he accuses him of specific wrongdoings. But the book shows that God himself declares Job blameless, and that Eliphaz was wrong in those accusations. Eliphaz assumes things he cannot prove.

For today: God cares for the weak, and we should too. Think of a vulnerable person near you, such as a widow, a child without support, or someone who is alone, and help them with something concrete this week. And avoid accusing others of sin when they are suffering.
exp.14:28:
The explanation says that the wicked man described here will not truly become rich, that his wealth will not last, and that his possessions will not spread across the land. The word "power" refers to his might or wealth, and "splendor" can be understood as his prosperity or what he yields. Scholars are not fully agreed on the exact sense of that last term, so its meaning remains somewhat uncertain.

Here Eliphaz, Job's friend, is speaking. He describes what, in his view, happens to the wicked: they may seem prosperous, but their end is ruin. In this way he suggests, without saying it directly, that Job is suffering because he is guilty. Later, God shows that Eliphaz's conclusion was mistaken.

For today: do not measure your life only by what you have or achieve. Wealth does not last; what endures is a life rooted in God. And be careful about judging someone who is suffering, for pain is not always punishment.
exp.38:14:
God asks Job whether he would trust the wild ox to bring home his harvest. The "wild ox" here is the grain already gathered, and the "threshing floor" is the flat ground where the grain was beaten out and piled together. The Hebrew word translated as "wild ox" most likely refers to a wild bull, an animal that is huge and strong but impossible to tame for farm work.

God speaks out of the whirlwind, answering Job after his long complaints. Through questions about wild animals, he shows Job that creation is full of things Job does not control and does not fully understand. The purpose is to help Job see the greatness and wisdom of God.

For today: we do not need to understand everything or control everything. We can rest in the knowledge that God sustains what we cannot manage.
exp.7:8:
He says that we were born yesterday, that is, we have lived a very short time, and so we know little. Our days on earth pass quickly, like a shadow that moves away.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He tries to convince Job that God is just and that Job should repent. To do this, he asks Job to listen to the wisdom of past generations. Be careful: in this book, the friends do not always speak rightly about God, and in the end God rebukes them. So this statement is true as an observation about our frailty, but Bildad uses it to judge Job unfairly.

Today, let us humbly admit that we know little. Let us listen to those who went before us in the faith, but without judging the suffering of others harshly.
exp.11:4:
He says that one whose feet are slipping, that is, one going through misfortune, is looked down on by those who are at ease, as if the suffering person's trouble made him worthless. The text describes those who live at ease as scornful of misfortune, treating the fate of the one whose feet are slipping as a thing to despise.

Job speaks, answering his friends with irony, especially Zophar. They believe that suffering is always punishment for sin. Job tells them that he is no less wise than they are, and that they mock him even though he is righteous. Then he points out that the wicked often prosper.

For today: do not judge someone by their pain or treat them with contempt. Approach them with patience, listen, and accompany them, instead of offering easy explanations.
exp.29:7:
It says that the people who now mock Job are a senseless and nameless brood, people with no respect and no standing. The verse describes them as worthless in the eyes of others, people who had no place in the community. The idea that they were driven off the land fits this picture of men cast out of society.

Job speaks in the midst of his great suffering. Before, people respected him, but now even young men of low social standing insult him and keep away from him. Job describes his pain over that humiliation. Keep in mind that this is his complaint, and not a judgment by God on those people.

For today: when you are humiliated or treated with contempt, you can honestly tell God how you feel, as Job did. And remember that no person has less value before God. Avoid speaking this way about others.
exp.6:0:
The explanation says that human life on earth is short and limited. A phrase like "consigned to labor" can also be understood as a time of service or assignment, much like a soldier's term of duty. It compares the days of man with those of a hired hand, a worker paid by the day, who labors hard and waits for his wages and his rest.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is answering his friend Eliphaz, who told him his suffering was the result of his sin. Job does not feel comforted; he expresses his weariness and pain with sincerity, and he speaks to God honestly.

For today: if you are exhausted or suffering, you can tell God frankly how you feel, without pretending. And remembering that life is brief invites us to live with purpose and to trust God.
exp.18:1:
Job asks his friends how long they will keep causing him pain. To "torment" him means to inflict deep suffering on him, and to "crush" him with words means to wear him down with harsh, repeated accusations. Job is worn out from hearing them.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. Instead of comforting him, his friends keep insisting that he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job defends himself and asks them to stop accusing him. He answers after listening to Bildad, who had just spoken in chapter 18.

For today: when someone is suffering, our words can either heal or wound. Before explaining or correcting, it is better to listen, to accompany, and to speak with tenderness. Sometimes the best help is a quiet and kind presence.
exp.36:10:
This verse says that God uses the clouds to water the earth with rain, and that he also spreads them out and scatters them. The Berean Standard Bible describes it as God loading the clouds with moisture and scattering his lightning through them. Some scholars understand the lightning in the verse as the brightness of the clouds, though the phrase is hard to render exactly.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of Job's discussions with his friends. In this speech he describes the weather as the work of God's power, to show that God is great and that we cannot understand all of his ways.

For today: when the weather gets in your way or your plans change, remember that God governs everything he has created. You can rest in the fact that he cares for the world, and trust him even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.37:0:
It says that God, here called "the LORD," spoke to Job from a whirlwind, that is, a strong, swirling wind, like a storm. The word "answered" indicates that God responds, after a long time of silence, to everything Job had said.

Job had suffered enormous losses and had asked God for an explanation. His friends had given him many speeches, and Elihu had also spoken. Now the one who speaks is God himself. He does not explain to Job why he suffered; rather, he invites him to look at the greatness of the Creator. Some scholars see in the whirlwind a sign of God's majesty.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, do not stop praying and listening. God remains wise and present, even when he does not give you all the answers. Trusting in him is a step of humility.
exp.6:6:
Job asks God to remember that his life is only a breath, meaning something brief, fragile, and quickly gone, that cannot be held onto. He also says that his eyes will never again see happiness, meaning that he no longer expects to experience good times again.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is covered with sores and pain. At this moment he answers his friends with an honest complaint addressed to God. He feels that life is slipping away without hope. This is his despairing feeling, not a final teaching; the book continues, and God later answers him.

For today: when you are tired or discouraged, you can speak to God with complete sincerity, as Job did. You do not have to pretend to be strong. Tell Him what you feel, and stay close to Him and to people you trust, even if you do not yet see a way out.
exp.41:7:
God tells Eliphaz to take seven bulls and seven rams, go to Job, and offer a burnt offering, a sacrifice burned whole for God. Job will pray for them, and God will accept his prayer so that he does not deal with them according to their folly. The reason is that the friends did not speak accurately about God, the way Job did.

God speaks after Job has repented. Eliphaz and his friends had insisted that Job was suffering for some hidden sin. God corrects them and calls Job "My servant." Job, who suffered so much, will now be the one who prays for them.

Today we can learn to speak about God and about other people's pain with humility, without offering easy answers. We can also learn to pray for those who have hurt us or judged us wrongly.
exp.28:17:
He says that Job thought he would die peacefully in his "nest," that is, in his home, surrounded by his family and his well-being. He also expected to live a great many years, as many as the sand, which cannot be counted. "Multiplying days" means lengthening one's life.

Job speaks in a long speech in which he looks back with longing on his past life, before he lost everything. He remembers when God watched over him, when people respected him, and when he helped the poor and restrained the unjust. He believed that his good conduct would assure him a peaceful end. Some interpreters see here a certain excessive confidence; others see only a sincere and painful memory.

It is wise to do good, but we should not place our security in our plans or our achievements. Let us trust in God, because life changes, and He remains faithful.
exp.12:3:
Here Job tells his three friends that they "smear with lies," meaning they spread falsehoods and cover the truth with them. He also calls them "worthless physicians," that is, doctors who are of no use and cannot heal anything. In today's language: "you spread lies, and you are counselors who do not help at all."

Job speaks in the middle of great suffering. His friends Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar insist that his pain is due to some hidden sin. Job disagrees and prefers to bring his case directly to God. His reaction is strong, and it comes from the pain of feeling wrongly judged.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us listen to them with humility before giving easy explanations. Sometimes staying beside them in silence and with compassion heals more than any speech.
exp.36:13:
This verse is an invitation to stop. "Listen to this" calls for paying attention. "Stand still" means keep still, rest, stop talking and stop being agitated. And "consider" means to think calmly about "the wonders of God," that is, his amazing works, such as the clouds, the rain, and the light.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who speaks after Job's three friends. He speaks of the storm and the weather to show that God governs everything with wisdom, even though we do not always understand his reasons. Some believe his speech prepares the way for God's answer that comes later, although the text does not say so in those words.

For today: pause in the middle of your questions and worries. Look at the sky or at nature for a few minutes and give thanks to God, trusting that he sustains what you cannot fully understand.
exp.8:10:
Job says that God passes by him and he does not see Him, and that God moves and he cannot recognize Him. "Were He to pass by me" describes God at work, and "I would not see Him" means that Job cannot understand God's ways. God is invisible and is beyond our sight and our understanding.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He has just described God's power in creation: the stars and the constellations. Job feels that God is so great that he cannot understand Him or call Him to account. His complaint is sincere, but his view is limited. Later God Himself will answer him.

Today, when you do not understand what God allows in your life, you can tell Him honestly what you feel. Not seeing His work does not mean that He is absent. Trust His character, even when you do not understand His ways.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that the wicked perish by the breath of God, and they are consumed by the blazing force of his anger. The word "breath" can also be understood as "wind," and the picture is of a powerful force that sweeps someone away. "Anger" here means a very strong wrath. "Consumed" means utterly finished off.

The speaker is Eliphaz, a friend of Job. He wants to comfort him, but he assumes that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. His view is that God always punishes the wicked and protects the innocent. The book later shows that God does not approve of that reasoning, since Job was in fact blameless.

For today: be careful not to conclude that someone's suffering is punishment for their sin. God is just, but we do not always know his reasons. Stand with the one who suffers with compassion, not with judgment.
exp.14:16:
Eliphaz asks Job to listen to him. He says he will explain things to him and tell him what he has seen himself. Here "inform" means to explain or make something understood. Eliphaz presents his words as a testimony based on what he has observed.

Eliphaz is from Teman, one of Job's three friends. In this second speech he insists that Job is wrong and that those who suffer deserve it. To support himself, he does not quote God directly, but rather his own experience and the wisdom of the ancients, which he continues in the following verses. Later, God will show that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

Today we can learn to be careful with personal experiences. What we have seen can teach us something, but it should not be used to judge the pain of others. Before giving advice, it is good to listen with humility and compassion, and to measure what we think against what God teaches in His Word.
exp.19:25:
He says that for the wicked person, all that is dark and disastrous is kept in reserve like a treasure laid up. The phrase "a fire unfanned" refers to a fire that no one has stirred up, perhaps a punishment that comes from God. That fire will consume him. And whatever is left in his tent will be devoured, which means his home and his household. Some believe that "total darkness" refers to his hidden treasures; others understand it to mean his hidden plans.

This is Zophar, one of Job's friends. He believes that every wicked person ends badly and that suffering always proves some sin. Here he describes the ruin of the godless with vivid images. But at the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak well of Him (Job 42:7).

For today: trust that God is just, but do not use that principle to judge someone who is suffering. Instead, come alongside them with compassion and humility.
exp.6:14:
It says that Job would prefer to be strangled, that is, to die by suffocation, rather than go on living in his suffering body. "Soul" here means his own self, his very person. "My bones" refers to his body, thin and aching. So Job is saying that death seemed better to him than bearing that pain.

Job speaks in the middle of his enormous suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. He cannot even rest at night, because his dreams torment him. His words are an honest outpouring before God, not a plan to take his own life. Some understand that he is expressing the despair of the moment. The Bible does not present him as an example to imitate, but as someone who wrestles with God in his pain.

If you feel so much pain that you wish you were not alive, do not keep it silent. God allowed Job to speak frankly. Tell it to God and also to someone you trust, to a pastor or a professional who can help you. You do not have to carry that weight alone.
exp.13:17:
This verse says that even a mountain can wear away and crumble, and that a great rock can be dislodged from where it stands. In the verse as you read it, "as a mountain erodes and crumbles" describes a mountain slowly breaking down, and "a rock is dislodged from its place" describes a rock being knocked loose from where it had stayed for ages.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. He is comparing human life with the natural world. Even what seems most solid and lasting wears away over time. In the verses that follow, he says that water wears down stones, and that in the same way God seems to bring an end to human hope. It is the sincere lament of an exhausted man, not a complete teaching about who God is.

For today: when everything that feels firm in your life seems to be crumbling, you can tell God your pain honestly, as Job did. He is not frightened by your questions, and your lament can also be prayer.
exp.35:1:
Elihu asks Job to bear with him a little longer, and he says there is more to be said on God's behalf. The request for patience is his opening, and his wording tells the reader that he still has things to say in God's defense.

Elihu is the young man who spoke after Job and his three friends finished arguing. He is upset because Job seemed to defend himself more than he defended God. Here his fourth speech begins. He says he speaks with wisdom, although the book does not fully confirm this, and some interpreters regard him more favorably than others.

For today: before speaking about God or correcting others, it is good to do so with patience, humility, and truth. It also reminds us to listen calmly, because no one has all the answers about suffering or about the ways of God.
exp.5:0:
This verse is only a transitional phrase. It says that Job speaks up to respond to what his friend has just said. "Replied" means that he speaks in reaction to another person, and "Job replied:" introduces his speech.

Here Job speaks, a man who lost everything and suffers a very great pain. His friend Eliphaz has just spoken to him in the previous chapter, and Job replies. His following words show that he feels misunderstood and that his suffering is heavier than the sand of the sea. Some understand that his broken words are a reflection of his anguish.

For today: when someone suffers, before advising or explaining, it is worth listening with patience. And if you are suffering, you can be honest with God and with others about your pain, as Job did.
exp.14:13:
This verse asks a pointed question: what is a human being, that he could think himself pure or entirely righteous before God? "One born of woman" is an old way of saying any person, with a frail and limited nature. The phrase "should be righteous" means to hold oneself to be without blame.

Eliphaz the Temanite, one of Job's friends, speaks here in his second speech. He rebukes Job because he believes Job's words against God are arrogant. Eliphaz maintains that no one is pure before God, but then he applies that idea harshly, as if Job's suffering proved his wickedness. The book itself shows that this conclusion was mistaken.

For today: humility is truth, not self-contempt. We can recognize that we need God's mercy without using our weakness to judge harshly the one who suffers. Let us accompany others with compassion, not with accusations.
exp.40:29:
The explanation says that the underside of Leviathan is covered with jagged pieces, like broken shards of pottery. When it drags itself across mud or soft ground, those sharp edges leave their marks, much like a threshing sledge spreads the mud behind it. Here "jagged potsherds" means broken fragments of pottery with rough, sharp edges, and "threshing sledge" refers to a heavy farm tool dragged over the ground.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful creature that cannot be tamed, perhaps a crocodile or a symbolic animal; scholars understand it in several ways. God wants Job to see that if he cannot subdue this creature, he cannot judge the ways of his Creator.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, remember his greatness and trust his wisdom. Resting in him is better than demanding explanations.
exp.36:3:
After the lightning comes the thunder, which roars with the majestic voice of God. "Roaring sound" is the phrase the verse uses, and "majestic" describes his greatness. The last sentence is hard: it may mean that once his voice sounds, nothing holds back the lightning or the storm God sends.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the conversation between Job and his friends. He uses a storm to show that God is great and that his works go beyond what we understand. He wants Job to listen with humility.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, do not despair. Stop, acknowledge his greatness, and trust that his wisdom surpasses yours, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.27:12:
Job says that human beings cannot know how much true wisdom is worth, and that it is not found among the living, that is, among the people of this world. The word "value" here means its worth or its great importance. And "the land of the living" is a way of saying "this world where we live."

Job is the speaker. In this poem (chapter 28) he describes how a man digs mines and finds metals and precious stones, but cannot find wisdom through his own effort. Job says this in the middle of his suffering and of long discussions with his friends.

For today: do not rely only on your intelligence or your achievements to understand life. Ask God for wisdom with humility, and value it more than money.
exp.37:26:
He says God sends rain even on empty places, to satisfy the parched wasteland and make it sprout with tender grass. "Satisfy" means to fill completely. "Parched" describes ground that is dry and cracked from lack of water. In other words, God cares for areas where no one lives.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God asks him questions about creation to show him his wisdom and his care. Rain in the wilderness benefits no human being, yet God sends it all the same. Interpreters see here that God governs with purposes broader than ours.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that God cares even for what no one sees. You can trust that he also cares for you, even when you do not see the reason why.
exp.33:13:
This verse says that if God were to turn his attention only to human beings and take back his spirit and his breath, the breath of life that he himself gives, everyone would stop living. The phrase "set his heart to it" means to fix his mind and will on something. "Withdraw" means to take back or draw in again.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's friends. He argues that God is just and does not pervert justice. His point is that God is the owner of all creation and sustains life, so no one has the right to accuse him.

Some readers believe Elihu speaks with wisdom, and others think he has a limited view of Job's suffering.

For today: every breath is a gift from God. Before complaining or demanding explanations, give thanks for life and trust that he continues to sustain you.
exp.39:1:
The explanation says that God asks Job to prepare himself with courage, like a person who gets ready for a hard task or a fight. The phrase "Gird up your loins" is an old expression: it means getting ready, standing firm and paying close attention. Then God tells him that now He will ask the questions and Job must answer.
