The one speaking is the LORD, who answers Job out of the storm (here, "the darkness"). Job had asked many times for God to give him an explanation for his suffering. Now God speaks, but He gives no reasons: He asks questions and shows Job how limited his view is. The following verses confirm this by contrasting God's power with Job's.

For today: when we do not understand our pain, we can be honest with God, but also have the humility to trust that He sees more than we see.
exp.30:5:
Here Job says that if God weighed him on honest scales, as gold or grain is weighed, God would find that his life is blameless. "Let God weigh me" means "let God put me on the scale," and "integrity" means a life that is honest and without deceit.

Job is a man who suffers greatly, and his friends believe he is suffering for some hidden sin. In this chapter he makes a solemn oath: he reviews his conduct and says he has not lied, deceived, or coveted. He does not claim that he never failed in anything, but he trusts that God knows his heart and will see that his accusers are wrong.

Today we can pray with humility: "Lord, examine me." Asking God to look over our words and decisions helps us live with sincerity, and to trust that He sees the truth when others judge us unfairly.
exp.30:8:
Job puts himself to the test: "If my heart has been enticed by my neighbor's wife, or I have lurked at his door…" Here "enticed" means drawn in and led astray by desire. "Lurked" means waiting in hiding for the right moment, in this case to commit adultery with another man's wife. The verse states the condition of a vow: if I have done this, I deserve punishment, which the following verse completes.

Job speaks as a man who suffers greatly and whom his friends accuse of having sinned in secret. To defend his integrity, he lists possible sins and declares that he did not commit them. He asks that, if he is guilty, a just punishment fall on him. He calls adultery a wickedness that judges must punish.

For today: sin begins in the heart, long before the actions. Take care with what you look at, imagine, and desire, and set clear limits that protect your faithfulness and the trust of others.
exp.3:6:
He asks Job to think carefully: has anyone ever been destroyed while innocent? Where has it been seen that upright people are wiped out? "Consider now" means think it over calmly. "Destroyed" means brought to ruin, and "upright" describes people who live honestly and do what is right.

Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, is speaking. Job has lost his children, his property, and his health, and Eliphaz tries to explain his suffering. He believes the pain comes from sin. However, the same book says Job was blameless (Job 1:1), and at the end God corrects the friends (Job 42:7). So this advice sounds logical, but it is wrong.

For today: let us not judge someone who suffers by assuming they did something wrong. It is better to walk alongside them with compassion, listening to them and helping them, and to trust that God knows what we cannot see.
exp.30:27:
It says that worshiping the sun or the moon, even in secret, would be a sin that deserves to be judged. "An iniquity to be judged" means a wrong that should be brought before the court and punished. And the reason is clear: it would be denying God on high, the one who rules over everything. Kissing the hand was a gesture of honor offered to the heavenly bodies.

Job speaks in his final defense. His friends accuse him of being a wicked man, and he answers by listing his upright conduct. Here he affirms that he never gave his heart to any power other than God. Some scholars point out that in that time the worship of the stars was a well-known temptation, although the details varied from region to region.

Today we may not worship the sun, but we can still give other things, such as money or success, the place that belongs to God. Ask yourself honestly: what secretly occupies my heart? Give it back to God.
exp.22:4:
Job says that if he could come before God, he would want to learn how God would answer him and consider carefully what God would say. The words "learn how He would answer" mean that he would find out God's reply, and "consider what He would say" means that he would think through the meaning of what God tells him. He is not seeking only to speak, but also to listen.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends tell him that he suffers because of some hidden sin, but he knows he has been sincere, and he feels that God is far away. For this reason he longs for a fair hearing where he can lay out his case. His desire is not entirely calm; there is pain and confusion in his words. Later, God does answer him, though in a way Job did not expect.

For today: when you are confused by a trial, pray honestly, but also leave room to listen. Read the Bible and stay silent for a moment, asking for understanding rather than explanations made to your own measure.
exp.20:17:
The verse says the wicked are like straw blown away before the wind, like chaff that a storm sweeps off. Chaff is the light, dry husk that surrounds the grain, and a storm lifts it away with force. It is an image of something without weight, without roots, and without firmness.

Job speaks, answering Zophar. His friends said that evil people always end up badly. Job questions that idea and reminds them that many wicked people seem to prosper. Here he repeats what his friends say, and the phrase "How often..." sounds like a question with a certain irony. Some understand it as a complaint and others as a statement that God's judgment does come, though not always when we expect it.

Today we can avoid judging others by appearances: neither success proves that someone is right with God, nor suffering proves that they are wrong. Let us trust in God's justice and seek to put down roots in Him.
exp.17:10:
Terrors surround the wicked person on every side. The word for "frighten" here means to scare or terrify. The verse says terrors also harass his every step, so fear dogs him wherever he goes and leaves him no peace along the way.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's friends. In this chapter he describes, with images of traps and snares, the miserable end he believes awaits the wicked. His aim is to suggest that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. However, the book itself shows that Bildad is wrong to apply this to Job, since Job was a blameless man.

Today it reminds us that living far from God often brings restlessness and fear. But it also warns us not to judge those who suffer, as if all pain were punishment. Rather, let us accompany them with compassion and trust in God.
exp.37:17:
Here God asks Job whether he has surveyed the extent of the earth. The word translated as "surveyed" means to observe and grasp something with close attention, and "extent" refers to how wide the earth is. Then God challenges him to tell Him if he knows all this. The question aims to lead Job to recognize how limited his knowledge is.

God himself speaks here, out of the whirlwind, after Job has suffered greatly and asked for explanations. God does not answer him with reasons for his pain, but with questions about creation: the sea, death, light and darkness. Through them he shows Job that his wisdom far surpasses that of any person.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that you do not need to know everything in order to trust. You can rest in a God who does know all things and cares for you, even in what you cannot comprehend.
exp.29:19:
He says that Job cries out to God for help, but feels that God does not answer him. When he stands before Him, that is, when he rises to pray or to make his complaint, he feels that God only looks at him and does nothing. The phrase "I cry out to You for help" means "I call out to you with everything I have", and "You do not answer" means "you give me no reply".

It is Job speaking, a man who lost everything and suffers from illness and mockery. In this chapter he complains painfully about his situation. He speaks from what he feels, not necessarily from what is true. Later in the book, God does answer him.

For today: if in your pain you feel that God is silent, do not hide it or pretend. Speak with Him honestly, as Job did. Continuing to cry out, even without feeling an answer, is a way of trusting that He listens.
exp.16:0:
It says that Job feels at the end of his strength. "Spirit" refers to his inner life force, and "broken" means damaged, spent, or worn down. "My days are extinguished" means he feels he has little time left. "Awaits" means waits in readiness: he feels the grave is already waiting for him.

Job speaks here, a man who has lost nearly everything: his children, his property, and his health. His friends accuse him of having sinned, and he feels misunderstood and surrounded by mockery. That is why he cries out to God, because he no longer finds support in anyone else. Scholars do not fully agree on every detail of these verses, but the tone of deep pain is clear.

When you feel exhausted and without strength, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Job did, and seek out people who will accompany you without judging you.
exp.2:16:
In that place, called "there," the raging of the wicked ceases and the weary find rest. "Raging" describes people who stir up agitation and cause turmoil for others. "The weary" are people without strength, worn down by suffering and toil.

Job speaks, a righteous man who lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is so overcome with pain that he wishes he had never been born. He imagines death as a place of rest where there is no oppression and no difference between rich and poor. It is the sincere lament of one who suffers, not a teaching about what happens after death.

When you are exhausted, do not hide your pain from God. Job spoke frankly, and God did not reject him. But seek help and rest today as well, from God and from people you can trust.
exp.35:25:
This verse says that God is so great that we cannot fully know him. The phrase "beyond our knowledge" means that no one can grasp him completely. The verse also says that the number of his years cannot be counted, because he has no beginning and no end.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the conversations between Job and his three friends. He wants to defend God's justice, so he invites his listeners to look at God's work in creation. Right after this, he speaks about the rain as an example of God's power and care. Some think Elihu is right about several things, though not everything he says applies to Job's situation.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, do not measure it with your limited mind. Look at his creation, give thanks for what you can see of his care, and trust that he knows more than you do.
exp.31:19:
Elihu says he must speak so that he can find relief. "I must speak" means he needs to unburden himself, like someone who has been holding their breath for a long time and finally breathes out. "I must open my lips" is his decision to begin talking, and "I must respond" means he will give his own view of what has been said.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who had waited in silence while Job and his three friends argued. He feels full of words, like new wine ready to burst its wineskins. He is angry because none of them has given an answer that satisfies him. He says he will speak frankly, without flattering anyone. Some see in him wisdom and others see excessive pride; the book does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you feel the pressure to say something, do not speak only to relieve yourself. First ask whether what you will say is true, kind, and helpful. Speak with honesty, but with humility.
exp.18:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that Job takes up the word to answer what he has just heard. "Answered" means he replies to someone, and the colon shows that his speech is coming next. Here there is no teaching yet, only the move into a new reply.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly and has lost his possessions, his children, and his health. He is answering Bildad, one of his friends, who has just spoken harshly in chapter 18. In the verses that follow, Job complains that his friends wound him with their words instead of comforting him. So his reply comes out of pain.

For today: before speaking to someone who is suffering, listen with patience. When we respond, let us aim for words that support and heal, not words that hurt. Sometimes being present in silence helps more than giving many explanations.
exp.24:1:
God has authority over all things, and he deserves deep reverence. "Dominion" means rule and authority; "awe" is a sense of wonder and respect before his greatness. The phrase "the heights of heaven" refers to the heavens, where God reigns. There he establishes harmony, bringing order and balance among the heavenly beings.

The speaker is Bildad the Shuhite, one of Job's three friends. This is his last speech, and it is very short. He wants to show that God is so great and pure that no one can stand before him as righteous. His words about God are true, but the way he applies them to Job, who is suffering, is often seen as harsh and inadequate.

When life seems disordered, remember that God governs with power and with harmony. Draw near to him with humility and trust, and comfort others without judging them.
exp.33:9:
Elihu says that people of good judgment should listen: God does not do wrong, and the Almighty does not act unjustly. The phrase "men of understanding" refers to people with good sense and insight. "Far be it from God" means that the very idea of God doing wrong is unthinkable, and the Almighty is the all-powerful God.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job and his three friends have finished arguing. Elihu responds to Job, whom he understands to have said that there is no benefit in pleasing God. To Elihu, that sounds like accusing God of being unjust, so he defends God's justice. Some scholars think Elihu is partly right but does not fully grasp Job's suffering. The book does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you suffer or do not understand what is happening, do not conclude that God is unjust. Be honest with him about your doubts, but trust that his character is good and just, even when you cannot yet see the answer.
exp.28:6:
He says that Job, when he went out to the city gate and took his seat in the public square, was a figure of respect and authority. The gate was the entrance to the city, where the elders gathered to settle disputes and make decisions. The public square was the open space beside that gate. His seat was a place of honor and authority.

Job speaks here while already suffering greatly. He looks back with longing on his good days, when God watched over him and everyone respected him. In the verses that follow, young and old show him honor. Job maintains that he used his position to do justice, not to show off. Some readers also see here a tone of grief over what he has lost.

For today: if God gives you some kind of influence, in your work, your family, or your church, use it to serve with justice and not to be admired.
exp.40:32:
It says that nothing on earth is the leviathan's equal. It is a creature without fear, one that is never startled or shaken by anyone. "Equal" means something that matches it in strength or nature, and "devoid of fear" means it has no sense of being frightened.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job from the whirlwind. After so much suffering, Job had asked many questions. God does not give him explanations one by one, but shows him his power in creation. The leviathan, an imposing creature, sometimes understood as a crocodile or as a sea monster, shows that God rules even over what human beings cannot control. Its exact identity is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if God sustains the most fearsome thing, he can also sustain you. When you do not understand what you are living through, trust his wisdom and rest in his care.
exp.16:15:
This verse speaks of death. The word translated "gates" refers to the entrance to Sheol, the place of the dead, and the grave is the dust where the body returns. Job asks whether his hope will go down there with him, and whether he and his hope will go down together into the dust. The Berean Standard Bible puts the verse as a question, so Job seems to be asking rather than declaring.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his friends accuse him instead of comforting him. In the verse before this one he calls the grave his father and the worms his mother and sister, as if they were his only family. He feels alone and without human hope.

For today: when pain makes you think there is no way out, do not hide it. You can speak to God honestly, as Job did. God does not turn away from someone who suffers. Also seek out a trusted person who will listen to you and keep you company.
exp.27:25:
It says that when God set a limit for the rain, he also marked out a path for the thunderbolt. "Set a limit" means he fixed boundaries, and "a path" refers to a set course. Even storms, which seem chaotic, follow an order that God determined.

The one speaking is Job, in a poem about wisdom. After saying that human beings can dig mines and search for treasure but cannot find wisdom, Job points out that only God knows it. When he ordered the wind, the water, and the rain, he saw wisdom and confirmed it. Job then concludes that fearing the Lord is wisdom.

For today: when life feels like a senseless storm, remember that God governs even what you do not control. Trust him, and seek wisdom by honoring him and turning away from evil.
exp.32:31:
If you have anything to say, answer me; speak up, for I would like to vindicate you. It says that if Job has something to say, he should say it with confidence. "Vindicate" here means to show him in the right, to grant him the point if he is right, and not to condemn him. Elihu tells him that he wants Job to be at peace and to have the truth made clear.

The speaker is Elihu, the young man who steps in almost at the end of the book. He has been speaking about how God corrects people through dreams, pain, and messengers to save them from death. Here he invites Job to reply. Some think Elihu speaks with sincerity and others that he is somewhat arrogant; the Bible does not make this entirely clear. Even so, his wish to hear Job out is a good gesture.

For today: when you talk with someone who is suffering or who thinks differently from you, listen first and let them express themselves. Aim to help them, not to win the argument.
exp.19:7:
He says that the wicked person will disappear quickly, like a dream that fades when we wake up. No one will be able to find him, and he will be driven off like a vision in the night. "Fly away" means he goes without leaving a trace; "like mist" in the sense of falling apart means he comes to nothing, like something that dissolves in the air; "a vision in the night" is a dream.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He believes that bad people end up badly and that the prosperity of the wicked does not last. He uses this to hint that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. Be aware: the book shows that Zophar is wrong to apply this to Job, although his general idea about the passing nature of wickedness sounds true in other biblical passages.

Today we can remember that success built on pride or injustice is not stable. Let us seek to build on what is honest and what endures. And let us take care not to judge others for their suffering, as Zophar did.
exp.31:15:
Elihu says that he waited while Job's three friends were silent. They had stopped speaking and no longer replied to anything. The phrase "they stood and no longer reply" means that they simply stayed where they were, without offering anything more.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who had listened quietly to the long debate between Job and his friends. The three men stopped answering Job because they had run out of arguments. Elihu asks whether he should keep waiting, and in the verses that follow he decides to speak. There are different opinions about whether what he says afterward is wise, since God does not mention him at the end of the book.

For today: before speaking, it is worth listening patiently and thinking carefully about what we will say. But we should also ask ourselves whether our words truly help someone who is suffering, or only aim to defend our own opinion.
exp.33:29:
This verse says that God does not allow godless men to rule or to set traps for the people. It describes someone who has no reverence for God and who uses power to deceive and harm others.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He argues that God is just and that he hears the cry of the poor. Some scholars understand that God removes wicked rulers; others, that he allows them to rule as a consequence of the people's sin. The text allows both readings. Note: not everything Elihu says applies to Job's case.

For today: if you have authority in your home, your work, or your church, exercise it with sincerity and service, never with abuse. And if you suffer injustice, trust that God hears your cry.
exp.9:14:
Job feels trapped. If he is guilty, he says, then he deserves to suffer, and woe to him. But even if he is righteous, he still cannot lift his head, meaning he cannot feel at peace or hold his dignity. He says he is full of shame and aware of his affliction.

Job speaks in the middle of his pain, addressing God. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He feels that God sees his suffering and does not relieve it. It is a sincere lament, not a complete teaching about God. Later in the same book, it shows that God did hear him, even though he did not give Job the answers Job hoped for.

For today: when pain weighs heavily on you, you can speak with God with complete honesty, as Job did. You do not have to pretend to be strong. Tell him what you feel, and also seek out people who will stay with you without judging you.
exp.29:26:
He says Job feels an inner churning that will not settle. The Berean wording describes this as churning within him and an inability to rest. "Churning" points to constant agitation inside the body, the place where strong feelings were understood to be felt. The phrase "days of affliction" speaks of hard seasons that came at him and left him overwhelmed.

Job speaks as a man who lost almost everything. In this chapter he complains because, although he helped those who suffered, now he hopes for good and receives evil. His friends do not comfort him, and he describes his pain honestly, without hiding it before God.

For today: if you are going through distress that does not let you rest, you do not have to pretend you are fine. Job shows us that one can speak to God with sincerity, and also seek trusted people who will listen without judging you.
exp.26:17:
The verse says the house the wicked build is fragile. It is compared to a moth's cocoon, which is delicate and easily destroyed, and to a hut set up by a watchman, a makeshift shelter put up for a short time and then abandoned. Here "watchman" refers to the one who keeps watch over a field or vineyard.

Job speaks, answering his friends. They hold that suffering is always punishment for sin. Job describes how the wicked end: even if he gathers a great deal of silver and clothing, others will enjoy them, and his wealth will not last. Some scholars think Job here repeats ideas of his friends; others think he affirms them as his own.

For today: let us not place our trust in what we accumulate, because it can disappear. Let us build our lives on justice and on God, who endures.
exp.36:18:
The speaker is Elihu, not Eleazar. Here is the point.

It says that God knows more than we do. Elihu asks Job: "Teach us what we should say to Him," because "we cannot draw up our case because of our darkness," that is, because of our ignorance and our limits. Drawing up our case here means building a clear argument.

Elihu is the young man who speaks in the book of Job toward the end of the speeches. He has just described God's power in nature: the wind, the heat, the firm sky. With irony he asks Job whether he can explain those things or bring his case before God. Elihu wants to show that the human being is too small to argue with the Creator. Some see here a wise humility; others notice that Elihu speaks with a certain arrogance.

When you do not understand what God is doing, do not despair for lacking all the answers. Speak with Him sincerely and humbly, and trust that He sees what you cannot reach.
exp.40:13:
It says that no one dares to open the jaws of this animal, called Leviathan. "His jaws" are what the reader sees here, and the teeth around them are fearsome, which means they cause fear. In other words: who would dare to force open that mouth and look at those teeth?

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful creature that cannot be subdued. Some believe it is the crocodile, others that it is a symbolic monster of chaos; it is not known for certain. God wants Job to see that if he cannot control this creature, he is far less able to question the Creator.

For today: there are things in life that we cannot control or understand. Instead of demanding answers, we can rest in the fact that God is wise and strong. Today, entrust to him in prayer a situation that worries you.
exp.17:20:
This verse says that this is how the homes of the wicked end: empty, without descendants, and without a good remembrance. The word "dwelling" means a house or a place where someone lives. The word "wicked" refers to someone who lives without reverence for God. The phrase "one who does not know God" does not speak only of ignoring Him, but of living without a relationship with Him or obedience to Him.

The speaker is Bildad, Job's friend. He holds that the wicked always suffer ruin, and he tries to convince Job that his misfortunes come from some sin. However, at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him. Therefore, his words contain general truths, but applied to Job they are unjust.

Today we can learn that living far from God leaves an emptiness, but we should not judge others by their suffering. Rather, let us accompany them with compassion and seek to know God truly.
exp.30:23:
Here Job says: "If I have put my trust in gold or called pure gold my security." To put trust in something means to rely on it to feel safe. Job denies having made money his place of safety.

The one speaking is Job, a wealthy man who suffers and is accused by his friends of being wicked. In this chapter 31 he defends himself with a series of oaths: "if I have done such a thing, let such a punishment come upon me." He wants to show that his life was blameless before God, including in regard to his riches. Mentioning gold and then his wealth shows that he did not love money more than God.

For today: having possessions is not a sin, but we can trust in them without realizing it. Ask yourself: what gives me peace, my bank account or God? Practice giving generously and thanking God for what you have.
exp.13:4:
This verse says that each person's life has a limit. Their days are determined, and God knows how many months they will live. The phrase "You have set limits that he cannot exceed" means that no one can go beyond what God has set. The phrase "is with You" suggests that God holds that number.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly and is full of pain. In this chapter he reflects on how brief and fragile human life is. He speaks with God and asks why he is being examined so harshly, since he is so weak. His words express anguish and should not be read as a complete explanation of life and death.

For today: although we do not control our time, we can entrust it to God. Keeping this in mind helps us not to waste our days, to value the people around us, and to trust that our lives are in the hands of someone who knows us.
exp.26:12:
This verse says that the wicked man's share from God is judgment, and that the ruthless will receive their lot from the Almighty. "Portion" means the fate or share that falls to a person. "Heritage" is what someone receives as their share. "Almighty" refers to God, the All-Powerful.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of a long discussion with his friends. They claimed his suffering came from some hidden sin. Job insists on his innocence, but here he states that he knows well how God deals with the wicked. Scholars debate whether Job speaks in earnest or repeats, with irony, what his friends maintained.

For today: do not envy those who prosper by doing harm; trust that God is just. Even so, avoid judging the suffering of others as punishment, because Job shows that this is not always the case.
exp.32:27:
This verse says that God rescues a person from death, the grave, which here is called the Pit, so that they do not go down into it. Instead of darkness, that person will live and see the light. "Redeem" means that God pays the price to save, or that he rescues.

Elihu, a young man, speaks in the dialogue with Job. He explains that God sometimes corrects people and speaks to them through suffering. If someone admits their wrong and says "I have sinned," God rescues them and restores them. Elihu is right that God is merciful, but not all suffering comes from a specific sin, as the book of Job itself shows.

For today: if God shows you something you need to correct, confess it simply and without fear. He does not seek to crush you, but to give you back life and hope.
exp.14:17:
Elifaz says he is going to tell Job what the wise have taught. They received that teaching from their forefathers and did not conceal it, but passed it on to others. The word "concealed" in the verse above means they did not keep it to themselves or say nothing about it.

The one speaking is Elifaz, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden wrongdoing, and to convince him he does not rely only on his own opinion but on the tradition of the elders. His aim is to maintain that the wicked always suffer. His argument has a flaw: God himself says later that Elifaz did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7).

It is wise to learn from those who came before us, but every teaching, even a traditional one, must be tested by the Word of God. Before we judge someone's pain, let us listen with humility and compassion.
exp.10:14:
It says that if a person turns back to God sincerely, they will be able to look others in the face without shame or guilt ("without blemish"). They will also have steadiness and will not live in fear. "Lift up your face" is a way of saying that a person no longer lowers their eyes because of guilt.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He tells Job that if he prepares his heart, prays, and puts away wickedness, God will restore him. His underlying idea is that Job suffers because of some hidden sin. At the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so their words are not to be taken as a rule for every kind of suffering. Even so, the promise of peace after turning back to God agrees with other parts of the Bible.

Today, if something weighs on your conscience, do not hide it. Bring it honestly before God, leave behind what harms you, and receive His forgiveness. But do not think that every pain is punishment for something you did.
exp.2:19:
Here Job asks why God gives light, that is, life, to the one who suffers greatly. The word rendered as "miserable" in the verse refers to someone weighed down by pain and exhaustion, and the phrase "the bitter of soul" describes people whose inner life is heavy with grief. Job is not explaining anything; he is asking with pain.

Job is speaking after losing his children, his property, and his health. His friends came to comfort him and sat in silence for seven days. Then Job breaks that silence and laments. In the verses just before this one, he imagines death as a place of rest. His complaint is sincere, and the Bible presents it without censoring it.

For today: if you are going through great sorrow, you can tell God what you feel, even with hard questions. And if thoughts of hopelessness weigh heavily on you, also seek out someone you trust or a professional who can walk with you.
exp.14:14:
If God puts no trust in His holy ones, and even the heavens are not pure in His eyes, then the point is about how great God's holiness is. The "holy ones" are the angels or heavenly beings who serve Him. Even the heavens, when measured against God's purity, fall short. "In His eyes" means "in His judgment." The idea is that God's holiness is so complete that everything He has made looks imperfect beside Him.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, Job's friend, in his second speech. He wants to rebuke Job and make him see that no human being can declare himself innocent before God. His argument has some truth in it, but he applies it wrongly, because he assumes Job's suffering proves a hidden sin. The book itself shows that Eliphaz was not right in his accusation.

For today: before God, humility is wise. We can acknowledge our faults without fear, but without using that truth to judge harshly someone who is suffering.
exp.21:14:
This verse is a question with a tone of warning. The phrase "the ancient path" refers to following the same road of life that others have already walked. Here it is the way of "wicked men," that is, people who live without respecting God. The question asks whether Job is willing to follow in their steps.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he accuses Job of thinking that God neither sees nor judges. He then recalls that those wicked men were "cut down before their time," as if a flood had swept away their foundation. We should note that, according to the book, Eliphaz is wrong to accuse Job, although his warning about living without God is serious.

Today we can ask ourselves which paths we follow out of habit or by imitating others. It is worth examining our decisions in the light of God, and choosing a path that honors him, without judging others harshly for their sufferings.
exp.26:6:
Job says here that his enemy or opponent should be treated like the wicked and the unjust, that is, like someone who is evil and unfair. It is a strong way of affirming that he is not a hypocrite. "Unjust" means unfair or wrongdoing; "enemy" is the one who opposes him.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his debate with his friends. They insist that he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job rejects that accusation and swears that he will keep his integrity until death. With these words he wishes that the fate of the wicked would fall on whoever accuses him falsely. Some readers see here a language of protest rather than a desire for revenge.

For today: when you are unjustly accused, you do not have to give up the truth or a clear conscience. Even so, entrust your cause to God and do not repay evil for evil.
exp.12:22:
Job asks God to show him what his faults are. He asks how many sins he has and wants God to reveal his transgression and sin. In other words, he asks God to tell him clearly what he did wrong.

Job speaks here in the middle of great suffering. His friends insist that everything is punishment for some hidden sin, but he feels there is no cause that explains it. So he turns directly to God, asking for a clear judgment and that God not treat him as an enemy. Job does not claim to be perfect; he wants to understand.

We can be honest with God and ask him to examine our hearts. However, not every pain is punishment for a specific sin. With humility, we can ask for light to see what we should correct, and trust that God is just even when we do not understand.
exp.37:10:
He says God spoke to the sea and set a limit for it: "You may come this far, but no farther; here your proud waves must stop." There the pride of its waves would be checked. "Proud waves" refers to the high, furious waves. The word "waves" means the sea's rolling water.

God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons, but asks him questions about creation. He wants to show him that He sustains a world that Job cannot control or fully understand. The sea appears as something powerful, but with limits that God himself set.

Today, when you feel your life is a storm without brakes, remember that God is still greater than whatever overwhelms you. You can rest and trust, even without understanding everything.
exp.36:4:
When God thunders, he does so in a way that inspires awe. The thunder is a sign of his power. The verse also says that God does great things that we cannot grasp. The word "wondrously" means in a way that stirs wonder.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who comes in almost at the end of the book, after the speeches of Job and his three friends. He describes the storm, the lightning, the snow and the rain to show that God governs nature and that no one can call him to account. Shortly afterward, God himself will speak to Job out of a whirlwind. Some think Elihu helps prepare that moment; others believe he speaks with too much certainty.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, do not stay alone with your questions. Look at his greatness, admit that there are things you do not understand, and rest in the fact that he knows what he is doing.
exp.30:13:
Job asks what he would do when God rises to judge, and how he would answer when called to account. The explanation of the verse's wording: "rises to judge" means God acts as judge, and "called to account" means God calls people to answer for how they have behaved. The question assumes that Job would have no answer if he had mistreated others.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, defending his integrity. In this chapter he reviews his life and says that he has not committed certain sins. Here he refers to his male and female servants: if he had dismissed their just complaints, he would have to give an account to God. Then he says that God made his servant just as He made him.

For today: treat with respect those who depend on you, such as employees, family members, or people with less power. Before deciding anything that affects them, remember that God sees, and that they are of equal worth before Him.
exp.19:11:
It says that evil was like a sweet treat for that person. He savored it with delight and kept it under his tongue, like someone who does not want the candy to run out. "Is sweet" means it tastes good to him, and "conceals it" means he keeps it out of sight so he can enjoy it for longer.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's friends. He is describing what, in his view, happens to the wicked: they enjoy their sin, but in the end it turns bitter. Zophar believes that all suffering comes as punishment for some specific sin. The book shows that this idea is incomplete, because God himself later corrects Job's friends. Even so, this picture of sin that is sweet at first and bitter afterward is true in many cases.

Today, ask yourself what wrong thing you are keeping hidden, something you enjoy in secret. Bring it to God honestly, before it turns bitter inside you.
exp.38:8:
The explanation says that God gave the wild ox its home in the desert and in dry lands where almost nothing grows. The word "wilderness" here does not speak of sadness, but of empty places, without people. The "dwellings" are the places where it lives, and "barren" means that these are dry lands.

The one speaking is God himself. In chapters 38 to 41, the Lord answers Job with many questions about creation. Job had suffered greatly and was questioning God. God shows him that he cares even for wild, free animals that no one tames, to remind Job that his wisdom and his care reach far beyond what Job understands.

For today: if God provides for the wild ox in dry lands, we can trust that he also cares for us when we go through dry or lonely seasons, even when we do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.37:22:
He says that God himself keeps the snow and the hail, as if they were weapons stored in a storehouse, to use them in times of trouble, of war and of battle. The word "hold" means kept back for a special moment. It is a question that God asks Job, not a loose explanation.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him reasons, but shows him his greatness in creation. The Bible mentions that God used hail on other occasions, as in Joshua 10:11, although the text does not say that God is referring to a specific case.

Today we can rest in the fact that God governs even what we do not understand. When something overwhelms us, instead of demanding answers, we can trust that the one who controls the storms also cares for us.
exp.23:12:
They are among those who rebel against the light. Rebelling against the light means rejecting what is good and true. Because of this, they do not know the light's ways, which is the just way of living, and they do not stay on its paths, meaning the routes it marks out.

Job speaks here in the middle of his conversation with his friends. He complains that many wicked people seem to get away with what they do while the poor suffer. The verses before describe exploited workers, and the verses after speak of murderers and adulterers who prefer the darkness. Job does not explain everything; he simply shows his pain at the injustice.

For today: examine whether in some area of your life you avoid the light, such as when you hide something or put off obeying. Ask God for the courage to live openly, for his way is safe.
exp.30:15:
Job asks whether he has ever denied the poor what they desired, or allowed the widow's eyes to fail. "Denied the desires of the poor" means he has never turned away from them what they needed to live with dignity. "Allowed the widow's eyes to fail" means he never made her wait for help until she grew weary and lost hope.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly, and his friends accuse him of being wicked. In this chapter he defends himself with a list of sins that he says he has not committed. Earlier, he reminded them that God made him and also made his servants, so all people are equal before God. If he were guilty of mistreating the weak, he would accept God's judgment.

Today, we might ask ourselves who is near us and needs help and is waiting for it. Perhaps it is a widow, a neighbor, or someone with few resources. Helping in time, with respect, and without making them wait is a concrete way to honor God.
exp.12:4:
Job tells his friends: "If only you would remain silent, because that would be your wisdom." The phrase "remain silent" is plain modern English for keeping quiet, and in this verse it carries the same sense. The phrase "that would be your wisdom" means it would be the wise thing for you to do, that is, it would be to your advantage.

Job speaks as one who suffers greatly and does not understand why. His friends insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job calls them "worthless physicians" because their advice heals nothing. He prefers to bring his case directly to God. Some readers see a note of irony here: silence would be their best contribution.

For today: when someone is suffering, they do not always need explanations or quick advice. Sometimes the wisest and most loving thing is to listen, to accompany in silence, and to let God speak to the heart. Before offering your opinion, ask yourself whether your words help or hurt.
exp.32:4:
Elihu says that he invites Job to refute him, if he is able. He asks Job to prepare his case and to face him directly.

"Prepare your case" means to get your argument ready and think through what you are going to say. The phrase "confront me" in the verse is a call to meet him face to face and stand your ground.

Elihu speaks, a young man who listened in silence to the debate between Job and his three friends. Now he steps in because he believes Job justified himself too much and that the friends did not answer him well. He presents himself as an equal to Job, formed by God from the clay, so that Job will not feel fear. Some see in Elihu a good messenger; others see him as somewhat presumptuous. The book does not make this entirely clear.

For today: before arguing with or correcting someone, listen with respect, speak in an orderly way, and treat the other person as an equal before God, without wanting to intimidate them.
exp.15:2:
The explanation says the word "ventosas" means full of air and without substance, so the speeches seem to go on with no end. Job asks his friend Eliphaz what keeps him answering. In plain modern English, the question is: "Is there no end to your long-winded speeches? What provokes you to continue testifying?"

Job speaks while suffering greatly, after listening to the long speeches of his three friends. They say they want to comfort him, but they repeat cold explanations and almost accuse him of having sinned. That is why Job calls them "miserable comforters." He feels their words bring him no relief.

For today: when someone suffers, it is often worth more to listen with kindness than to give speeches. Before speaking, ask yourself whether your words help or only fill the air. A hug, a simple prayer, or a respectful silence can comfort more than many arguments.
exp.14:10:
Eliphaz asks Job whether the comfort God offers seems too little to him. He also asks whether Job is hiding some private reason or secret wisdom that justifies his attitude.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He is upset because Job insists on his innocence and does not accept his advice. Eliphaz believes that his words and those of the other friends come from God, and he appeals to age and experience. Note: the book later shows that Eliphaz was wrong in the way he judged Job (Job 42:7).

Today we can learn not to make light of God's comfort when we suffer. But we can also learn not to speak harshly in God's name to someone who is suffering. Listening with humility and offering gentle presence is worth more than being right.
exp.20:6:
Job asks why the wicked, that is, those who live without respecting God, still go on living, keep growing older, and keep gaining power and possessions. "Growing older" means they reach old age, and "gaining power" means their influence and wealth keep increasing.

The one speaking is Job, in the midst of his great suffering. His friends had been telling him that God always punishes the wicked and blesses the righteous. Job answers with a fact that troubles him: many evil people prosper, have children, and live at ease. For this reason he asks them to listen carefully, and he admits that this fills him with dread.

Today we can learn not to judge anyone's life only by their success or their pain. When we see others doing well without deserving it, or when we ourselves suffer, we can bring our honest questions to God and keep trusting in Him, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.7:6:
He says that, although your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish. The phrase "latter days" in the verse refers to the later stage of life, and the verse uses the word "flourish" to describe growth and well-being that come in time.

This is spoken by Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some sin, and he tells him that if he seeks God sincerely, God will restore him. Be aware, though: God himself later says that Job's friends did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7), so their words are not a rule for every case. Even so, the image of hope is a beautiful one.

Today we can remember that a modest or difficult beginning does not decide our future. Let us seek God with honesty, trusting in him, and without judging someone who suffers as if they were guilty.
exp.7:7:
He says Job should ask the generations that came before and take the trouble to look into what his ancestors discovered. "Past generations" means people who lived in earlier times, and "inquire" means to investigate or find out. The point is not to rely only on one's own experience.

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some sin, and so he asks Job to listen to the wisdom of earlier generations. Although his words sound wise, God later says that these friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). Their inherited teaching did not explain Job's case.

For today: learning from those who came before us is very valuable, and it is wise to seek counsel from older people and people of faith. But we should be careful not to use tradition to judge someone who is suffering harshly. Listening and standing alongside others is worth more than offering easy explanations.
exp.0:8:
Satan answers God with a question: "Does Job fear God for nothing?" The word "nothing" points to the question of whether Job gains anything from his devotion. Satan is hinting that Job does not truly love God, but loves what God gives him.

Here Satan, the accuser, speaks after God has praised Job as a blameless and upright man. Satan doubts Job's sincerity and points out that God has protected and blessed him greatly. The book presents this scene to raise the question of whether Job's faith is genuine or self-interested.

For today: examine why you follow God. It is natural to thank Him for His blessings, but mature faith loves Him for who He is, also when losses come and we understand nothing.
exp.2:0:
It says that after seven days of silence with his friends, Job finally spoke. "After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth" is a plain way of saying that he began to speak and expressed his pain by wishing that the day he was born had never happened. He does not curse God, but the day on which he was born.

The one speaking is Job, an upright man who lost everything at once: his children, his possessions, and his health. Chapters 1 and 2 tell that he remained silent, sitting with his friends. Here his pain overflows. The book neither approves nor condemns this outpouring at this point; it simply presents it with honesty.

For today: when the pain is very great, do not pretend you are fine. You can tell God honestly what you feel, and seek out someone you trust who will listen with patience, without rushing you or judging you.
exp.12:18:
Job asks a bold question: "Can anyone indict me?" He is confident that no one can prove he is guilty of what his friends say. He adds that if he were to keep silent, he would die. The word "indict" means to formally charge someone with a crime, that is, to bring a case against them in a court of law. "Die" here means to come to an end.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything and is suffering greatly. His friends insist that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job does not accept that explanation and wants to present his case before God. For him, staying silent would mean surrender and being left without hope. Some readers see courage here; others see a boldness that God will later correct.

When you suffer, you do not have to hide your pain or pretend. You can speak to God with honesty, even with hard questions. Do so with respect, and listen also for his answer.
exp.11:7:
It says that if someone speaks to the earth, it will teach, and that the fish of the sea will inform you. It is a poetic way of saying that all of creation has something to teach. The word "inform" here means to make known or to explain.

Job speaks, answering Zophar and his other friends. They held that bad things happen to the wicked and good things to the righteous. Job replies that this does not always hold, since sometimes the wicked prosper. He says that even the animals know that everything is under the hand of God, though we do not always understand his ways. Some scholars see a touch of irony in his words.

Today we can look at nature with humility and remember that God sustains life. When something has no explanation, let us trust in him instead of quickly judging others.
exp.39:13:
The explanation above was written for a verse that reads differently in your Bible. Job 40:14 in the Berean Standard Bible says: "Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you." The phrase about "confessing" and "the right hand" is what the commentary is pointing to, so the three parts below follow that wording.

The text refers to Behemoth, the great creature God describes, as "the chief of the ways of God," meaning one of the most impressive works of his creation. It also speaks of the one who made it being able to approach its "sword," that is, its blade. Only the Creator has the power to subdue it. The word translated "chief" can also mean "first," and scholars read it in several ways.

God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned how God runs the world. God then shows him a powerful animal that Job cannot control. Many think it is the hippopotamus or a similar animal, while others believe it is a legendary creature. There is no complete agreement among scholars.

For today, when you do not understand what God allows, remember that he sustains even what seems unmanageable to you. Rest in his wisdom, and do not demand explanations in order to trust him.
exp.21:9:
It says that, because of something already mentioned, there are now snares all around Job, and that sudden peril terrifies him. (The word "snares" refers to traps.) "Terrifies" means to frighten greatly or fill with dread.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes that suffering is always punishment for sin, and so he accuses Job of oppressing widows and orphans. The Bible shows that Job was righteous, and in the end God rebukes Eliphaz for speaking wrongly about Him. So this verse is a mistaken accusation, not a correct explanation of Job's pain.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us not judge them or offer easy explanations. Better to walk alongside them with compassion, listen, and pray, knowing that we do not always understand what God allows.
exp.40:5:
It says that no one could make a feast of Leviathan to share with their partners, or cut it up to sell to traders. "Partners" are people who join together for a shared venture, in this case a fishing trip or a business deal. "Traders" are those who buy and sell. The idea is that this creature cannot be caught and turned into goods.

God speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He presents Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome animal. Some think it is the crocodile; others see a symbolic or mythical creature. God uses questions to show that Job does not control even one creature, much less the order of the world.

For today: when we do not understand what we are going through, let us remember that we do not control everything, but God does. We can rest in his wisdom and trust him with humility.
exp.35:26:
This verse says that God draws up the drops of water and gathers them toward himself. In other words, he takes them from the mist that rises from the earth, and then they fall again as rain. The Berean wording describes the drops being drawn up and distilled into rain from the mist, so the rain comes from the mist, which is the picture the verse gives.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in at the end of the discussions between Job and his friends. He wants to defend the greatness and justice of God. He uses rain as an example of something ordinary that, even so, is beyond us and shows that God is far greater than we can understand.

For today: the next time it rains, pause for a moment to give thanks. What is common is also the work of God, and remembering this helps us trust him when we do not understand everything.
exp.2:23:
This verse says Job's pain is so constant that, when food is placed in front of him, his response is a sigh rather than hunger or a desire to eat. Instead of appetite, what comes out of him is groaning, and it pours out without stopping, like water that keeps running.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. After seven days of silence with his friends, he opens his mouth and expresses his anguish, even wishing he had never been born. The verses that follow show that he lived with deep fear and without rest. His complaint is sincere, though not everything he says is a model to follow.

For today: if you are suffering, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Job put his pain into words before God, and the Bible records it. Speak to God honestly, and seek out someone you trust who can stay with you, without rushing you.
exp.35:12:
The godless in heart are those who look religious on the outside but do not truly submit to God within. They harbor resentment and grow more stubborn. The verse says they "harbor resentment," meaning they nurse their anger and let it build up. The phrase "even when He binds them" refers to God holding them back through hardship or discipline. Even then, they do not cry out to God for help.

The speaker is Elihu, the young friend of Job, who speaks after the other three. He holds that God uses suffering to correct, and that whoever listens is restored. Whoever hardens the heart is lost. This is his point of view; the book itself shows that Job's suffering was not due to godlessness.

For today: when a difficulty comes, do not shut yourself up in pride or outward appearances. Speak to God with sincerity, ask him for help, and listen to what he may want to teach you. And be careful not to judge others for their pain.
exp.19:16:
The verse says that the wicked person will not enjoy abundance. The streams, rivers and flowing waters of honey and cream are images of a rich and prosperous life, like a land where everything is plentiful. The "cream" here means the rich, thick dairy that was prized as a sign of wealth. The verse says that this man will not enjoy that abundance.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. He believes the wicked always come to a bad end, and for that reason he suggests that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. Zophar describes well what happens to someone who oppresses the poor, but he is wrong to apply it to Job, because God himself says that Job was blameless.

For today: do not put your hope in riches gained through injustice. And be careful not to judge others by their suffering; instead, help them with humility and compassion.
exp.41:6:
He says that, after God had finished speaking with Job, he turned to Eliphaz the Temanite and expressed his anger. "My wrath is kindled against you" means that God was very displeased. He, along with his two friends, had not spoken about God accurately, unlike Job, whom God calls "My servant."

It is the LORD who speaks. Earlier, Job humbled himself before God, admitting that he had known him only by hearsay. Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar had insisted that Job was suffering because of some hidden sin. God corrects that idea. Some understand that Job was commended because he spoke sincerely, even in his complaint. How all of his words fit together is a matter of debate.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us avoid giving quick explanations about what God is doing. It is better to accompany them with humility, to listen, and to pray.
exp.19:15:
He says that the wicked man "will suck the poison of cobras," that is, of deadly snakes, and that "the fangs of a viper will kill him." The word "kill" carries the same meaning as "slay." It is a picture: what seemed sweet to him turns into deadly poison.

It is Zophar, one of Job's friends, who speaks. He is describing what, in his view, always happens to the wicked person who grows rich through injustice. His idea is that God brings the wicked down. But the book shows that Zophar applies this wrongly to Job, who was suffering without being punished for any such wickedness. His general teaching does not explain all suffering.

For today: be wary of unjust gains, even when they seem sweet now. And be careful not to judge the pain of others with easy answers; sometimes it is better to keep someone company with humility.
exp.37:31:
God asks Job whether he can bring out the constellations in their seasons and lead out the Bear with her cubs. The phrase "in their seasons" means at the right times of the year. The Bear and her cubs seems to be the Great Bear with its nearby stars, though scholars are not sure which group of stars is meant.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered terribly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons, but shows him his wisdom in creation. The questions are meant to help Job see his limits and trust the one who holds the universe together.

For today: when you do not understand what you are going through, remember that the God who orders the stars also cares for your life. Pray honestly, but rest in the knowledge that he knows what you cannot see.
exp.33:14:
This verse says that if God withdrew his breath of life, every living creature would die at the same time, and human beings would return to the dust. "Flesh" means every living thing, and "all would perish together" means all at once. "Return to the dust" means going back to the earth from which man was formed.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He argues that God is just and does not act with wickedness. Here he argues that God does not need anyone to grant him authority over the world, and that the life of everyone depends on him. Some readers think Elihu is right about what he says concerning God, but that he misapplies it to Job's case.

For today: remember that every breath is a gift from God. That invites us to live with humility and gratitude, and to trust him even when we do not understand what we are going through.
exp.31:21:
He says that Elihu does not know how to flatter, that is, to speak with pretty but false words in order to win someone's favor. If he did so, he says, his Maker, meaning God, would remove him in an instant. The phrase "remove me in an instant" here means to bring an end to him or take his life. "Instant" means "very quickly."

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who listened quietly to the debate between Job and his three friends. He was angry because none of them had managed to give a satisfying answer. Here he says he will speak frankly, without favoring anyone or offering empty praise. Scholars disagree about whether Elihu is entirely right or whether he speaks with excessive confidence, but his desire not to flatter is easy to understand.

For today: try to speak the truth with respect and love, without exaggerating praise to please people, and without keeping silent about what matters out of fear. Before you speak, pray and examine your motive: are you seeking to help, or only to look good?
exp.32:13:
God does speak, and he does so in one way and in another, yet people often fail to notice it and do not understand. The phrase "in one way and in another" means that God uses different means to communicate, and does not limit himself to just one.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He rebukes Job for complaining that God does not answer or give explanations. Elihu maintains that God does communicate, and right away he mentions dreams in the night. Note that Elihu is not presented as an infallible teacher, so his words should be read carefully, although here he expresses something that the Bible confirms in other places.

Today we can ask God for an attentive heart. He speaks through his Word, through wise counsel, through conscience, and through circumstances. Set aside a moment each day to read the Bible and listen with humility, comparing everything with what it teaches.
exp.30:31:
It says that no stranger had to spend the night on the street, because Job kept his door open to the traveler who was passing by. The phrase "on the street" means outdoors, out in the open, during the night. The traveler is the person on the road who had no place to stay.

Job speaks, a righteous man who suffers greatly. His friends accuse him of having done wrong, and he answers by defending his life. In this chapter he reviews how he treated others: the poor, his servants, and foreigners. In that time, welcoming the traveler was a very important duty, because the roads were dangerous and there were few inns.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we might open our door to: a lonely neighbor, an immigrant, a brother or sister in need. Offering hospitality does not always mean giving a bed; it can be a meal, a little company, or concrete help.
exp.13:13:
It says that Job asks whether a person who dies can live again. His answer is one of waiting: all the days of his "hard service" (that is, his time of struggle in this life) he will wait until his "renewal" comes. The word renewal means a change or relief, like a guard being replaced at the end of a shift. It may refer to death or to a renewal after death; it is understood in several ways.

Job speaks here as a man who suffers greatly and has lost everything. In the chapter he compares human life to a fragile flower and to a tree that can sprout again. As he speaks with God, he longs to hide in the grave until the pain passes, and yet he lets a spark of hope show through: that God will call him, and he will answer.

For today: when you do not understand your suffering, do not keep silent before God. Tell Him your questions honestly, and wait on Him patiently, trusting that He has the last word.
exp.33:33:
This verse says that people with good judgment and understanding will speak up in agreement with the one who is talking, and that the wise will listen closely to what he says. "Men of understanding" refers to sensible people who think carefully about what is right.

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends have finished. He is upset because Job defended his own innocence. Elihu presents himself as someone who speaks for the sensible, and in the verses that follow he criticizes Job. Scholars disagree about how right Elihu is, since God does not directly correct him, but neither does God directly approve of him.

Today the verse reminds us that we should seek wise counsel, but also examine with humility whether the person speaking truly does so. No one should be followed simply because they claim to speak for "the wise." We should test everything against the Word of God.
exp.18:18:
This verse says that the people closest to Job turned their backs on him. "Best friends" are the intimate friends, the ones to whom one tells one's secrets. "Despise" means they looked down on him with contempt. And "turned against me" means they became his opponents, precisely the ones he had wanted on his side.

Job speaks here, a man who lost almost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends insist that he suffers for some hidden sin, and he defends his innocence. Here he describes his deepest pain: loneliness. Even his wife and the young men reject him, and he feels that God himself has struck him.

For today: if someone you love has hurt you or left you alone, you can speak your pain to God honestly, as Job did. And if you know someone who is suffering, stand beside them with patience and kindness, without judging them.
exp.5:8:
Job wishes that God would be willing to crush him, that is, to destroy him. The idea of God being willing to do it can be understood as God being pleased to do it or as it seeming good to him. The image of God unleashing His hand and cutting him off is like letting His hand fall and bringing Job's life to an end. The idea of being cut off means being brought to a complete end.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. He is answering his friend Eliphaz, who kept insisting that his suffering was caused by some sin. Job is in such pain that he would rather die than go on like this. Even in that despair, he does not turn away from God; he speaks to Him, and says that he has not denied His words. This is not advice, but the honest cry of a broken man.

For today: if you are in very great pain, you can tell God with complete sincerity what you feel, without pretending to be strong. And do not carry the pain alone: also seek out someone you trust who will listen to you and stay with you.
exp.16:2:
Here Job asks God to give him the pledge that God himself demands, so that he can defend his case. "Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand" is a request to be given a guarantee right now. "To go to court" is to enter a legal dispute, and "who else will be my guarantor" asks who else would stand up to answer for him, the way a person would vouch for someone in a binding agreement.

Job speaks while suffering greatly, his health broken and close to death. His friends mock him instead of comforting him. For that reason he feels that no one stands with him, and he asks that God himself be his guarantor. Some understand that Job speaks to God as both judge and guarantor; others see a desperate plea, without its being fully clear who could answer for him.

For today: when no one understands you or defends you, you can speak with God with complete honesty. He is not frightened by your questions. Christians also see in Jesus the one who answers for us before God.
exp.39:7:
God tells Job to do something only God can do: to bring down the proud and hide them in the dust, meaning in death or the grave, and to bury their faces in darkness, the way the dead are covered. The wording of the verse here is Would you really annul My justice? Would you condemn Me to justify yourself? Job had challenged God's justice, so God presses him with this question.

God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned God's justice, and now God challenges him: if you think you could govern the world better than I do, start by humbling the proud and the wicked. If Job could do this, God will admit that God's own strength can save him.

Today, this passage invites us to humility. Before we judge how God runs the world, let us remember that we cannot even control the pride of our own hearts. Let us trust that God is just, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.5:28:
Job asks his friends to reconsider what they are saying. He pleads with them not to be unjust toward him. He says that his righteousness is at stake, meaning that his innocence and uprightness in this matter are what he is asking them to take seriously.

Job speaks while suffering greatly. His friends, especially Eliphaz, have told him that his pain must be punishment for some sin. Job feels judged and without comfort, and he asks them to listen to him with honesty. Some scholars hear in his words a firm demand; others, a wounded plea. Both ideas fit.

When someone suffers, we should not rush to judge them or explain their pain with easy answers. Before speaking, let us listen with humility, be willing to reconsider our ideas, and offer companionship instead of condemnation.
exp.12:17:
He says that Job has already prepared his case to bring before God, like someone getting ready for a trial. The phrase "I have prepared my case" means he is getting ready to be judged, or to present his defense. To be "vindicated" means to be shown to be innocent, or to be in the right. Job confidently affirms that, in the end, his case will turn out well.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. His friends insist that he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job does not think himself perfect, but he knows he has not lived in the hypocrisy they accuse him of. For that reason he wants to bring his complaint directly before God. Later on, God himself will correct Job, so his confidence does not explain everything.

For today: when you suffer and others judge you without understanding, do not stay silent or pull away from God. Bring your heart and your questions to him honestly, and at the same time remain willing to listen and to learn from him.
exp.5:29:
Job asks his friends whether there is wickedness or falsehood on his lips. He asks whether his mouth is unable to discern malice. He is saying that he can tell what is wrong from what is right, and that he is not speaking with deceit.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. His friend Eliphaz has suggested that his troubles come from some hidden sin. Job defends himself and asks them to look at him honestly and reconsider their judgment. He does not claim to be perfect, but he maintains that his complaint is sincere.

For today: when someone suffers, let us listen before we accuse. And if we are the ones who suffer, we can speak with sincerity before God and others, without pretending. Let us ask for wisdom to discern with humility and compassion.
exp.8:32:
He says that Job finds no one standing between him and God who could judge the case fairly. A "mediator" is someone who stands between two parties to bring them together. The phrase about someone who could lay a hand on both of us suggests a person with the authority to reach out and bring both sides together. Job feels that there is no one who can do this.

Job speaks here in the midst of enormous suffering. He is answering his friend Bildad, and he acknowledges that God is so great that a man cannot argue with Him as an equal. That is why he longs for a mediator who could give him a fair hearing. His words are a sincere cry, not a complete teaching about God.

For today: when you feel that your pain separates you from God, you can tell Him so honestly. Christians see in Jesus the answer to this longing, since the Bible calls him the mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5).
exp.0:15:
This messenger reports that the "fire of God fell from heaven" and burned up the sheep and the servants. The servants who tended the flocks are the young attendants. To "consumed" them means the fire destroyed them completely. Only one escaped to bring the news to Job.

He is the third messenger to come to Job, one after another, on the same day. Job was a rich and upright man, and he is losing his possessions within a matter of hours. The phrase "fire of God" may refer to a lightning strike or some other powerful natural event; the text does not explain how it happened. The book later shows that behind it was a trial permitted by God, although Job did not know this.

For today: when blows come one after another and we understand nothing, we do not have to have all the answers. We can keep trusting God, weep honestly, and look for support from other believers.
exp.33:21:
There is no place dark enough where wicked people can hide from God. "Deep shadow" describes a very thick darkness. "Workers of iniquity" refers to those who do evil.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in at the end of the conversations between Job and his friends. He wants to defend that God is just and that he sees everything human beings do. His words are addressed to Job, whom he believes is too sure of himself. Later, the book shows that Elihu does not explain everything correctly, so it is wise to read him carefully.

For today: there is no need to pretend before God. If there is something hidden in your life, bring it to Him sincerely, ask for forgiveness, and ask for help to change. His gaze is not a threat to anyone who seeks the truth, but an invitation to live in the light.
exp.8:9:
It says that God does great things, too deep to fully search out, and wonders so numerous that they cannot be counted. The word "and" in the verse is simply the ordinary connecting word meaning "and." "Beyond searching out" means that the human mind cannot grasp them completely.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly, and he is answering his friend Bildad. Job acknowledges the power of God as he looks at creation: the heavens, the sea, and the constellations. But he says it with pain, because he feels that God is so great that he cannot call Him to account or understand what is happening to him. The verses that follow show that tension: God passes by and Job does not see Him.

For today: when you do not understand what you are living through, do not stay only with the question. Look at what God has already done, and remember that His wisdom is greater than yours. You can be honest with Him in prayer, and even without understanding everything, keep trusting Him.
exp.27:27:
It says that God spoke to humankind and showed where true wisdom is found: in the fear of the Lord, which means respecting him and honoring him with reverence. It also says that turning away from evil is understanding, that is, sound judgment for living well. Here "Lord" stands for the Hebrew word in the original text.

The speaker is Job, in a poem about wisdom. First he shows that people can dig mines and uncover treasures, but they cannot find wisdom on their own. Only God knows it, since he set the rain and the lightning in their place. Then Job closes with this verse. Some think it is a pause before Job continues speaking; others see it as the central answer of the chapter.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself whether it pleases God. And if there is something wrong you need to leave behind, begin today with one concrete step.
exp.13:18:
The explanation says that water, with its force and constant flow, wears away even stones and carries off the fine earth. Job uses that image to say that God, in the same way, destroys a person's hope. "Destroy" means to bring to an end. The words are harsh because they express what Job feels, not a complete explanation of what God is like.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, during the dialogue with his friends. He is reflecting on how fragile and brief life is. Earlier he said that a cut tree can sprout again, but that a person, once dead, seems to have no such chance. His lament is sincere and desperate.

For today: when you feel your hope wearing away little by little, do not hide it. Tell God honestly, as Job did, and seek the support of people of faith who walk with you.
exp.27:22:
It says that only God knows the way to wisdom and knows where it is. "Its" refers to wisdom, the subject of the whole chapter. "Its way" is the route to reach it, and "its place" is where it is found. What no human being or animal can see, God understands completely.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his dialogue with his friends. Earlier he describes how people dig mines and search for treasure, yet they cannot find wisdom through their own effort. Here he answers that God knows it because he sees everything and governs creation. Some read this chapter as a reflective pause in Job's speech; others see it as a poem that prepares what follows.

For today: when you face hard decisions or pain without explanation, do not rely only on your own understanding. Ask God for wisdom with humility, because he knows the way that you cannot see.
exp.7:1:
