Bildad asks Job how long he is going to keep talking like this. He says Job's words are like a blustering wind: loud and forceful, but empty, and they blow everything around without building anything up. The phrase "these things" refers to Job's complaints.

Bildad is one of Job's three friends. Job has just cried out in pain and said that God is treating him unfairly. Bildad feels offended and believes Job is accusing God. His view is that suffering always comes because of sin, and later the book will show that this idea is incomplete.

For today: when someone is suffering, let us listen before we correct. Pain is not healed by quick explanations. Sometimes the best help is to stay with someone patiently, tenderly, and humbly.
exp.12:6:
Job asks his friends whether they really plan to speak wickedly and deceitfully on God's behalf. It is a question that rebukes them: they believe they are defending God, but Job tells them that dishonesty never serves him.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends insist that he must have sinned seriously, because they think all pain is punishment. Job knows his situation is not like that, and he tells them that their defense of God is full of mistakes. The book itself later shows that they had not spoken rightly about God (Job 42:7).

For today: when someone suffers, let us avoid giving easy explanations or judgments we do not have the knowledge to make. It is better to stand beside others with humility and honesty, and sometimes to keep silent, than to defend God with words he has not spoken.
exp.40:4:
It says that Leviathan cannot be treated like a pet. "Can you pet him like a bird" and "put him on a leash for your maidens" picture someone amusing young women with a creature kept on a cord, the way one would handle a tame bird. "Maidens" here means young women. The question expects a firm "no."

Here God speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He presents Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature. Scholars do not agree on which animal this is: some think of the crocodile, others of a symbolic figure of chaos. God wants Job to see that there are things in creation he cannot control, and that God does govern them.

For today: recognize that you do not control everything. When something overwhelms you, rest in the fact that God does have control and trust his wisdom, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.11:23:
This verse says that God deprives the leaders of the earth of their reason and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland. The phrase "deprives of reason" describes leaders who lose sound judgment, and the image of the trackless wasteland describes people walking without any clear direction. The idea is that God leaves rulers confused, so they wander lost with no clear path ahead.

Job speaks here in reply to his friends, who were saying that God only punishes the wicked. Job answers that God has power over everything: nations, rulers, and history. Some understand that Job exaggerates his anger and pain; others see that he expresses a real truth about God's sovereignty. Even so, Job does not yet understand why he is suffering.

Today it reminds us that no human power is absolute. Let us not place our hope only in leaders or in our own wisdom. Let us ask God for direction with humility, as Proverbs 3:5-6 says.
exp.32:17:
He says God holds people back so that their soul does not fall into the "pit," that is, the grave or death, and so that their life is preserved from perishing by the sword, which means dying violently. The word "preserve" speaks of guarding someone in time, before they reach disaster.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins in near the end of the dialogues with Job. He explains that God sometimes speaks in dreams and through pain to correct pride and save people. Some scholars understand Elihu to suggest that Job's suffering is correction; the book itself does not confirm this at the end.

Today: when something holds you back or makes you uncomfortable, ask yourself humbly whether God is looking after you from a harmful path. Listen for his voice in the Bible and in prayer, and do not harden your heart.
exp.1:6:
Job 2:7 says that Satan left the presence of the LORD and infected Job with terrible boils, from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head. "Terrible boils" means painful sores on the skin, and "from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head" means they covered his whole body, from his feet to the top of his head. His whole body was affected.

God had allowed this trial, but with a limit: Satan could touch Job's body, but could not take his life. Satan had claimed that Job only served God for what he received, and that Job would curse God if he suffered in his own body. The text does not describe the exact illness. Scholars have proposed several possibilities, but no one can say with certainty what it was.

For today: when suffering comes without explanation, remember that God remains God and that pain has a limit under his watchful eye. You will not always understand the why, but you can keep trusting him and seek support from people who walk alongside you with compassion.
exp.19:14:
He swallows down wealth the way someone swallows food, but he will have to vomit it up. God himself will force it out of his stomach. The word "vomit" and the phrase "force it out" match the wording of this reader's verse, so they are used here as plain verbs. Wealth gained unjustly seems sweet at first, but afterward it turns into poison.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's friends. He believes the wicked always lose what they gained, and he uses this image to suggest that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. The book shows that Zophar is wrong to apply this idea to Job, although his general statement about wealth gained dishonestly has some truth to it.

For today: do not cling to dishonest gains or to greed, because they do not bring lasting peace. And when someone is suffering, let us avoid judging them quickly. It is better to stand with them in humility, without accusing them.
exp.2:5:
Here Job wishes that the night of his birth would be swallowed up in total darkness. He asks that it not be counted as part of the calendar, that it not appear among the days of the year or be entered in any of the months. He wants that night erased from the record of time, as if it had never happened.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. After seven days of silence with his friends, he finally voices his pain. He does not curse God, but the day of his birth. It is poetic and very intense language, born of deep suffering.

For today: if you are going through a very great pain, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. The Bible shows that one can speak honestly about suffering. Tell God how you feel, and seek out someone you trust who will listen.
exp.22:10:
It says that Job followed closely in God's footsteps, like someone walking right behind a trail. "My feet have followed in His tracks" means his feet stayed on the path God had marked. "I have kept His way" means he cared for that path and obeyed it. And "without turning aside" means he did not step off it, neither to one side nor the other.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends tell him he is suffering because of some hidden sin. Job defends himself: he does not feel perfect, but he is faithful. Although he cannot see or find God, he trusts that God knows his way and will test him, as gold is tested in the fire.

When you do not understand what God is doing, do not stop walking with Him. Keep obeying in the small things of each day, such as praying, being honest, and forgiving, trusting that He sees you even when you do not feel Him close.
exp.34:9:
People suffer and cry out for help, yet almost no one asks, "Where is God, my Maker, who gives us songs in the night?" In other words, few people turn to God, the Creator, who gives comfort and hope even in the darkest moments. "Maker" refers to the one who made us.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He corrects Job because he believes Job complains about his suffering without turning his eyes toward God. Elihu does not always get everything right, and in the end God does not rebuke him as He rebukes the other friends, but He does not explicitly approve of him either. His point here is that pain can make us cry out without truly seeking God.

For today: when a difficult "night" comes, do not stay only in complaint. Ask sincerely, "Where are you, God?" and pray, trusting that He will give you comfort, even if it is a song in the darkness.
exp.4:9:
It says that God is the one who gives rain to the earth and sends water upon the fields. The surface of the earth is the setting for this, a fitting picture of the many great things God does every day that we cannot fully trace.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He advises Job to seek God and entrust his concerns to Him. Eliphaz is right to speak of God's greatness, but later in the book God says that his friends did not speak rightly of Him, so their counsel should be read with care.

Today, whenever you see rain fall, you can remember that God cares for what you need. Give thanks for the everyday and bring your worries to Him in prayer, trusting that He continues to sustain life.
exp.5:18:
The caravans of Tema look for water, and the travelers of Sheba hope to find it. "It" refers to the streams of water in the wadis, which Job mentioned before. Tema and Sheba were regions known for their caravans in dry lands. To hope here means to trust in finding water.

Job is speaking, answering his friend Eliphaz. He is suffering greatly and feels let down because his friends are not giving him support. He compares his friends to streams that dry up in the heat: they seem to bring relief, but they fail just when they are needed. The caravan travelers arrive full of hope and are left disappointed.

For today: when someone suffers, they do not need cold speeches, but compassion and presence. Let us be like cool water for the one who is tired. And when people fail us, let us remember that God is a faithful spring that never runs dry.
exp.29:12:
He says that his enemies have torn up his path, that is, his plans and his way of life. They profited from his brokenness, that is, his downfall and weakness. And he adds that there was no one to restrain them.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. He was once respected, but now young men without honor mock him and attack him. Job believes God took away his strength, and that is why they dare to mistreat him. His friends do not comfort him, and he feels alone. It is a sincere lament, not a final explanation from God.

When someone is weak, there are those who take advantage, but we can be helpers. Today you can draw near to someone who is suffering, listen to them without judging, and offer concrete help. And if you are suffering, you can express your pain to God with sincerity, as Job did.
exp.9:4:
Here Job asks God a pointed question: are your days like those of a mortal, or your years like those of a man? The phrase "human times" refers to the brief life of a person, but that phrase is not in the verse you are reading, so I will simply say that the question points to the short span of human life. Job does not claim that God is weak; he uses the question to contrast the limited view of people with God's view.

Job speaks in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends accuse him of having sinned, and he, with a bitter soul, speaks directly to God. He wonders why God seems to be searching for his guilt as if He needed time to investigate it, when Job knows he is not wicked. These are words of sincere pain, not a teaching about what God is like. Some read them as an honest complaint, others as the exaggeration of a wounded man.

For today: when you suffer, you can speak to God with complete sincerity, but remember that He sees further than you can see. Bring Him your questions without ceasing to trust in Him.
exp.33:2:
This verse compares two senses: just as the mouth tests food to know whether it is good, the ear examines words to tell whether they are true or not. The part of the mouth that perceives flavors is the palate, and here "to test" means to examine or put to the test.

It is Elihu who speaks, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He addresses those who consider themselves wise and asks them to listen carefully. He wants them to judge together what Job has said, because he believes Job has spoken wrongly about God. Elihu is not always right, and the book does not fully approve of him.

Today we can apply it this way: let us not accept everything we hear, even when it sounds good or comes from someone who is sure of themselves. Let us test words calmly, comparing them with the Bible and with prayer, before we believe them or repeat them.
exp.38:28:
This verse is a question that God puts to Job. The bird here is a hawk, a bird of prey. God asks whether the hawk rises and spreads its wings toward the south because of Job's wisdom or ability. It is suggested that the bird migrates or glides toward the south, although some read it only as its safe flight.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and had asked for explanations. God does not give him a list of reasons, but shows him creation: the horse, the hawk, the eagle. With these questions he teaches Job that he does not govern the world or understand it completely. Job answers with humility and falls silent.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that God sustains things you do not control. Rest in his wisdom and trust him, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.20:1:
Job asks his friends to listen carefully to what he is about to say. The word for "listen" here is the one that appears in the verse, and "consolation" refers to what they might give him. Job tells them that if they truly want to comfort him, the best comfort will be to hear him well, without interrupting.

Job is speaking, and he is suffering greatly. His friends, like Zophar in the previous chapter, have told him that he suffers because of his sin. Job does not agree, and he feels that they are not listening to him. In this chapter he points out that the wicked sometimes prosper, and so the simple explanations of his friends are not enough.

Often, the one who suffers does not need quick advice, but someone who will listen with patience. This week, try to listen calmly to a person who is going through pain, without judging or correcting them right away. Listening can also be a way of showing love.
exp.35:30:
This verse says that God uses the clouds, the rain and the storms for two purposes. With them he judges the nations, and with them he also provides food in abundance for many people. The word "judges" here can be understood as "corrects" or "governs." Some translators understand "judges" as "corrects."

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who, after Job's three friends, defends the greatness and justice of God. He is describing divine power in nature: the clouds, the light and the thunder. His aim is for Job to recognize that God is far greater than we can understand. Interpreters debate whether everything Elihu says is accurate, since God himself speaks afterward.

For today: when you see rain or a storm, remember that God sustains life and that his power deserves respect and gratitude. Give thanks for daily bread and trust him even when you do not understand everything.
exp.28:0:
It says that Job kept speaking. The phrase "returned... to take up his theme" is an old way of saying he resumed his speech or his argument. The Hebrew word is usually translated as "proverb" or "discourse." In other words, Job does not stop, but goes on with another block of words.

Job is a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends have already spoken, and they accuse him of suffering because of some sin. Here begins his last great speech (chapters 29 to 31), in which he first looks back with longing on his past life, when he felt God's care.

For today: when you suffer, you can speak honestly before God, without pretending. Remembering with gratitude what you have lived through is good, but also ask for strength to trust Him in the present, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.25:10:
The explanation says that even the "foundations of heaven," a poetic image of the most firm and lofty parts of creation, quake and are astounded when God rebukes them. The words "astounded" mean that they are filled with awe and fear. "Rebuke" is a strong word of authority. The foundations should not be taken literally: this is the language of poetry.

Here Job is speaking, answering his friend Bildad. Job describes God's power over the heavens, the sea, and the limits of light and darkness. He wants to show that God is greater than we can understand. Some think the "foundations" recall ancient images of earth and sky; the text does not make this clear.

For today: if the most solid things in the universe bow before God, our fears are not greater than He is. You can rest, pray with humility, and trust that his power also cares for you.
exp.6:15:
Job says he is sick of his life and cannot stand his suffering. The phrase "I loathe my life" expresses real hatred of the misery he is living through. He knows he will not live forever, and he asks God to leave him alone. The phrase "a breath" pictures his days as brief and fleeting, here one moment and gone the next.

Job speaks in the middle of his pain, answering his friends and crying out to God. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health, and his nights bring him nightmares. That is why he longs for death. Some understand "leave me alone" as a desperate plea, not as a lack of faith, since Job keeps speaking with God.

When you are worn down by pain, you do not need to hide it. You can tell God honestly what you feel, even if it comes out as complaints. He listens. And if the weight is more than you can carry, seek the support of someone you trust or of a professional as well.
exp.36:12:
This verse says that God uses the clouds and the rain for different purposes: sometimes as a punishment, sometimes for the good of the land, and other times as an expression of his loving devotion. The phrase "he accomplishes this" means "he carries it out" or "he brings it about."

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who tries to explain to Job that God governs nature with wisdom. He sees in the storms and the rain a sign of God's power and of the fact that his ways are higher than ours. Some think Elihu is right in part, though he does not see the whole picture of Job's suffering.

For today: when you go through difficult or unexpected times, remember that God is still wise and present. We will not always understand his reasons, but we can trust that his character is good. Today, give thanks for the rain, the sun, or the weather, and pray with confidence.
exp.4:20:
It says that God will shelter the person from the "scourge of the tongue," that is, from words that wound, such as slander, cruel criticism, or cursing. It also promises that you will not fear when havoc comes, a word that here refers to ruin or disaster.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to comfort Job by saying that God takes care of those who are faithful to him. However, at the end of the book God says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly (Job 42:7). His words contain truths, but he applied them wrongly, since he assumed Job was suffering because of some sin.

For today: when others hurt you with words, do not live in fear. Trust that God sustains you, and make sure your own words bring blessing and not wounds.
exp.11:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that Job spoke up to answer what he had just heard. "Then Job answered" means it was his turn to speak after someone else. It does not yet give the content of his answer.

Here Job speaks, a man who suffers greatly and who has lost his possessions, his children, and his health. Zophar, one of his three friends, has just spoken to him and hints that he suffers because of some hidden sin. Job answers with irony and pain, because he feels that his friends claim to be wise without understanding his situation. That is the idea of the following verse.

For today: before answering someone who suffers, it is good to listen with humility. Often another person's pain needs company and compassion, not quick explanations or judgments. Let us ask God for wise words and a kind heart.
exp.18:5:
Job says he feels that God has wronged him and drawn His net around him, as if he were an animal caught with no way out. Here the net stands for a situation that closes in on every side.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. His friends insist that his misfortune is punishment for some sin. Job answers that, even if he had made a mistake, that error would be his own concern, and that they have no right to humiliate him. He feels that God has treated him unjustly, although the book shows that his view was limited and that he did not know what was happening in heaven.

For today: when you feel trapped and without answers, you can express your pain to God honestly, without pretending. And avoid judging others' suffering lightly; sometimes the person needs company, not explanations.
exp.7:10:
The explanation says that papyrus, a plant that grows in marshy places, cannot grow where there is no marsh, and that reeds cannot flourish without water. These are two rhetorical questions: the obvious answer is "no." Plants need their source of life in order to survive.

The one speaking is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. He believes that Job is suffering because of some sin, and he uses examples from nature to say that whoever forgets God loses his support and dries up. Note: in the book, God later says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so their teaching does not apply to Job.

For today: take care of your roots. Seek God steadily in prayer and in His Word, because there is your strength. But do not use this idea to judge someone who is suffering; pain is not always punishment.
exp.40:20:
His breath sets coals ablaze, and flames pour from his mouth. It is a striking picture: a creature that breathes out fire, with heat so strong it lights the embers. The wording here says the breath sets coals ablaze, and the coals are glowing pieces of wood.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the storm. He describes Leviathan, a huge and fearsome creature. Scholars disagree about what it is, whether a crocodile, a mythical beast, or a symbol of chaos. God is not giving a lesson in zoology but showing Job that Job cannot control or fully understand all of creation, while God can.

For today: when life overwhelms you and you do not understand what is happening, remember that God governs even what seems unmanageable to you. Rest in his power and wisdom, and trust him even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.9:16:
Job says that God keeps bringing new accusations against him and keeps increasing His anger. The "witnesses" he speaks of are fresh charges and proofs brought against him, and "anger" is strong displeasure. "Hardships assault me in wave after wave" means that trouble keeps arriving, one blow after another, with no time to recover. Job feels that the pain never stops and only grows.

Job speaks here in the middle of his suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and his friends accuse him of having sinned. He feels cornered by God and speaks to Him with pain and without disguise. This is his complaint, not a teaching about what God is like. The book later shows that Job did not see the whole picture.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, you can tell God what you feel, honestly and without pretending. He is not offended by your cry. Speak with Him, and also seek someone you trust who can walk with you without judging you.
exp.29:28:
He says he feels like a companion to lonely, sorrowful animals. "Jackals" here are not fantasy creatures; they are wild animals of the desert. The "ostriches" are a bird that also lives in lonely wilderness places. What matters is the image: Job lives in solitude, and his weeping sounds like the howling and crying of those desert animals.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He has lost his health, his fortune, and his good name, and people despise him. In this chapter he compares his former honor with his present humiliation. Even so, he keeps crying out to God and does not hide his pain.

For today: if you are going through a time of loneliness or pain, you do not need to pretend otherwise. You can be honest with God, as Job was, and seek out someone you trust who can walk alongside you, instead of isolating yourself.
exp.37:34:
God asks Job whether he can send the lightning bolts on their way, as a master sends out his servants, and whether they would report back to him, "Here we are." The question assumes the answer is no.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and had asked for explanations. God does not give him a specific reason for his pain, but leads him to look at creation: the heavens, the clouds, the rain and the lightning. In this way he shows Job how limited human beings are and how great divine wisdom is.

Today, this verse invites us to rest in the fact that we do not control everything. When something is beyond us, we can hand over to God what we do not understand and trust that he still governs with wisdom.
exp.21:24:
The explanation says that God Almighty will be your gold and the finest silver, meaning He will be your treasure and your greatest good. The phrase "in heaps" is not in your verse, so it is left out. Some scholars note that the Hebrew can also be read as the Almighty being a protection for Job, but the basic meaning stays much the same.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he urges him to turn back to God so that he can be restored. But at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So this advice is not a safe rule.

For today: seek God for who He is, not as a way of gaining wealth. And when someone is suffering, stand beside them with compassion, without accusing them or assuming that their pain is punishment.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that one day the "sons of God" came to present themselves before the LORD, that is, before God. Satan also came with them. The word "Satan" means "accuser" or "adversary."

The book of Job tells the story from the outside, as a narrative that lets us see a scene in heaven. Earlier we saw Job caring for his family through prayer and burnt offerings. Now we are shown something Job did not know. The "sons of God" are usually understood as heavenly beings or angels, though some scholars interpret them differently. What is clear is that Satan answers before God and has no power of his own.

For today: when you suffer without understanding why, remember that God is still in control, even when you cannot see what is happening behind the scene. You can trust Him and keep seeking Him honestly.
exp.25:9:
He has drawn a horizon on the face of the waters, a clearly marked line where light and darkness meet, that is, the boundary between day and night. The wording "He has inscribed a horizon on the face of the waters" means that he set a firm limit on the surface of the sea. Some understand this as the circular horizon seen over the water; others see it as a general order God gave to creation. It is not certain which image the author had in mind.

Here Job is speaking, answering Bildad. He is describing God's power over the clouds, the sea, and the heavens. He does so in the middle of his suffering, and he acknowledges that God governs everything with wisdom.

Today we can rest in the fact that God sets limits even on what seems out of control. When your life feels like a restless sea, remember that God still marks the edge. Bring your anxiety to him in prayer and trust his control.
exp.21:20:
It says you should be reconciled to God and live at peace with Him. The words "reconcile now" mean bring yourself back into friendship with Him. The words "good will come to you" mean you will receive good things, or blessing.

It is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, who speaks. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and so he urges him to repent. Although his words sound wise, God later said that Eliphaz and his friends had not spoken rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So the advice is good in general, but wrongly applied to Job.

For today: draw near to God with sincerity, not using Him as a formula to obtain things. And when someone is suffering, stand with them in kindness rather than accusing them. Peace with God is a precious gift, even when life remains hard.
exp.11:6:
Job invites his friend to ask the animals, the birds, and then the earth and the fish. The old Spanish phrase "te lo mostrarán" means that they will make it plain to you. The text does not say that the animals speak. It says that creation teaches something to anyone who observes it with attention.

Here Job speaks, answering Zophar and his friends, who tell him he suffers because of his sin. Job replies that he sees wicked people living at ease, so their explanation falls short. He says that even the animals know that everything is in the hand of God (verse 9). Interpreters debate whether Job speaks with irony or with seriousness; probably both.

For today: when you do not understand pain or injustice, go out and look at creation. Observing it can remind you that God is still great and that his wisdom surpasses your explanations.
exp.27:18:
This verse says that no jewel can compare with wisdom. The "topaz from Cush" is a precious stone from the region of Cush, although some scholars think it was a different gem. "Pure gold" is very fine gold. "Cannot be valued in pure gold" means that wisdom is worth so much that it cannot be priced even in gold.

Job speaks in the middle of his long debate with his friends. This chapter is a poem about wisdom. Job describes how people dig mines and find treasures, but they cannot find wisdom through their own effort. At the end of the chapter he says that true wisdom is to fear the Lord.

Today we can ask ourselves what we pursue with the most determination: money or wisdom. Let us ask God, in prayer and by reading his Word, to teach us to make decisions with prudence and to live with reverence toward him.
exp.41:14:
It says that in the whole land there were no women as beautiful as Job's three daughters. Their father also granted them an inheritance among their brothers. The daughters received a share of the property, which was unusual for that time.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book, who tells the ending of the story. After Job suffered greatly and trusted God, the Lord restored him and gave him a new family. According to many scholars, the names of the daughters mean something like "dove," "cinnamon," and "horn of perfume," though the exact meaning is debated. The text does not explain why Job granted them an inheritance; it simply reports it.

For today: Job honored his daughters by giving them a place and a worth equal to that of their brothers. We can follow his example by treating everyone in our family fairly and generously, without unjust distinctions.
exp.37:20:
God asks Job with irony: "Surely you know, for you were already born! And the number of your days is great!" In other words, you should know, because you have been alive long enough to have learned it. God speaks of light and darkness, and points out that Job was not present when they were created.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him a reason for his pain, but shows him the greatness of creation and the limits of human knowledge. Some think the irony aims to humble Job; others, that it aims to lead him to trust.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that you do not see the whole picture. You can rest in the knowledge that God does see it, and trust his wisdom and his care.
exp.10:19:
The verse says the wicked will be left without strength. "Their eyes will fail" pictures them staring anxiously, waiting for help that never comes. They will have no escape, meaning no way out and no safe place to run to. And their hope will be like a final breath: the one thing they are counting on fades away, the way life slips out with the last breath.

The speaker is Zophar, one of Job's three friends. With this closing image he sets the person who turns back to God, who lives secure, against the wicked person, who has no way to escape. Zophar believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. At the end of the book, God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so this speech should not be treated as a rule for judging others.

For today: do not use this verse to say that everyone who suffers deserves it. Instead, examine your own heart with humility and seek refuge in God, who does listen and sustain those who cry out to Him.
exp.13:1:
It says that human life is very brief. It is like a flower that comes out and then withers away, or like a fleeting shadow that does not endure. "Withers away" means that it fades and dies. "Fleeting" means that it passes quickly.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly and is grieved by the loss of his children, his possessions, and his health. He speaks to God with sincerity and almost with complaint. He compares human frailty with God's attention, and asks why God would examine so closely someone so fleeting. It is a lament, not a complete teaching about God.

For today: since life is brief, do not spend it on things that do not matter. Seek God, forgive quickly, and love those closest to you. And if you are suffering, you can speak to God honestly, as Job did.
exp.22:9:
He says that God does know the way I take, even though I cannot see him. "He knows the way I take" means that God knows my life and my steps. "When he has tested me" is the same idea as "when he has tried me." And "I will come forth as gold" means that, after the trial, I will come out clean and precious, like gold that passes through the fire.

Job speaks here, a man who suffers greatly without understanding why. His friends accuse him of having sinned, but he feels innocent. In the verses before this one he searches for God everywhere and cannot find him. Even so, he affirms that God knows him. Then he says that he has followed God's paths and his word.

For today: when you go through a difficult season and feel God far away, remember that he sees you and knows your situation. Keep obeying and praying, trusting that he can use the trial to strengthen your faith.
exp.13:7:
It says that a tree can grow old: its roots grow old in the ground, and its stump seems dead, dry in the soil. It is an image of something that no longer shows signs of life. The words "If its roots grow old in the ground" describe the roots growing old, and "its stump dies in the soil" describes the stump appearing to have died.

Job speaks, a man who suffers greatly and reflects on how brief and fragile human life is. Here he compares a person to a tree. According to Job, a tree that has been cut still has hope, because with water it can sprout again. A person, however, dies and does not see that he will bud again. This is Job's lament, not a full explanation of what God will do afterward.

For today: when you feel that something in your life seems dry or without a future, be honest with God, as Job was, and place it in his hands. He can give hope where you do not see any.
exp.40:14:
This verse describes the skin of Leviathan as if it were armor. "His scales" refers to its outer covering, that is, its scales. They are described as its pride, the thing most admired about this creature, and they are "tightly sealed together," meaning they fit so closely that there are no gaps.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He shows Job Leviathan, a powerful creature that no one can subdue. Some believe it is the crocodile; others think it is a symbolic monster. Nobody knows for certain. God wants Job to understand that He governs what human beings cannot control.

For today: when life seems unmanageable, remember that God is still in charge. Trust Him with humility, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.27:8:
The miner strikes the flint and overturns mountains at their base. "Flint" is a very hard stone. "Overturns" means turns over or stirs up. It speaks of the miners who dig deep into the earth in search of treasure.

It is Job who speaks, in the middle of his dialogue with his friends. In this chapter, Job describes the human skill for finding silver, gold, and precious stones under the earth. He does this to contrast it with something harder: finding wisdom. Human beings reach places where no bird or wild beast has gone, but true wisdom is not obtained by that kind of strength.

For today: we can admire what human ingenuity accomplishes, but we should not confuse it with wisdom. To live well we need to ask God for direction, and to revere him, for Job concludes that the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
exp.40:31:
It says that the Leviathan, as it swims, leaves a glistening wake behind it, so much so that the sea seems to have white hair. A "wake" is the trail of disturbed water that stays on the surface behind a moving creature. The image is of bright, churned-up foam marking where it has passed.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. He describes the Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature. Some think it is a crocodile, others a whale or a symbolic monster of chaos; there is no certain agreement. God wants to show that Job cannot master or understand all of creation, and that God can.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God governs even what is beyond you. Rest in his wisdom, and speak to him with humility and trust, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.8:29:
Job says that even if he washed himself with snow and cleansed his hands with lye, making them as clean as they could possibly be, it would still do him no good. Snow is pure and white, a picture of complete cleanness, and lye is a strong cleaning agent, so together the images stress the most thorough cleansing Job can imagine.

Job speaks here in the midst of his great suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He feels cornered: he believes God is so great and holy that he cannot defend himself before Him. The verses that follow show that he imagines himself thrown into the mud. Keep in mind that Job speaks out of pain, and some of his ideas about God are not correct, as the book itself shows later on.

For today: we cannot cleanse our hearts by our own effort. When you feel dirty because of guilt or pain, do not try to fix yourself alone; come to God sincerely and trust in His forgiveness, which He offers with grace (1 John 1:9).
exp.28:10:
Job 29:11 says that those who heard about Job called him happy and blessed. Those who saw him commended him, meaning they spoke well of him and confirmed that he was a good man. "Commended me" means they praised him sincerely.

The one speaking is Job. He is suffering greatly and remembers with longing how his life was before, when everyone respected him. The verses that follow explain the reason: he helped the poor, the fatherless, and the widow. His good reputation did not come from his wealth, but from his righteousness and his compassion. Job tells this to defend his integrity before his friends, who were unjustly accusing him.

For today: aim for your good reputation to come from serving others, not from putting on an appearance. Help someone in need this week, without expecting applause. And if you are ever judged unfairly, remember that God knows your heart.
exp.27:24:
When God fixed the weight of the wind and measured out the waters, he set the strength of the wind and gave the waters their exact amount. The verse is part of a passage that continues in the verses that follow: God did all this with order and purpose.

Here Job speaks in the middle of his debate with his friends. The whole chapter asks where wisdom can be found. Job answers that human beings cannot buy it or discover it on their own, but God knows it, because he sees everything and governs creation. The details of the wind and the water show that God acts with wisdom.

For today: if God takes care of every detail of the wind and the water, he can also guide your life with wisdom. When you do not understand what is happening, do not rely only on your own ideas. Ask God for direction and trust that he knows what he is doing.
exp.8:12:
The verse says that God does not restrain his anger when he decides to act, and that even the mighty forces that come to the aid of the proud end up cowering beneath him. The word that is used for "restrain" means "hold back," and the word for "cower" means they shrink down or give way. The verse mentions "the helpers of Rahab," a chaos monster from ancient poetry; the sense is that not even the most fearsome forces can stand against God.

The speaker is Job, in the middle of his suffering. He is answering his friend Bildad. Job acknowledges God's power, but he feels that God is so great and beyond reach that there is no way to bring a complaint against him or to win a case against him. His words express pain, not a complete teaching about what God is like.

Today, when we do not understand what we are suffering, we can be honest with God, as Job was, and remember that he is greater than any power. Let us trust him, even without answers.
exp.8:3:
This verse says that God is wise in the depths of his being and mighty in power. Then it asks: who has resisted him and prospered? The word "resisted" in this verse means that someone set themselves against God. The expected answer is: no one.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly and feels that his situation is unjust. He is answering his friend Bildad, and he acknowledges that no one can win a debate with God. He speaks with pain and sometimes with a bitter tone; his words are not always the final word about God, but here he expresses a real truth about God's greatness.

For today: when you do not understand what you are living through, do not fight against God with pride. Bring him your questions with sincerity and humility, trusting that his wisdom and power exceed what you are able to see.
exp.39:17:
It says that the behemoth, the great creature God describes, drinks up an entire river without being startled. "Without being startled" means without being disturbed or feeling fear. "Confident" means he is sure of himself. Even if the whole Jordan rushed into his mouth, he would swallow it calmly. It is a poetic way of exaggerating his strength.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job from the whirlwind. He shows Job the behemoth to make him see that there are creatures Job cannot master, and that God made them. Scholars do not agree on which animal it is: some think of the hippopotamus, others of the elephant, and others of a symbolic or mysterious creature.

For today: when life overwhelms you, remember that God governs even what seems to you enormous and uncontrollable. Rest in his wisdom, and take care not to demand explanations from him as if you could be in control of everything.
exp.27:11:
This verse asks a deep question: where can wisdom be found? The word "but" marks a contrast, and the question points to good judgment for acting well. The text suggests that, although human beings accomplish great things, wisdom is not obtained as easily.

The one speaking is Job, in the midst of his suffering and his debates with his friends. Before this, he speaks of human skill in digging into the earth and uncovering hidden treasures. Now he contrasts that with wisdom, which is beyond human reach. Many scholars see this chapter as a separate poem within the book, though not all agree on its exact function.

Today we can remember that having information or success is not the same as having wisdom. Before deciding something important, stop to pray and ask God for his guidance, with humility and a willingness to learn.
exp.9:13:
If I sinned, You would take note, and You would not let my guilt go unpunished. Job means that God notices sin at once and does not leave it uncorrected. "You would take note" means that God keeps close watch over him. "Guilt" is evil or wrongdoing. Job feels that God has him under a gaze that overlooks nothing.

Job speaks here, in the middle of his great suffering, addressing God with pain and confusion. He remembers that God gave him life and mercy, but now he feels that God treats him as an enemy. Note well: this is Job's lament, not necessarily the complete truth about God. At the end of the book, God himself corrects Job, and the text makes clear that his suffering was not a punishment for some hidden sin.

For today: when you suffer, you can tell God honestly your complaints and fears, as Job did. But do not let go of what you know of his goodness. Ask him to cleanse you of whatever is sin, and to give you peace where there are only questions.
exp.5:10:
Job wonders where he will find the strength to go on waiting. Here "strength" means his energy and endurance, and the question of whether he should be patient asks how long he can keep going. In other words: "What future do I have to wait for, and how long can I keep enduring?" It is the cry of an exhausted man.

Job speaks after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. He is answering Eliphaz, who gave him a speech with little compassion. Job wants God to bring his suffering to an end, yet he affirms that he has not denied the words of the Holy One. His words are desperate, and the Bible leaves them without any disguise.

For today: if you are tired, you can honestly tell God that you no longer have the strength. You do not have to pretend to be strong. Also, seek out someone you trust who will listen to you with kindness, without lectures, like a true friend.
exp.5:1:
Job wishes that his grief and his suffering could be placed on a scale, together with his calamity, so that their true weight could be seen. Here "grief" means his lament, the outpouring of pain that he has been pouring out, and "calamity" is the deep anguish he feels. The verse asks for an honest measure of how heavy his suffering truly is.

Job is speaking in reply to his friend Eliphaz, who had told him that his suffering was a sign of sin. Job has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. He feels that his harsh words seem exaggerated, but he asks that someone weigh fairly how much he hurts.

Today, before judging the words of someone who is suffering, let us listen with patience. The one who hurts does not need quick sermons but compassion. Like Job, we too can bring our honest complaint before God.
exp.17:19:
It says that the day of the wicked man's fall will leave the people appalled. "Those in the west" and "those in the east" are the two groups named in the verse, so the phrase covers people in distant places, and the idea is that his ruin will shock everyone, from one side of the world to the other.

Bildad, Job's friend, speaks here in his second speech. He believes that suffering is always punishment for wickedness, and he describes the end of the godless to hint that Job is in sin. The book shows that this conclusion is mistaken: Job was blameless, and God himself later corrects his friends.

For today: avoid judging others by their pain, as if every suffering were a punishment. Walk alongside them with compassion and listening, and trust that God sees the heart better than we do.
exp.38:21:
Here God asks Job whether it was he who gave the horse its strength. The verse about the horse's "neck" and "snort" appears in the explanation as well. Some translations say the neck is clothed with a flowing mane; the Hebrew text is difficult and can be understood in several ways, but the central idea is the animal's strength and spirit.

God speaks out of the whirlwind, answering Job after his long complaints and questions about suffering. Instead of giving explanations, he shows him creation: the horse, the ostrich, the eagle. The purpose is to remind Job of the wisdom and power of the one who sustains all things.

For today: we do not need to understand everything to trust God. When something in your life has no explanation, look at what God sustains each day, and rest in the fact that he is wise and faithful.
exp.18:21:
Job asks his friends why they pursue him as though they were God, and why they will never get enough of tormenting his body. He is saying that they keep attacking him and speaking against him without stopping, as if they could never have their fill.

Job speaks while sick and in pain, after losing his children, his possessions, and his health. His friends insist that he suffers because of some hidden sin. Job feels that God is striking him, and that instead of comforting him, they add to his anguish. Soon after, he wishes that his words could be written down forever.

For today: when someone is suffering, there is no need to explain why or to judge them. Accompany them with patience, listening and compassion. And if you yourself are suffering, you may express your pain honestly before God.
exp.29:22:
Here Job says he is sure that God will bring him down to death, to the place appointed for all the living, that is, the grave, the place set aside for every human being. The phrase "you will bring me down" carries the sense of "you will lead me down" or "you will take me there." "All the living" means everyone who is alive.

Job speaks in the midst of great suffering. He has lost his health, his possessions, and the respect of others. He feels that God, once so close, has now become harsh toward him. His complaint is sincere and desperate, and it should not be taken as the final word of the book, since God himself will answer later on.

For today: when suffering makes you doubt God, do not hide your pain. You can tell him honestly what you feel, as Job did, and keep seeking him even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.24:5:
This verse compares human beings to a maggot and a worm to show how small and frail we are before God. The phrase "how much less" means "much less": if even the moon and the stars do not shine bright enough before God, then how much less does a human being. The phrase "son of man" is another way of saying "human being."

The speaker is Bildad, one of Job's three friends. This is his last and shortest speech. He wants to prove that no one can stand clean before God. His idea of God's greatness is true, but he uses it to silence Job, and at the end God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: acknowledge with humility that you need God, but do not stay in discouragement. Other parts of the Bible show that God cares for us and values us. Ask Him for forgiveness and help with confidence, without pride and without looking down on yourself.
exp.19:27:
It says that what the wicked person leaves behind, such as his possessions and his household, will be removed and swept away. The phrase "flowing away" pictures wealth draining off like water, so that nothing is left to hold onto. "On the day of God's wrath" points to the time when God judges wickedness, and the loss is tied to that judgment.

Zophar, one of Job's three friends, is the speaker. He believes that anyone who suffers this way is a wicked person being punished by God. He describes well the final fate of the wicked, but he is wrong to apply it to Job, who was innocent. The book itself shows that his reasoning was incomplete.

For today: do not build your life on what does not last. Seek justice and trust in God. And when someone suffers, do not judge them quickly; walk alongside them with compassion.
exp.32:23:
This verse speaks of a messenger who tells the sick person that God has shown compassion toward them. It says that God spares them from going down to the Pit, that is, to death, and that God has found a ransom, a phrase that here can be understood as a price paid that sets someone free. The wording can also be understood as God himself speaking and saying: "Spare him; I have found his ransom."

The one speaking is Elihu, a young man who steps in at the end of Job's discussions with his friends. He explains that God sometimes corrects a person through suffering. If a faithful messenger reminds the sufferer of his duty and announces God's mercy, the sick person may be restored. Scholars debate the exact meaning of "ransom" in this passage.

For today: when someone is suffering, do not judge them; approach them with words of hope and remind them that God is merciful and can give new life.
exp.22:13:
He says that God carries out his decree against him, and that God has many plans like it. "Carries out" means he brings it to completion, and "decree" means something firmly decided. "Has many such plans" means God has many more of the same kind held in reserve.

Job speaks here as a man who suffers greatly and does not understand why. He feels innocent, for he says he treasured the words of God more than his daily food. He longs to find God and state his case, but cannot locate him. So he acknowledges that no one can stop what God has decided, and this fills him with fear and confusion.

For today: when you do not understand what you are going through, you can trust that God is still at work, even when you cannot see the reason. Bring your confusion honestly before him, as Job did, and keep following him one step at a time.
exp.19:28:
This is what God prepares for the wicked person: the share he has set aside for him. The phrase "is the portion" points to a share that falls to someone, and "God has appointed" shows that it is a sentence decided by God.

Zophar, one of Job's three friends, speaks. With this speech he closes his contribution, describing how the wicked man ends: his possessions are lost and everything rises against him. Zophar takes it for granted that Job suffers because of his wickedness. The book itself later shows that this conclusion was mistaken, and that God rebukes these friends.

For today: God's justice is real, but we should not use this verse to judge someone who is suffering. Instead, let us trust that God is just, and accompany those who suffer with compassion, without accusing them.
exp.18:14:
Here Job says that even the people who lived in his own house, including his maidservants, treated him as a stranger. His guests and servants saw him as an outsider, as if he were a foreigner among them. Job felt like a foreigner in his own home.

Job speaks as a man who lost everything: his possessions, his children, and his health. His friends accuse him that his suffering is punishment for some sin. In this chapter Job describes his loneliness: relatives, acquaintances, servants, and even his wife withdrew from him. He is crying out in pain and does not hide what he feels.

For today: if you are going through a trial and feel that others are pulling away, you are not alone. You can tell God honestly about your pain, as Job did. And if you know someone who is suffering, draw near to them with kindness, without judging them.
exp.7:3:
This verse says: "When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion." The phrase "gave them over to their rebellion" means that He left them to the result of what they chose to do.

Bildad speaks, one of Job's three friends. Job had just lost his children and everything else. Bildad believes that God never bends justice, so he assumes the children died because of their own guilt. In the end, God himself says that the friends did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7). Their view is partial and very harsh.

For today: when someone suffers, let us not explain it with quick answers or place the blame on them. Better to accompany them with presence, prayer and tenderness, trusting that God is just even when we do not understand everything.
exp.18:20:
Job begs his friends to show him compassion. He says it twice, because his pain is very great. In the verse you are reading, the words "have pity on me" appear, and the two requests together show how desperate he feels. Job believes that "the hand of God" has struck him, meaning that his suffering comes from God or is allowed by Him.

Job speaks as a man who has lost everything: his children, his possessions, and his health. His three friends came to comfort him, but they ended up accusing him, saying he was suffering because of some hidden sin. Job feels alone, rejected by relatives and acquaintances. Here he stops arguing and asks for tenderness, not explanations.

For today: when someone is suffering, they often do not need us to correct them or explain why it is happening. They need presence, listening, and kindness. And if you are suffering, you can ask for help honestly, as Job did, without pretending you are fine.
exp.4:25:
The explanation says that the person who trusts in God will reach a long and peaceful old age, and that their death will be like that of a heap of grain gathered in when it is ripe. The word for "grave" is the tomb. The word "gathered" means "gathered in" or "harvested."

Eliphaz, a friend of Job, speaks in his first speech. He wants to comfort Job and promises him that, if he humbles himself before God and accepts his correction, God will restore him. However, Eliphaz assumes that Job's suffering is due to his sin, and at the end of the book God says that his friends did not speak well of Him. For this reason, this promise is beautiful, but it is not a rule for every case.

For today: trust that your life is in God's hands, and live each stage with gratitude, without judging others for their sufferings.
exp.22:16:
Job wonders why he was not taken out of life before the darkness arrived, and why God has hidden the darkness from his sight. "Taken out of life" simply means he would rather have died than endured this. The darkness stands for his pain and confusion. This verse is hard to read, and scholars differ in how they understand it, but its overall meaning is clear: Job is in deep anguish.

Job speaks from the middle of his suffering. His friends insist that he must have sinned, but he knows he has done nothing to deserve this and wants to lay his case before God. Yet he cannot find him, and this fills him with fear and bewilderment. That is why he says God has troubled him.

For today: when darkness surrounds you and you cannot understand what God is doing, you can bring him your complaint with honesty, as Job did. The Bible does not hide pain; it teaches us to be sincere before God and to keep seeking him, even without answers.
exp.8:5:
This verse says that God shakes the earth from its place, so that its foundations tremble. It is poetic language: the earth is pictured as a structure resting on foundations. It does not describe a scientific explanation, but rather the enormous power of God.

Job, a man who suffers greatly, is speaking. He is answering his friend Bildad and acknowledges that God is wise and powerful. But he says it with pain: he wonders how a human being could defend himself before someone so great. For this reason he lists things God controls: mountains, earth, sun and stars.

For today: when you feel that everything is being shaken in your life, remember that God is greater than whatever makes you tremble. You can draw near to Him with humility and sincerity, even with your questions and your pain, trusting that He continues to hold up what you cannot.
exp.34:3:
Elihu says to Job: "I will reply to you and to your friends as well." The word "arguments" is not in this verse, so it is left out here, along with the comment about the old spelling of "to."

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who listened quietly to the debate between Job and his three friends. He thinks Job has defended himself too much, as if he were more righteous than God. So he wants to correct him, and at the same time correct the friends, who had not managed to convince him. Some readers see Elihu as wise and others see him as somewhat presumptuous; the Bible does not make this entirely clear.

For today: before answering someone who is suffering, or defending ourselves, it is good to listen carefully and speak with humility. God is greater than our complaints, and we can come to Him with sincerity, without thinking ourselves more righteous than He is.
exp.29:27:
He says Job goes about blackened, meaning darkened or gloomy, though not from the sun. His face and his spirit are shadowed by suffering. He also stands up in the assembly and cries out for help. Some readers understand the blackening as the darkness of his grief, while others see it as pointing to his diseased skin.

Job speaks here in the midst of his pain. He had hoped for good and light, but received evil and darkness. He lost his possessions, his children, and his health. Here he complains that he finds no relief even among people. His friends judge him instead of comforting him.

For today: if you are going through a dark season, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. Job cried out honestly. Be open with God and seek out someone you trust who will listen to you with patience and without judging you.
exp.41:9:
God restored Job's fortunes after he prayed for his friends. The phrase "restored his prosperity" means that God brought back what Job had lost, or made his situation good again. "Doubled" means that God gave him back twice what he had before.

The narrator is the author of the book. After many speeches, God had corrected Job's three friends, because they had not spoken rightly about him. God asked them to offer a sacrifice and to have Job pray for them. Job obeyed, although those friends had wounded him with their words.

For today: when someone has hurt you, praying for that person can heal your heart. It is not a formula for receiving things, but it is a step toward forgiveness and peace, and God cares for those who trust in him.
exp.3:20:
It says that what makes a person valuable or admirable ends when they die. They die without having reached true wisdom. The verse here uses the image of tent cords being pulled up, so that the whole dwelling collapses and comes down. The Hebrew text can be understood in several ways.

It is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, who speaks. He describes a night vision to show that human beings are frail and imperfect before God. His intention is to suggest that Job is suffering because of some sin. But at the end of the book God says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him, so we should read their speeches with care.

Today: live with humility, remembering that our life is brief and that true wisdom is trusting in God. And do not judge another person's suffering as if it were punishment; rather, accompany them with compassion.
exp.33:20:
He says that God looks closely at the life of every person. "His eyes are on the ways of a man" means that he observes the way we live, and "He sees his every step" means that nothing we do escapes him. In the text, "He" refers to God.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job and his three friends have argued. Elihu maintains that God is just, that he has no favorites and is not swayed by power or wealth. Because God sees everything, there is no place where the wicked can hide. Some scholars think Elihu is right in general, but that he applies these truths poorly to Job's suffering.

For today: live with integrity, even when no one sees you. And if you feel overlooked, remember that God sees your path and your steps.
exp.8:15:
He says that Job, even if he called out to God and God answered him, would still doubt that God had really listened to him. The word "called" in the verse you see means calling out to someone, and "answered" means replying. It is not that Job denies that God hears, but that he feels so much pain and confusion that even an answer would not give him certainty.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering, replying to his friend Bildad. He has lost his children, his possessions and his health, and he feels that God treats him harshly without explaining why. He admits that God is so great that no one can face him as in a trial. It is the honest language of a wounded man; not everything Job says is correct, and in the end God himself answers him.

Today, if you feel that God is far away or silent, you can be honest with him, as Job was. Keep praying even with doubts, and seek support from people of faith and from his Word.
exp.27:16:
It says that wisdom is worth more than gold and any jewel. Neither gold, nor crystal (the Hebrew word may refer to glass or crystal, and it is not known for certain), nor jewels of fine gold can be exchanged for it. "Cannot compare to it" means that no amount of gold or jewels can match wisdom's value.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering and his debates with his friends. This chapter is a poem showing that people know how to draw treasures out of the earth, but cannot discover wisdom on their own. At the end, Job says that wisdom is to fear the Lord (v. 28).

For today: before seeking money or success, ask God for wisdom to decide well. Set aside time each day to listen to him in his Word, because that is worth more than any gain.
exp.39:6:
First, a detail: in some Spanish Bibles this text appears as Job 40:11-12, not 40:7. Verse 11 says that Job should look at every proud person and bring him low, and tread down the wicked where they stand. "Bring him low" means to cast him down, to make him come down.

Here God is speaking, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had questioned divine justice, and God challenges him, with irony, to brace himself like a man and rule the world. If Job could himself overcome pride and wickedness, God would admit that Job's own hand could save him. The point is that Job cannot, and that only God governs with justice.

For today: when the injustice or pride of others frustrates you, remember that judging the world belongs to God, not to you. Trust in his justice, and examine your own heart as well.
exp.28:13:
He says Job "put on" righteousness, meaning that doing what is right was part of his everyday life, like the clothing a person puts on. Righteousness fit him like a cloak, a covering that wrapped around him. Where the verse speaks of a "turban," it means a headpiece worn on the head, and "justice" here means acting with uprightness and fairness.

Job speaks in the middle of his suffering. He remembers with longing what his life was like before he lost everything. The verses before and after show that he helped the poor, the fatherless, and the widow. Job maintains that his conduct was honest and compassionate, while his friends accuse him of wickedness. Some scholars see here a sincere defense; others note that Job focuses a great deal on himself.

For today: ask yourself whether your way of treating others, at work, at home, or in business, is just and compassionate, like a garment you always wear. This week, concretely help someone who has no one to defend them.
exp.18:4:
Job 19:5 in the wording of your verse: "If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me and use my disgrace against me." Here Job says that his friends consider themselves better than he is and use his suffering and his shame as an argument to accuse him. The phrase "exalt yourselves above me" means rising up with pride, looking down on another from above. "Disgrace" means dishonor or humiliation. "Use against me" means putting it forward as proof.

Job speaks here in the middle of his pain. His friends, such as Bildad, insist that he suffers because of some hidden sin. Job has already told them that, if he has done wrong, that error is his own concern. He does not deny being a sinner, but he rejects the idea that his suffering is proof of guilt. He feels wounded by those who should be comforting him.

For today: when someone suffers, let us avoid quick explanations and judgments. It is better to accompany them with presence, listening and humility, because we do not always know what God is doing in another person's life.
exp.34:7:
Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of man. This verse says that the wrong you do touches people like you, and the good you do also benefits them. "Wickedness" means living without reverence for God, and "righteousness" means living in what is right and good before Him. "Son of man" here simply means an ordinary human being.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the debate between Job and his friends. He wants to correct Job, because he believes Job has suggested that his righteousness should oblige God to act. Elihu answers that God does not depend on our conduct. Some scholars think his arguments have a measure of truth, but that they are misapplied to Job's suffering.

For today: our decisions are never only private. What we do, good or bad, touches our family, friends, and neighbors. Today you can choose one concrete act of kindness or honesty that blesses someone close to you, not thinking that in this way you are "paying" God back, but loving Him and others.
exp.37:1:
Here God asks a sharp question: who is the one who obscures God's counsel by speaking without understanding? "Counsel" means the purpose or design of God. "Obscures" means making it unclear. And "without knowledge" points to words spoken without true understanding.

The LORD speaks, and he does so out of a whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and, after many speeches from himself and his friends, was asking God for answers. Now God responds, but he does not explain the reason for the suffering; he invites Job to consider his greatness. Some think the question is aimed mainly at Job, although the friends had also spoken wrongly.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, speak with humility. You may weep and ask questions, but do not conclude that God is unjust. Trust that his wisdom is greater than yours.
exp.40:0:
Here God asks whether a person could catch Leviathan, a huge and fearsome creature, by using a hook or by tying down its tongue with a rope. The question expects a "no": no one is able to subdue that creature.

God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind, almost at the end of the book. Job had suffered greatly and had questioned God. God does not explain his reasons to him; instead, he shows him his power in creation. It is not known with certainty what animal Leviathan is; some think of the crocodile, others of a symbolic creature of chaos.

Today, this verse invites us to recognize that we do not control everything. When something overwhelms us, we can rest in the fact that God does govern, even when we do not understand why.
exp.15:20:
This verse expresses a wish of Job: that someone could plead his case before God in the same way a person pleads with a neighbor. "Plead" means to argue or make a case, and the neighbor is the person who lives next door. Some readers understand that Job is longing for someone to stand between him and God and speak on his behalf.

The one speaking is Job, a man who suffers greatly and does not understand why. His friends accuse him and judge him without giving him comfort. For this reason Job looks up to heaven and says that there he has a witness. He feels that God is so great that he cannot speak to Him as an equal, and he longs for fair treatment. He also sees his death drawing near.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand, do not keep silent or pretend to a strength you do not have. Bring your questions to God with sincerity, for He listens to the one who cries out honestly. Look also for friends who will walk with you, not ones who will judge you.
exp.0:14:
Some men called Sabeans attacked, carried off the oxen and the donkeys, and put the servants to the sword. The word "servants" here means young servants or workers, and the phrase "put to the sword" means they were killed with weapons. The messenger is the only one who managed to escape to tell what happened.

A messenger speaks, one of Job's workers. He arrives with news of the first blow in a series of misfortunes that Job receives in a single day. The Sabeans were a people from southern Arabia, as is commonly thought. The book has already told us that Job was an upright and very wealthy man, and that God allowed this trial.

When bad news comes, sometimes one after another, we are not alone. We can bring our pain honestly to God, as Job did, and ask him for strength for the next step.
exp.39:12:
1) What it says: This text appears in most Bibles as Job 40:18. It describes the strength of a creature called Behemoth. Its bones are as strong as bronze, and its limbs are as firm as iron bars. The "members" are the legs or the body. It is not known for certain which animal this is: some think of a hippopotamus or an elephant, and others of a more symbolic creature.

2) Context: God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. After so much suffering and so many questions, God shows him his power in creation. If Job cannot master this creature, neither can he judge the plans of the one who made it.

3) For today: When you do not understand what you are going through, remember that God is greater than any force that frightens you. Rest in his wisdom and trust him with humility.
exp.31:11:
Elihu says that he paid full attention to Job's three friends. After listening to them, he states that none of them was able to prove Job wrong, and none of them rebutted his arguments. "I paid full attention to you" is what the phrase about listening closely means.

Elihu, a young man who had kept silent out of respect for his elders, now speaks up. He waited while listening to Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, but they stopped talking without proving Job wrong. Elihu is angry because Job was justifying himself before God and the friends did not answer his arguments well. The verses that follow show that he does not want them to excuse themselves by saying that only God could correct Job.

For today: before correcting someone, listen with patience and speak with truth, not just with many words. A good answer requires attention, humility, and arguments that truly help.
exp.20:7:
It says the wicked see their descendants become firmly established around them and prosper. "Descendants" means their children and grandchildren, and "offspring" refers to the young ones who are growing up. "Established" means firm and well settled. They take delight in watching their family grow.

Job speaks in reply to his friends, who maintain that things always go badly for the wicked. Job points to what he himself observes: many who live without God enjoy family, health and wealth. For this reason he confesses that he is amazed and trembles. His complaint is sincere, and he seeks to understand the apparent injustice.

For today: when you see that someone who lives badly is doing well, do not become bitter or doubt God. Bring that question to Him honestly, as Job did, and remember that prosperity in this life is nobody's final judgment.
exp.15:21:
This verse says that only a few years of life are left to him, and that he will soon set out on a road from which there is no return, that is, death. The phrase "only a few years are past" means a limited number of years that are almost used up. "I will go the way" is a poetic way of speaking about dying. The phrase "the way of no return" shows that there will be no coming back to this life.

The one speaking is Job, in the middle of enormous suffering. His friends accuse him and argue with him instead of comforting him, so he weeps before God and longs for a righteous advocate. He feels close to death and wants someone to recognize his innocence before he departs.

For today: life is brief, and that invites us not to put off what is important. When you suffer, bring your pain to God with sincerity, as Job did. And when you accompany someone who is suffering, listen and comfort more than you argue.
exp.37:32:
God asks Job whether he knows the laws that govern the heavens, that is, the order of the stars and the seasons. He also asks whether Job can make that order rule over the earth. The verse's word "laws" means the fixed rules that the heavens follow, and "dominion" means power or rule. The expected answer is: no.

Here God speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him the reasons for his pain, but shows him his wisdom in creation, so that Job can see how limited his knowledge is. The names of the constellations are translated in different ways, and not all scholars agree on which they are.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening to you, remember that God sustains an orderly universe that you do not control. You can rest in his care, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.2:2:
Job wishes that the day of his birth would vanish, and also the night when someone announced that a boy had been conceived. The word "perish" means that it would come to an end and cease to exist. Job is not cursing God, but the day of his birth, and he expresses a grief so great that he would rather never have been born.

Job speaks after losing nearly everything: his children, his property, and his health. Until now he had kept silent beside his friends. Here he breaks that silence and opens the book of his laments. Scholars see these words as poetry of deep grief, not as teaching about what we should think of life.

For today: if you are suffering, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you feel, even your darkest thoughts. He hears honest pain. And if someone close to you speaks this way, stay with them patiently, without rushing to give them answers.
exp.14:34:
He says that the wicked "conceive trouble," meaning they plan or carry evil within them, and what they give birth to is "evil," that is, wickedness and injustice. Their inner being is full of "deceit," thoughts of lies and trickery, and that is what they produce. It is an image of pregnancy and birth: what is carried inside ends up coming out.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. In this speech he describes the fate of the wicked, and he implies that Job is suffering because of some hidden sin. Although his words sound wise, God later says that the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7). So this general principle does not apply to Job.

For today: take care what you feed in your heart, because thoughts end up in actions. And do not judge the suffering of others as if it were always punishment.
exp.41:1:
Job tells God that he acknowledges that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted. The word "know" here means that he has understood it and admits it. The idea of a "plan" stands out in this verse: God's purposes cannot be blocked or overturned, and nothing human thought can keep hidden from Him.
