Job speaks after God answered him out of the whirlwind, showing him His greatness in creation. Before this, Job had suffered greatly and had asked many questions about his pain. Now he answers with humility. The lines that follow, which Job repeats from what God said to him, show that he recognizes he spoke about things he could not understand.

For today: when you do not understand why things happen, you can rest in the fact that God does not lose control and does not ignore what you think and feel. Speak to Him with sincerity, but with humility, trusting that He knows more than you can see.
exp.4:12:
It says that God catches those who think they are wise in their own craftiness, and that the plans of cunning people get swept away. The word translated "catches" means to seize or take hold of. The word for "craftiness" refers to skill in deceiving or manipulating others.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. He tries to comfort and encourage Job to trust God, since God lifts up the humble and frustrates the crafty. Notice that the apostle Paul quotes this line in 1 Corinthians 3:19, but the book of Job shows that Eliphaz's advice was not always correct. So this general truth about God is certain, even though Eliphaz applies it wrongly to Job.

Today, do not rely on tricks, shortcuts, or deceit to get ahead. Seek to act with honesty and humility, and leave justice in God's hands, because human wisdom without God is fragile.
exp.37:23:
God asks in which direction the lightning is spread out and how the east wind is scattered over the earth. The east wind is the wind that blows from the east, which in that region was often dry and strong. "Dispersed" means the lightning is sent out or carried to different places. Some scholars understand the word for lightning here as the light of day, since the Hebrew allows either reading.

Here God himself speaks, answering Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered greatly and was asking for explanations. God does not give him reasons for his pain, but asks him questions about creation, to show him how great his wisdom is and how small human knowledge is.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God governs things you cannot control, such as the lightning and the wind. Rest in the fact that he is wise and trustworthy, even when you do not have all the answers.
exp.20:16:
The verse says that the lamp of the wicked goes out, meaning that their prosperity or their life comes to an end. Then disaster falls on them, and God, in his anger, apportions destruction to them.

Job speaks here in reply to his friends, who insisted that the wicked always suffer quickly. Job shows them that many wicked people live at ease and prosper (vv. 7-16). For this reason, some understand this verse as a question: "How often is the lamp of the wicked put out?", with the sense of "rarely." Others read it as a statement, or as an idea of the friends that Job quotes. Scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: let us not judge the lives of others by their success or their pain. Let us trust that God is just, even when we cannot see everything now.
exp.5:14:
He says that his friends, whom he calls "brothers," have proven faithless, like the wadis of a dry land that seem dependable but fail. "Faithless" means they did not keep the support they promised. The wadis are seasonal streams that overflow in the rainy season and then run dry, leaving the traveler with nothing.

Job speaks in the middle of great suffering. He has lost his children, his possessions, and his health. His friend Eliphaz answered him with reproaches instead of comfort. Job hoped for compassion but found criticism. That is why he compares his friends to the seasonal streams: they promise water, but they fail when the traveler most needs it.

For today: when someone suffers, they do not need speeches first, but presence, listening, and tenderness. Try to be a steady friend who walks alongside others with patience, without rushing to judge. And if people fail you, remember that God does remain faithful.
exp.3:0:
Here begins the first speech of Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends. "Replied" means that he responds to Job's complaints in chapter 3. "Temanite" means that he came from Teman, a place associated with Edom, and he was known for his wisdom.

Job had just lamented his pain and wished he had never been born. His friends had come to comfort him, and they had sat with him in silence for seven days. Now Eliphaz speaks first, with a tone that is at first kind. Later, however, he will suggest that Job is suffering because of some sin, and God will say afterward that the friends did not speak rightly about Him.

For today: before answering someone who is suffering, learn to listen with patience. Ask yourself whether your words of comfort truly encourage them, or whether they only defend your own ideas about suffering.
exp.35:24:
Everyone can see God's work. The "it" refers to the work of the Lord described in the previous verse. The phrase "men behold it from afar" means that people see it from a distance, so they cannot fully understand it, but they can still look upon it and take notice.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who spoke after Job's three friends. He maintains that God is just and that no one can correct him. He invites Job to praise God for his creation, especially for the rain and the storms, which are described in the verses that follow. Some scholars see his words as wise, others as somewhat presumptuous.

Today we can stop to look at the sky, the rain, or a sunrise, and give thanks. Even though we do not understand everything, we can trust that God is great and good.
exp.1:2:
God asks Satan whether he has noticed Job. He calls him "my servant" and says there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil. God adds that Job still keeps his integrity, meaning he remains steadfast, even though Satan incited God against him to ruin him without cause, that is, without any just reason.

This happens in a scene where Satan appears before God for a second time. Job had already lost his children and his possessions, yet he had not cursed God. Satan will answer that Job only endures because his body has been spared. The text does not explain every mystery of suffering; it shows only that Job was not suffering because of some hidden sin.

For today: not all suffering is punishment. If you go through a trial, keep trusting God, and do not judge harshly those who suffer.
exp.3:11:
It says that a word came to him in secret. The word "word" here means a message, not a business deal. "Secretly" means it had not been shown to him openly. And "my ears caught a whisper of it" means he heard only a faint sound, a small part of what was being said.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. He wants to comfort and correct Job in his suffering, and to give weight to his words he relates a night-time experience he says he had. What follows is a vision that filled him with fear. Note: the Bible records his words, but later God says that Eliphaz and his friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).

For today: not everything that sounds spiritual or claims to come from a deep experience is the word of God. Test what you hear against the Scriptures, and be careful when you comfort others.
exp.21:16:
These are wicked people who said to God, "Depart from us." Then they ask, "What can the Almighty do to us?" That is, they pushed God away as if he could do nothing to them.

The speaker is Eliphaz, one of Job's friends. By recalling these wicked people of the past, who were suddenly destroyed, he tries to warn Job, since he takes for granted that Job's suffering is punishment for his sin. But the book later shows that Eliphaz was wrong to judge Job (Job 42:7). Some think the verse alludes to the flood, but the text does not say so clearly.

For today: God has given us many blessings, and it is easy to live without thanking him or taking him into account. Thank God today for something specific. And do not judge the pain of others as if it were always punishment.
exp.40:24:
When Leviathan rises up, even the mightiest are terrified, and they withdraw before his thrashing. Their courage gives way, and they are left unable to stand their ground.

The one speaking is God, who answers Job out of the whirlwind. He describes Leviathan, a powerful and fearsome creature, to show Job that he cannot stand against it. If Job cannot deal with this creature, how much less can he argue with the Creator.

For today: when something frightens you because it is greater than you, remember that God is greater. Come to Him with humility and trust, without pretending to understand everything.
exp.38:11:
God says the wild ox cannot be tamed. He asks Job whether that animal would agree to serve him or stay the night at his feeding trough. The Hebrew word refers to a wild bull, strong and impossible to subdue. It is probably the aurochs, now extinct, although scholars are not completely sure. It is not the magical horse of the stories.

God himself speaks to Job out of the whirlwind. After Job suffered greatly and asked for explanations, God shows him wild animals that live outside human control. With this he reminds him that creation is far greater than Job can manage or understand.

Today, this invites us to humility. We cannot control or understand everything that happens. When something slips out of our hands, we can rest in the knowledge that God does know what he is doing and cares for his creation.
exp.37:38:
The verse you are reading says: "Can you hunt the prey for a lioness or satisfy the hunger of young lions?" God is asking Job whether he could find food for a lioness and fill the hunger of her young. The "prey" is the animal the lion hunts to eat, and to "satisfy the hunger" means to leave the lions full, with nothing left to crave.

Here God himself speaks, from the whirlwind, answering Job. Job had spent chapters complaining and asking for explanations of his suffering. God does not give him explanations; instead he asks questions about creation to show Job his wisdom and his care. The verses before speak of the rain and the dry ground, and God continues with the animals that follow.

For today: if God feeds the lion, he also cares for you. When you do not understand what you are living through, trust the one who sustains all creation.
exp.21:26:
It says that if a person turns back to God, they will be able to pray to him with confidence, and God will listen. Then that person will fulfill their vows, that is, the promises they made to God. The verse says that you will pray to Him, He will hear you, and you will fulfill your vows.

The one speaking is Eliphaz, a friend of Job. He believes Job is suffering because of some sin, and he advises him to repent so that he can be restored. His idea that suffering is always punishment is not correct, because at the end of the book God rebukes Eliphaz and his companions for not speaking rightly about Him. Even so, this verse reflects a truth: God hears those who draw near to Him.

Today we can pray with the assurance that God hears us, and be faithful in keeping the commitments we make to Him, without making promises lightly.
exp.0:3:
This verse tells us that Job's sons held feasts with food and drink, each one hosting in his own home and taking turns. The verse says they would take turns, so each son had his day to host. They also invited their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not Job. He describes the life of a large, close, and blessed family. Some understand that these feasts lasted several days and were repeated in cycles; the text gives no further detail. What follows shows that Job, concerned for his children, offered sacrifices on their behalf.

For today: value the times of family fellowship and, like Job, pray for your own family. Enjoying one another's company is good, but it also helps to regularly place your family before God.
exp.33:25:
It says that God punishes the wicked in a public way, in full view of everyone. The phrase "for their wickedness" means "because of the evil they have done," and "strikes them" means he hits them or brings them down. The idea is that his judgment is not hidden.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who joins the conversation in the book of Job after the three friends. He tries to argue that God is just and does not act with evil. The verses that follow say these wicked people turned away from God and ignored the cry of the poor. Elihu does not always get everything right, and later God corrects Job's friends, so it is wise to read him with care.

For today: God sees injustice and hears the needy. We can trust that he will judge with justice, and in the meantime we should treat those who suffer with compassion and honesty.
exp.21:29:
He says that God will deliver even one who is not innocent, and that you will be rescued through the cleanness of your hands, that is, an honest life. The phrase "one who is not innocent" is the key here: the verse speaks of God's mercy reaching someone who has done wrong, not only someone who has never sinned. The rescue comes through the cleanness of your hands, which points to a life turned back toward what is right.

The speaker is Eliphaz, a friend of Job. He believes Job is suffering because of some hidden sin, and he encourages him to turn back to God so that he may be restored. But God later says that Eliphaz did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7), so his advice should not be taken as a rule.

For today: God cares for those who seek Him sincerely, but let us not judge anyone who suffers as if it were punishment. Let us accompany them with compassion and live with clean hands out of love for God.
exp.8:26:
Here Job says: "If I were to say, 'I will forget my complaint and change my expression and smile.'" His complaint is the lament and pain he has been voicing, and changing his expression and smile means putting on a cheerful face and pretending his sorrow is gone.

Job speaks in the midst of great suffering, answering his friend Bildad. He has just said that his days pass swiftly and without joy. Although he tries to encourage himself, the next verse shows that his pains frighten him and he feels that God will not declare him innocent. His determination clashes with his anguish.

For today: when you suffer, do not pressure yourself to pretend everything is fine. It is honest to tell God that it is hard for you to take heart. Pour out your pain to him sincerely, and also seek the support of brothers and sisters who will listen to you without judging you.
exp.13:2:
Here Job asks God: "Do You open Your eyes to one like this?" He is speaking of the human being, whom he has just described as frail and short-lived. To open one's eyes to someone means to watch that person closely. To bring someone into judgment means to bring them before a court. Job is amazed that God would fix His gaze so closely on a creature so weak and fleeting.

Job speaks here in the midst of his great suffering. He feels examined and judged by God, though he acknowledges that man is like a flower that is cut down and a shadow that flees. His complaint is sincere, and some scholars see it as a cry for compassion rather than a cold accusation.

For today: when you feel frail or worn out, you can bring your questions to God with complete honesty, as Job did. He is not frightened by your weakness, and you can ask him for mercy and rest.
exp.30:25:
It says that Job did not look at the radiant sun or the splendid moon in order to worship them. The phrase is part of a condition: "if I have done this...". In this verse, looking is not simply seeing, but looking with admiration that leads to devotion.

Job speaks as he defends his integrity before his friends, who accuse him of having sinned. In this chapter he lists possible sins and states that he did not commit them. Earlier he spoke of not trusting in gold; now he speaks of not worshiping the heavenly bodies. For him, both would be giving to creation the place that belongs to God.

We can enjoy the beauty of creation, but we should not place our hearts in it. Today the "heavenly bodies" may be success, image, or money. Give thanks to God for the good things you have, and ask yourself: what do I admire so much that it could take the place of God?
exp.13:20:
He says that after a person dies, he no longer knows what happens to his children. If they receive honor, he does not know it; if they are brought low, he is unaware. The phrase "ó" means "o," and "no entenderá de ellos" means that he will have no knowledge of their situation.

Job speaks here in the middle of enormous suffering, answering his friends. He reflects on the frailty of human life and feels weak before God. In this passage he expresses what he sees from within his pain: death seems to cut every bond with this life. It is the lament of a man, not a complete teaching on what happens after death; the Bible develops that subject more fully in other passages.

Today, this truth invites us not to postpone love. Bless, advise and embrace your children and your family while you can, and entrust them to God, who always cares for them.
exp.33:35:
Elihu says he wants Job to be examined or tested to the utmost. The reason is that Job answered like a wicked man. The word "tried" here refers to being examined, not necessarily punished. Some translators understand the wish as a plea, while others read it with a harsher tone.

The speaker is Elihu, a young man who steps in after Job's three friends. He believes Job has justified himself and has spoken wrongly about God. For this reason he accuses Job of adding rebellion to his sin. Keep in mind that at the end of the book, God does not fully support either Job or his friends, and does not mention Elihu, so his words should be read with care.

For today: before judging harshly someone who is suffering, listen to them with patience and humility. Only God sees the heart completely.
exp.35:32:
This verse is difficult and is translated in several ways. The thunder declares God's presence, and the storm it announces is about to arrive. Some readers take the cattle's reaction to mean that even the animals sense the storm coming.

Elihu, the young man who speaks before Job and his friends, describes the clouds, the light and the thunder to show that God is powerful and just. He wants Job to recognize God's greatness and not to judge him.

For today: just as thunder warns before the rain falls, creation reminds us that God is real and great. When you notice your pride, stop, humble yourself and pray calmly.
exp.6:20:
Job asks God why he does not pardon his offense (his failing or wrongdoing) and take away his guilt (his evil or fault). He says that soon he will "lie down in the dust," meaning he will die and be buried. He adds that when God seeks him, he will be gone.

Job speaks as a man who is suffering greatly, answering his friend Eliphaz. He feels worn out and believes God is watching him closely. Although he admits that he has sinned, he does not accept that his pain is punishment for any particular sin. Some scholars see here a complaint; others, a sincere prayer. His life seems brief and fragile to him.

For today: when you suffer, you can speak to God with complete honesty, even with painful questions. And do not wait until life is over to ask for forgiveness and mercy; he hears you now.
exp.30:3:
Here Job says that God sees everything he does: where he walks and every step he takes. "Ways" refers to his manner of life, and "count my every step" shows that nothing escapes God. The question is rhetorical, since the answer is plainly yes.

Job speaks in the midst of his suffering. His friends suggest that he suffers because of some hidden sin. In chapter 31 he defends himself and makes a list of what he has avoided: lust, deceit, injustice. He recalls that God punishes wickedness, and so he wishes to be examined on the scales of justice, confident of his integrity.

For today: living as someone who knows God sees them need not produce fear, but sincerity. Before deciding something in private, ask yourself: "Could I present this to God with a clear conscience?" And if you fail, come to Him in humility.
exp.17:8:
He says the wicked person will be caught like an animal in a trap. The "snare" is a rope with a sliding knot that will grip him by the heel. "A trap seizes his heel" means the trap will snap shut on him with force, and he will not be able to get free.

Bildad speaks, one of Job's three friends. He takes for granted that Job is suffering because he is wicked, and so he describes how the wicked person falls. Although some of his ideas sound wise, the same book shows that he is wrong to apply them to Job, since God declares him blameless (Job 1:8; 42:7).

For today: be careful about explaining other people's pain with quick answers. Before judging someone who is suffering, walk alongside them with humility and listen. And examine your own ways honestly, because sin often does entangle us.
exp.18:16:
Job says that his breath, meaning the smell of his mouth or his breathing, has become repulsive to his wife. He says he is loathsome to his own family, so even though he pleaded with her for the sake of the children, she would not come near him.

Job speaks after losing his possessions and his children and falling seriously ill. He feels rejected by everyone: his servants, his wife, his friends. Some understand "my own family" to refer to children who had already died, or perhaps to his brothers; the Hebrew text allows more than one reading.

When someone suffers, sometimes the people closest to them pull away. We can do the opposite: draw near to the one who is going through pain, listen without judging, and accompany them with patience, even when we do not know what to say.
exp.35:0:
This verse says that Elihu went on speaking. The word "continued" in this translation shows that he carries on with his speech. It is a transitional phrase, but it signals that a new part of his words is coming.

Elihu is a young man who had listened in silence to the debate between Job and his three friends. From chapter 32 on he speaks because he is upset with everyone: with Job for defending himself so much, and with the friends for not answering him well. Here he begins his fourth speech, and right away he says he wants to defend the justice of God. Some readers see in him a wise voice; others see a voice that is somewhat arrogant. The Bible does not make this entirely clear.

For today: before speaking about God or advising someone who is suffering, let us listen with patience. And when we speak, let us do so with humility, without assuming that we understand everything.
exp.12:2:
It says that Job prefers to speak directly with the Almighty. "Argue my case" means presenting his matter and making his point, as in an honest conversation. Job no longer wants to keep debating with people; he wants to bring his matter before God himself.

Job is speaking, a man who suffers greatly and does not understand why. His three friends tell him that his pain is punishment for some hidden sin. Job replies that he knows just as much about God as they do, and that their explanations do him no good. That is why he calls them useless physicians: counselors who heal nothing. His desire to speak with God shows both his pain and his trust that God hears him.

When you suffer and other people's explanations do not comfort you, do not stay silent. Bring your questions to God with sincerity and respect, trusting that he listens to you.
exp.41:10:
After Job's trial, his brothers, his sisters, and all who had known him before came to visit him. They ate bread with him in his house, shared his sorrow, and comforted him over all the evil that God had allowed to come upon him. Each one gave him a piece of money (a coin of value, probably silver) and a gold earring (a ring or earring).

This is part of the book's ending. The narrator tells how God restored Job after Job prayed for his friends. It is striking that these people appear only now; the text does not explain why they were not there before. Their gifts helped Job start over.

For today: do not wait for someone to recover before you stand by them. Even so, it is never too late to draw near, to sit at the table with someone who is suffering, to listen to them, and to offer concrete help.
exp.15:18:
Job says that even though no one on earth defends him, he has a witness in heaven. The word "behold" is an old way of saying "look" or "pay attention," as if Job wants us to notice what he is declaring. The phrase "on high" is another way of speaking of heaven, where God lives. Job trusts that someone there knows the truth about him and will speak on his behalf.

Job is speaking here in great suffering, having lost almost everything. His friends tell him he suffers because of some hidden sin, and he denies it. He feels misunderstood and weeps before God. Earlier in this chapter he asks that his blood not be covered, meaning that the wrong done to him not be forgotten. It is not entirely clear who he means by "my witness" or "my advocate." Many believe it is God himself, and others think of a heavenly defender. The text does not make this fully clear.

When people misunderstand or judge you, you do not have to win every argument. You can bring your pain to God honestly, knowing that he sees the whole truth.

sum.37: In Job 38, God answers Job out of a whirlwind and challenges him with many questions about creation: the earth, the sea, light, snow, rain, the stars, and the clouds. Through these questions, God shows Job that his wisdom and power are vast, and that Job cannot understand everything.
sum.3: Eliphaz answers Job. He reminds him that in the past Job encouraged others, but now he is shaken by his own suffering. Eliphaz believes that the innocent are not destroyed and that those who sow wickedness reap it. He tells of a night vision in which he was told that no one is more righteous than God. Interpreters debate whether his reasoning applies to Job.
sum.28: In this chapter Job looks back with longing on his past days, when God watched over him, his family surrounded him, and everyone respected him. He recounts that he defended the poor, the fatherless, the widow, and the blind, and that his advice was highly valued. He expected a long and peaceful life, but now all of that has been left behind.
sum.32: Elihu asks Job to listen to him and tells him that Job was wrong to claim he was innocent and that God was treating him like an enemy. According to Elihu, God is greater than any human and speaks to people through dreams and through suffering to turn them away from pride and save them from death. If a person admits their sin, God redeems them and restores their light.
sum.20: Job answers his friends and asks them to listen carefully. He tells them that many wicked people live well, with wealth, children, and secure homes, even though they reject God. He also says that in the end both the evil person and the good person die and are covered by the dust. For this reason, their comforts seem empty and false to him.
sum.13: In Job 14, Job reflects on how brief and fragile human life is, and he begs God to show him compassion. He compares a person to a cut-down tree that can sprout again, while a man dies and does not rise. Even so, Job longs for God to remember him and hopes for a change, though he feels weighed down.
sum.30: In this chapter, Job defends his life before God. He says he guarded his eyes, was fair to his servants, helped the poor, did not put his trust in gold, did not rejoice at the misfortune of his enemy, and opened his home to the stranger. He asks that God examine him and answer him.
sum.6: In Job 7, Job answers in pain: human life is short and hard, like that of a day laborer, and he spends sleepless nights with a sick body and no hope. He decides not to keep quiet about his complaint and speaks directly to God, asking why God watches over him and tests him so much. He asks God to forgive him and leave him alone, since soon he will no longer be here.
sum.35: In Job 36, Elihu continues speaking and affirms that God is great and just. He punishes the wicked, cares for the afflicted, and corrects those who obey him so that they may prosper. He warns Job not to turn back to wickedness. Then he praises God's power, seen in the rain, the clouds, and the thunder.
sum.24: Bildad, the third of Job's friends, speaks briefly. He says that God has absolute power, that he establishes peace in the heights, and that his light reaches everyone. He concludes that no human being can be righteous or clean before God, since even the moon and the stars grow dim before him, and man is like a worm.
sum.27: Job 28 describes how people dig deep into the earth and find silver, gold, iron, and precious stones, yet they cannot find wisdom, which is worth more than any treasure. Only God knows where it is, because he saw it when he created the world. He tells humankind that wisdom is to fear the Lord and turn away from evil.
sum.11: Job answers his friends with irony. He tells them that he has understanding too, and that they mock him even though he is righteous, while the wicked live at ease. He reminds them that even the animals know that everything comes from the hand of God, and that wisdom and power belong to him. God brings down kings, judges, and nations, and no one can stop him.
sum.4: Eliphaz tells Job that foolishness and envy bring destruction, and that suffering is part of human life. He advises him to seek God, who lifts up the humble, frustrates the schemes of the crafty, and heals the one who has been wounded. He promises that if Job accepts his correction, he will receive protection, peace, and a long life.
sum.39: God answers Job out of the whirlwind and asks him whether he really intends to argue with the Almighty. Does he dare to correct God, or to condemn him in order to prove himself right? God challenges him to show a power like his own, to clothe himself in majesty and splendor, and to humble the proud. Then God describes Behemoth, a mighty creature that God made, to show that only God has power over it.
sum.2: Job breaks his silence and curses the day he was born, wishing he had died at birth so that he could rest in the grave, where there is no more weariness or oppression. He asks why life is given to someone who suffers in bitterness. He confesses that the thing he feared most has happened to him, and he finds no peace.
sum.5: In Job 6, Job answers Eliphaz and describes his pain as heavier than the sand of the sea. He wishes that God would put an end to his life, but he says he has not denied the words of the Holy One. He complains that his friends have failed him like dry streambeds, and he asks them to show him where he went wrong.
sum.25: Job answers Bildad with irony: his words have not helped the weak, nor offered any real wisdom. Then Job describes God's power over death, the earth, the waters, the sky, and the sea. He concludes that all of this is only a small part of God's ways, and that his greatness is impossible to fully grasp.
sum.40: In this chapter God continues speaking with Job and describes Leviathan, a powerful and frightening creature that no one can catch, tame, or defeat. If no one dares to face it, then no one can stand before God, the owner of everything that exists. The lesson is that we should humbly acknowledge the greatness of God.
sum.41: Job acknowledges that God can do all things and that he spoke about things he did not understand. Now, having seen God, he repents with humility. God rebukes Job's three friends and asks Job to pray for them. Then God restores Job, giving him twice what he had before, new children, and a long life.
sum.29: In Job 30, Job describes how he is now looked down on, even by young men of low standing, who mock him and spit at him. He feels broken, sick, and abandoned, and he cries out to God, but he feels that God does not answer him. He remembers that he used to weep for those in need, and now his joy has turned to mourning.
sum.23: In Job 24, Job asks why God seems not to step in when wicked people steal from orphans and widows, leave the poor without clothing or bread, and act in the dark with crimes and adultery. Although he says that in the end such people vanish like grain stalks cut down, he also complains that God does not put a stop to the cries of the wounded. He ends by challenging anyone who would contradict him.
sum.17: In Job 18, Bildad becomes annoyed with Job and describes the fate of the wicked in harsh images: their light goes out, they fall into traps, they live in terror, they lose their family, and their memory disappears. Bildad implies that Job is suffering because he is wicked, although the book shows that this explanation is incomplete.
sum.36: Elihú describes God as the one who commands the thunder, the snow, the rain, the ice, and the clouds, with a power that no one can fully understand. He invites Job to stop and reflect on these wonders. He concludes that God is great, just, and worthy of respect, and that people should fear Him.
sum.34: Elihu rebukes Job for claiming that he is more righteous than God and that there is no benefit in not sinning. He tells him to look up at the heavens: God is so high that our sin or our righteousness affects us, not him. The oppressed cry out, but they do not seek God with their whole heart, and Elihu says that Job speaks without wisdom.
sum.31: The three friends stopped answering Job, and then Elihu, a young man who had waited out of respect for his elders, became angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and with the friends for failing to answer him. Elihu says that wisdom comes from the Spirit of God, not just from age, and that he will speak honestly, without flattering anyone.
sum.38: God asks Job a series of questions about animals: the lion, the raven, the wild goats, the wild donkey, the ostrich, the horse, and the eagle. Through these questions he shows that he cares for and governs them, and that Job has neither that power nor that wisdom. In the end, Job, humbled, acknowledges how small he is and falls silent.
sum.8: In Job 9, Job replies to Bildad and acknowledges that God is wise, powerful, and the creator of all things, and that no one can argue with Him. He feels broken and without justice, and he wishes there were an arbiter between him and God so that he could speak without fear. His words express pain and confusion, not necessarily truths about God.
sum.15: Job replies to his friends, telling them they are miserable comforters, and he says that if they were in his place, he could speak to them the same way. He describes his suffering. He feels that God has attacked him and that people have turned against him, even though he is innocent. Even so, he trusts that he has a witness in heaven, and he weeps before God.
sum.12: Job tells his friends that he understands everything they know, just as they do. He accuses them of defending God with lies. He decides that he will speak directly to God and trust Him even if God kills him, and he will argue his case, hoping to be proven right. Then he asks God to take away His heavy hand and to show him what his sin is.
sum.16: Job, his spirit broken and feeling death close by, complains that his friends only mock him and have no real wisdom. Even so, he affirms that the righteous will keep to their path and grow stronger. But Job sees his hope fading and thinks that his only home will be the grave.
sum.22: Job responds bitterly and longs to find God so that he can bring his case before him, but he cannot see him in any direction. Even so, he trusts that God knows his way and that he will come out like gold, for he has always kept God's commandments. Yet he fears before God's sovereign will and feels troubled.
sum.14: Eliphaz accuses Job of speaking empty and arrogant words, and asks him whether he thinks he knows more than the elders and even God himself. He says that no one is clean before God, and he describes how the wicked man lives in fear and ends in ruin for rising up against the Almighty.
sum.18: Job answers his friends in pain. He feels cornered by God and abandoned by his family and acquaintances, and he asks them for compassion instead of more accusations. In the midst of his suffering he declares with confidence that his Redeemer lives, and that even after he dies he will see God. He ends by warning his friends that God judges injustice.
sum.9: In Job 10, Job, weary of living, speaks to God in bitterness. He asks God to explain why he treats him like an enemy, when it was God who formed him with such care and gave him life. He says he does not understand his suffering, wishes he had never been born, and begs for a little relief before he dies.
sum.19: In Job 20, Zophar responds harshly and says that the joy of the wicked lasts only a short time. He claims that whoever gets rich through theft and the oppression of the poor will lose everything, will suffer distress, and will fall under God's punishment. However, the book shows that Job does not fit this idea, since his suffering is not because of wickedness.
sum.7: In Job 8, Bildad answers Job and tells him that God does not pervert justice. He asks Job to seek God sincerely and assures him that in this way he will prosper again. Using examples from nature, such as the reed that grows without water, he states that those who forget God lose their hope.
sum.10: In Job 11, Zophar responds to Job harshly. He accuses him of talking too much and of thinking himself innocent. He tells him that God is infinite and that Job cannot understand his ways. He invites him to put away wickedness and return to God, promising him peace and hope, while the wicked will have no refuge.
sum.1: Satan asks God for permission to strike Job's health, and God allows it, but forbids him to take Job's life. Job is covered with sores, and his wife tells him to curse God, but he keeps trusting and does not sin with his lips. Three friends come and sit with him in silence for seven days.
sum.33: Elihu speaks to the wise men and accuses Job of claiming that he is righteous and that God has taken away his right. He insists that God is never unjust, that he sees everything, that he judges kings and the poor alike, and that he hears the cry of the needy. He asks Job to humble himself, and he rebukes him for his words.
sum.21: Eliphaz accuses Job of great wrongdoing, without any proof. He says Job took advantage of the poor, the widows, and the orphans, and that this is why suffering has come upon him. He urges Job to turn back to God, accept his words, and seek peace, with the promise that Job will be restored. Note: later in the book, God will show that these accusations were not correct.
sum.26: Job swears by God that he will never speak falsely and that he will not give up his integrity, even though his friends insist he is guilty. He then declares that the wicked person, however much wealth and children he gathers, will have no hope: God will bring him down, his possessions will pass to the righteous, and he will end in terror and ruin.
sum.0: Job was a wealthy, upright man who feared God, and he would even offer sacrifices on behalf of his children. Satan said that Job served God only because of his blessings, and God allowed Satan to take everything from him, but not to touch his body. Job lost his property and his children, and even so he worshiped God and did not blame him.
